News.title: Chilling signs paranoid Putin is building huge doomsday nuclear bunker dubbed ‘Dead Hand’ hidden under remote mountain
News.content:
Next

VLADIMIR Putin looks to be building a doomsday nuclear bunker hidden under a mountain as the tyrant revives a Cold War programme.

Guarded by a machine gun turret, the underground command centre is one of Russia’s most top-secret facilities and could be used to hide a paranoid Putin should nuclear war break out.



The 24-room tunnel is at the centre of a strategy to guarantee retaliatory nuclear strikes against the West, a bombshell investigation has revealed.

Fitted with air filtration units to screen chemical, biological, and radioactive fallout, the bunker has been discovered beneath Kosvinsky Kamen mountain in the Urals region.



Codenamed Facility 1335, the cocoon was first built during the Cold War to ensure mutual destruction against the West in the event of a nuclear strike.

Dubbed the “Dead Hand project”, it would see back-up control channels activated if communication was lost with the Kremlin’s top brass.



These would transmit long-wave radio signals to mobilise missile launchers.

An investigation by The Sunday Times, Danish media group Danwatch and the Dossier Center has now revealed the site has been rebuilt.



The new, massive structure at the foothills of Kosvinsky Kamen is costing hundreds of millions of pounds.

Since 2018 Moscow has ferried heavy excavation and rock-drilling equipment, steel, piping and cabling into the mountain, procurement data shows.

The site has already used three million litres of fuel, 823,000 litres of gas and about 20,000 tonnes of steel – the weight of roughly three Eiffel Towers.

It is estimated that the concrete used would build at least 150,000 square meters of surface area, which is enough for a multi-storey building.

Mine ventilation systems and air filtration units capable of screening chemical, biological, and radioactive fallout have also been delivered to the site, the investigation found.



The bulk work was carried out between 2020 and 2021, records show.

A senior Russian military figure said “strategic missile forces will fulfil their historic mission of retaliation against any enemy” with Facility 1335.

The chilling findings come after Putin said publicly he would be ready to use a tactical nuclear weapon against Ukraine if the conflict escalated.



Clues of the project’s revival first appeared in 2020 when the Kremlin released transcripts of a meeting between Putin and his top brass.

During the meeting, Mad Vlad discussed the creation of a system to ensure Russia’s nuclear command and control infrastructure would survive an attack.

He said: “We are aware that a lot depends on the survivability of these systems and their ability to continue operating in a combat environment.

“They have told me that the creation of an absolutely secure facility for controlling strategic nuclear forces, among others, is nearing completion, and that it will have a very high safety margin.”

Putin has become increasingly paranoid about a US strike carried out with its bunker-buster bombs capable of hitting targets deep underground.



Norwegian Staff College and armed forces’ Russian security policy expert Tom Roseth told The Sunday Times: “It appears that the Russians are securing this facility against every type of attack.

“To protect 1335 and the command-and-control facilities of the nuclear forces, they therefore have to dig even deeper and reinforce the site even more.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“The expansion of Facility 1335 follows a major upgrade of Russia’s nuclear forces, which has been given high priority within the Russian armed forces.

“The perimeter will once again be given priority now, in a more tense geopolitical situation in which Russia sees itself as being in conflict with the West.”

News.title: Ranulph Fiennes’ family say police snubbed pleas to check on explorer after claims Brit ‘unlawfully’ kept in care homes
News.content:
Next

THE family of legendary explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes has claimed police have snubbed their pleas to check on the Brit’s wellbeing.

His stepson Alexander Millington-Cotes said he had had “no luck” getting cops to update them on the case after worrying claims Ranulph has been “unlawfully deprived of his liberty” inside a care home.



The 82-year-old polar hero has not been seen in public for two years, amid growing concerns about his care.

His second wife Louise Millington-Cotes, 59, has lasting power of attorney for the explorer and is accused of moving her husband between care homes under false identities.



His current whereabouts are unknown, sparking desperate pleas from his loved ones for police to help find him.

Alexander, 31, said he had been trying for months to establish where his stepfather was and what police were doing.

He told The Sunday Telegraph: “It’s a real challenge because I don’t think anyone quite knows where he is.

“I’m trying to establish from the police what they’re doing… I’ve tried to get in touch but no luck so far.”



He has contacted forces in areas where he believes Sir Ranulph may have been staying, including Cheshire Constabulary and West Mercia Police.

Sir Ranulph is known to have been in a Cheshire care home, while the family home is in an area covered by West Mercia Police.

A manager at one care home where the explorer was staying was also sufficiently concerned about his care arrangements to contact the Office of the Public Guardian.

The care watchdog previously concluded that Sir Ranulph was being “unlawfully deprived of his liberty” at the start of this year because the correct protocols were not being followed.

His family now want the Office of the Public Guardian to investigate his circumstances and care arrangements.



Alexander, who is estranged from his mother, has also launched a fundraising appeal for a legal challenge to her lasting power of attorney over Sir Ranulph.

The explorer’s celebrity friends have joined calls for action, with Bear Grylls and Ben Fogle among those expressing concern.

Grylls said: “We have been desperately trying to connect with Ran for a year now to no avail. But truth always wins out.”



He added: “These reports of his isolation from his loved ones and treatment in care homes are so deeply disturbing.

“That a hero like Ran should have to face this is very hard to read.

“It’s past time for the Office for the Public Guardian and the police to investigate urgently. We owe it to him. Ran, we are coming.”

Fogle, who has summited Everest and walked to the South Pole, said he was “deeply disturbed” by the reports.

He said: “That such a great man, hero of mine and a national treasure, should be treated in this way, isolated and kept away from family and friends, is very troubling.”



Alexander said he believed action was needed quickly and questioned whether his stepfather would have chosen to be isolated from those closest to him.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “I just want to be able to see him, for him to be able to see who he wants to, go where he wants with any support that he might need.

“This just seems like a really bad dream.”

News.title: Anonymous evidence from NINE key Lucy Letby witnesses ‘fuelled conspiracy theories about her case’
News.content:
Next

ANONYMOUS evidence from nine key witnesses in the trial of baby killer Lucy Letby has fuelled ­conspiracy theories about the case, experts warn.

The doctors and nurses at the Countess of Chester Hospital won the right not to be named amid fears for their mental health and claims that public identification would harm their evidence.



But media specialist partner ­Martin Soames, of law firm SMB, told The Sun on Sunday: “Anonymity takes away the human aspect.

“It may also give rise to a ­suspicion that professionals are not being called to account. Any erosion of open justice is bad news.”



Now, The Sun on Sunday can reveal that the controversial anonymity orders used in the trial are widespread across the ­justice system.

We analysed publicly available data and can reveal that the number of such orders issued by courts in England and Wales has rocketed in six years, sparking concerns for open justice.

The Courts and Tribunals Judiciary database shows orders granted, mainly in High Court cases, soared from 54 in 2019 to 1,479 last year — a 2,638 per cent rise.

Others were allowed at inquests, tribunals and public inquiries, so the true total is likely much higher.

The Government has not published official statistics on witness anonymity orders since 2009, when 232 applications were made in Crown, Magistrate and Youth Courts — with 206 granted and 26 refused.

Leading barrister Geoffrey Robertson KC blasted “tender-hearted judges” for being easily swayed by lawyers.



He said: “The open justice principle is fundamental to all trials, and that includes the right to report the names and evidence given by witnesses unless, like rape victims, they are especially vulnerable.

“The decision to anonymise some of the witnesses in the Lucy Letby case was wrong, especially the ­professional witnesses who had a duty to explain themselves publicly.

“We need judges to not allow ­witnesses to withhold their names.



“Many judges today are tender-hearted and easily swayed by advocates who exaggerate the danger that witnesses in controversial cases may be demonised by the media.”

Goldsmiths media professor Tim Crook insisted one of the “justice purposes” of identifying witnesses in criminal trials was “that public scrutiny enhances the qualities of veracity and integrity”.

In his briefing, The Lucy Letby Trial and Open Justice, he wrote: “One of the risks of too much secrecy in criminal trials and the anonymising of trial participants is that the lack of key and specific information undermines the credibility and confidence of the public in the trial process.”

This week, there were calls for Letby to face a retrial after an exclusive Sun and Channel 5 documentary questioned whether the nurse — currently serving 15 whole life terms — was made a scapegoat.

The unprecedented decision to grant lifelong anonymity to nine key witnesses was made after medical professionals claimed public identification would harm their evidence or cause extreme workplace distress.



Judges allowed the orders to remain in place after Letby’s conviction and during the Thirlwall Inquiry into why she was able to murder seven babies and attempt to murder seven others at the hospital between 2015 and 2016.

Only one witness has since been identified: consultant Dr Mark Deakin, previously referred to as Doctor U or Doctor A.

He was granted lifetime anonymity after being described as Letby’s “boyfriend” and permitted to give evidence from behind a screen at Manchester Crown Court.



Following his death from ­suspected “unnatural causes” in July, he can now be named.

Crossbench peer Lord Walney, a former government adviser on ­political violence, said: “It is troubling so many witnesses in the Letby trial were given anonymity.

“Intimidation and harassment can be real, but so many NHS scandals in recent decades have been made much worse by clinicians closing ranks to save their own skin.

“Social media ridicule or trolling is grim, but it should not trump the principle of open justice, which is vital to protect confidence in our increasingly battered justice system.

“If people in public positions like doctors and nurses are routinely granted anonymity, it will further increase the sense that the NHS circles the wagons to protect itself when things go wrong and shuts out patients who have been failed.”



Last week, three council workers set to give evidence at the inquest into the death of murdered ten-year-old Sara Sharif had a bid to protect their identities rejected.

Sara was found dead in bed at home in Woking, Surrey, in 2023. Her father and stepmother — jailed for murder the next year — were already known to social services.

A review found serious errors by agencies including Surrey County Council, who visited the wrong address the day before Sara died and failed to question why she suddenly wore a hijab to cover bruising for “fear of causing offence”.



The council lost its bid to shield the workers’ identities when they testify at Sara’s inquest next year.

Children and sexual offence ­victims automatically get anonymity in UK courts.

Some witnesses, such as undercover police or those in the Omagh and Bloody Sunday inquiries, are protected from retaliation.

However, legal experts warn adults fearing a social media backlash are increasingly using anonymity orders to protect personal reputations.

Anonymity on medical grounds was also granted to 59 witnesses by chair Sir Brian Langstaff during the Infected Blood Inquiry, which issued a 2024 report exposing systemic failures in a scandal where 3,000 people died.



Anonymity orders were also granted in the Post Office Horizon inquiry, launched after 900 sub- postmasters were wrongly ­prosecuted for theft due to a faulty computer system.

Chair Sir Wyn Williams allowed at least nine “core participants” to testify anonymously.

Some parents of surviving victims in the Southport knife attack — in which three girls were killed by Axel Rudakubana in July 2024 — said that anonymity orders at the trial left them feeling sidelined.



The mother of Daisy, who was seven when stabbed 33 times, said: “It’s more comfortable to forget these girls survived because remembering what they went through is really horrendous.”

Dawn Alford, chief executive of the Society of Editors, warned routine anonymity risks eroding public scrutiny. She said: “Some people plainly need their identities protected, including children and victims of sexual offences.

“Others may face a genuine risk if they are named. But anonymity should not become a routine feature of a trial, tribunal or inquiry because giving evidence may be difficult or attract attention.”

The Sun on Sunday’s analysis reveals over 500 anonymity orders have been granted since 2019 in asylum seeker deportation cases.

Among them is “XAG”, a Ghanaian migrant with convictions for battery, fraud, shoplifting, and possessing extreme pornographic images, granted anonymity while fighting deportation.



Meanwhile, an anonymised Eritrean small-boat migrant is fighting Home Office placement in adult housing after social workers determined he was “significantly over 18,” despite claiming to be 16.

However, Richard Garside, Director of the Centre for Crime and Justice Studies, said social media makes anonymity essential, adding: “It doesn’t serve the interests of justice if witnesses do not come forward or refuse to testify for fear of social media exposure, threats and rumour.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Given this, lifetime anonymity orders decided on a case-by-case basis might be the price we have to pay.”



It is understood the Ministry of Justice does not publish overall ­figures on anonymity orders as they span differing jurisdictions.

News.title: Fury as Heathrow’s third runway delayed by another four years in ‘huge blow to British economy’
News.content:
Next

HEATHROW’S third runway is to be delayed by another four years — meaning it will not be up and running until 2039.

The setback follows reports that PM Andy Burnham has plunged the entire project into fresh doubt after privately telling MPs he has always opposed the expansion.



The airport’s £49billion enlargement — which would involve demolishing hundreds of homes and rerouting the M25 — was first approved by ex-PM Gordon Brown in 2009.

It is projected to be worth £1.4billion a year to the economy and create 100,000 jobs.



Reform UK Treasury chief Robert Jenrick slammed the hold-up.

He told The Sun on Sunday: “This is a huge blow to the British economy.

“A third runway would bring thousands of well-paid jobs — we cannot afford any more delays.

“If Andy Burnham does not pass emergency legislation to make it happen, a Reform government will.”

Airport chiefs are understood to have told ministers they could not hit their deadline to have the runway operational by 2035.

Heathrow still hopes to get their planning permission by 2029 — though London Mayor Sadiq Khan is among those strongly opposed, citing climate change plus noise and air pollution.

Building a third runway at London’s Heathrow was first proposed in 1946.



Meanwhile, Mr Burnham has reportedly told party colleagues that he has doubts over the entire project.

A Labour MP told The Financial Times: “He said he’s never been in favour of Heathrow expansion, but he’s not indicated one way or another what he will do now.”

A Department for Transport spokesman said: “There is no live planning application for a third runway, and we cannot comment on ongoing consultation processes or prejudice them in a way that will only delay progress.



“The timeline has always been ambitious.”

A spokesman for Heathrow said: “It’s right that ambitious targets were set. The sooner expansion begins, the sooner the whole UK will benefit.

“Our focus has always been to secure planning permission by 2029.

“Once achieved, the runway will be open within a decade — and the benefits of expansion can be felt from today.”

News.title: Burnham must be explicit about how he’ll ‘bring back hope’ because so far we’ve had little more than feelgood vibes
News.content:
UK needs hope not hopeless posturing







Next

ANDY BURNHAM will address the Labour conference on the theme of bringing back hope.

So the new PM must be explicit about how he plans to go about it.



Because so far we’ve had little more than feelgood vibes and tinkering around the edges.

Britain’s workers would be given real hope if he lifted the tax burden which weighs in at a post-war record.



Bosses running businesses would be filled with hope if they were freed from the ruinous NI costs which have crippled firms and thrown a million young people on the dole.

And the whole country would radiate hope if there was a new attitude to planning and investment which allowed big building projects to thrive.

But on all these fronts Mr Burnham is unlikely to deliver.

Because instead of cutting taxes next month’s budget seems likely to raise them.

Rather than freeing up private enterprise, the PM is planning to take energy, water and housing back into public ownership at untold cost.

And as for big projects he seems happy to sit tight as the potential bonanza of Heathrow’s third runway is delayed yet again, this time for four more years.



No doubt Mr Burnham’s words from the podium will be effectively delivered and warmly received inside the conference.

Outside, in the real world, it is not his words but his actions which will count.

It is all very well talking about hope.

But unless he cuts spending and supports the economy things will seem increasingly hopeless.

Political Ed ache

SIR ED DAVEY is a political buffoon.



The Lib Dem leader’s pratfalling and gurning photo opportunities are almost as tedious as his demands to rejoin the EU.

He lives in a world of fantasy policies and grotesque posturing.

In any normal era his self-inflated Lib Dems would spiral off into the hot air like a deflated balloon.

But these are not normal times.

If the polls are right Ed Davey is closer to power than either Kemi Badenoch or Nigel Farage.



And although Andy Burnham has ruled out calling an early election Sir Ed is plotting his demands for propping up Labour in a future coalition of chaos.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

This terrifying prospect should knock some sense into the Tories and Reform.

Whenever the next election comes one thing is clear. A disunited right will condemn Britain to five years of the Andy and Ed show.

News.title: Woman who took part in £54m benefits scam now on Universal Credit after leaving prison – and she’s only paid back £18k
News.content:
Next

A WOMAN who took part in a £54million benefit scam is living free on Universal Credit — despite having paid back just £18,000.

Tsvetka Todorova, 54, was in a gang which made thousands of false claims.



The five Bulgarians spent the money on luxury cars, designer clothes and flashy watches.

Todorova was jailed for three years in May 2024 but released in late 2025 having served half of her sentence.



She was told in January to return £101,201.78 at a London confiscation order hearing.

But a Freedom of Information request shows the fraudster has coughed up only £18,228.14.



Earlier this year, Todorova boasted of her taxpayer-funded lifestyle, telling reporters: “I love it here, it is good and has helped me I’ve been back on benefits since December 30.

“It’ll be about £200 a month. I don’t have a right to work. My husband gets over £1,000 for Universal Credit.”

But she has now claimed: “My husband is depressed.

“I’m depressed as well. I have had high blood pressure because of the case. My husband also has a lot of back pain.”



Todorova, of Erith, South East London, is fighting efforts to be deported, and could be sent back to jail over failing to meet the confiscation order.

The Crown Prosecution Service said: “Enforcement of this matter is ongoing.”

News.title: Bizarre moment pregnant & ‘drunk’ monkey seen dozing off inside shop as owner finds half empty vodka bottle by its side
News.content:
Next

THIS is the bizarre moment a pregnant monkey is found passed out inside a local shop after appearing to be drunk on vodka.

Viral footage shows a female monkey dozing off on top of boxes of booze with a half empty bottle of strong liquor discovered with its cap ripped off close by.



The monkey was caught passed out inside a wine shop in Block Chowk, Ranchi by the shopkeeper and several shoppers.

Video shows the bewildered storekeeper continuing to serve customers while the monkey sleeps behind him.



The monkey ran into the liquor shop while the workers were inside on Friday around 7.30pm, according to reports.

Locals say the monkey had been spotted over the past few days drinking leftover alcohol from discarded bottles outside before it decided to raid the shop.

The shopkeeper initially tried to drive the monkey away, even offering biscuits to lure her outside.

However, the primate ignored their pleas and instead broke open a bottle of vodka and started swigging it, causing chaos in the store, witnesses claimed.



One of the workers sustained injuries to his arms and legs and was treated at a local hospital after being attacked by the animal.

The drunk monkey got drowsy very quickly and fell asleep on some crates of beers, leaving onlookers stunned by her antics.

She remained asleep for a while whilst the shop continued serving as normal.

People that passed by recorded the viral moment and shared it on social media.

After becoming sober, the primate wreaked havoc again causing the shopkeepers to keep their distance.



They later contacted the Birsa Biological Park to handle the situation.

Biologists Vivekananda and Rakesh Awasthi, along with their team, captured the monkey and took it away safely.

The pregnant monkey is currently being assessed at Bhagwan Birsa Biological Park’s veterinary hospital, and will be released back into the wild when she is healthy.

It comes after Kalua, a drunken monkey in the Mirzapur district of India, was given a life sentence for biting over 250 people, one of whom died.

In 2020, the six-year-old primate was taken to Kanpur zoo where he will remain in captivity for the rest of his life.



Kalua’s owner used to give him alcohol, but after he died, the monkey went on a biting spree and caused mayhem for the local residents.

News.title: Two men stabbed during alleyway brawl as pair both arrested after being rushed to hospital with serious injuries
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

KNIFE FIGHT Two men stabbed during alleyway brawl as pair both arrested after being rushed to hospital with serious injuries







Next

TWO men were stabbed in an alleyway brawl before cops arrested them both when they arrived at hospital.

The pair suffered serious stab wounds during the violent scenes in Oldham on Friday night.

Cops were called to the area at around 8.15pm following reports of at least one stabbing.

Witnesses said a major disturbance broke out in an alleyway leading to St Stephen Street just after 8pm.





Officers found one man at the scene with stab wounds before rushing him to hospital.

The second man later turned up at The Royal Oldham Hospital himself with knife injuries.

Both men were arrested in connection with the incident soon after.

They remain in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, Greater Manchester Police said.



A police cordon was put in place across part of the alleyway as officers launched an investigation.

Cops remained at the scene for several hours carrying out enquiries into the bloodshed.

Pictures from the scene showed a large police presence on Bridgewater Street.

A Tactical Aid Unit van was also pictured parked on the road as officers worked at the scene.



The circumstances surrounding the brawl and how the two men came to suffer stab wounds remain under investigation.

No further details about the men involved have been released.

A Greater Manchester Police spokesperson said: “Officers were called to reports of a stabbing on Bridgewater Street at 8.15pm last night (25/09/26).

“Officers located one man with stab wounds at the scene and another man presented himself at Oldham Hospital with stab wounds.

“Both men have been arrested.



“Both remain in hospital with non-life threatening injuries as enquiries continue.”

Enquiries into the incident are ongoing.

News.title: Earl Spencer is 'doing a Meghan' with very own  Spencer Farms jam brand
News.content:
Earl Spencer is 'doing a Meghan' with very own Spencer Farms jam brand

A source has confirmed the Earl plans to take a leaf out of Meghan Markle's playbook with a new range of market goods... including jams

View 5 Images Earl Spencer plans to pivot into a range of homemade jams

Princess Diana's brother appears to be taking inspiration from Meghan Markle's business strategy, with Earl Charles Spencer launching a new commercial venture following his controversial memoir about his sister: He's planning to produce homemade preserves.

‌



Much like Prince Harry's wife, the Earl intends to use his Althorp Estate in Northants as the base for producing honey, tea, marmalade, cheeses, wines, ciders, and other goods.

‌



The shift towards market produce comes as the 62 year old Spencer faces ongoing criticism over his contentious book about his late sister Princess Diana, with accusations he's profiting from her death decades later.

‌



Intellectual Property Office records show the Earl has also registered his name for public speaking engagements, personal appearances, and voice-over work.

View 5 Images Netflix and Meghan’s lifestyle brand As Ever ended their formal collaboration (Image: CBSNEWS)

A UK trademark is a legally protected identifier—whether a word, logo, shape, or sound—used to differentiate one business's goods or services from competitors.

‌



A source told The Sun: "First Spencer imitated Prince Harry with attacks on the royal family, and now he is doing a Meghan - and appears to be planning to make jam."

View 5 Images Meghan's As Ever business has faced almost constant scrutiny since its launch in April 2025 (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

This new branding initiative follows Princess Diana's former butler Paul Burrell accusing Earl Spencer—whose explosive memoir Swan Song has generated considerable backlash—of abandoning his sister during her time of need. He told the Sun: "I'd think those last five years . . . are pretty vague in the book because he knows nothing about them. She said, 'My family only want me when they want the best seats in the best restaurants or want to sit in the Royal Box at Wimbledon'."

‌



Speaking on Piers Morgan Uncensored, Burrell, 68, continued: "They barely spoke. He was not part of her world."

Diana and her younger brother experienced a rift when he

View 5 Images Diana's butler said he "did not recognise" much of what was said in Earl Spencer's book (Image: Pier Morgan Uncensored)

‌



refused to allow her to reside in the Garden House at Althorp, the family's 13,000-acre estate, after her public separation from then-Prince Charles in 1992.

Earl Spencer, who inherited the estate that year aged 27, pointed to the Garden House's closeness to a road as a security risk.

He maintained he had made available every appropriate property on the Northamptonshire estate.

‌



Amongst his criticisms of the now King Charles, Spencer claimed that he told him following his father's funeral that he was "so lucky" to inherit at such a young age.

View 5 Images Diana, Princess of Wales, died in a car crash in Paris in August 1997 (Image: Getty)

He has also accused Charles of being "giddily elated" after Diana's death in 1997 and alleges he said "we will forget her soon enough."

Article continues below

Buckingham Palace suggested that the "pain of fraternal grief" may have clouded the Earl's recollections.

Burrell voiced his opinion that the Earl made the wrong decision by burying Diana on an island within his estate.

While members of the public can visit the estate for a fee, only family members are allowed to visit the grave itself. He maintained that Diana should have been laid to rest somewhere the public could properly pay their respects.

News.title: Mount Etna eruption RECAP: Catania Airport flights suspended as 4km ash cloud sparks red alert
News.content:
Smoke rises from the crater of the Etna volcano as it erupts.

Flights at Catania Airport have been suspended until 4pm as Mount Etna sends a 4km-high ash cloud into the sky, with a red aviation alert in force.

Flights were suspended at Catania Airport after Mount Etna sent a 4km-high volcanic ash cloud into the sky.

Ash was emitted from Etna’s north-east crater and dispersing southwards, while a violent storm also battered Catania throughout the night.

The airport’s Operational Coordination Unit has closed sector C1 of the airspace and imposed a restriction of zero landings and zero take-offs. A red VONA aviation warning — the highest alert level on a four-point scale — is also in force.

Ten flights had already been diverted before operations were suspended, with five sent to Palermo, three to Trapani and two to Comiso. A Volotea flight between Catania and Verona was also able to depart from Comiso instead.

Earlier restrictions had limited Catania Airport to just four landings per hour, compared with 12 during normal operations, before flights were halted altogether.

This blog is now closed.

News.title: Murder probe after e-bike cyclist killed in horror crash in Kensington
News.content:
Murder probe after e-bike cyclist killed in horror crash in Kensington

Police were called to reports of a man found seriously injured in North Pole Road in Kensington, west London, at 1am on Friday

View Image The scene on North Pole Road, North Kensington (Image: UKNIP)

Police have launched a murder probe after a 24-year-old e-bike rider was killed in a crash with a moped which is thought to have been chasing him.

‌



The crash took place in Kensington, west London, at 1am on Friday, the Metropolitan Police said.

‌



Police were called to reports of a man found seriously injured in North Pole Road, west London, about 20 minutes later.

‌



Paramedics from London Ambulance Service also rushed to the incident but he was pronounced dead at the scene.

The Met is searching for the moped rider and investigators are appealing for witnesses to the collision and preceding events.

‌



Detective Chief Inspector Neil John, leading the investigation, said: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family at what is a very difficult time.

"We have launched a full investigation and are working hard to get answers and establish exactly what happened.

"Our team are pursuing a number of lines of inquiry, including efforts to identify and trace the rider of the moped."

Article continues below

He added: "As part of this, we’re urging anyone who was in the area at the time and may have seen the e-bike or the moped to get in touch with us as soon as possible.

"If you have any information that could help, please come forward."

Anyone with information is asked to contact the Met on 101 quoting 414/25SEP26 or Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111 to remain anonymous.

News.title: ‘Dry 2 washing machine loads’ with £10 Lidl like £17 B&Q and £22 Tesco in stores now
News.content:
‘Dry 2 washing machine loads’ with £10 Lidl like £17 B&Q and £22 Tesco in stores now

Lidl claims the item could make a 'weather-resistant and durable' option for homeowners

View 4 Images An in-store only deal now at Lidl (Image: Getty Images)

A new accessory is now available at every Lidl store across the country, and it could be a life-saver for homeowners hoping to dry their clothes indoors. The supermarket, which has over 1,000 locations UK wide, claims it could make a "weather-resistant and durable" option - all at a budget price.

‌



Available for just £9.99, the 18m Clothes Airer can be found in the iconic 'Middle of Lidl Aisle' while stocks last. It is claimed it has space for "up to 2 washing machine loads" which could be especially useful with weather now a far cry from the scorching heatwaves of the summer.

‌



It's instantly obvious the item isn't the simple tiered airer that can be found in your average British household. Instead of the traditional vertical design synonymous with an airer, this one in particular takes advantage of width to dry your wet clothes.

‌



View 4 Images The 18m Clothes Airer at Lidl (Image: Lidl)

To add to its versatility, this Lidl accessory boasts a foldable design that could prove especially useful for smaller homes. Yes, it may stretch out to 180cm when fully deployed, but it can be folded away when not in use.

Product features - full list

Space for up to 2 washing machine loads (8kg each)

Also suitable for large items of laundry

Total drying length: 18m

Can be folded out to a length of 1.8m

Folds flat to save space

Comfortable height

Weather-resistant and durable tubular steel frame with robust joints and floor-friendly caps

With a child safety lock to prevent accidental folding

Max. load: 17kg

Size (unfolded): L180 x W54.5 x H106cm

Size (folded): L128 x W54.5 x H3.5cm

3-year warranty

‌



Shoppers hoping to find out more should visit the Lidl website. It bears a striking resemblance to high-end options available at other retailers.

View 4 Images The Foldable Clothes Airer at B&Q (Image: B&Q)

Take B&Q, for instance, which has the Foldable Clothes Airer for £16.99. The product description reads: "This white foldable clothes airer is a strong, space-saving solution for drying laundry indoors or outdoors. Designed with 22 wide bars, it provides up to 18 metres of drying space - perfect for towels, bed linen, or a full load of clothes.

‌



"With two winged extensions, you can easily hang longer items without creasing or overlapping. Made from premium stainless steel, this laundry airer offers a rust-resistant and weather-resistant build that can be used in any environment. Its foldable structure means it can be stored flat in tight spaces, ideal for homes with limited storage. Lightweight yet durable, the airer is easy to carry, open, and close, giving you convenience with every use."

View 4 Images The Clothes Airer Drying Rack at Tesco (Image: Tesco)

Then there's Tesco which stocks the all-too-similar Clothes Airer Drying Rack with a £21.99 price tag. Tesco explains: "Dry your clothes easily with this beautiful rack. This drying rack from Lifetime Clean offers space for all your clean laundry.

Article continues below

"The rack is almost two meters wide and therefore good for hanging up a lot of laundry. After use you can fold the rack and store it easily. You can hang up the clothes conveniently so that everything gets nicely dry and is ready to use again."

Both options have a similar look to the Lidl version, but there's one big difference, and it's nothing to do with how much it hits your wallet. Tesco and B&Q offer home delivery, an amenity not available at their budget supermarket rivals.

News.title: Met Office maps show heavy downpours for 35 areas on Sunday- full list
News.content:
Met Office maps show heavy downpours for 35 areas on Sunday- full list

Met Office weather maps show heavy rain hitting much of the UK on Sunday, with 35 areas forecast to see downpours of up to 4mm an hour or more.

View 3 Images Heavy rain is forecast to move across Britain from the west throughout Sunday (Image: Derby Telegraph)

Britain is set to be drenched by a huge wall of rain on Sunday as heavy downpours sweep across much of the country.

‌



Met Office maps show the wet weather moving in from the west and spreading across large parts of the UK throughout the day, with some areas forecast to see heavier bursts of 4mm of rain an hour or more.

‌



The forecaster says: "A largely dry and cloudy start on Sunday, and turning increasingly windy. Heavy rain moves in from the west, but warm sunny spells develop in the east."

‌



Rain is forecast to reach Northern Ireland, parts of Wales and the far north of Scotland, including Stornoway, by around 9.15am on Sunday.

View 3 Images Heavy rain is forecast to move across Britain from the west throughout Sunday (Image: Met Office)

The band of wet weather then gradually moves eastwards, reaching northern England during the afternoon as well as parts of the south, including Plymouth.

‌



Scotland is forecast to see some of the heaviest downpours, with Met Office maps turning blue and yellow across much of the country from around noon. Yellow areas indicate heavier rainfall of 4mm or more an hour.

The maps show much of the rain clearing by early evening at around 6pm, although showers are still forecast around Sheffield, Swindon and Birmingham.

View 3 Images Met Office maps show heavier downpours developing across parts of the UK on Sunday (Image: Met Office)

‌



Conditions are expected to improve on Monday as the rain clears, leaving a "fine day with sunny spells". Tuesday is forecast to turn "rather warm", although it will also become windy with another spell of rain moving in from the west.

Fresher conditions and showers are then expected on Wednesday.

What the Met Office says for October

Looking further ahead, drier and more settled weather is expected to become increasingly likely across the UK between October 1 and 10, according to the Met Office.

Higher pressure is forecast to build, although there remains uncertainty over whether the most settled conditions will be focused across northern or southern parts of the country.

Some shorter spells of rain or showers are still expected as areas of lower pressure occasionally move in, but the period overall is forecast to be drier than average.

Temperatures are forecast to remain warmer than average.

News.title: Jay Slater's mum shares impact of horror moment she saw images of dead son
News.content:
Jay Slater's mum shares impact of horror moment she saw images of dead son

Debbie Duncan, 57, retraced the final steps taken by her son, Jay Slater, before he fell from height in the mountains of northern Tenerife during his first holiday without his family

View 4 Images Debbie Duncan revealed the moment she was shown photos of Jay Slater's body (Image: ©5 Broadcasting Limited / Candour Productions Press Enquiries: press@channel5.com NOTE: Paramount images are for the use of Press outlets only. Any blogs requesting access to these images are required to seek approval from Paramount directly. Contact press@channel5.com While we will continue to send out the weekly PI booklet every Friday, we have now launched the ViacomCBS Media Hub. This is an all-encompassing press centre where you can find the latest PI, press releases and other relevant information.)

The mum of Jay Slater has revealed the impact that seeing images of her dead son had on her.

‌



Debbie Duncan returned to the Spanish island of Tenerife, where Jay disappeared in June 2024. The disappearance sparked a massive manhunt across the holiday hotspot for a month until his body was found in the hills of northern Tenerife.

‌



The 57-year-old revealed she was shown photos of her son's dead body by police when she went to collect his phone. Speaking in Channel 5's Cause of Death, she added: "I did think about it (viewing his body) and thought, I don't think I can.

‌



"But then, when we had to go back to Tenerife to get paperwork from the courts and to collect his phone, to my horror there were images of Jay. I thought my heart was going to stop beating."

View 4 Images Jay died after falling from height in the hills of Tenerife (Image: Family Handout/LBT Global/PA)

Jay Slater's mum accidentally glanced photos of his dead body in return to Tenerife to retrace his final steps READ MORE :

She continued: "Whenever people say, 'How did you know it was Jay?' Well, it was Jay. My beautiful boy."

‌



Debbie was joined by Jay's uncle Glen Duncan when she retraced his final steps at Tenerife's Rural de Teno national park. The Channel 5 documentary was filmed just weeks after Debbie received the delayed Spanish post-mortem report on her son's death, that confirmed he died after he fell into a ravine.

Dr Richard Shepherd, who carried out the Home Office post-mortem, said he believed it was important Debbie "knew the truth" due to the "trolling" and memes she received following 19-year-old Jay's death. Speaking to The Sun, he said: "She wanted to know how his injuries would have affected him.

View 4 Images Jay's body was found about a month after he went missing (Image: PA)

‌



"I was able to tell her that yes, it was an awful injury, and yes, it killed him. But the head injury was so severe that it probably would have killed him immediately. It was the end — there was no pain and suffering."

Fabricated claims spread online about the case and persisted after an inquest in 2025 found he died on June 17, 2024, following a "heavy fall from height." Earlier this year, Debbie told This Morning that she still deals with personal attacks about her son.

"[Trolls have been] calling his family, calling me [saying] 'they're drug dealers... he had a bad upbringing', it just got really personal," she said. "They don't know us, they don't know our family, they don't know Jay but yet they just judge... and the conspiracies started almost immediately."

Jay called his friend Lucy Law after he left an AirBnB to say he was lost in the mountains. He was reported missing after he did not return to his accommodation and his body was found weeks later.

News.title: Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers on to housing ladder
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help young people get on the property ladder.

The "Your First Home" scheme would be open to first-time buyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their new build property's value to help pay for the purchase.

Burnham said people who do not have support from the "bank of mum and dad" are among those the scheme would aim to help.

There would be an initial interest-free period for the equity loan, with more details expected in next month's Budget.

The Conservatives warned the policy would leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risks "pushing up the price of new homes".

Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own.

"So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder."

The PM added he believes the scheme will give builders the "confidence to deliver the high-quality new homes the country needs".

Funding for the scheme is expected to come from reprioritising existing budgets, but housing developers will pay towards the running costs.

Ministers have not yet confirmed whether there is an age restriction on the scheme, or a cap on the price on the value of the property.

The policy is similar to initiatives from previous governments, including the coalition's Help To Buy scheme, introduced in 2013 by then-Chancellor George Osborne.

It expanded a previous scheme, known as FirstBuy, which was aimed solely at first-time buyers.

Help to Buy initially enabled all purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home, with a value of up to a Â£600,000.

Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.

The first version of the programme was active until 2021. A second iteration of the scheme, which ran until 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties that could be bought.

An evaluation of the scheme, external found more than 387,000 properties were purchased through it, of which 328,000 were by first-time buyers.

In its conclusion, the report noted Help to Buy was "effective in supporting people into home ownership in some areas, but did not remove affordability barriers for first-time buyers in areas that were already relatively expensive".

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said "Your First Home" would "build on the lessons learned from previous schemes, while retaining the benefits".

The Home Builders Federation welcomed the proposals, saying it had "long called for action to improve access to home ownership".

"Our analysis shows a well-designed scheme can make a meaningful difference for households struggling to get on to the property ladder," it added.

Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam accused Labour of wanting first-time buyers to "take on even more debt to afford the few homes that have been built".

She added taxpayers would take a "stake in their homes" and be "picking up the bill for months".

Lam said: "Slapping another levy on developers risks pushing up the price of new homes too.

"This is a colossal admission of failure. This Labour government is making homes harder to build, then asking buyers to borrow more to pay for them."

Lam said the Conservatives want to scrap stamp duty, "back British house builders" and ensure that houses are "built in the places that people actually want to live".

Rayner told the BBC earlier this month that there was only a "slim chance" the government would meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election, but said she was "not giving it up".

Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.

BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.

News.title: Controversial Orange Order march to go ahead for first time in nearly 30 years after late night drama
News.content:
The Orange Order, is the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland.

The decision banning Sunday's parade was successfully appealed following an emergency court sitting late on Saturday night after a challenge was taken by an Orange Order member.

A large crowd gathered on the Garvaghy Road in the wake of the Appeal judges' ruling.

Masked men also blocked the north end of the Garvaghy Road, towards Drumcree.

Earlier Breandan Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition said: "There's no such thing as justice or rights for our community. I'm going back to help defend my community."

SÃ­nn FÃ©in leader Mary Lou McDonald described the latest development as a "disgrace".

"This march is steeped in a history of hate, sectarian violence, and murder, and championed by Unionist leaders."

Stormont First Minister Michelle O'Neill said: "Our message tonight is clear. There is no going back. Not tomorrow. Not ever.

"Sinn FÃ©in stands fully with the Garvaghy Road community, and they have the full support of Nationalists from right across Ireland in the period ahead."

Judge Patricia Smyth issued the injunction after Portadown District Orange Lodge declined her request to postpone the parade until all issues were properly considered.

The judge, who has been hearing the legal challenge to the Parades Commission's decision, said the temporary injunction would apply until the judicial review application could be properly determined.

Supporters had gathered at the Drumcree Centre off the Garvaghy Road while the Order's appeal was being heard.

News.title: Faisal Islam: The two big calls the chancellor has to make ahead of the Budget
News.content:
"It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?

"Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted.

The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimed at boosting confidence in the economy.

But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October.

Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence.

In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%.

Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget.

News.title: Heathrow Airport warns third runway could be delayed by four years
News.content:
Heathrow Airport has warned that its planned third runway might be delayed by four years due to planning and regulatory issues.

The government had hoped the new runway at the UK's busiest airport, estimated to cost Â£33bn, would open by 2035.

But Heathrow sees this deadline as increasingly difficult to deliver without further steps to simplify the planning process. It said on Saturday that it hoped to secure planning permission by 2029 and then open the runway "within a decade".

The Department for Transport (DfT) said the project's timeline had "always been ambitious" and that it would continue to work with stakeholders "at pace" on the matter.

The airport said its "core scenario" had always been to open a new runway within a decade of securing planning permission.

It said it was encouraged by the chancellor's efforts to streamline infrastructure and remove regulatory bottlenecks, and promised to continue to work with ministers, airlines and stakeholders to "progress the planning application with pace".

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced the government's support for the project in January 2025 as a means to grow the economy, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham - who was previously critical - said he was "open-minded" about the scheme when he came to office.

Despite attracting wide opposition from environmental campaigners and local resident groups, the project is expected to create around 100,000 jobs and provide a major boost to the economy as part of a wider Â£49bn modernisation of the airport.

The expansion would mean demolishing hundreds of homes, diverting rivers, and rerouting the M25 motorway between junctions 14 and 15 through a tunnel under the new runway.

The number of flights from the site, currently capped at 480,000 a year, could go up to 720,000 - or nearly 2,000 a day on average.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors 2 cast: Who are this year's 'big dogs' and dark horses?
News.content:
If Carr was the star of last year's show, then perhaps his fellow TV funnymen could be the ones to watch this time around.

Naturally good readers of a room and skilled at misdirection, comedians can inject some comic relief into those tense roundtable moments.

It worked for Carr, who was considered to be less of a threat and more out of his depth by the other sleuths.

This time around, stand-up star Joe Lycett, 38, is one of the leading candidates for the role of class clown. Known for his quick wit and political stunts, Lycett told the BBC he asked Carr for advice on "how to spot a rotten little traitor like you".

Last year's winner replied: "Just anyone that's sweating and giggling."

With his brightly coloured outfits, Lycett will bring some glamour to the castle, if and when he's not donning the famous dark cloak.

"There's a lot of variety and silly stuff that I might not get to wear at all if I end up doing a Paloma," he noted, with reference to Paloma Faith, who was brutally killed off early doors last year by her supposed friend, Carr.

If laughing all the way to the winning line is to work again, then it's hard to look beyond James Acaster.

Anyone who has seen his Netflix special Repertoire or heard his podcast Off Menu will know his deadpan, absurdist humour and whimsical flights of fancy could make it difficult to tell whether he is telling the truth or not.

A "huge fan" of the show since the first non-celebrity edition in 2022, Acaster, 41, said he would prefer to be a faithful as he wasn't good at lying - though Carr did previously say something similar...

News.title: Can you eat ultra-processed foods and still be healthy? A dietitian analysed my weekly shop
News.content:
First things first, what is a UPF?

It depends who you ask. A basic rule of thumb is that to be ultra-processed a product needs more than five ingredients, with at least one not normally found in your kitchen - things like emulsifiers, additives and flavourings.

There is a large and growing body of evidence that shows UPFs are linked to obesity, cardiovascular disease and metabolic disorders such as diabetes, as well as mental health problems and even premature death.

But scientists, doctors and dietitians can't agree on why. Is it purely down to the high fat, sugar, salt and calorie content? Or is the ultra-processing also a factor?

Studies show more than half the calories we consume in the UK come from ultra-processed food, external. Dr Chris van Tulleken has written books and made documentaries about how bad these foods can be, and he tells me they're "almost impossible to avoid" - even his own family's diet includes a few.

And my shopping list isn't UPF-free either.

Maeve Hanan, a member of the British Dietetic Association, pauses as she scans through some of my weekly shopping list (there was more fruit and veg, honest) and points to a box of bran flakes.

"This is ultra-processed, but I often buy this for my family. It's got so many health benefits."

Hanan says there's a "growing hysteria" about UPFs.

"Mainly because the messaging around them is so black and white," she says. "This food is good. This food is bad.

"It just fuels fear - and fear around food is never good."

News.title: Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim too
News.content:
Ashlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.

Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed.

"She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.

Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.

Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.

Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.

A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole.

Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.

Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".

News.title: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
News.content:
"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".

Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.

And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.

China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up.

"The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home.

"People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."

She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".

Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University â one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full. "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.

News.title: Man City chairman confident club will prove innocence
News.content:
Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak says he is still confident of proving the club's innocence after they were found guilty of breaking the Premier League's financial rules.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.

On Friday, it was announced City had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them and Al Mubarak has responded with a letter to fans on the club's website.

"Following Friday's media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I," Al Mubarak said.

"Here's what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

"But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.

Sanctions on the club are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine.

Al Mubarak, who was appointed as City's chairman after their 2008 takeover, also said his club was being "undermined".

"While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed," he added.

"There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity."

News.title: 'No turning back' in independence journey, says first minister at rally
News.content:
Wales' first minister has said there is "no turning back" on the journey to independence for the country, as he attended a rally on Saturday.

In a speech addressing the crowd gathered in Aberystwyth, Ceredigion, Rhun ap Iorwerth said the "next step" for Wales had to be "equality with Scotland, as a minimum".

Thousands were in attendance, with the event organisers, campaign group Yes Cymru, saying it estimated the march attracted between 8,000 and 9,000 people.

"[Wales is] on a journey, and there's no turning back," ap Iorwerth said.

Since 2019, thousands have taken part in independence marches across Wales, including in Cardiff, Swansea, Wrexham, Merthyr Tydfil, Rhyl and Barry.

But this was the first time the first minister of Wales had attended a Yes Cymru march.

A Reform Cymru Member of the Senedd (MS) said he was "disappointed" by the first minister's decision to attend, while a Welsh Conservative MS said it would be "better for him to be behind his desk in Cathays sorting the problems he said he would sort out".

News.title: PM pledges £210m to regenerate UK's high streets
News.content:
The prime minister has announced a Â£210m package to regenerate the UK's communities and high streets.

Empty spaces will be put back into use, Andy Burnham said, turning them into "community hubs, health centres, shared workspaces, cafÃ©s and the local services that people actually want to see."

The scheme is part of funding earmarked by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government for high street support and regeneration.

It comes ahead of Burnham's first Labour Party conference as prime minister, where he is set to emphasise his plans for the UK will have "making life more affordable" at its core.

As part of Burnham's high streets scheme, a Â£125 million derelict buildings fund will be available to transform mothballed and dilapidated buildings.

And an Â£85m pot will enable communities to take over neglected spaces including pubs, clubs and shops, the government said.

There will also be Â£65m allocated to rescuing businesses and buildings at risk of closure, and a further Â£20m allocated to help communities set up co-operative businesses and let out empty units.

The prime minister said: "People don't measure growth by looking at a spreadsheet. They measure it by looking at their local high street. Are shops opening or are the shutters down? Does the place feel like it's moving forward or being left behind?

"Today's funding will help put power back into the hands of locals who know their area best."

Communities Secretary Angela Rayner said the scheme showed the government would mean communities see "boarded-up buildings that have been left to rack and ruin turned into places people are proud to visit again".

Meanwhile First Secretary of State Louise Haigh said the investment would give local people the resources they need to make change, adding: "This is what devolution means in practice".

The move follows Burnham's announcement in the summer that pubs, clubs and social venues would see 20% cuts to business rates from April.

But Peter Kyle, business secretary to former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, suggested Burnham needs to act with "more urgency" to boost growth, as the PM arrives in Liverpool for Labour's party conference this weekend.

The Conservatives' own plan for "stronger high streets" would abolish business rates for thousands of businesses, and would "defend key pillars of the community such as post offices, pubs and pharmacies", according to the party.

News.title: Met to re-examine CCTV from Jill Dando murder case
News.content:
The Met Police has confirmed it will re-examine CCTV footage relating to the unsolved murder of Jill Dando, 27 years ago.

The BBC presenter and journalist was shot dead with a single bullet on her doorstep in Fulham in April 1999. Despite one of the biggest and most high-profile murder investigations in British history, the case remains unsolved.

A Met spokesperson said recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology had "provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station".

The CCTV includes an unidentified man who was seen sprinting near the scene of the shooting, 20 minutes after the event.

The Met said in the 27 years since Dando's death, the investigation had been "subject to numerous reviews", aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

It warned this latest review was part of "ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter".

News.title: Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in Britain after six years in US
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said it feels "great" to be back in Britain after spending six years living in California.

He told Canadian network CTV: "It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil. The kids are happy in school and it gives me a chance to be able to really focus on the Invictus Games in Birmingham in July next year."

Prince Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020, before returning to live in Britain last month.

It is thought the family are basing themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, had to be moved to a different school only days after they started over security concerns about the school run.

It is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had raised concerns about the distance and heavy traffic on the route to the school.

Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has been marked by tensions with the Royal Family.

News.title: Mayfair club shuts as Met investigates weapon claim
News.content:
A private members' club popular with celebrities has temporarily closed while police investigate allegations of threatening behaviour and whether a weapon was brandished in a nearby street.

The Metropolitan Police said it asked Westminster City Council to review Maison Estelle's alcohol licence as the premises was "allegedly associated with serious crime, or serious disorder, or both".

It related to an incident on 19 September, the force said. No injuries were reported.

Councillors suspended the licence at a private hearing on Thursday. The Mayfair venue, which has hosted Princess Beatrice, Idris Elba and Kim Kardashian, said it would be closed for "a few weeks" while investigations took place.

"A further hearing will be held in due course," a Met spokesperson said.

"The circumstances remain under investigation, including whether a firearm â or imitation firearm â was involved."

News.title: E-motorbikes seized by police sold on at auction, BBC finds
News.content:
Electric motorbikes seized by police forces in the UK are being sold on at auction, despite some fears they could end up back in the hands of criminals, the BBC can reveal.

Thousands are confiscated annually because they are suspected of being driven illegally, or used in a crime - most are later destroyed, but a BBC investigation has found some are sold on to members of the public in online auctions.

Across the UK, police sold 161 e-bikes and e-motorcycles last year and 54 in 2024, although the real number could be higher because not every force responded to the BBC's Freedom of Information request.

Some of the forces said they had now ended the practice, but others defended it as a way of putting "money back into policing".

Six forces responded to say some of the vehicles they had seized had been sold, including large forces such as West Midlands Police and Police Scotland.

The figure includes electrically-assisted pedal cycles, which look similar to bicycles and have a motor that kicks in as a rider pedals, as well as electric motorbikes, which are usually more powerful and are propelled only by their motor.

E-bikes and e-motorcycles have become controversial because some think they are linked to crime and anti-social behaviour.

Recent BBC reporting has highlighted cases across the country of balaclava-clad young men riding illegally on footpaths and intimidating residents.

There have also been a number of pedestrian deaths, including 86-year-old grandmother Gloria Stephenson, who was struck at a zebra crossing in Sunderland last year by an illegal e-motorbike.

News.title: Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference
News.content:
Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.

She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.

In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British".

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."

Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".

Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".

The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.

She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."

Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here.

But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.

But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.

The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this month.

Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.

She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

China and Russia got their turns to speak at the United Nations on Saturday, but that wasn't call.

Watchers from across the globe could find news that affected their lives at the U.N. General Assembly meetings. Here are a few moments:

___

Redefining Netanyahu's words

The foreign minister of Iceland, Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, used part of her time on the world stage Saturday to turn Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's words on Friday upside down.

Netanyahu, addressing people who were walking out on his remarks, called them “moral cowards.”

A day later, Gunnarsdóttir was having none of it. Speaking about Gaza, she said:

“We have heard the words ‘moral cowards’ from this podium. To me, moral cowards are those leaders around the world who refuse to sit down and negotiate a just and lasting peace. Those who deny access to humanitarian aid for people in desperate need. And moral cowards are those leaders who repeatedly go against and disrespect international law."

In diplomacy, Canada looks past the usual horizon

In a stormy year for the usually calm U.S.-Canada relationship, Canada’s top diplomat stressed to the world that her country is looking elsewhere.

“We can no longer afford to be overly reliant on any one partner,” Foreign Minister Anita Anand told the assembly. She spotlighted the government’s efforts to bolster economic ties with Europe, India, China and African countries, and a roster of new security, defense and economic deals inked with various countries this year.

Canada is increasing its defense spending in line with NATO commitments, and it’s expanding its diplomatic footprint, recently opening a new consulate in Greenland to help foster connections around the Arctic, she noted.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has made a splash in diplomatic circles this year by arguing that “middle powers” need to look out for themselves and for the very concept of international order. He has held Canada out as a pathfinder.

Anand echoed that message, telling the assembly: “In a rapidly changing world, Canada is a reliable partner, and we are ready to work together.”

Was he or wasn't he? Only his pilot knew for sure

For a brief moment Friday afternoon, a rumor circulated that Chinese leader Xi Jinping would leave Washington and President Donald Trump and come to New York. Was that true? And if so, would he speak on behalf of China at the United Nations?

As reporters scrambled to meet contingencies, we checked around the United Nations and found a definitive answer. Someone inside the U.N. compound who would know, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were giving out information that would normally be issued by the Chinese, had heard nothing and confirmed there was no Chinese advance team on site — as there would always be if Xi was on the way.

That was definitive. After all, the someone said, “The Chinese don't improvise."

And that's exactly the way it happened — or didn't. Vice President Han Zheng spoke Saturday, exactly as scheduled, and Xi headed home to Beijing.

___

Associated Press journalists Jennifer Peltz, Edith M. Lederer and Ted Anthony contributed to this report.
