Sports.title: Noel Gallagher begs Premier League bosses not to punish Manchester City fans despite 'breaking financial rules'
Sports.content:
Noel Gallagher begs Premier League bosses not to punish Manchester City fans despite 'breaking financial rules'

Noel Gallagher, who will tour with Oasis again next year, has responded to the bombshell development Manchester City have been found guilty on 114 of the 115 charges

View 4 Images Noel Gallagher reacts during a Premier League match involving Manchester City (Image: Getty Images)

Noel Gallagher has begged Premier League bosses not to punish fans of his beloved Manchester City for more than 100 alleged breaches of financial rules.

‌



The Oasis star was shocked by reports the football giants have been found guilty of 114 alleged offences and could now face a massive fine, point deductions, stripped trophies, or even enforced relegation. Noel, 59, said: "Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it's nothing to do with the supporters or the players. Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw. They won it on the pitch.

‌



"Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that's nothing to do with the fans. We were there, we know what we saw. Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt."

‌



Man City star's dad left Oasis legend Noel Gallagher with two black eyes after headbutt READ MORE :

Stripping Man City of Premier League titles 'unlikely' as new charges punishment theory given READ MORE :

View 4 Images City won seven Premier League titles when the alleged breaches took place (Image: Getty Images)

Noel, who is pals with the club's former boss Pep Guardiola, added: "I'm sad for the fans and the players and a little surprised because all along the club reassured us and vehemently denied all the charges. It was a shock to hear we were guilty on all but one of them."

Man City, owned by mega-rich Emirati royal Sheikh Mansour, are expected to appeal the verdicts, which were first reported on Friday after a three and a half year probe by an independent Premier League commission. At least four clubs, including Arsenal, Man United, Liverpool and Tottenham, have already reportedly preserved their rights to claim compensation for loss of earnings under Section W of Premier League rules. Other clubs are also tonight understood to be taking legal advice about the possibility of legal action.

‌



Christian Purslow, who has previously held top executive roles at Liverpool, Chelsea and Aston Villa, today warned the verdicts could kick-off a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game". Mr Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss.

"Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3million. Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated.

"Let's say the team that finished 18th would've finished 17th if Manchester City weren't there. And they, of course, suffered huge loss. If you add all those claims up, over nine years, and that's just in the Premier League, you can see that the potential here for this to spiral out of control is huge."

‌



View 4 Images Noel pictured in the stands after a City game this month (Image: Peter Byrne/PA Wire)

Mr Purslow added: "I really hope that common sense prevails here and that there is a comprehensive solution between the authorities and Manchester City that looks at all these issues and tries to draw a line in the sand. Because a never-ending waterfall of legal claims and uncertainties for another four or five years would be absolutely appalling for the game."

Writing on X, Noel's younger brother Liam, 54, today wrote: "We'll win the appeal and all the WETWIPES from other clubs begging for our titles need to sit down... embarrassing."

‌



The alleged breaches took place between the 2009-10 and 2022-23 seasons, during which time Man City won seven Premier League titles, a Champions League, three FA Cups and six League Cups. They relate to a number of areas, with the most serious linked to claims the club failed to provide “accurate financial information” to the league.

They were accused of a wide range of rule breaches centring on claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.

Uefa previously found Man City in breach of football fair play rules in 2014, a decision that resulted in the club paying a €20m fine. By 2020, Uefa had suspended City from the Champions League for “overstating its sponsorship revenue in its accounts”. But the suspension was later overturned by the club on appeal to the court of arbitration for sport.

‌



View 4 Images Erling Haaland is one of Manchester City's stars (Image: Getty Images)

The Premier League or Man City, whose executives are said to have signed non-disclosure agreements, have so far refused to publicly confirm the latest alleged verdicts.

A Man City spokesperson said: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.

‌



“The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

'Our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began'

In an open letter today published on Man City's website, the club's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak wrote: "Following Friday’s media reporting, many of you will have spent your evening answering questions and responding to messages from friends, family and colleagues. So have I. Here’s what I said to my family: The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position. But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies. "I ask you to please carefully read the statement below, which we gave on Friday, and the statement we issued in February 2023. Every word matters and holds true.

Article continues below

"While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our Club. We will not give them that opportunity.

Arsenal fan Piers Morgan today wrote on X: "Let’s be clear: Manchester City have been found guilty of being the biggest cheats in English football history, and the punishment must fit their crimes. At very minimum, they must be relegated from Premier League and stripped of all fraudulently ‘won’ titles."

Former Man City chairman David Bernstein told Times Radio: “I’m a fan of Manchester City and have been a fan for 70 years. “First of all, the timing of this I think is crucial. This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because…you’ve got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it’s just not viable. “I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty. All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland player 'boycotts' Israel match as teammates call emergency meeting
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland player 'boycotts' Israel match as teammates call emergency meeting

Republic of Ireland are scheduled to face Israel in a Nations League match in Hungary on Sunday night, amid vocal opposition to the game taking place

View 2 Images Gavin Bazunu has informed Republic of Ireland bosses of his final decision

More Republic of Ireland players could boycott Sunday’s match with Israel after Gavin Bazunu confirmed he does not want to play in the fixture.

‌



The Bolton Wanderers goalkeeper, who is his country’s second choice, told bosses on Friday about his intention to not play, according to the Telegraph.

‌



His teammates are now considering their options and it's thought more could follow the same path throwing the UEFA Nations League match into major doubt. There have been increasingly vocal calls for Ireland to boycott the fixture, amid the backdrop of the humanitarian crisis in Gaza.

‌



A UN-commissioned inquiry previously found Israel has committed genocide against Palestinians in war-torn Gaza. More than 73,000 people have been killed after Israeli military action was launched in response to the Hamas attack on the Nova Festival in southern Israel of October 7 2023, which killed approximately 1,200 people.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

‌



An open letter from more than 160 Irish athletes urged the Irish Football Association (FAI) to withdraw from the fixture, with protests outside the team’s hotel in Dublin earlier this week.

It was expected that Ireland’s players would issue a statement at Saturday morning’s pre-match press conference. However, that was cancelled and rearranged minutes before the scheduled time, with no reason offered.

Last year, the FAI voted to submit a motion to UEFA that would have seen Israel banned from club and international competitions. The FAI cited two alleged violations of UEFA rules, including organising clubs in occupied Palestine without the permission of the Palestinian FA and the failure to enforce an effective anti-racism policy.

‌



Ireland captain Dara O’Shea made clear it was important that the opinions of all players were heard in the build-up. He said: “We’ve got to respect each other’s opinions and each other’s views and really sit down and take the time, because it deserves the time to talk about.

View 2 Images Heimir Hallgrimsson, Head Coach of Republic of Ireland (Image: Charles McQuillan/Getty Images)

“It’s the main thing and it’s something that can’t be brushed over. Whatever decision that we go through as players is taken as one and everybody’s view is respected as well.”

‌



Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson elicited a response from the Israeli FA earlier this week when he said “we are not playing with genocide. We are playing against genocide. We are playing against Israel; we are not playing with Israel.”

In response the Israeli FA issued a statement which read: We have contributed to the world and humanity in countless fields, earning an impressive number of Nobel Prizes along the way.

“Unfortunately, we have not yet found a cure for stupidity, ignorance and hypocrisy displayed by the @IrelandFootball team coach. We’re not playing with ignorance, hypocrisy and stupidity, we’re playing against the coach who embodies them.”

Article continues below

Israel are currently prohibited from playing games at home, due to security concerns, with this weekend’s match scheduled to take place in Hungary. The return fixture will also be played on neutral ground - in Serbia - amid the opposition to the game taking place.

Sports.title: Internationals take shock lead over USA into singles after late drama
Sports.content:
The International Team moved another step closer to a historic Presidents Cup win on American soil by taking a 10.5-7.5 lead over Team USA into the Sunday singles.

Geoff Ogilvy's side held a four-point advantage after the first two days at Medinah Country Club, following their historic foursomes sessions sweep on Friday, then added 1.5 points from four matches during a tight Saturday fourballs session.

Team USA captain Brandt Snedeker benched world No 1 Scottie Scheffler for the afternoon foursomes, where they threatened their own session sweep after grabbing the early lead in all four matches.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from Scottie Scheffler and Sam Burns' fourballs victory over Hideki Matsuyama and Ryo Hisatsune on Saturday morning

Cameron Young and Chris Gotterup thrashed Adam Scott and Sungjae Im 6&4, before Patrick Cantlay and Xander Schauffele saw off Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim 2&1 to reduce the deficit further, only for the Internationals to fight back in an impressive finish.

Ryan Fox and Min Woo Lee bounced back from falling behind early to defeat Sam Burns and Wyndham Clark 3&2 in the bottom match, guaranteeing the Internationals would start the Sunday singles ahead for just the fourth time ever.

The International Team require five more points from the 12 singles matches to complete their unlikely success, while Team USA need 7.5 points on the final day to avoid an embarrassing home upset or eight points for a comeback victory.

Snedeker reveals 'mistakes' as Internationals 'weathered the storm'

Team USA captain Brandt Snedeker:

"I thought our guys battled hard. It was a tough day out there. This golf course got really tough this afternoon. There's such a fine line between good shots and bad shots and I was proud of the way the guys hung in there and battled.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Team USA captain Brandt Snedeker forgot the name of Cameron Young, one of his players, during a live interview ahead of the Presidents Cup Saturday fourballs

"I challenged the guys this afternoon to go out there and be that team that we need them to be and got Scottie (Scheffler) some much-needed rest, so he can go out there tomorrow and be the Scheffler that we know he is.

"It's going to be a long, hard day tomorrow. I've got the right guys in that team room. They're going to compete. So proud of how they've kind of hung in there this week, despite all of my mistakes. Can't wait to see them go out there tomorrow and compete."

Image: Snedeker left Scheffler out of Team USA's line-up for the afternoon foursomes

International Team captain Geoff Ogilvy:

"What a day! They (Team USA) came out firing, as we knew they would. They were up in all four in the morning and we thought we stole a point and a half a little bit, to get out of that with only 2.5-1.5.

"This afternoon, same thing. The United States came out playing well, which we know they're going to. They're some of the best players in the world, but the boys hung tough and sort of weathered the storm if you like and started making a few putts.

Image: Tom Kim and Si Woo Kim have won three of their four matches together this week

"It's tough when there's all red on the board, but to get 2-2 out of that afternoon session and to go into tomorrow with a lead, which was the goal at the start of the week, I'm very proud of them."

What happened in the morning fourballs?

Min Woo Lee and Im recovered from being two down with four to play to tie the top match against American duo Jackson Koivun and Justin Thomas, who said post-match that he felt like he 'let down' his rookie team-mate.

Sports.title: Keane disagrees with Gordon: There is a gap between Spain and England
Sports.content:
Roy Keane disagreed with Anthony Gordon's assessment that England are at the same level as Spain after the World Cup winners came from behind to beat Thomas Tuchel's side 3-2 in their Nations League opener.

Spain extend their unbeaten run to 39 games with the win at Wembley, but the game could have had a very different outcome had Harry Kane not missed a second-half penalty after he headed England 2-1 in front before the break.

The momentum shifted in Spain's favour after Kane's slip, with Alex Baena equalising off the bench before setting up the winner, scored by fellow substitute Mikel Oyarzabal, who broke England hearts in the Euro 2024 final.

Image: England's Harry Kane slips and fires his penalty against the bar in the match with Spain

Gordon, who scored England's equaliser from a terrific counter-attacking move, felt the performance was enough to win them the game and showed that they are a top team.

"I don't think there is a gap [to Spain] I feel like we're right there," Gordon told ITV Sport. "We can win that game so easily. If the penalty goes in we can go on and win the game. In hindsight it's always easy to say that. But I felt good in the game.

"I don't think there is a gap and I think if we played them in the final I would've felt confident. Being confident doesn't always translate into a win, but I think you've seen here tonight that we're a top team."

Responding to the England forward, Sky Sports pundit Roy Keane said on ITV Sport: "I disagree with Gordon, I think there is a gap. I think there is, obviously [Spain are] world champions, European champions."

Tuchel: We thought we had Spain at half-time

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Tuchel reflects on England's loss against Spain.

England scored two goals in the space of four first-half minutes just before half-time - more goals than Spain conceded in the entire World Cup - but failed to capitalise on their dominance after the restart with Kane's spurned penalty proving to be the turning point.

Spain, meanwhile, were ruthless with Lamine Yamal pouncing on Marc Guehi's error to open the scoring after two minutes and Baena's second-half equaliser coming directly after a misplaced pass from Nico O'Reilly.

"We did everything today to beat Spain," Tuchel said after the game. "Details matter on this level. Clear-cut mistakes were too high on our side unfortunately. In the last 20 metres they were more clinical and composed to convert our ball losses into clear-cut chances.

"Still we had them and we had our chance to beat them."

He added: "We wanted desperately to be the team to beat them. We thought we had them at half-time. That was the way the team showed up after half-time.

"It happens too often today and we get punished on the highest level. The execution and composure in the final 20 metres was on the highest level from our opponents."

Spain boss: We had the game under control

Image: Lamine Yamal celebrates scoring against England

Spain boss Luis de la Fuente felt his side were in charge of the game save for the final stages of the first half when England came from behind to lead at the break.

"The game was under control most of the time, except for six to seven minutes, when England dominated us," he said.

"We got disconnected. Against a rival like England, a superpower, this can happen. I think we had the game under control."

Analysis: 'Missed penalty and a missed opportunity for England'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Gordon reflects on a tough match against Spain in the Nations League.

Sky Sports News senior correspondent Rob Dorsett at Wembley Stadium:

"One captain's slip, one memorable scalp that slipped away.

"A missed penalty and a missed opportunity for England - though it's hard to argue that Spain weren't the far superior side over 90 minutes.

"The world champions could have been out of sight within 30 minutes, after a dominant display of their prowess. And a couple of self-destructive England passes.

"The fact that Spain were only a goal ahead, gave England hope, and it was a stunning 10-minute spell that saw England grab the lead.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Kane reacts to England's loss against Spain and his penalty kick miss.

"Firstly, a brilliant goal from their best player on the night, Anthony Gordon, and then from captain Kane with a header.

"But the home side started the second half really well, and when Kane missed from the spot to give England a two-goal lead, Spain sensed blood. Their response with strikes from Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal was decisive and deserved.

"A defeat with some merit then, for Tuchel's England. But there still seems to be a gulf in class."

Sports.title: Over inside four rounds? Whyte 'well up' for showdown with Fisher
Sports.content:
Dillian Whyte says he is "well up" for a fight against Johnny Fisher and has vowed to stop 'The Romford Bull' inside four rounds.

The Brixton heavyweight was watching from ringside as Fisher battled to a majority-decision victory over Michael Pirotton at The Copper Box on Saturday night.

Whyte is ready to return following his loss to Moses Itauma last August and has welcomed a verbal challenge from Fisher.

"Johnny Fisher has been calling me out for a while. He wants to fight me. I'm well up for that fight," Whyte told Sky Sports.

"I knock Johnny Fisher out. It's heavyweight boxing, anything can happen. I could get caught high on the head like I did last time out, but I'll knock Johnny Fisher out.

"I'll be surprised if it goes past three or four rounds. I'm an ageing dog but I still have all of my teeth."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Pirotton mocks Johnny Fisher after he got hit with a huge right hand!

Whyte, who holds wins over the likes of Joseph Parker and Alexander Povetkin, insists he would relish an explosive showdown with Fisher, who has 12 knockouts in his 15 victories.

"He's a bit erratic and he's open in lots of areas but he's dangerous," said Whyte. "He's swinging big punches, a big man, and he hits hard so yeah, I think it would be an exciting fight while it lasts."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Zuffa Boxing 11 fight between Johnny Fisher and Michael Pirotton.

Asked about Fisher's biggest threat, Whyte added: "Big overhand rights really. That's it really, but I've fought the best of my generation. The reason this fight attracts me is because it's dangerous. My last fight lasted a round so people could be thinking I'm washed up and finished now so let them run with that.

"I don't mind being a stepping stone because you need a stepping stone to step somewhere else. Let's go. They want to fight me. I was at home relaxing, they offered me out, so let's get it on."

Nelson warns Fisher about Whyte threat

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Johnny Nelson says that Johnny Fisher needs to be smart with who he fights next and that Dillian Whyte should not be his next opponent.

Sky Sports expert Johnny Nelson has warned that Whyte could be 'too much' for Fisher.

"No he can't [keep having fights like that]," Nelson told Sky Sports.

"I spoke to Dillian Whyte, who is kind of looking at being a potential opponent for Johnny Fisher.

"I think Dillian knows too much for him, regardless of what stage of his career he's at.

"They need to think smartly, matchmaking him, if they want to get him to a British title attempt.

"I wouldn't put him in with Dillian Whyte, because Dillian knows too much.

"He's strong, he's rugged and he's experienced."

Sports.title: Fisher overcomes Pirotton in heavyweight brawl
Sports.content:
Johnny Fisher came through a bruising battle as he outslugged Michael Pirotton to win their heavyweight clash at the Copper Box Arena.

Fisher punched forward to take a lead, but as his energy reserves waned he began to look increasingly vulnerable while the Belgian battled back.

The Romford favourite forced himself through to the finish, taking a majority decision win, but it was testing.

Having just watched gym-mate Craig Richards lose in the chief support, Fisher looked to banish any nerves by plunging forward onto the front foot. He went straight for the Belgian with double jabs.

Pirotton hefted a left hook across, but Fisher's "Romford Bull Army" of supporters had found their voice. Feet stamping, voices raised, they chanted Fisher's name to create a raucous atmosphere in the Copper Box.

Fisher responded driving himself into Pirotton, but leaving himself open when he leaned over his front leg.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Pirotton mocks Johnny Fisher after he got hit with a huge right hand!

The Belgian did catch Fisher with his right cross. But the "Romford Bull" also showed off some of his work with new trainer Tony Sims, every now and then bobbing and weaving under an attack to stay in the pocket and pummel Pirotton's body.

Fisher was landing head shots and Pirotton was cut over the left eye early on. It was in a bad position and the doctor had a close look at it in the fourth round.

On resumption, Fisher stormed forward, sensing his moment. He hit Pirotton with a hard left hook to body, and then launched his right down on his head. That combination worked for him and Fisher tenderised the body to open up the head.

He shook up Pirotton and directed him back into the ropes. But getting through the fourth, Pirotton fired back in the fifth round.

Power began to drain away from Fisher's punches and he held his feet. Pirotton blasted his right into a tiring Fisher and caught him with following head shots.

Fisher struck back before the end of the fifth round but he was flagging. In the sixth round, his supporters bellowed him on as Fisher searched for his second wind. He did find chopping hooks that rattled Pirotton round the head.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Johnny Nelson says that Johnny Fisher needs to be smart with who he fights next and that Dillian Whyte should not be his next opponent.

In the seventh round Fisher's right swung wildly, missing, but he launched himself back in with an explosive left to drive Pirotton into the ropes.

The Belgian, increasingly on the offensive, continued to make it a bruising night's work for Fisher.

He threaded his right over Fisher's jab, a fine shot. Even though he'd picked up a second cut round his left eye, Pirotton was undaunted, looking to chip into Fisher's lead and he managed to stand his ground.

Pirotton's left eye was almost fully closed by the last round. Fisher hurt him, lashing in shots as the crowd roared. He summoned up his final dregs of energy, windmilling rights at Pirotton as he went for him.

Fisher, exhausted at the end of the battle, couldn't find a decisive finish and one judge had the two heavyweights level at 95-95. A second saw it close at 96-95 but the third had Fisher ahead 98-92.

Sports.title: Spain show their class as errors cost England in Nations League loss
Sports.content:
Spain showed why they are the best national team in the world by emerging 3-2 winners from a thrilling, chaotic Nations League clash at Wembley, in which England's flaws undermined their exciting attacking play.

It was the World Cup final that might have been had England not squandered their advantage against Argentina this summer - but Spain showed the gap in quality in a result which is a major blow to Thomas Tuchel's stated aim of winning this competition.

Bad errors from Marc Guehi and Nico O'Reilly helped Lamine Yamal and Alex Baena score Spain's first two and England were cut open through the match, including for Mikel Oyarzabal's winner which came with 16 minutes to play.

Image: Mikel Oyarzabal puts Spain 3-2 up against England in the Nations League

But while England's defence suffered, there was brilliant forward play, too.

Anthony Gordon had urged England to lean into their traditional strengths this week and they did just that with an exceptional counter-attack to make it 1-1, which saw the winger combine with Jude Bellingham before precisely applying the finish. Harry Kane's header from O'Reilly's cross made it 2-1 and capped an incredible transformation in the match.

In four minutes, Spain had conceded more goals than in their eight World Cup games combined.

Croatia beat Czech Republic Croatia won 2-1 away to Czech Republic in the other A3 Nations League game on Saturday, meaning England are third in the group.

There was then a pivotal moment, when England were awarded a penalty at the start of the second half, when Rodri was judged to have fouled Bellingham, following a VAR check. But Kane slipped and sent his spot-kick against the bar - and Spain capitalised.

Ferran Torres may have passed up two one-on-one chances in the first half, but Spain were clinical after the missed spot-kick to go top of Nations League Group A3.

Image: England's Harry Kane slips and fires his penalty against the bar in the match with Spain

With this result, Spain's record-breaking unbeaten streak is also extended to 39 games. England will now have to find a way to beat them in Madrid in November - and win against Czech Republic and Croatia in the meantime - if they are to make it to the Nations League finals and show they are capable of toppling the best when it matters.

England team news: Trafford made surprise start James Trafford was a surprise starter for England in goal, taking the spot of regular No 1 Jordan Pickford.

Jarell Quansah started at right-back ahead of Trent Alexander-Arnold; Myles Lewis-Skelly started in midfield.

England fielded their first-choice front-four of Harry Kane, Jude Bellingham, Bukayo Saka and Anthony Gordon.

The key moments from Wembley

Spain make fastest start against England at Wembley in 70 years Lamine Yamal scored the third quickest goal England have ever conceded at Wembley Stadium, behind only first minute goals for Scotland in 1957 and Hungary in 1953.

2: GOAL! Marc Guehi's blunder allows Lamine Yamal to take the ball, run in on goal and score. An early gift for the world champions!

Image: Lamine Yamal celebrates scoring against England

9: NO GOAL! Ferran Torres heads in after a corner which comes from a Myles Lewis-Skelly misplaced pass. But the Spain forward is flagged offside.

16: BIG SAVE! James Trafford saves a one-on-one with Ferran Torres after England's defence is cut wide open.

27: HUGE CHANCE! But Ferran Torres sends his shot wide of the goal after Rodri plays him in following a Lamine Yamal interception from Elliot Anderson's pass.

36: GOAL! Anthony Gordon combines with Jude Bellingham before completing an exceptional counter-attack move to level the match.

Image: Anthony Gordon celebrates his equaliser for England against Spain at Wembley

39: SO CLOSE! Harry Kane drops to his knees as his shot flies narrowly wide as England almost grab a quickfire second. The home fans inside Wembley roar their team forwards.

40: ENGLAND LEAD! An incredible transformation in mood, momentum and scoreline as Kane heads in Nico O'Reilly's cross despite Marc Cucurella's attempts to block.

45: CROSSBAR! Cucurella's mis-hit cross kisses the face of the England crossbar.

54: PENALTY MISS! Rodri is punished after a VAR check for his challenge on Bellingham in the box… but Kane slips as he takes the spot-kick and fires it against the bar!

60: GOAL! Spain punish Kane's miss when they pounce on an error from O'Reilly and tee up sub Alex Baena to clip in the equaliser from the edge of the box.

74: GOAL! England drop deep under pressure but it's a through pass from Baena which releases Mikel Oyarzabal to tuck away the eventual winner.

Tuchel: We had them - but made too many mistakes

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Thomas Tuchel reflects on England's loss against Spain.

England boss Thomas Tuchel:

"We did everything today to beat Spain. Details matter on this level. Clear-cut mistakes were too high on our side. In the last 20 metres they were more clinical and composed to convert our ball losses into clear-cut chances.

"We had them, we had our chance to beat them. We will keep on pushing. But I think the way we played was enough to beat them.

"We had the worst possible start against a team like Spain who loves to control the game. We could have won it. We have to recover from it, learn from it. Do what we did good and reduce and improve on our mistakes."

Kane: We went toe-to-toe with Spain

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Harry Kane reacts to England's loss against Spain and his penalty miss.

England captain Harry Kane to ITV Sport:

"We reached good levels in the World Cup but didn't put a full 90 mins together. Similar today.

"We went toe to toe with Spain. On another day we would have won. It's disappointing, but we have to take the positives."

De La Fuente: We had the game under control

Spain boss Luis de la Fuente:

"The game was under control most of the time, except for six to seven minutes, when England dominated us. We got disconnected. Against a rival like England, a superpower, this can happen.

"I respect [the Spain squad's] ambition, they want to grow. There is still room for improvement and new players are coming on. This generation of players is exceptional. They are still hungry, they want to keep growing and playing."

Analysis: A statement win slips away from England

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Gordon reflects on a tough match against Spain in the Nations League.

Sky Sports News' Rob Dorsett at Wembley:

"One captain's slip, one memorable scalp that slipped away. A missed penalty and a missed opportunity for England. Though it's hard to argue that Spain weren't the far superior side over 90 minutes.

"The world champions could have been out of sight within 30 minutes, after a dominant display of their prowess. And a couple of self-destructive England passes. The fact that Spain were only a goal ahead, gave England hope and it was a brilliant 10-minute spell that saw England grab the lead. Firstly a brilliant goal from their best player on the night, Anthony Gordon, and then from captain Kane with a header.

"The home side started the second half really well but when Kane missed from the spot to give England a two-goal lead, Spain sensed blood. Their response with strikes from Alex Baena and Mikel Oyarzabal was decisive and deserved.

"A defeat with some merit then, for Tuchel's England. But there still seemed to be a gulf in class."

Sports.title: Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty miss
Sports.content:
It was another high-profile game when Thomas Tuchel’s England let a lead slip in the second half and went on to lose. But unlike the last time, it was not one for recriminations. The England support can accept losing when their team plays with cut and thrust. More to the point, they can accept losing to Spain who, at times, played football from a different stratosphere.

England were game. They were driven by Jude Bellingham, who ran on adrenaline and played to the point of maximum expression. They had positive surges either side of the interval, especially the one towards the end of the first half when goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put them in charge, hauling them back after Lamine Yamal’s second-minute goal.

The biggest takeaway was Spain’s slickness. There is a reason why they won the World Cup in the summer. Why they won the European Championship before that. They are the best team in the international game by a distance. Nobody can live with them. England did well to stay within a puncher’s chance of a result in this Nations League opener; Bellingham was still throwing them in stoppage time. Crucially, as Tuchel and England try to look forward after the heartbreak of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina, there was no negativity from the Wembley crowd. Even in the face of England’s defending, which was dreadfully loose.

We were denied the chance to see how the fans would react to the announcement of Tuchel’s name when the teams were read out in the countdown to kick-off. Because, after going through the starting XI and the 12 substitutes, Tuchel’s name was not read out. But there were none of the dreaded boos at the full-time whistle.

The match turned on a Kane penalty miss in the 54th minute. Had the captain scored rather than hitting the crossbar after his standing foot gave way in the turf, England would have been 3-1 up. Shortly afterwards, they were pegged back to 2-2 by the Spain substitute Álex Baena and there was a degree of inevitability about the winner from another replacement. Mikel Oyarzabal’s dinked finish was impudently brilliant. Spain had been fantastic for the opening 30 minutes and when they went again after the Kane penalty, they had too much. It was a statement of intent from them, an illustration of their remorseless desire.

“Campeones” was the chant from the enclosure housing the travelling fans before kick-off and it is fair to say the visiting radio commentators were excited about seeing Spain for the first time since the second star was stitched on to their shirt. Their fervour went up a few notches in the early running when Lamine Yamal opened the scoring.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane’s left foot gives away as he takes the penalty. He hit the crossbar and the ball bounced out to safety. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

The goal was a personal disaster for Marc Guéhi; it was almost as if the Manchester City defender had other things on his mind. It was of a piece with England’s struggles against the Spanish press. Guéhi was facing upfield as he tried to build a move from deep but his passing lanes were blocked. So he checked back and walked straight into Lamine Yamal, who robbed him and was clean through. He made the finish past James Trafford look easy.

Tuchel had started Trafford ahead of Jordan Pickford, a major deviation from his stated intention for continuity from the World Cup. Pickford was erratic in the summer and was punished for some of his mistakes. Trafford has been outstanding for Leeds since joining them over the summer. Tuchel’s idea is to share the minutes between Trafford and Pickford during this window. Trafford could hear the knock of opportunity and he helped to keep England in the game as Spain pushed to add to Lamine Yamal’s goal.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

How Spain pushed. They shimmered with menace. It was the movements, the speed of them – plus the breathtaking assurance on the ball. They had so many options in possession that it felt at times as if they had more men on the pitch.

Ferran Torres had the ball in the net only to be pulled back for offside while Trafford stood up to make a big one-on-one block against the Spain striker after Lamine Yamal had played the through-ball. England’s backline was all over the place. Torres blew another one-on-one on 28 minutes, with Trafford making himself big while Dani Olmo rifled just wide after a sumptuous Lamine Yamal flick.

England tried to throw counterpunches as they hung on. The resistance was impressive. Gordon was to the fore and so was Bellingham. They showed their personality when the chips were down. When the two combined for an equaliser that had not really been advertised, it was the prompt for a wild turnaround.

It was Spain pushing only for Nico Williams to lose his footing and then the ball to Elliot Anderson. England swept forward in thrilling style, Gordon flicking to Bellingham, getting it back and surging in on goal. The low finish was nerveless.

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane (on the ground) watches his header come off the thigh of Marc Cucurella to make it it 2-1 to England. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Enter Kane. He was unlucky when he banged inches wide from the edge of the area after a Bukayo Saka burst. He was lucky when his header from a Nico O’Reilly cross, which Unai Simón looked to have covered, drew a panicked reaction from Marc Cucurella. The left-back jutted out his thigh to turn the ball past his goalkeeper. The fates were against Cucurella. When his mishit cross on 45 minutes sailed over Trafford, the ball came back off the far post.

Bellingham appeared particularly determined to leave his imprint. The Real Madrid midfielder was in the mood for bragging rights back in La Liga. It was the power and directness of his running; the smoothness of it, the quickness of his moves. Spain could not contain him. It was his persistence after yet another surge that led to the penalty.

Gordon played the pass back inside from the left and Bellingham got there before Rodri, who invited trouble when he hung out a leg. Down went Bellingham and after a review, it was decided that the contact trumped the feeling that the England player had tried to engineer it. Kane could not convert.

Back came Spain. Lamine Yamal pushed a shot wide after a give and go with Baena, whose backheel was beautiful. Then Baena equalised after O’Reilly gave away the ball and Olmo quickly shifted it to the edge of the area. Baena bought himself the space for the shot with an expert drop of the shoulder.

Saka curled just wide at the other end after more good work by Bellingham but the tide had turned. You could not take your eyes off Lamine Yamal while Luis de la Fuente’s attack-minded changes worked. It was Oyarzabal who made the difference from a Baena pass. England could have no complaints.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland will fulfil their fixture against Israel in Hungary on Sunday night, but only after lengthy deliberations between the players resulted in a “significant majority” voting to play. The Bolton goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, however, will not be involved, after pulling out in protest.

After a week in which the Irish team and officials have come under increasing domestic pressure to boycott the match due to Israel’s military actions in Gaza, training was delayed by five hours on Saturday while the squad discussed whether to go ahead.

“This morning, a player expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad,” said the FAI’s chief David Courell, referring to Bazunu.

“What proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves, but also at times with the coaching staff and the executive. Ultimately we carried out a vote amongst the squad ... and it was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue.”

Courell said the squad had also agreed a number of measures to signal their unease with the fixture taking place. Players are to wear black armbands “in recognition of all the lives lost in the conflict” he said, adding that there will be “elements of the pre-match ceremony” that will “not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland” players, namely the pre-match handshake and exchange of pennants.

Bazunu, writing on Instagram, said: “Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people.

“However, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.

View image in fullscreen The Republic of Ireland head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson (left), and the FAI CEO, David Courell, confer during the delayed press conference. Photograph: Ben McShane/Sportsfile/Getty Images

“My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.

“There are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them.”

The Republic’s head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, meanwhile, said “nobody is comfortable playing these games for many reasons” as he was once again put under pressure over remarks in which he described his team as “playing against genocide” earlier this week.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Hallgrímsson said he had used a “strong” word and now regretted it. “It was a wrong word for me to use,” he said, arguing that he had meant to say that “by playing we are not accepting what is happening”. If a player chooses to play in the fixture “he is not supporting or agreeing with anything in Gaza” Hallgrímsson said. “We are not playing with that word, we are playing against it.”

The leadership of the Israel team used their press conference to read a statement congratulating Ireland on their decision to play. “What we have seen today is that football has won,” it read. “The separation between football and politics must continue. Anything else spells chaos and creates consequences for the game we love. The Irish took the right decision in agreeing to this. Even if it took longer than it should, it was welcome.”

Israeli officials said they would engage in all of the pre-match formalities with the head coach Ran Ben-Shimon confirming: “I will shake hands with Hallgrímsson.”

The Israel FA will also appeal both yellow cards awarded to Saied Abu Farchi during Thursday’s defeat to Austria. Farchi was given a second yellow after he celebrated scoring an equaliser by uprooting the corner flag, an action interpreted by officials as mimicking the firing of a rifle.

Israel dispute this interpretation. “Anyone familiar with him knows it was an imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty,” their spokesperson said.

Sports.title: Pocognoli’s reign as Scotland coach begins with stalemate in Slovenia
Sports.content:
Sébastien Pocognoli grimaced on Friday when recalling his debut as an international player for Belgium. Alessandro del Piero and Italy discovered favourable opposition when preparing for the 2006 World Cup. Pocognoli will also look back, in time, at his first game as the manager of Scotland.

Blue skies, a dainty stadium in Ljubljana and a second-half display that provided glimpses of optimism in respect of Scotland’s world, post-Steve Clarke. The best-forgotten first 45 minutes can be explained away by a squad operating under a new regime. By full time, Slovenia were grateful for their point. Scotland’s players took deserved applause.

Scotland’s failing here was a familiar one. A lack of goals haunted Clarke. Nonetheless, this version of Scotland did at least create a series of openings. Scott McTominay, a key attacking threat, was missing. Instilling ruthlessness in a team is no easy task; it is one, however, Pocognoli has the coaching credentials to meet. Slovenia, on this evidence, have the more significant challenges.

“The feeling in the dressing room is positive because of the second half,” said Pocognoli. “We should have scored but I am very happy with the general performance of the strikers. It was only the last details we missed.” His demeanour was upbeat.

Ninety-four days had passed since Scotland’s loss to Brazil all but confirmed World Cup elimination. When that meek exit was certain, Clarke announced his resignation. Players and supporters alike seem caught between being highly grateful to Clarke for materially altering Scotland’s fortunes and heralding regime change.

In Slovenia, Pocognoli sampled international management for the first time at the age of 39. Slovenia failed to reach the World Cup, with the rows of empty seats telling the story of a country that is not at all convinced by its footballing outlook. The absence of Benjamin Sesko did nothing to help a shot-shy side.

Scotland could hardly bemoan poor preparation. Pocognoli had whipped his squad and mini-army of backroom staff to La Manga in the buildup to this Nations League game. With a sense of revolution in the air, the head coach unleashed a hitherto unseen front two: Robbie Ure was making his international debut while Oli McBurnie returned after years in the wilderness. The opening half only proved there is little point deploying multiple strikers if there is no adequate means of supplying them.

Scotland were awful in that first period. The football was passive and directionless. Players looked well-enough drilled off the ball, but descended into a state of panic when in possession. Slovenia, who were little better than ordinary, should have seized upon these shortcomings. To his credit, whatever message Pocognoli forcefully pressed home during the break had an effect.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli barks instructions during his first game in charge of Scotland. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

Andraz Sporar had the ball in the net for the hosts in the eighth minute only for an offside flag to go up. Sporar subsequently missed a golden opportunity from six yards after fine work from Danijel Sturm. As Aljosa Matko shanked wide of Angus Gunn’s goal, the Tartan Army’s groans were audible.

Save a Ure shot from 20 yards that clipped the outside of a post, Scotland were nonexistent as an attacking force. An overhit Billy Gilmour pass that flew out of play when intended for the marauding Andy Robertson rather summed things up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

McBurnie should have marked his Scotland return with a goal within five minutes of the restart. He opted to try to jink around Jan Oblak rather than slam a shot past the goalkeeper. Oblak morphed into Inspector Gadget, stretching out his arms while grounded to pinch the ball from McBurnie’s feet.

This triggered Scottish improvement; Gilmour forced a save after a one-two with McBurnie. Aaron Hickey could not quite divert a John McGinn corner on target. Oblak had to be sharp to deny the Scotland substitute Kieron Bowie before doing likewise to McBurnie from the resultant corner.

Second-half Scotland involved a huge upturn. McBurnie said he would not be able to sleep due to his profligacy. Seventeen Scotland caps are yet to yield a goal.

Bowie’s miss, 12 minutes from time, was in the category of howler. Gilmour, increasingly influential as Scotland dominated, had fed his teammate. Pocognoli was emboldened, sending on Ben Gannon-Doak to replace Hickey. In old money, that represented a winger for a full-back.

Scotland huffed, puffed, pushed and wheezed. Slovenia stood firm. Pocognoli nodded with approval as the whistle blew. Next up, a Hampden Park bow against Switzerland on Tuesday.

Sports.title: Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
It isn’t quite over yet. Lionel Messi will return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.

Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.

Then Messi retired, distraught after a missing a penalty in the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision.

Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more.

This retirement will not be overturned. Messi is 39. Those who persuaded him to change his mind in 2016 were perhaps imagining – hoping for – six more years: they got 10. There will be no second thoughts this time. The rupture is real. No longer when things are going awry will Argentina be able to turn to the superhero in their midst and ask him to fix it.

The best example came almost at the end, when Argentina trailed Egypt 2-0 with 11 minutes of their World Cup last-16 tie remaining. Barcelona youth team coaches used to speak of the teenage Messi “getting the face on”, at which point he would be unstoppable. It happened in Atlanta: it was as though Messi simply decided that wasn’t going to be his last World Cup game. Argentina won without needing extra time.

Optimists will draw solace from the fact that Argentina’s best performance under Lionel Scaloni probably came in their 4-1 victory against Brazil in a World Cup qualifier in March 2025, when Messi did not play. Even allowing for the odd tactical choices of the opposing coach, Dorival Júnior, Argentina were exceptional. Leandro Paredes anchored a midfield as Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernández linked exhilaratingly with Rodrigo De Paul and Thiago Almada on the flanks and Julián Alvarez at centre-forward.

But football is not just about when things are going well. Even in the bleak times, the years of doubt under Edgardo Bauza and Jorge Sampaoli, when games were spiralling out of control, there was always the possibility Messi would put things right. But Argentina now have to deal with a future without that get-out potential.

The post-Messi future begins next week with games against Bolivia and Burkina Faso. Scaloni, has hinted he will sign a contract extension that would take him through to the 2028 Copa América with an option to the 2030 World Cup. That, at least, would provide a measure of stability, but there is little disguising the fact that a new cycle is beginning, just as Scaloni instituted a new era after the 2018 World Cup.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi cries at the end of the World Cup final after Argentina’s loss to Spain. Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

Other than Messi and Nicolás Otamendi, who are retiring after the Benin valediction, Scaloni named a 35-man squad. Of those, 20 were at the World Cup; given Paredes and Nahuel Molina are serving lengthy bans, that represents a remarkable degree of continuity, although Nicolás Tagliafico, at 34, is also understood to be considering his future. But 12 of the squad had played three internationals or fewer and De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso, who are in their thirties, will play only against Benin, giving the new cohort space to impress in the first two friendlies.

The biggest opportunities, at least in the short term, look to be at the back. Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez, both 28, look likely to be the first-choice central defensive pair, but Valentín Gómez of Real Betis and Tomás Palacios, on loan at Estudiantes from Inter, are competing to be back-up.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

With Molina suspended, Tagliafico ageing and Gonzalo Montiel injured, the real interest, though, is at full-back, where a pair of 22 year olds could stake a claim to be the future: Agustín Giay of Palmeiras and Román Vega of Zenit.

In Messi’s absence, there remains a question of formation. Although that Brazil game demonstrates what is possible through inter-movement even without a huge amount of overt creativity, it maybe that Scaloni opts for more traditional wingers. Again there are young options: Leonel Flores of Boca Juniors and Roma’s Matias Soulé are likely to make their debuts over the next few days.

And replacing Messi? That’s just not possible, either at a tactical level or, perhaps more significantly, in terms of what he meant for the spirit of the team. It’s not that Argentina need Messi to play well. Indeed, a purist could even argue that Argentina played better in that game that they ever could have played with Messi (or at least the pedestrian Messi of late), because of his lack of movement and the way the game had to be built around him.

That is always the danger with individualists, but Messi was so spectacularly consistent that the percentage option was to rely on his extraordinary genius, the true extraordinariness of which was how reliable it was.

No matter how well-organised an opposition defence, there was also the possibility – the probability even – that he would find an opening, no matter how badly things were going, there was always the chance he would get the face on and sort everything out single-handed.

Plenty of sides have found a new fluency, a more team-based dynamic, after a major star has moved on. Argentina’s ceiling could conceivably rise, but Messi offered a reassurance, a possibility of salvation, that will be sorely missed.

Sports.title: Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?
Sports.content:
What happens next?

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 134 disciplinary charges brought against them by the Premier League.

In keeping with the history of this case which has been conducted exclusively in private and with every party sworn to secrecy, there is a lot we don’t know. We do not even have an official confirmation that the three-person judicial panel has reached a verdict. All of football is acting as if they have, however, and that reports of a big win for the Premier League are correct.

If these assumptions are accurate, and neither party have formally denied them at least, then the immediate thing to watch out for is news of an appeal. Under Premier League rules, City would have 14 days from the announcement of the verdict to submit an appeal and the process that follows should be completed in less than 12 weeks from then. Once the appeal has been heard – which should happen in one block of no more than five days – and a verdict reached, the appeal panel are also expected to publish written reasons behind their decisions. We should also see the written reasons from the original judicial panel too, but the unique scale of this case has meant that normal procedures have not always been followed, and the date of publication for these reasons remains unknown.

If City do appeal, what happens?

The club would be submitting an appeal based solely on the decision and not any resulting punishment, which is yet to be determined. In hoping to make the case that the judicial panel were wrong in their observations, City would be allowed to submit new evidence, providing it had not been previously available to them, and make new oral presentations. Once the hearing is concluded, a verdict would be expected in 30 days.

If an appeal fails, what then?

According to Premier League rule W.97, “the decision of an Appeal Board shall be final”, but even this is subject to one final route, that of arbitration. This would mean appearing in front of another panel of eminent legal figures, but the criteria for any hearing would be a lot stricter and successful arbitration only possible in the main if the judicial panel or appeal board was found to have abused the legal process. City have recently been through the arbitration process with the Premier League over its rules related to associated party transactions and, after an initial verdict challenged two applications of the rules but otherwise found them to be sound, City and the Premier League reached a settlement which stopped the case from going to court.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

When and how would City be punished?

If City managed to overturn the verdict, there would of course be no sanction. If City’s appeals failed, there are a number of measures available to the panel. They start at fines and end at complete expulsion from the league, with a variety of sporting sanctions including point deductions falling in between. Given the magnitude of the verdict, City can expect to receive a punishment at the sharper end of the scale should any appeal not prove successful.

Could relegation be the end of it?

It seems unlikely. Premier League clubs and those who have been relegated from the division are understood to have been assessing any financial losses they may have incurred during the period City were winning and, appeal pending, breaking the rules. A wave of lawsuits is likely to follow, with Manchester United, for example, having finished second behind City in 2017-18 and potentially denied a record-breaking 21st league title in the process. It is possible that clubs who were relegated could argue that they were sent down because of points denied them by a City side subsequently found to have cheated. Premier League clubs reportedly lost their appetite for legal action after an estimated £50m cost to the competition last season, but if the verdict against City revealed this week is ultimately upheld, a new wave of lawsuits will surely follow.

Sports.title: Manchester City chair al-Mubarak insists ‘nothing has changed’ after guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the Manchester City chair, has spoken for the first time since the club was found guilty on virtually all counts of breaching Premier League financial rules. He said “nothing has changed” and “our confidence and intent in proving the club’s innocence is just as strong as when this began”.

News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied.

The club did not comment on the verdict until Saturday afternoon when al-Mubarak said on social media: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.

“We have some exciting moments to look forward to after this international break. We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family. Thank you, as always, for your constant support.”

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak (right) has been Manchester City’s chair since the Abu Dhabi takeover of the club from Thaksin Shinawatra (left) in 2008. Photograph: Nigel Roddis/Reuters

Earlier, City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, posted a cryptic message on social media reading “I know nothing”.

On Saturday morning, Maresca was approached for comment about whether he is seeking reassurance from the club on their continued stance of innocence. The Guardian was sent by his representatives a screenshot of a quote attributed to Socrates, the Greek philosopher, which Maresca posted on Instagram.

The quote reads: “The only thing I know is that I know nothing.” Maresca also wrote: “Time to breathe. Time to analyse. Time to learn.”

Elsewhere, there wwere contrasting reactions to the outcome of the Premier League investigation. Oasis’ Noel Gallagher, a longtime City fan, described his shock at the news, while the club’s former chair David Bernstein believes any potential punishment should not be only financial. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, described the case as unsettling.

On the Let Me Talk podcast, Gallagher said: “A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges.

“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really just quite sad. Sad for the fans and for the players.”

View image in fullscreen Noel Gallagher, a longtime Manchester City fan, maintains that even if the guilty verdict stands, the club’s fans will not feel any differently about their success. Photograph: Shaun Brooks/CameraSport/Getty Images

Asked if it changes the context of moments like Sergio Agüero’s title-winning goal in 2012, Gallagher said: “Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw.

“Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it’s nothing to do with the supporters or the players. The players won that game and won that title on the pitch. Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that’s nothing to do with the fans.

“Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt.”

Bernstein, City’s chair from 1998-2003, told Times Radio: “I felt absolutely awful, I felt in shock yesterday. You’ve asked me on the programme because of my time as chair of City and the FA, but basically I’m a fan of Manchester City and have been a fan for 70 years.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“When I was chair I think I helped get the club out of a very difficult period and started the road to better things. But to see all this tarnished in this way is very sad.

“I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who’ve stayed with the club through thick and thin. It’s a pretty bad day for the fans in blue of Manchester.”

As for the correct punishment, Bernstein said: “First of all, the timing is crucial. This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process has to be done quickly because you’ve got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it’s just not viable.

“The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, that would be a disaster. Not just for this particular case, but for English football generally.

“I can’t give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty. All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that.”

On BBC Radio 5 Live, Nandy said: “Most football fans will be feeling this is not a good moment for football as a whole and Manchester City fans will be feeling very anxious about what happens next. This is a really longstanding investigation, it dates all the way back to allegations that begin in 2009.

“The football fans need to know the rules are applied fairly and consistently, they need to know they’re upheld and they need to know the right decision has been reached.

“We do have a way to go with this, it’s very unsettling for football fans and I hope it can be resolved as swiftly as possible.”

Nigel Huddleston, who was the shadow secretary of state for culture until last month, said on social media: “Whatever the next steps are, they must be conducted in an accelerated and more transparent manner or risk further damage to the reputation and integrity of English football and more unnecessary anxiety for millions of football fans.”

A City spokesperson said on Friday: “The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality. As such Manchester City FC’s position remains consistent with the club’s statement of February 2023.” In that statement, City said they had a ‘comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence’ of their innocence.

Friday’s statement from City continued: “The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.”

Sports.title: We Manchester City fans fear relegation and losing trophies … but club are bang to rights
Sports.content:
It couldn’t have been more prophetic. In 2008, 15 years before Manchester City were charged with financial fraud, fans started singing “City’s going down with a billion in the bank” to the tune of Yellow Submarine. This was because the former Thailand president Thaksin Shinawatra’s 15-month ownership of City had come to an abrupt end when more than £1bn of his assets were frozen. And although Sheikh Mansour of the UAE had stepped in to save City, we were sinking fast.

Despite the UAE’s untold riches, by December we were in the relegation zone. It’s called Cityitis – shorthand for our tendency to self-destruct when things appear to be going well. In fact we won trophy after trophy. But we continued to sing the song about going down with a billion in the bank. When the financial fair play investigation was launched in 2018, the chant got louder. Then in 2023 we learned there were more than 100 charges. The chant became even louder and more cavalier. And now that our grubby, griftin’, cheatin’ chicken has come home to roost, you can bank on one thing (if banks still deal with us) – the chanting will be louder and more cavalier than ever.

After all, this is a club that believes schadenfreude starts at home. We brag about our failings. Other songs we sing include “Empty seats at home” (to the tune of the Beautiful South’s Rotterdam) because we can’t sell out our tickets and “Is This the Etihad?” (to La donna è mobile from Verdi’s Rigoletto, natch) at deathly quiet away grounds.

It’s not about tempting fate. Nor is it hubristic irony – we can’t sell out despite winning all these trophies. It’s simply an acceptance that one way or another we’ll always be City, always suffer from Cityitis, and come the day, despite our endless UAE riches, we’ll do a City.

And that day has come. We don’t know what our fate, or sentence, is yet. When I interviewed Wayne Rooney recently he suggested we would have 60 points docked, making it virtually impossible for us to avoid relegation.

It could be worse, of course. We could lose all eight trophies we won in the period (2009-10 to 2017-18) we flouted fair play, including three Premier League titles and our record-breaking centurions season when we won with 100 points in 2017-18. To me, that would be disproportionate and would in effect mean the Premier League eating itself.

But is the verdict itself unjust? City will say yes because they don’t want anything as petty as fair-play rules thwarting their bid for global domination. The lawyers will say yes because they’re paid to do so. Many fans will say yes because they’re fans. But some of us believe we’re bang to rights.

Everton and Nottingham Forest have been docked points for lesser offences, so it would be embarrassing if City had got away with it; an undeniable case of one rule for the rich. Despite City’s shocking attempts to legally filibuster the charges out of existence for the past three years, we’ve rightfully failed. Although it appears this is not the end because City intend to appeal.

View image in fullscreen The 2017-18 Premier League title may be one of eight trophies that Manchester City fear losing. Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty Images

Our behaviour has been pretty outrageous at Dodge City. Failing to provide accurate and up-to-date financial reports, concealing salary details and bonuses, inflating sponsorship revenues and failing to cooperate or supply requested documents during the investigation all feature on the charge sheet. We used lawyers to royally take the piss. And when it comes down to it, that is not very City. After all, this is a club founded in 1880 as St Mark’s (West Gorton) by members of St Mark’s Church of England for humanitarian and social rescue purposes to serve the deprived area of east Manchester, where Shameless was filmed a century later.

So what happens next? We may lose trophies. We will almost certainly get relegated. We almost certainly lose our best players and say ha det bra to Erling Haaland, the great Nordic God of goalscoring (having said that he may stay just to see how many he could get in a Championship season). And we start building again.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

If the very worst happens, and we lose all those trophies, at least we still have our anni mirabiles when we did the unprecedented domestic quadruple (2018-19), and treble including the Champions League (2022-23). There was barely a whiff of scandal in these years. We were simply obscenely wealthy, brilliantly run and managed by the world’s numero uno Pep Guardiola.

And plenty of positives will come out of our disgrace. The biggest being that justice is done. But there is so much more. City may get to play in the Championship where we enjoyed some of our finest moments (“We’ve got Kevin Keegan 100 goals a season,” sung to the tune of Let’s All Do the Conga a mere 24 years ago). League One? Halcyon days. For City fans of a certain age and disposition, beating Gillingham in the playoff is our top footballing memory. League Two? Thrill of the unknown. The only way is up, as the song goes.

Ticket prices come down, allowing regular civilians back into the Etihad. Prices become so low that we fill the ground. Fans begin to realise Wembley visits and winning trophies are to be treasured. Pep has already gone so there’s no danger of losing him. We learn some humility and stop coming over all sullen because we’ve only won the League Cup and FA Cup in one season.

Perhaps the biggest positive is that rather than simply pulling out the chequebook and signing the world’s best, we learn to think imaginatively. I noticed the God of Bermudan goalscoring Shaun Goater this year left his job coaching Aston Villa Women. He’s only 56, never relied entirely on pace, and I bet he’s a free agent.

Sports.title: Anthony Gordon makes bullish ‘coward’ claim after England slip up against Spain
Sports.content:
England's Anthony Gordon has claimed that he'd rather lose in the way England lost to Spain than in a 'cowardly' way.

The Three Lions kicked off their Nations League campaign with a 3-2 defeat on home soil, but it was an entertaining match.



4 England have now lost back-to-back competitive games Credit: Getty

It was the first time the Three Lions had played since that infamous World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina.

Gordon had put England 1-0 up, but as the game went on, Thomas Tuchel's side sat deeper and deeper with more and more defenders being thrown on.

In the end, they lost 2-1 and went out with a whimper.

It was another defeat for England, which came against the eventual winners of the tournament but Gordon was satisfied with the approach from the Three Lions for this game.



Asked if he felt England at least played without a fear of losing, Gordon told talkSPORT: "I don't think we did that at all, which I am very proud of. After the summer and all the controversy and everything people have spoken about.

"We lost a game against the best team in the world. It was 3-2. It was very entertaining, and I would rather lose this way.



"I would rather lose through a mistake than retreating. I don't want to feel like a coward on the pitch.

"I don't feel like a coward tonight. I feel proud of our performance. We just lost the game.



"But we didn't retreat, we went for it."

Gordon's comments were subsequently put to England boss Thomas Tuchel, and he responded: "I don't really know what that means… in the end, we have to say we made too many mistakes and were not clinical enough in the decisive moments. But we played our way and it worked in phases of the game."

4 Gordon has now got five England goals and is locking down that left wing spot Credit: Getty

What did Gordon mean?

Gordon was directly referencing the defeat to Argentina in the World Cup, a game for which Tuchel has received heavy criticism for his tactics and changes.

But it was different at Wembley on Saturday evening, with Gordon outlining his pride at England going after the world and European champions.



He added: "I feel like we did everything people wanted us to do, and what we've asked of ourselves.

"Plenty of positives. I felt like we went for the throat, and at 2-1, we get the penalty, but that was a massive momentum shift.

"Ultimately, if you make the mistakes we did when playing out, a team like that are always going to punish you.

"I felt like they were on the back foot, and we really went for them.

4 Harry Kane's missed penalty was his first for England since the 2022 World Cup quarter-final against France Credit: Getty



"H [Kane] is probably the best penalty taker in football, and he slips, so you have to take that on the chin.

"And at 3-2, it's so hard to get the ball back off them. They are the best in the world at controlling possession when they have a lead."

What happened in the game?

Spain arrived at Wembley having only conceded one goal across the whole World Cup.

And it took just 95 seconds for them to gain the lead as Marc Guehi twisted and turned himself into knots, allowing Lamine Yamal to pinch his pocket and find the net via the far post.



Spain could have been 3-0 up as Ferran Torres missed a one-on-on and saw James Trafford make a good save to deny him before England equalised.

It came via a rapid counter-attack, starting with Elliot Anderson playing a pass into Gordon, who delicately flicked it around the corner for Jude Bellingham.

4 Kane's missed penalty swung the momentum of the game and England couldn't regain control Credit: Getty

Bellingham returned the favour and played Gordon in on goal, and he fired it under Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon.



The game was turned around moments later as Nico O'Reilly crossed for Harry Kane and his header looked easy for Simon to deal with.

Marc Cucurella raised his thigh, and the ball diverted into the net off his leg to leave England in the lead at half time.

The hosts started the second half brilliantly and won a penalty as Rodri tripped Bellingham in the box.

Kane stepped up, slipped, double touched the ball, and it hit the crossbar.



Spain made it 2-2 shortly after O'Reilly lost possession at left-back, regained it, and then passed the ball straight to Dani Olmo.

He couldn't believe his luck as he rolled a pass to Alex Baena on the edge of the area, who curled home.

And Mikel Oyarzabal scored the winner following a delightful move that saw Baena slip a pass into the striker, who chipped Trafford to seal the win.

England piled the pressure on at the end but created no further clear chances.
