Local suppliers will have opportunities to provide goods and services to manufacturers, logistics operators, construction companies and other businesses within the corridor. If properly integrated into emerging value chains, Ogun’s SMEs could become suppliers and producers within the new economic ecosystem.

The fourth is agricultural transformation.

Ogun has a substantial agricultural base, but production alone does not guarantee prosperity. The real opportunity comes when agricultural commodities are processed, packaged, stored and exported competitively. The Blue Marine Special Economic Zone could provide the industrial and logistics platform for moving agricultural production further up the value chain, creating greater income for farmers and businesses while reducing the export of raw commodities without value addition.

The fifth is logistics and supply-chain development.

The port, the Blue Marine Special Economic Zone, the Gateway International Airport, dry ports and the coastal highway can collectively create a multimodal transportation network. Rather than isolated infrastructure projects, they can operate as interconnected economic assets, allowing goods, people, raw materials and finished products to move more efficiently.

The proposed 28-kilometre Ogun section of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway is particularly important in this regard. President Tinubu described the highway as central to the commercial viability of the emerging corridor, linking the port and industrial zone with Lagos, the Nigerian hinterland and wider African markets.

There is also a fiscal multiplier.

As more businesses establish operations, the economic base from which government derives revenue expands. Increased commercial activity means greater demand for property, transportation, professional services, hospitality and other economic activities. Over time, this can translate into a broader and more diversified revenue base for Ogun.

The project could equally deepen Ogun’s position as an industrial gateway.

The state already possesses a concentration of manufacturing and industrial activities and sits within close proximity to Lagos. The addition of a major deep-sea port and a large integrated economic zone could strengthen that advantage by giving industries located in Ogun more direct access to international shipping and export markets.

But perhaps the most consequential implication is maritime.

For decades, Nigeria has possessed an enormous coastline, a large consumer market and a strategic geographical position along the Gulf of Guinea, yet it has not fully translated these advantages into the kind of maritime dominance its size and economic potential should command.

The Gateway Deep Sea Port could help change that equation.

If successfully developed alongside the Blue Marine Special Economic Zone and the supporting road, rail, airport and logistics infrastructure, Ogun could provide Nigeria with a new maritime gateway capable of attracting larger vessels, facilitating regional trade and connecting Nigerian production more efficiently to international markets.

In doing so, Nigeria could once again—and this time decisively—occupy its pride of place as the maritime hub of the West African subregion.

The ambition should not be limited to serving Nigerian cargo. A truly competitive port can attract transit cargo, regional distribution, trans-shipment and logistics activities from across the subregion. That means Nigeria can move from merely being a large market at the end of global supply chains to becoming a strategic node through which goods move into and out of West Africa.

The economic consequences could be profound.

A stronger maritime ecosystem would stimulate demand for shipping, freight forwarding, warehousing, ship-related services, insurance, finance, customs services, logistics technology, maritime training and a broad range of ancillary businesses. It could also strengthen Nigeria’s capacity to compete for regional trade currently routed through other West African ports.

This is where the Ogun project takes on a significance beyond the boundaries of the state.

Nigeria has long faced the challenge of moving from an economy that exports substantial volumes of raw commodities to one that exports more finished and semi-finished products. An integrated port and industrial zone directly addresses that challenge by creating infrastructure around which production and export can take place.

It can also strengthen Nigeria’s position within the African Continental Free Trade Area by providing a competitive platform for Nigerian manufacturers to produce at scale and reach markets across Africa.

This is why President Tinubu described the initiative as economic diversification and industrialisation made tangible.

For Ogun, however, the story is also about the evolution of the state’s economic identity.

The state has spent years building the infrastructure and investment environment necessary to consolidate its position as Nigeria’s industrial hub. The emerging coastal corridor adds another dimension to that strategy: linking industrial production inland with maritime trade on the coast.

Governor Dapo Abiodun has consistently presented the deep seaport not as a standalone project but as part of a wider multimodal economic vision involving the Gateway International Airport, dry ports, the coastal highway and the Blue Marine Special Economic Zone.

His reference to DP World’s Jebel Ali Free Zone is instructive. The objective is not simply to have ships berth at Ogun’s coastline, but to create an ecosystem in which cargo arriving at the port feeds production, processing, logistics and exports within the wider economy.

The journey to this point, as Abiodun acknowledged in Paris, has involved sustained collaboration among political leadership, government institutions, investors, technical advisers and the host communities.

The governor specifically acknowledged President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for providing the political leadership that helped revive a deep-seaport vision that had remained largely unrealised for more than three decades. He also recognised the contributions of the Minister of Marine and Blue Economy, Adegboyega Oyetola, the Nigerian Ports Authority and other federal institutions for their support.

Abiodun also acknowledged the strategic contributions of DP World, SkyCapital, Supo Sasore Projects and the ALP team, whose investment, advisory, project-development and technical inputs have contributed to advancing the initiative. Equally important, he recognised the host communities, whose cooperation and partnership remain critical to the successful development of the port and the wider Blue Marine economic corridor.

President Tinubu, in turn, commended Governor Abiodun and the Ogun State Government for securing the land, structuring the investment framework and reducing project risks for global investors. He also acknowledged DP World, SkyCapital, financial advisers and other investors and partners whose commitment helped bring the agreements to the signing stage.

That convergence of federal leadership, state initiative, private capital, technical expertise and community partnership is perhaps one of the most important features of the project.

Tinubu described it as “cooperative federalism”—a model in which a subnational government develops a strategic economic vision while the Federal Government provides the institutional, regulatory and infrastructure support required to make that vision investable.

And that may ultimately prove to be as important as the port itself.

Because the real test of the Paris agreements will not be the elegance of the documents or the ceremony surrounding their signing. It will be whether the agreements translate into construction, industries, jobs, exports, businesses, stronger supply chains and measurable improvements in the lives of people.

Governor Abiodun captured that challenge in his own words: “History will judge us not by the elegance of documents signed, but by the transformation that follows. Ceremonies proclaim intentions; only implementation creates prosperity.”

That is the real significance of the Ogun-DP World partnership.

The deep seaport can move cargo. The Blue Marine Special Economic Zone can create the productive capacity to transform that cargo into economic value. The coastal highway can provide connectivity. The airport and dry ports can widen the logistics network. Manufacturers can create products. Farmers can feed processing industries. SMEs can supply emerging value chains. Young people can find new employment opportunities. And exports can travel from Ogun to Nigeria, Africa and the wider world.

If successfully implemented, the initiative could therefore become more than another major infrastructure project.

It could represent a shift from infrastructure as an end in itself to infrastructure as an engine of production, investment and wealth creation.

For Ogun State, that is the game-changing opportunity.

For Nigeria, it is the possibility of turning a coastline into an economic corridor, a port into an industrial gateway and an investment agreement into a broader platform for diversification, export growth and sustainable economic expansion.

More importantly, it offers Nigeria the opportunity to reclaim a strategic position that its size, location and economic potential have long suggested it should occupy: the maritime and logistics hub of West Africa, with Ogun serving as one of the principal engines of that ambition.

The signatures were made in Paris.

The real story—and the real economic transformation—will unfold in Ogun.

*Akinmade is the Special Adviser to Ogun State Governor on Information and Strategy

World.title: 2027: Umahi says Wike’s Rainbow Coalition not in Ebonyi
World.content:
Minister of Works David Umahi has rejected claims that the Rainbow Coalition Movement was plotting to wrestle power from Governor Francis Nwifuru of Ebonyi State, saying the movement does not exist in the state.

Mr Umahi, the immediate past governor of Ebonyi State, spoke during an inspection of the Calabar-Abuja Superhighway in Benue State on Friday.

A video clip which showed the minister making the remarks has been circulating on Facebook.

Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT) Nyesom Wike runs the Rainbow Coalition, a multi-party political arrangement, to support President Bola Tinubu’s 2027 re-election bid.

Mr Umahi’s comment follows controversies and disagreement between Mr Wike and some members of the All Progressives (APC), particularly Nigerian governors under the party’s platform over the coalition.

Mr Wike has said the coalition will back candidates of his party, the People Democratic Party (PDP) for other elective positions whilst supporting APC’s Mr Tinubu re-election as president in 2027.

The FCT minister is officially a national leader of the PDP faction recognised by the court and the Independent National Electoral Commission.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

However, he works in the administration of Mr Tinubu, who is a member of the ruling APC.

He has continued to openly express support for the re-election of the president in 2027.

‘No Rainbow Coalition in Ebonyi’

But reacting, Mr Umahi, also a member of the ruling APC, said he was unaware if Mr Wike has a governorship candidate in Ebonyi State.

“Wike is my good friend and brother, (but) there is no (Rainbow) Coalition in Ebonyi State. There is none. And if Wike has (a governorship) candidate here, he has not told me.”

“And his candidates cannot break our relationship. But his candidate is not part of our relationship,” he said.

The works minister, who exited PDP in 2020, jokingly said he did not know that the PDP was still in existence in Ebonyi State.

“I killed PDP when I left PDP. Whether they are alive again, (I don’t know). And if they are alive, we have to unalive them because PDP did not treat the people of South-east well.

“We supported the PDP. We voted for presidents in the PDP. when it was our time for them to, you know, honour us (with presidential ticket), they did not honour us. We have hope in APC,” he said.

‘We’ll fight’

Mr Umahi said his position and that of Governor Nwifuru is that opposition candidates and politicians are free to campaign in Ebonyi State without causing “troubles.”

“But if you think you can foment (a) crisis, we will run you out of the state. Nobody can foment crisis in Ebonyi State.

“Anybody that wants to campaign, come and campaign. But don’t dish out hate speeches. And you want to dish out hate speeches and you want us to make a red carpet for you. We will not do that. And If you want (to) fight, we will fight,” he said.

‘Nwifuru, Tinubu’s second term bids guaranteed’

Mr Umahi then boasted that there are no threats against the victory of Mr Nwifuru and President Tinubu in Ebonyi State in 2027.

“I don’t think we have any threat either for the president or for the governor or for any of the APC candidates in this Ebony State.

“I fought the battle alone before. Today, I have the governor. He has me. And there are so many leaders that are with us. So there is nothing to fear (other) than to calculate our votes ahead of time,” the minister claimed.

“If we win 95 percent (of votes), that will be our dream come true.”

Background

Messrs Wike and Nwifuru appeared to be fighting cold war in June this year when the Ebonyi governor threatened to “consume” the FCT minister if he dared to challenge him in the south-eastern state ahead of the state’s governorship election in 2027.

The governor’s outburst followed claims by Mr Wike’s unnamed allies that Mr Tinubu had handed over Ebonyi to the FCT minister and his PDP faction.

In recent times, the friction between Mr Wike and APC governors has also heightened tension and fears that the FCT minister might use the Rainbow Coalition Movement against the governors in the 2027 elections.

World.title: Nigeria demands fairer pandemic financing, vaccine access at UN meeting
World.content:
Nigeria has called for a more equitable global pandemic preparedness system, urging increased financing, technology transfer and stronger manufacturing capacity in Africa to enable developing countries to respond effectively to future health emergencies.

The Minister of State for Health and Social Welfare, Iziaq Salako, made the call while delivering Nigeria’s national statement on behalf of President Bola Tinubu at a high-level meeting on Pandemic Prevention, Preparedness and Response (PPPR) at the United Nations Headquarters in New York.

The meeting was held on the sidelines of the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Mr Salako said effective pandemic preparedness must begin with strong public health systems capable of preventing, detecting and responding to health threats before they become emergencies.

“Prevention is preparedness and the strength of everyday public health systems determines how effectively nations detect threats early, respond rapidly, and maintain essential services during crises,” he said.

He said Nigeria was strengthening its legal and institutional frameworks, expanding digital disease surveillance, institutionalising the 7-1-7 approach, enhancing genomic sequencing capacity and improving multi-hazard preparedness.

The 7-1-7 approach requires countries to aim to detect a suspected public health threat within seven days, notify the relevant authorities within one day and complete the initial response within seven days.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Greater equity

Mr Salako said equity must remain central to the global PPPR agenda, particularly in ensuring that countries that provide access to pathogens receive fair and timely benefits from the development of vaccines, diagnostics and therapeutics.

He called for sustainable and rapidly accessible financing for low- and middle-income countries, alongside technology transfer and stronger domestic manufacturing capacity, particularly in Africa.

Nigeria’s priorities, he said, include stronger national ownership, governance and legal preparedness; prevention-focused health systems; integrated and resilient One Health systems; equitable access to financing and African manufacturing; and greater regional and global solidarity and accountability.

“National ownership and global solidarity must advance together,” he said.

Mr Salako said Nigeria was also advancing the One Health approach, strengthening antimicrobial resistance (AMR) governance and infection prevention and control programmes, and expanding emergency workforce capacity at national and sub-national levels.

The country’s public health laboratory network now covers all 36 states, while Public Health Emergency Operations Centres support responses to outbreaks including Lassa fever, cholera, diphtheria and meningitis, he said.

Nigeria’s Joint External Evaluation score also improved from 39 per cent in 2017 to 54 per cent in 2023.

In addition, the World Bank’s $250 million Health Security Programme is supporting health security capacity at federal and state levels under a One Health approach, Mr Salako said.

Nigeria to host global AMR meeting

Mr Salako said Nigeria also wanted antimicrobial resistance to remain firmly embedded in the global pandemic preparedness agenda, describing it as “both a current public health threat and a multiplier of pandemic risks”.

Against this background, he announced that Nigeria would host the fifth Global High-Level Ministerial Conference on Antimicrobial Resistance in December 2026.

The conference will be the first edition to be held in Africa and will provide an opportunity to accelerate measurable One Health action and advance the priorities of low- and middle-income countries, he said.

Mr Salako also stressed the importance of involving communities in pandemic preparedness, saying public trust could not be built only after an outbreak had begun.

He called for sustained investment in risk communication and community engagement, social listening, community hygiene and infodemic management between emergencies.

He said Nigeria remained committed to strengthening national and regional capacity to prevent, detect and respond to public health threats, while supporting a global pandemic preparedness framework that is equitable, sustainable and accountable.

World.title: We are building strong foundations for agricultural transformation in Jigawa – Namadi
World.content:
Jigawa State Governor, Umar Namadi has said his administration is laying strong and sustainable foundations for the transformation of agriculture into a productive, technology-driven, and commercially viable sector capable of improving livelihoods and creating opportunities for the people.

The governor stated this on Friday during the formal launch of the Nigeria AgriConnect initiative and the CGIAR System Board Dinner held at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), Ibadan, where he reflected on Jigawa State’s agricultural transformation and its growing partnership with IITA.

According to him, the state’s agriculture-first strategy under the 12-Point Agenda for Greater Jigawa is already translating into concrete investments and institutional reforms aimed at increasing productivity, strengthening value chains, and making agriculture more resilient and profitable.

“Jigawa is a leading producer of rice, wheat, and sesame. We are expanding irrigation and dry-season farming, strengthening extension services, and extending mobile veterinary services across all 287 wards,” he said.

He further said that the state had also established the Agricultural Transformation Agency and the Ministry of Livestock Development to provide focused leadership, coordination, and accountability in driving agricultural development.

Namadi said the administration’s investments were deliberately designed to address critical constraints to agricultural productivity, including access to mechanization, extension services, entrepreneurship, research, and innovation.

He disclosed that the state had established 60 mechanization centers, supported by 400 tractors and 60 combine harvesters, while the number of agricultural extension agents had grown to nearly 2,000.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The governor further revealed that Jigawa had entered into a partnership for an agribusiness incubation programme aimed at developing 10,000 entrepreneurs and supporting the emergence of at least 500 new small and medium-sized enterprises.

He said the initiative was part of the administration’s broader effort to move agriculture beyond subsistence production by connecting farmers with technology, finance, processing, markets, and viable business opportunities.

Namadi also explained the transformation of the Jigawa State Agricultural Research Institute, saying the institution was being repositioned to ensure that agricultural research more effectively responds to practical challenges facing farmers and the wider agricultural sector.

He said the research focus covers critical areas including seed systems, soil fertility, irrigation, livestock productivity, post-harvest management, and agro-processing, while targeted research scholarships and specialist training, including MSc and PhD programmes, are strengthening the human capacity required to sustain the transformation.

The governor said the investments were being complemented by the state’s partnership with IITA, which provides a platform for applying science, research, and innovation to the specific agricultural challenges and opportunities in Jigawa.

He stated that the partnership focuses, among other areas, on improved varieties of maize, soybean, and cassava; soil health and mapping; stronger seed systems; pest and disease management; competitive value chains; and youth-led agribusiness.

“What excites us most is the opportunity to connect IITA’s science and innovation with Jigawa’s land, farmers, institutions, and entrepreneurial energy,” the governor said.

He stressed that the ultimate objective was to ensure that research reaches farmers, improved technologies raise productivity, increased production connects to processing and markets, and agriculture generates viable businesses and decent employment for young people.

The governor said Jigawa State remained committed to working with IITA, CGIAR, the Federal Government, development partners, financial institutions, and investors to translate knowledge and innovation into measurable improvements in agricultural productivity and livelihoods.

He noted that the success of the partnership would ultimately be measured by improved yields, healthier soils, reliable seed systems, reduced post-harvest losses, stronger value chains, thriving agribusinesses, higher farm incomes, and improved access to nutritious food.

He invited the leadership of the CGIAR System Board and other partners to visit Jigawa State to see firsthand the transformation taking place in the agricultural sector.

“Together, let us demonstrate what becomes possible when science, government, farmers, young people, and markets work as one,” he said.

World.title: Court dismisses suit seeking fresh investigation into Mohbad’s death
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja has thrown out a suit by a non-governmental organisation (NGO), Registered Trustees of Break the Silence Foundation, seeking to compel the police to reopen investigations into the death of Afrobeats singer Ilerioluwa “Mohbad” Aloba.

PREMIUM TIMES gathered that the suit listed the Inspector-General of Police (IGP), the Nigeria Police Force and the Commissioner of Police, Lagos State Command, as respondents.

Justice James Omotosho dismissed the application after finding that the foundation had not shown sufficient legal interest in the matter to warrant its joinder.

He granted the organisation leave to commence the proceedings through an ex parte application seeking judicial review and an order of mandamus to compel the police to carry out a fresh investigation into Mr Aloba’s death.

Ruling

Delivering judgment in the suit, which was earlier postponed after none of the respondents appeared in court when the matter was called, Justice Omotosho held that the applicant lacked the legal right to institute the case, Leadership newspaper reported on Friday.

He further described the suit as meritless and maintained that the court would not entertain claims based solely on speculation without concrete evidence.

“This suit is therefore without credible evidence and thus without merit. I must say here that lawyers are bound to know the elementary principle of law and not flood the courts with frivolous and baseless cases which take the precious time of the court, which should be reserved for serious matters”, Justice Omotosho said in his ruling.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The judge said the group provided no copy of the initial police report to demonstrate that the earlier investigation was inadequate.

Report

Additionally, the judge said the NGO did not provide the initial investigation report needed to assess the propriety of the probe, despite its argument that the police had earlier investigated the matter without conducting a comprehensive investigation.

“The applicant stated that the police had earlier investigated the matter, but that the police did not investigate the same well, as some relatives of the deceased were not investigated. Hence, the applicant seeks a reinvestigation of the matter.

“Now the applicant did not attach the investigation report of the first investigation to conclude that those persons it mentioned, such as the wife and the father of the deceased, were indeed not investigated.”

The judge noted that the applicant failed to place the investigation report before the court, leaving nothing to establish whether the persons concerned underwent any investigation.

Justice Omotosho said the omission weakened the applicant’s case, as the claim amounted to speculation and conjecture without documentary evidence.

He maintained that mere assertions could not suffice, adding that an allegation unsupported by evidence could not justify the relief being sought.

Caution

Justice Omotosho warned counsel involved in the matter to refrain from speaking publicly about the proceedings, including through media interviews and social media posts.

He said any lawyer who disregards the court’s directive by discussing the case publicly could face contempt proceedings.

The “KPK” hitmaker died on 12 September 2023 and was buried the following day. Nine days later, his remains were exhumed and taken for an autopsy as part of efforts to determine what caused his death.

Three years after his death, several questions surrounding his death remain unresolved, including the paternity of his son, Liam, and the ownership of his properties, among others.

The lingering controversies also contributed to his father, Joseph Aloba’s decision not to proceed with his son’s final burial.

Mr Aloba has repeatedly demanded justice and answers over the circumstances surrounding his son’s death.

World.title: Five killed at Plateau mining site as soldiers rescue district head
World.content:
At least five miners were killed and two others injured when gunmen attacked a mining site in Marit village, Barkin Ladi Local Government Area of Plateau State, on Saturday, according to community sources.

The attack came amid renewed tension in parts of the state, with troops also rescuing a district head who was reportedly attacked by youths in Jos East Local Government Area following the killing of a resident at an illegal mining site.

Rwang Tengwong, spokesperson for the Berom Youth Moulders-Association (BYM), confirmed the Marit attack in a statement on Saturday.

“Five persons were killed while two others sustained injuries in the attack,” Mr Tengwong said, describing the incident as a painful development for communities that have repeatedly suffered violence.

He called on security agencies to strengthen their presence in affected communities and prevent further attacks.

A resident, Simon Mundat, also confirmed the deaths and appealed to the authorities to improve security in the area.

The police and the Nigerian Army had yet to respond to requests for confirmation of the Marit attack at the time of filing this report.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

District head rescued

Meanwhile, soldiers rescued Musa Usman, the district head of Fursum in Jos East Local Government Area, after youths reportedly attacked his residence in Ninseng community.

According to security sources cited by counter-insurgency publication, Zagazola Makama, the incident occurred at about 1:45 p.m. on Friday.

The youths allegedly accused Mr Usman of supporting Fulani residents.

Mr Usman reportedly sustained injuries and was evacuated to the Jos University Teaching Hospital (JUTH) for treatment.

His vehicle was also reportedly set ablaze during the attack.

The incident was said to have followed the killing of a resident at an illegal mining site in Nabar Dutse community.

Troops from Sector 1, Sub-Sector 12, reportedly intervened after receiving a distress call, brought the situation under control and secured the area against further violence and possible reprisals.

The two incidents occurred as Plateau continues to grapple with renewed attacks and communal tensions in several parts of the state.

Earlier, security operatives, supported by local hunters, reportedly repelled an attack on Latok in Qua’an-Pan Local Government Area.

A community member, Danat Noel, said the operatives engaged the attackers and forced them to withdraw.

The latest attacks come days after the state government imposed a dusk-to-dawn curfew on three local government areas, including Barkin Ladi, following a series of attacks and killings.

The state Commissioner for Information, Joyce Ramnap, had urged residents to remain calm and law-abiding while security agencies worked to restore peace.

The recurrence of violence around mining locations has also raised fresh concerns over the security of mining communities and the activities of illegal miners in the state.

World.title: The diplomacy of politics: The eighty-first UNGA and impunity, By Owei Lakemfa
World.content:
The United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) is the global platform for all countries. So, no country can bar another speaking from its podium.

But the United States (US) at the on-going UNGA decided that the voice of the Palestinian State will not be heard. Only that of the State of Israel would be permitted. It therefore denied Palestinian Authority (PA), President Mahmoud Abbas an entry visa into the US, effectively barring a Head of State from attending UNGA.

The US decided to illegally bar the Palestinian state from UNGA for having the nerve to take legal actions against Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and the International Criminal Court (ICC). The Palestinian Case at these courts challenge the legality of Israel’s occupation of Gaza and the West Bank; its settlement policies under which Palestinian lands are stolen and given out to illegal Israeli settlers, and gross violations of international treaties and humanitarian law.

A second reason US gave is that the PA rather than abandon its citizens convicted by the opaque Israeli courts, continues to provide financial stipends to their families. To the US, this amounts to the PA glorifying or supporting terrorism.

The ICC in investigating war crimes and crimes against humanity perpetuated by the Israeli regime against the Palestinian people, had on 21 November, 2024 issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the its former Minister of Defence, Yoav Gallant. So, essentially, the US is sitting on appeal against the ICC decision and is in a retaliatory mode against the Palestinians.

But the US action in denying President Abass and the Palestinian delegation visa to attend UNGA, is a gross violation of the UN-USA Headquarters Agreement signed on 26 June, 1947, and approved by UNGA on 31 October, 1947. The Agreement signed by then UN Secretary-General Trygve LIE and, former US Secretary of State George C Marshall, provides under Article IV Sections 11, 12, and 13 that regardless of bilateral relations, the US would issue visas to State delegations and UN representatives promptly and without charge.

It provides under Section 11 that: “The federal, state or local authorities of the United States shall not impose any impediments to transit to or from the headquarters district…” for these officials.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Sections 12 and 13 further stated that: “The provisions of Section 11 shall be applicable irrespective of the relations existing between the Governments of the persons referred to in that section and the Government of the United States.” “Laws and regulations in force in the United States regarding the entry of aliens shall not be applied in such manner as to interfere with the privileges referred to in Section 11. When visas are required for persons referred to in that section, they shall be granted without charge and as promptly as possible.”

For UNGA, this was not the time to discuss the US violating the Agreement or, hear demands that the UN headquarters be moved to a more receptive country. What was important was to hear him. It was therefore proposed that Abass should be heard via video link.

But even this, irked the US which staked his reputation by urging UNGA not to accept this minimum compromise. US Deputy Ambassador to the UN Tammy Bruce argued that: “If the PA wants to be treated as a partner, it must stop subsidizing terror and stop using diplomatic theater as a substitute for serious governance.” The American representative added: “We will not relent on our insistence that the Palestinian Authority and the PLO [Palestine Liberation Organisation] completely and unequivocally renounce terrorism. They have not yet done so.”

The matter was put to vote and 152 countries voted for the resolution while only three countries voted for the US position. These were Paraguay, the US itself and its partner, Israel. Four abstained; Panama, Honduras, Peru and Colombia.

Thus, the world sat and listened to the Palestinian leader who described the Israeli war in the Palestine as genocide and urged humanity to act and, not fold its arms. He demanded that the Israeli attacks and military occupation of the Palestine be brought to an end. Abass posited that a permanent solution should be effected whereby the Israelis and Palestinians would live in their various countries with guaranteed security and, in peace.

In contrast to the treatment meted out to President Abass, US welcomed Prime Minister Netanyahu. But UNGA did not welcome him. When he began to speak, 77 Delegations walked out rather than listen to a man who has an international warrant of arrest hanging round his neck. He had no choice but to address a virtually empty hall.

But he is not a man capable of reading a simple situation. Rather than present his country’s case, he ranted how Israel and its allies have been eliminating people and destroying countries: “Half the Houthi leadership in Yemen – gone. Yahya Sinwar in Gaza – gone. Hassan Nasrallah in Lebanon – gone. The Assad regime in Syria – gone. Those Militias in Iraq? Well, they’re still deterred. And their leaders, if they attack Israel, will also be gone. And for Iran’s top military commanders and its top nuclear scientists… Well, they’re gone too.”

When President Trump arrived the UN Headquarters on Tuesday, 22 September, it was like a theatre. He had banned the CNN from the White House and might have been oblivious of the fact that the UN is not US territory, so his ban had no effect there.

He told the news channel: “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me. You should not be here covering me. You said you weren’t going to cover me” CNN reporter Kaitlan Collins replied: “The United Nations allowed us in, sir.” The response was clear; Trump did not call the shots in the UN.

Playing God, Trump told UNGA about his assumed choices on Iran: “Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before? Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic?…. Do I drive them into hell with no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness or generations?”

But Iran is no country to bully or, backdown. Its President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country will fight to its last breath: “The United States president described us as terrorists. We have been the victims of terrorism,” “Are we the sources of instability? We only seek to live independently,” “We are the ones who cause instability? Those who are committing terrorism and committing crimes, are they the protectors of peace and stability?”

On the side lines, the US and Iran held a three-hour meeting. Perhaps it is an admission that impunity and bullying will ultimately, not pay.

Owei Lakemfa, a former secretary general of African workers, is a human rights activist, journalist and author.

World.title: Soludo’s wife reacts to Peter Obi’s godfather claims
World.content:
Nonye Soludo, wife of Governor Charles Soludo of Anambra State, has refuted claims by Peter Obi that he and his wife are godparents to Mr Soludo’s children.

PREMIUM TIMES earlier reported that Mr Obi, the presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), claimed on Friday that he and his wife are godparents to the Anambra governor’s children.

“People might not know. My wife and I are godparents to Soludo’s children.

“We are that close. We are not quarrelling. I will never quarrel with him. If I see him anyday, he and I will hug. If they say anything, I’ll answer them,” he said when he spoke as a guest at the Nigerian Guild of Editors’ 22nd Conference in Enugu on Friday.

Mr Obi’s comment came amid debt debate between him and Mr Soludo’s administration.

The former governor did not say how many of Mr Soludo’s children they serve as godparents to.

PREMIUM TIMES reports that Mr Soludo has four daughters and two sons.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A godparent is someone who serves as a witness at a child’s baptism.

Children’s godparents are usually chosen by their biological parents, often because of existing close relationships between the two families.

‘It’s false’

Reacting in a statement on Saturday by her media aide Dan Ezeigwe, Mrs Soludo described Mr Obi’s claim as “false.”

The Anambra first lady stressed that the clarification became necessary after the family received several calls from people who wanted to know the true position.

“Mr Peter Obi is not a godfather to any of the children of Professor Chukwuma and Nonye Soludo,” she said.

“We urge members of the public, the media and all concerned to take note of this clarification and disregard any impression created by the statement that Mr. Peter Obi is godfather to any of Governor Soludo’s children,” she added.

Mrs Soludo stressed that she is a “confirmation godmother” to Mr Obi’s daughter while Mr Obi’s wife, Margaret Obi, is “the baptismal godmother” to one of Mr Soludo’s daughters.

The first lady’s submission means that only Mr Obi’s wife is a godparent to one of Mr Soludo’s daughters.

“Neither Mr Obi nor Professor Soludo has served as a godparent to the other’s children,” she maintained.

Background

Messrs Obi and Mr Soludo have been engaged in a war of words in recent years.

The face-off between the two politicians took a fresh twist in early September when the Commissioner for Finance in the state, Izuchukwu Okafor, claimed that Governor Soludo’s administration was still repaying loans and other debts incurred by Mr Obi and other past governors of the state.

Responding to the claim in a now-viral clip, Mr Obi said he was not owing any debt in Anambra when he left office as governor of the state.

The NDC candidate subsequently reiterated that he did not incur any debt as governor but rather saved over N75 billion in the state’s account.

In response, the Anambra government released loan records arguing that Mr Obi’s administration took eight external loans worth $123.7 million, with $92.35 million outstanding.

On Thursday, Mr Obi again reiterated that he left over $150 million in savings for Anambra State Government when he exited office as governor in 2014.

World.title: Mad rush into deadly pits for gold: 374 illegal mining sites in 17 states uncovered
World.content:
•Reports say 156 dead

•NASS C’ttee: This is a sophisticated national threat…with implications for security, revenue generation

•How it fuels child labour

By Shina Abubakar, Femi Bolaji, Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo, Golok Nanmwa, Jeff Agbodo, James Ogunnaike and Deola Badru

Illegal mining, an economic and environmental offence, has assumed a more troubling dimension in Nigeria, with security agencies, regulators and community leaders increasingly warning that the illicit exploitation of the country’s mineral resources is becoming a national security concern.

In parts of the North-West and North-Central, the activity has intersected with banditry, kidnapping and other forms of organised crime, while in other parts of the country, it is fuelling conflicts over land, destroying farmlands and forests, polluting water sources and leaving behind dangerous mining pits.

Recently, the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps, NSCDC, which has responsibility for the Mining Marshals, described illegal mining as a major national security threat, saying the problem had gone beyond an economic crime and required intelligence-driven and coordinated enforcement.

Concern

The concern has also reached the National Assembly, with the House of Representatives Committee on Mineral Exploitation, Security and Anti-Money Laundering describing illegal mining as a “sophisticated national threat” with far-reaching implications for security, revenue generation, environmental sustainability and governance.

Concerned by the situation, the Federal Government responded with a combination of enforcement, prosecution and attempts to formalise artisanal mining.

However, concerns remain over the effectiveness of these measures.

Accordingly, Mining Marshals, established under the NSCDC, have been deployed across the country to identify and shut illegal sites, arrest suspects and protect licensed mining areas.

Last month, the Minister of Solid Minerals Development, Dele Alake, said the Mining Marshals had identified 374 illegal mining sites, cleared 108, arrested 743 suspects and prosecuted 165 cases involving 430 accused persons, with five convictions secured.

Operations

Also, NSCDC reported hundreds of arrests and the shutdown of numerous illegal sites, insisting that its operations are increasingly based on intelligence gathering and collaboration with other security and regulatory agencies.

But the actors behind the illicit trade are not limited to rural miners who wield shovels and pickaxes at the sites.

Checks by Sunday Vanguard showed a multilayered chain involving artisanal miners, labourers, mineral buyers, middlemen, financiers, processors and, in some cases, foreign nationals.

The authorities have particularly raised concerns about the participation of some foreigners in unauthorised mining and mineral trading.

In May 2026, Alake disclosed that more than 327 people, including foreign nationals, had been apprehended for illegal mining, with some cases involving suspected links to terrorism handed over to the Office of the National Security Adviser for further investigation.

He said the government had also revoked about 3,000 mining licences as part of efforts to sanitise the sector.

Among the foreign nationals repeatedly appearing in recent enforcement operations are Chinese nationals.

In May, the NSCDC Mining Marshals arraigned 15 Chinese nationals and nine Nigerians before the Federal High Court in Abuja over alleged illegal lithium mining in Kokona Local Government Area of Nasarawa State.

In September, four Chinese nationals were arrested in Maiya’aki, Lapai Local Government Area of Niger State, over alleged unauthorised mining activities at a site where they reportedly had no valid licences.

Earlier, an EFCC court filing alleged that Chinese and Nigerian nationals were involved in the illegal extraction and trading of mica and lithium, with some of the minerals allegedly moved to Ogun State for processing and export through Lagos.

Character

Sunday Vanguard observed that the scale and character of illegal mining vary from state to state. In Zamfara, gold mining has intersected with banditry and other forms of insecurity.

In Plateau, unsafe mining practices have been linked to repeated deaths, while Taraba has witnessed repeated government orders suspending mining activities.

In Osun, illegal gold mining has been associated with environmental degradation and clashes involving enforcement personnel.

Nasarawa has emerged as a major lithium-mining frontier, attracting both local and foreign operators, while in Benue, mining activities have taken place alongside displacement and insecurity.

State-by-state findings revealed the locations of mining activities, the minerals involved, the actors operating in the sector, the environmental consequences, reported deaths and the response of governments and security agencies.

ZAMFARA: Gold, banditry

Illegal gold mining remains a major concern in Zamfara State, particularly around Maru, Anka, Bukkuyum, Talata Mafara and Zurmi.

Not every miner operating in these areas is involved in criminal activity.

Many rural residents depend on artisanal mining for income.

However, security concerns become more pronounced where unregulated mining overlaps with armed groups and weak state control.

In April 2025, an attack in Gobirawar Chali, Maru Local Government Area, reportedly left at least 19 people dead, while Amnesty International said more than 20 people were killed.

There have also been reports alleging that a terror kingpin demanded protection levies from gold miners in Zurmi.

The allegations could not be independently verified.

In September 2025, a mining pit collapsed in Kadauri, Maru Local Government Area, with reports indicating casualties, although the exact number was not immediately established.

The environmental consequences have also been serious, with mining activities affecting farmland and vegetation and raising concerns about the pollution of water sources.

Despite repeated enforcement operations, illegal mining has persisted, highlighting the challenge of combining surveillance and enforcement with formalisation and alternative livelihoods for communities dependent on artisanal mining.

NIGER: Gold, multiple minerals

Illegal and unauthorised mining activities have been reported across several parts of Niger State, including Lapai, Katcha, Kontagora, Mariga, Minna, Shiroro, Rafi, Suleja, Agwara, Borgu, Munya and Paikoro.

Gold mining is particularly prominent in areas including Minna, Kontagora, Rafi, Paikoro, Magama and Shiroro, while the state also has deposits of talc, feldspar, iron ore, beryl, amethyst, tourmaline, graphite, kyanite, manganese, mica, wolframite, marble, lead, copper and topaz.

In Lapai, four Chinese nationals were arrested in September 2026 at Maiya’aki over alleged unauthorised mining activities.

Similar concerns have been raised in Katcha, including the Zuzungi area, where alleged unauthorised mining by Chinese nationals attracted enforcement attention.

Authorities have also shut down mineral-processing sites in Kontagora as part of efforts to curb illegal activities.

The state came under national attention in September 2026 after 37 suspected illegal miners died while in NSCDC custody.

The circumstances surrounding the deaths are under investigation, while the Federal Government has constituted an independent 10-member committee to investigate the incident.

PLATEAU: Multiple disasters, deaths

Plateau State has witnessed a succession of mining-related accidents, attacks and other incidents resulting in significant loss of lives.

Mining activities are concentrated in areas including Barkin Ladi, Jos South, Bassa, Riyom, Wase, Bokkos and Mangu.

In November 2024, 13 people reportedly died following a mining-site collapse around the boundary of Bassa, Jos South and Jos North local government areas.

Four people died in another mining-site collapse in Dura, Jos South, in September 2025.

In December 2025, 12 people were reportedly killed in an attack at Ratoso Fan in Barkin Ladi, while seven others were killed in a shooting incident at Kuru, Jos South, in January 2026.

In February 2026, at least 37 people died at Kampanin Zurak in Wase Local Government Area following exposure to toxic gas at a mining site.

Five people were killed at Gero Village, Gyel, in Jos South, on June 16, 2026, while three others were killed at Nyango-Gyere on June 30, with two others injured.

On August 12, seven people died in a mining-pit collapse in Kassa, Barkin Ladi, while two others were killed in another incident in Gangare, Barkin Ladi, on September 23.

The reported deaths amount to 90.

Concerned by the situation, Governor Caleb Mutfwang, in February 2025, issued Executive Order 001 suspending mining activities across 17 local government areas.

In May 2025, the state government said 159 operators had been cleared to operate under various categories, including six mining licences, 15 small-scale mining leases, 15 exploration licences, five artisanal and small-scale mining permits, one quarry lease and 118 tin sheds and buying centres.

However, the remote and scattered nature of mining sites, coupled with reports of night operations, has continued to pose challenges to effective monitoring.

KOGI: Battle for gold, others

Kogi State Government has expressed concern over illegal mining, particularly in areas where mining activities have affected communities and the environment.

In September 2026, Alake, while responding to protesting youths in the state, described illegal mining as a major concern.

He said Mining Marshals had dislodged illegal miners operating in a licensed area in Yagba East Local Government Area.

The minister said investigations indicated that some of the illegal miners were indigenes and alleged that some elders, traditional rulers and local government functionaries supported the activities.

The Concerned Kogi Youths Against Environmental Degradation had protested against the impact of mining in areas including Ankpa and Omala, alleging that the activities had damaged roads, destroyed farmland and polluted water sources.

Kogi is endowed with coal and other mineral resources, making regulation and monitoring of mining activities a continuing challenge.

NASARAWA: Lithium frontier

Nasarawa State has emerged as one of the country’s important lithium-mining areas, with activities particularly reported in Kokona, Wamba and Nasarawa Eggon local government areas.

The state has attracted both local and foreign operators, leading to increased regulatory and security attention.

In May 2026, 15 Chinese nationals and nine Nigerians were arraigned before the Federal High Court in Abuja over alleged illegal lithium mining in Kokona Local Government Area.

Concerns have also been raised over the safety of workers and possible child labour at mining sites.

In September, special monitoring and enforcement teams intensified checks on mining operations, particularly to ensure that operators remained within licensed coordinates.

TARABA: Repeated suspensions

Across the forests, rugged mountains and river basins of Taraba State, illegal mining has emerged as a major environmental and security concern. Taraba sits atop deposits of gold, blue sapphire, topaz, lead, zinc and lithium.

Yet, over the years, these resources have increasingly attracted unauthorised mining activities.

Unauthorised miners have moved into parts of the state, including forest reserves and rural settlements. The most intense activities have been reported around Mayokam and Gangtu in Bali, the Mambilla Plateau in Sardauna, Takum, Ardo-Kola and Gassol.

Security profiling and intelligence reports indicate that some mining camps involve migrant labourers and undocumented foreigners from Cameroon.

Security agencies have carried out raids in several areas, arresting hundreds of miners reportedly from Zamfara, Katsina and Bauchi states.

The activities also involve networks of middlemen, mineral buyers, financiers and operators of heavy equipment.

Governor Agbu Kefas has issued three Executive Orders suspending mining activities since 2023, including another suspension in June 2026.

Illegal mining has been documented across Sardauna, Karim Lamido, Bali, Gashaka, Kurmi, Ussa and Yorro local government areas.

A Premium Times investigation estimated that the state could lose more than N10 billion annually to illegal mining.

On September 18, 2026, five alleged illegal miners died following a mining-pit collapse in Mayokam, Bali Local Government Area.

A task force subsequently dispersed miners and seized equipment, with reports indicating that some of the miners were from Zamfara, Bauchi and Sokoto states, as well as Cameroon and Chad.

EBONYI: Abandoned pits, deaths

Ebonyi State is endowed with mineral resources including limestone, zinc, lead, chalcopyrite and oxide.

While mining licences are issued by the Federal Government, the state government has environmental and community-level responsibilities, creating an additional layer of regulation and enforcement.

The state has faced allegations of unlicensed mining operations, poor environmental practices and failure by some operators to carry out required environmental impact assessments.

Mining activities and abandoned pits have been reported in areas including Abakaliki, Ikwo, Izzi, Ezza South, Ebonyi and Ishielu.

The state government, in collaboration with the NSCDC, has announced measures against illegal mining and unauthorised mineral trading.

Abandoned mining pits have remained a major concern in communities including Okposi Umuoghara, Enyigba, Ameka and Ishiagu.

There have also been allegations of child labour and the involvement of pregnant women in mining activities.

The state government inaugurated a Solid Minerals Task Force to seal illegal sites, confiscate equipment and stop night-time rock crushing and the movement of mineral-laden trucks.

Licensed operators are expected to comply with the Mining Act, display appropriate signposts, pay required revenue, refrain from night operations, conduct environmental impact assessments and enter into Community Development Agreements where applicable.

The Commissioner for Solid Minerals, Mt Magnus Nkah, during visits to mining communities in Ishielu and Ohaukwu, warned operators to comply with safety requirements.

“The welfare of workers is equally important because these workers are our people. Many companies have not paid sufficient attention to their welfare,” he said.

The government has also raised concerns about inadequate safety standards and delays in implementing community development agreements and other obligations, including scholarships.

The ministry said it would issue compliance templates and deadlines, while the task force would monitor operations and work to eliminate revenue leakages.

Night-time transportation of minerals has also been declared illegal in affected areas.

The dangers posed by abandoned pits have already resulted in deaths.

Community youth leader Ogochukwu Elem said one abandoned pit had remained open for about 10 years after an earlier incident.

At Okposi Umuoghara, a truck driver and his assistant reportedly died after falling into a mining pit. A motorcycle operator later died after falling into the same pit when his brakes reportedly failed, while a cyclist also died in the area.

The incidents accounted for at least five deaths.

In Ezza North, three suspects were arrested by the NSCDC over alleged illegal mining, while the site was sealed.

BAUCHI: Mining, insecurity concerns

Illegal mining has become a security concern in parts of Bauchi State, particularly in Alkaleri and neighbouring border communities.

In August 2026, Governor Bala Mohammed identified illegal mining in the area as a major contributor to insecurity and banditry and warned influential individuals allegedly involved in the activities that they could face prosecution.

Illegal mining does not automatically cause banditry. However, the presence of valuable minerals and uncontrolled mining operations can create opportunities for armed groups and other criminal networks to exploit weak regulation and security gaps.

KADUNA: Gold, tin, lithium

Mining activities have been reported in Birnin Gwari, Sanga, Jema’a and Kubau local government areas of Kaduna State.

The state has deposits of gold, tin, tantalum, lithium and gemstones.

A 2024 study identified 103 mining sites across 36 communities in four local government areas, comprising 53 active and 50 abandoned sites.

The study identified Jema’a and Birnin Gwari as major areas of activity, while Sanga and Kajuru also recorded mining operations.

In Birnin Gwari, communities including Fara Ruwa, Bugai, Dagara, Awaro, Tashan Keji, Sabon Layi, Dawakin Basa, Kungi, Janruwa, Maganda, Tsohon Gwari, Randagi and Rema have reported mining activities involving gold, tin, tantalum and tourmaline.

At a gold-mining site around Bugai, about 16 kilometres from Birnin Gwari, miners described the activity as an important source of livelihood, although many operators remain outside the formal licensing system.

The Birnin Gwari Emirate Progressive Union, BEPU, has called for stronger security around mining communities.

In Jema’a, the study identified 64 mining sites, accounting for more than 60 per cent of its sample. Communities mentioned include Godogodo, Gidan Waya, Antang, Nisama, Kanufi, Zankan-Nindem, Gwaska, Dangoma, Garti, Farin Hawa and Ambam.

Minerals reported in the area include tantalite, tourmaline, tin, lithium, mica, zircon, sapphire and nickel.

In May 2025, illegal tin-mining operations in Damau, Kubau Local Government Area, were shut down.

The Kaduna State development plan has also identified indiscriminate mining, particularly in Birnin Gwari and Jema’a, as a cause of land degradation.

KEBBI: Gold, informal operations

In February 2026, Mining Marshals, supported by the Department of State Services, the Army and the Police, dislodged thousands of people from mining areas under the Presidential Artisanal Gold Mining Development Initiative, PAGMI, in Yauri Local Government Area.

Gold is the dominant mineral in the affected areas. The government has sought to formalise artisanal mining through initiatives such as PAGMI, but informal operations have continued to pose challenges.

Environmental concerns include land degradation and pollution of water sources.

The continuing challenge is how to prevent operators displaced by enforcement operations from simply moving to other unregulated mining locations.

ADAMAWA: Mining, security concerns

Mining activities in Adamawa State have also attracted security concerns.

The state has deposits of gold, limestone and gypsum, with mining activities reported in Song, Mubi, Maiha, Jada, Toungo and Michika.

In June 2026, Governor Ahmadu Fintiri ordered an immediate ban on illegal mining in Lamurde following a preliminary report on a crisis in the area and directed security agencies to enforce the order.

As in other states, mining does not automatically create every conflict, but uncontrolled mining can deepen tensions over land, access to resources and local revenue.

BENUE: Displacement

Mining activities have continued in parts of Benue State, particularly in Kwande and Logo local government areas.

Communities affected include Mbagber, Tombo, Ukemberagya/Tswarev and Ayilamo.

The activities have taken place alongside attacks and displacement in parts of the state.

Federal lawmaker Terseer Ugbor has linked illegal mining to insecurity in the state, although such claims represent a political assessment and should not be taken as proof of a direct causal relationship.

The Turan Development Association suspended mining activities in May, citing insecurity, environmental degradation and alleged exploitation.

The state government has also cautioned traditional rulers against issuing mining permits without the necessary approvals.

OSUN: Foreign illegal miners

Illegal mining in Osun State is not only disrupting livelihoods, especially on ancient farmlands, including cocoa and kolanut plantations, but is also creating environmental hazards that constitute inherent dangers to the lives and property of residents and indigenes of affected communities.

The menace mostly affects Osun-East Senatorial District, particularly Ifeland and Ijesaland, but the environmental impact extends to Osogbo, Asejire and the Osun River.

There has been an influx of illegal miners from northern Nigeria, Niger Republic and Mali, with concerns over inadequate documentation and the security implications.

In Ijesaland, affected communities include Ibodi, Ijanna Wasare, Itagunmodi, Ayegunle, Iwara, Igangan, Kajola, Iponda, Ikinyinwa and Ilase. Ile-Ife, Ifetedo and Ifewara have also recorded mining activities.

Farmlands have reportedly been destroyed, forcing some farmers and farm owners to abandon their lands, while residents living close to mining sites have also abandoned their houses.

There have been allegations that some influential indigenes backed illegal mining activities for pecuniary gains, while officials allegedly shielded miners through a ticketing system operated by third parties.

During a visit by Sunday Vanguard to Ibodi alongside officials of the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development and four local government chairmen, security personnel were allegedly seen providing cover for miners and preventing enforcement officers from carrying out arrests, citing legal tickets issued to the operators.

The situation reportedly led to a standoff, with Sanya Omirin intervening. Military and police personnel were also reported to have raised weapons against one another during the confrontation.

At Ijanna Wasare, NSCDC personnel were allegedly accused of alerting miners and helping some of them escape, thereby preventing arrests.

The Osun-Osogbo River serves more than 20 communities, and pollution allegedly linked to gold mining has raised concerns about its use and consumption.

Concerned by the development, Urban Alert called for urgent intervention by federal government, Osun State government and international partners.

The organisation said the river stretches about 213 kilometres from Ekiti through Osun, Oyo and Ogun to Lagos, with five dams and about two million people depending on it.

Urban Alert said testing had detected substances including cyanide, mercury and lead, raising concerns about possible health risks.

Chairman of Ilesa West Local Government Area, Lanre Balogun, said many mining sites had no records with the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development and were operating without licences.

He said the local government had sought information from the Osun Mining Office but had not received a satisfactory response, adding that unknown individuals were collecting revenue through ticketing.

“We discovered that many of these mining sites have no records whatsoever with the Federal Ministry of Solid Minerals Development. They are unregistered, unlicensed and largely untraceable. Rather than enforcement, what we observed was the unlawful collection of revenue by unknown artisanal miners at the expense of the safety of our communities,” Balogun said.

OYO: Gold, gemstones, marble

Illegal mining activities have been reported across Oke-Ogun, Iwajowa, Iseyin, Itesiwaju, Atisbo, Kajola and Irepo, as well as parts of Ido, Egbeda and Lagelu local government areas.

The Lagos-Ibadan quarry axis has also recorded mining activities, while Itasa in Iwajowa has attracted attention over mineral exploitation.

Minerals found across the state include gold, tantalite, tourmaline, gemstones, aquamarine, sapphire, talc, marble, kaolin, quartz, cassiterite, columbite, bismuth, granite, feldspar and clay.

Parts of Ibarapa are known for tantalite, aquamarine, tourmaline and sapphire, while Irepo has marble and tantalite deposits. Igbeti in Olorunsogo is also known for marble and dolomite.

There have been allegations of the involvement of some traditional rulers in mining activities.

In January 2026, the state government suspended the Sobaloju of Ofiki, Atisbo Local Government Area, over allegations that he issued unauthorised consent letters to mining companies and permitted mining activities in a government reserve.

The case has also highlighted tensions between federal control of mining titles and state and community interests in environmental protection and local development.

OGUN: Lithium, gold, quarrying

Illegal mining has been reported around Ogere in Ikenne, Ode-Remo in Remo North, the Omi-Ogunmakin-Odede axis and other border communities.

Minerals found in the state include lithium, mica, gold, tantalite, granite, feldspar, kaolin, silica sand and clay.

The expansion of mining activities has raised concerns over environmental degradation, land use and the regulation of operators working outside the formal licensing framework.

EDO: Gold, lithium, other minerals

Mining activities have been reported across Edo North, including Okpella, Ososo and the Egbetua forest axis in Etsako East and Akoko-Edo local government areas.

Other locations include Erhua near Ehor and Iruekpen.

Minerals associated with the state include gold, lithium, iron ore, titanium, granite, marble, limestone, kaolin, feldspar and silica.

The spread of unauthorised mining has raised concerns over forest degradation, land use and the environmental impact of mining operations.

KWARA: Gold, lithium

Illegal mining activities have been reported in Kaiama and Bani, with gold and lithium among the minerals attracting operators.

Kwara is also endowed with tantalite, cassiterite, columbite, tourmaline, aquamarine, sapphire, emerald, amethyst, beryl, marble, dolomite, kaolin, quartz, feldspar, granite and talc.

The expansion of unauthorised mining has raised concerns over environmental degradation, revenue leakage and the difficulty of monitoring remote mining locations.

National security

Security expert, Dr Bamaiyi Altine, said the government should treat illegal mining as a national security issue, arguing that proceeds from the activities could provide resources for armed groups.

“Government should treat this as a national security issue. These people are unregulated and mean. They are lawless in areas they operate. I don’t think the Mining Marshals alone can checkmate their activities. As long as these activities continue unchecked, banditry will remain active,” Altine said.

Another security expert, Mr Okwuonye Eziashi, called for urgent government action, warning against allowing illegal mining to develop into another major security crisis.

He said: “Government needs to act fast. We should not wait until illegal mining becomes another full-blown security crisis before we respond. What we are seeing in some parts of the country should concern everybody because wherever you have valuable minerals being exploited outside the law, you can also have criminal elements taking advantage of the situation.

“We have the experience of the Democratic Republic of Congo to learn from. The battle for control of mineral resources has been intertwined with armed conflict in eastern Congo for decades. Different armed groups have benefited from the illicit exploitation and trade in minerals. We cannot afford to allow a similar pattern to develop here.

“The lesson for Nigeria is clear: we must secure our mining communities, regulate the sector properly and ensure that proceeds from our mineral resources do not end up financing banditry, terrorism or other criminal activities. The earlier government moves decisively, the easier it will be to prevent illegal mining from becoming a major driver of insecurity.”

ILLEGAL MINING: Children face brain, lung, reproductive damage—Experts

By Chioma Obinna

For children growing up around mining sites, danger can be difficult to see.

It may be in the fine dust hanging in the air, the water flowing from a contaminated stream, the soil beneath bare feet, or the food produced near where minerals are extracted. It may also be in the long hours spent at a mining site instead of sitting in a classroom.

The issue was recently brought into focus when young children in Niger and Plateau states were found involved in illegal mining, once again drawing attention to the growing vulnerability of minors around mining communities.

But beyond child labour and lost schooling lies another danger that may be less visible and far more enduring. What exposure to the mining environment can do to a developing child.

Experts in pharmacology, toxicology, public health and reproductive health said that exposure to mining activities can cause neurological, respiratory and developmental damage. At the same time, heavy metals and other contaminants may threaten reproductive health and contaminate entire communities.

For Prof. Omoniyi Yemitan, Professor of Pharmacology and Toxicology at the Lagos State University College of Medicine, Ikeja, in an interview with Sunday Vanguard, the problem is not mining itself but what happens when basic safety precautions are ignored, particularly in artisanal mining.

“Mining is a problem all over the world. It’s not only in Nigeria, but it is more problematic when necessary precautions are not carried out for miners,” he said.

In a properly regulated environment, miners are expected to use protective equipment, including helmets, gas or nose masks, coveralls and safety boots. But many artisanal miners lack the knowledge, resources or discipline to adhere to such safety measures.

That becomes particularly troubling when children live, play or work around the same sites.

Yemitan said children could inhale heavy metals associated with minerals being extracted, as well as other metals present in surrounding soil and rock.

Gold, tin and, increasingly, lithium have attracted attention in Nigeria, but the minerals being extracted may occur alongside other substances capable of causing harm.

“They always have some lead in their environment, mercury in the environment and all that. And all those, when they are inhaled, they have health implications, especially in children,” he said.

Problem

Mining environments can contain large quantities of dust carrying particles from soil, rock and chemicals present at mining sites. Prolonged inhalation can damage the respiratory system.

For Yemitan, however, one of the most worrying consequences for children is neurological damage.

“Toxic metal poisoning can cause brain damage,” he said, adding that prolonged exposure could interfere with cognitive development.

The concern is not necessarily about an immediate and visible injury. A child may continue to attend school, play and appear healthy while toxic exposure gradually affects development.

The professor said children exposed to mining could eventually have lower IQ levels than children who were not exposed, indicating that parts of the developing brain could be affected by toxic substances.

But the danger does not stop with the brain.

Yemitan identified the lungs as another major organ at risk, stressing that children could be particularly vulnerable because their respiratory systems were still developing.

One of the conditions associated with prolonged exposure to dust from mining is silicosis, a lung disease caused by inhalation of respirable crystalline silica.

“When scarring occurs, the functions of the lungs will be reduced,” he said.

The consequences can spread throughout the body because inadequate oxygen supply affects vital organs, including the brain.

“If enough oxygen is not getting to the brain, especially in children, then all the health issues which I mentioned originally about brain damage and low IQ will generally occur,” he said.

Chronic cough, asthma and hypoxia, a condition in which the body does not receive sufficient oxygen, are also among the possible consequences of prolonged exposure, he added.

Yet toxic exposure is only one layer of the danger.

Mining site

“The earth can at any time collapse on anybody, but more particularly children that don’t have enough guard for themselves,” Yemitan said.

Nigeria has already witnessed the devastating consequences of unsafe mining, particularly in Zamfara State, where lead poisoning linked to artisanal gold mining has affected communities, including children.

Yemitan recalled the health crises associated with mining in Zamfara and said other parts of the country had also experienced mining-related incidents.

For children, he stressed, vulnerability is heightened by their stage of physical development.

“Children are particularly more vulnerable when it comes to mining sites because their guard is, of course, reduced. Their bodies are still developing, so more prone to some of these health effects,” he said.

But the hidden toll of mining does not necessarily stop at the edge of a mining site.

Once toxic substances enter the environment, they can travel through water, soil, air and food.

For Dr Casmier Ifeanyi, public health and medical research scientist and National President of the Association of Medical Laboratory Scientists of Nigeria, the consequences of poorly regulated mining are “very far-reaching” and potentially devastating.

He said: “The implications of mining in any area, particularly the health-related implications, are very far-reaching. They are very devastating, and sometimes they lead up to lifelong debilitation. Nigeria’s experience with lead poisoning in Zamfara is a clear example of the consequences of illegal, unregulated and unsafe mining.

“So the issue and the risks associated with mining for any community are well-documented.’’

According to him, mining exposes people to both physical hazards and toxicological risks.

Children living near mining areas, as well as those directly involved in mining, could be exposed to heavy metals and chemicals through air, water, soil and other environmental pathways.

He identified lead and mercury among substances of particular concern.

Lead poisoning associated with artisanal gold mining, he said, could cause kidney damage and other serious health consequences, while mercury exposure could cause neurological damage.

“Children who are exposed to mining may end up with brain damage, and would, of course, have developmental issues. This is well established,” he said.

But perhaps one of the most troubling aspects of environmental contamination is that people may not know they are being exposed.

Mining operations can pollute surface water and groundwater when minerals and mining waste are washed into water bodies. People may then be exposed through drinking water, farming and livestock.

“The air in that environment again becomes very much polluted. If you aggregate it, people absorb this, the soil absorbs it, it ends up in the food we eat,” he said.

The contamination can move far beyond the immediate mining community.

“If you consume livestock produced in that area, the food you have grown in those areas that end up in Lagos and Abuja, and any other part of the world for that matter, would have absorbed these heavy metals,” he said.

The concern is particularly significant in communities where people depend on groundwater, including boreholes, for domestic use.

Ifeanyi said mining activities could contaminate water bodies used for farming, livestock production and domestic purposes.

“People dig up anything, and they go to the freshwater body where people fetch for farming, where they fetch for livestock production, where they fetch for domestic use, and they go there to wash them. And as they wash, they are contaminating the water bodies. They are contaminating groundwater bodies,” he said.

The implication is that a mining operation can affect people who have never entered a mining pit.

Childhood

There is another cost that cannot be measured through laboratory tests.

Children drawn into mining can lose something that is difficult to recover later — their education and childhood.

Ifeanyi said mining often involves hard labour and child labour, depriving children of education while exposing them to exploitation.

Some children, he noted, are introduced to mining because they can earn small amounts of money from the activity.

“That child will tell you, education is a scam. I am already making money,” he said.

What appears to be an immediate opportunity to earn money can become a cycle of poverty in which children abandon school, become trapped in hazardous work and grow up with fewer opportunities to escape poverty.

“It is exploitative. It’s exploitative, taking undue advantage of them,” he said.

The consequences, however, may extend beyond childhood.

Ifeanyi said some toxic metals associated with mining could affect reproductive health, creating risks that could extend beyond the individual who was exposed.

He also raised concerns about sexual exploitation and early pregnancies around mining communities, saying children and young people in such environments could face multiple forms of vulnerability.

“Exposing children to mining affects not only their health; it has psychological and social effects, it affects reproductive health, it has a transgenerational impact, and the communities where this happens are also not spared at all,” he said.

That possibility introduces another dimension to the mining problem: the health of generations yet unborn.

Generations

For Prof. Oladapo Ashiru, renowned Nigerian professor of anatomy, reproductive endocrinologist and pioneer of In Vitro Fertilisation in West Africa, the reproductive-health consequences of mining exposure deserve particular attention.

Ashiru warned that children exposed to toxic substances could face risks that affect their future ability to have healthy children.

According to him, the mining environment creates a combination of physical hazards, toxic exposure and developmental vulnerability.

Toxic substances such as lead and mercury can cross the placental barrier, potentially exposing unborn children and increasing the risk of developmental problems, impaired cognition, low birth weight and premature birth.

He said exposure could also affect reproductive health before conception.

“For women, hazardous exposure can contribute to reduced fertility, menstrual disorders and premature menopause, while in men it can affect hormone production, sperm count and sperm movement,” Ashiru said.

“The reproductive implications are therefore not limited to children who are currently working in mining. Exposure among adults of reproductive age can potentially affect pregnancies and future generations.”

For children actually working at mining sites, the risks begin much earlier.

They may be injured in tunnel collapses, while handling explosives or using unsuitable tools. Carrying heavy loads can cause musculoskeletal injuries and deformities, particularly in growing bodies.

The respiratory system is another major target.

“Children who inhale rock dust over extended periods can develop serious respiratory disease, including silicosis.
