This month, Bannon formed an unlikely partnership with independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, a socialist, to call for significant restrictions on AI development, government oversight and corporate accountability at the Pro-Human Assembly conference in Washington, D.C.

toggle caption Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images

Still, the two have differing stances on what any of those measures should look like. Sanders called for an immediate pause on AI development until clear safety rules are established by scientists, a permanent ban on the development of artificial "superintelligence" (AI systems that are more intelligent than humans in all domains), and an international treaty with China in an effort to avoid an AI arms race. Bannon, meanwhile, argued for slowing the pace of AI development, the formation of a national regulatory organization and for cutting off China from U.S. AI technology.

"So why are we letting the Chinese Communist Party drive us? Oh, we have to do this or China wins," said Bannon in his speech at the event in Washington. "We should quarantine now every aspect of the ecosystem of artificial intelligence away from the Chinese Communist Party today. We should cut them off."

Sponsor Message

Safetyists

Safetyists are primarily concerned with the potential risks of the rapid advancement of AI. Their worries center on the possibility of catastrophic or existential outcomes, such as the death of humanity at the hands of autonomous machines.

High-profile members of the safetyist community include Geoffrey Hinton, who is commonly referred to as the "Godfather of AI" because of his pioneering work in deep learning that helped launch the modern era of AI. In recent years, Hinton, who previously worked at Google, has issued a series of warnings about existential risks associated with AI, particularly if an AI model surpasses human intelligence and becomes autonomous.

Another vocal AI safetyist is Daniel Kokotajlo, a former researcher at OpenAI and co-author of AI 2027, a paper published last year that discusses how super-intelligent AI could lead to human extinction by the mid-2030s.

Effective altruists

Effective altruists (often shortened to "EA") generally believe in maximizing humanity's long-term welfare. The movement originally focused on material ways to reduce global poverty. But more recently, many EA thinkers have focused their concerns on the possibility of existential risks from advanced AI and other potential societal-scale disasters such as nuclear war, climate change and pandemics. They particularly worry about the consequences for future generations. People from the EA camp prioritize AI safety, alignment – which is the science of making sure AI systems behave in a way that is reflective of human values and in line with safety rules – and reducing the probability of catastrophic outcomes.

The key difference between EAs and safetyists is that EAs generally provide funding for AI safety research and risk mitigation, whereas safetyists are researchers and advocates undertaking AI safety work and publicly calling for regulation.

Other AI factions often derisively describe effective altruists as so-called "AI Doomers." EA has also become a focus of criticism from the Trump administration since Coxon's resignation from Anthropic.

Sponsor Message

"Americanism, not effective altruism. The United States will continue to be AI DOMINANT!" said one Defense Department post this month.

toggle caption Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

Well-known people in the EA movement include Eliezer Yudkowsky, co-founder of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), which focuses on mathematical approaches to making advanced AI systems safe. He is also the author of Harry Potter fan fiction that helped popularize ideas associated with EA. Holden Karnofsky, an American entrepreneur and philanthropist, founded Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), an organization that funds causes central to the EA mission, including AI and biosecurity. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei is considered to be aligned with effective altruism. Karnofsky also works at Anthropic and is married to Daniela Amodei, who is a co-founder of Anthropic and the sister of Dario Amodei, the CEO.

Another high-profile supporter of the EA movement is Sam Bankman-Fried, who founded major cryptocurrency exchange FTX. In 2023, he was convicted of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy related to the misuse of customer and investor funds and is currently serving a 25-year prison sentence.

AI ethics

The AI ethics camp argues that society should focus on the harms AI is already causing, rather than on hypothetical existential risks. Some proponents contend that emphasizing existential threats from a hypothetical future superintelligence can serve as a distraction from the more immediate harms and accountability issues surrounding AI today.

AI ethicists' concerns include how AI systems can be biased due to the content of their training data, for example, the ways in which AI facial recognition or job application systems might perpetuate existing societal biases. They are also concerned with how AI could be used to exploit workers and to enable mass surveillance, as well as about the environmental costs of data centers, autonomous weapons, and the concentration of power among technology companies.

A notable voice of the AI ethics faction is Timnit Gebru, a computer scientist and former co-lead of Google's Ethical AI team. Gebru left the company in 2020 because of a dispute with the company over a research paper she wrote exposing problems with large language models (LLMs), including their tendency to generate harmful or misleading language.

Sponsor Message

AI as a normal technology

People belonging to the "AI as a Normal Technology" group reject both the utopian and dystopian narratives about AI. Instead, this faction sees AI as a powerful but ultimately normal technology, comparable to the internet or electricity. They believe the focus should be on understanding and regulating specific applications and harms instead of treating AI as an unprecedented threat or as a path to inevitable superintelligence.

toggle caption Big Event Media/Getty Images

Notable people associated with this worldview include Fei-Fei Li, a computer scientist and co-director of the Stanford Human-Centered AI Institute. Li is famous for creating ImageNet, a vastly large dataset of images which provided the training data for large neural networks, which led to several major developments in AI.

Katie McQue's reporting is supported by the Tarbell Center for AI Journalism, which is a grantee of Coefficient Giving. Neither Tarbell nor Coefficient have any editorial input into her work.

World.title: Meal deliveries can save money and improve health. Will they survive Medicaid cuts?
World.content:
Meal deliveries can save money and improve health. Will they survive Medicaid cuts?

toggle caption Robin Lubbock/WBUR

On a weekday morning in a quiet Boston neighborhood, a kitchen bustled with activity. Volunteers sliced chicken breasts, stuffed bell peppers, filled trays, and carefully labeled each item.

This story was produced in partnership with KFF Health News.

It was part of an experiment to offer nutritious and medicall- tailored meals to Medicaid patients who are unable to shop for groceries and cook for themselves.

"Once I started to eat these meals that were geared toward my illness, I built up my muscle mass again, built up my strength, built up my confidence in myself," said Vanessa Georges, who is in remission from throat cancer and said she would struggle to consume enough calories without the deliveries.

"These meals have given me a second chance."

Sponsor Message

Georges said she noticed another benefit from the meals: She spends less time at the doctor's office.

Researchers have found evidence backing her observation. About 1,900 Massachusetts residents who, like Georges, received medically-tailored meals for at least three months needed less medical care, according to a study published in the journal Nature Medicine. They had 20% fewer emergency department visits and 31% fewer hospitalizations than similar patients who did not receive meals.

toggle caption Robin Lubbock/WBUR

"It actually saves the healthcare system money," said Dariush Mozaffarian, a cardiologist and professor at Tufts University who led the study. "That's a really big deal, because most things in healthcare don't."

The research from Massachusetts adds to evidence that medically-tailored meals could save states money — in addition to improving health. Yet such programs could land on the chopping block as states look to tighten spending under Trump administration budget cuts, even as federal officials argue that food is a critical component of health.

Medicaid budget cuts loom

The 2025 law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act slashed projected Medicaid funding by more than $900 billion. Many Republicans who backed the bill believe federal health spending is too high and riddled with fraud. Sen. John Kennedy, a Louisiana Republican, for example, has accused California of "outrageous fraud" for using Medicaid dollars to fund housing and nutrition programs.

Sponsor Message

Amaya Diana, a policy analyst at KFF, said states will have to make tough choices in the next few years as they figure out how to fill funding gaps. "If states are not able to offset the loss of federal funds with new taxes or reductions in other state spending, they may have to make program cuts," she said. (KFF is a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News.)

toggle caption Robin Lubbock/WBUR

Thirteen states have received federal waivers to use Medicaid dollars to pay for meals — part of an approach known as "food is medicine." Three other programs are awaiting federal approval.

President Donald Trump's support for social services has wavered. While the first Trump administration allowed states to pursue medically-tailored meals and other social supports, the second Trump administration rescinded Biden-era guidance for Medicaid initiatives that address social needs. It hasn't detailed a new policy.

Administration officials have warned that they will be more focused on the budget impacts of such initiatives.

"They signaled they're going to be a lot more skeptical," said Kurt Hager, an assistant professor at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School who studies nutrition programs and helped lead the Massachusetts study. "Instead of using a broad-based approach nationwide, they're going to make decisions on a state-by-state basis."

At the same time, health leaders in Trump's administration have made nutrition a major focus, including by promoting less-processed foods. Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who leads the Department of Health and Human Services, and Mehmet Oz, administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, have pushed hospitals to serve healthier foods to boost patient outcomes.

toggle caption Robin Lubbock/WBUR

The healthcare system is often willing to pay for surgeries, Oz said in a social media video in June, "but not always willing to pay for the nutrition that might help prevent those outcomes in the first place. That's bothered me my whole career."

Sponsor Message

He added that the agency is evaluating several strategies, including medically tailored meals, to prevent illness and hospitalization. CMS officials did not respond to several emailed requests for comment for this article.

Katie Garfield, who studies social determinants of health at Harvard Law School's Center for Health Law and Policy Innovation, said the lack of federal guidance is stirring uncertainty for states that want to pursue nutrition programs in Medicaid. "We're still waiting to see that big step forward around 'food is medicine' interventions," she said. "We need to see that step forward to resolve some of the uncertainty."

Lawmakers have had a hard time engaging administration officials on medically-tailored meals, said U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, who sponsored a bill that would pilot meal deliveries for some chronically-ill seniors on Medicare. The legislation has yet to come up for a vote.

"I had thought, based on some of his rhetoric before he entered the Trump administration, that RFK Jr. would be a natural ally on this," McGovern said. "But we can't seem to get his attention."

The costs of poor nutrition

Some companies have been accused of billing Medicaid for meals that were neither healthy nor nutritious, raising concerns about lax regulation of these programs.

But at Community Servings in Boston, the food is prepared with specific attention to sugar, salt, fat, vitamins, and minerals and is based on a person's health needs, said David Waters, chief executive of the nonprofit. Many recipients require food that is mild or low in fiber, for example.

"What we're able to do is to work with your healthcare provider to understand your health realities — what your diagnoses are, what your medications are, side effects, food allergies, cultural norms — and then prescribe a diet for you that is scratch-made," Waters said.

Sponsor Message

The Massachusetts researchers found that the meals — at a cost of $125 per person per week — essentially paid for themselves. Patients with heart disease used about $10,000 less in healthcare services over six months, and patients with kidney disease used $12,000 less in healthcare. There were also savings for people with diabetes, depression, and anxiety.

"Those are pretty big numbers when you think of how expensive those diseases can be and the prevalence in the population," Waters said.

Nationally, researchers estimate, 10 million Americans would benefit from medically tailored meals, though only a small fraction are enrolled.

"Poor nutrition is the top cause of poor health in this country. It's the top cause of preventable healthcare spending," said Mozaffarian, director of the Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts. He has estimated that medically tailored meals could help patients avoid 1.6 million hospitalizations and save the U.S. $13.6 billion in healthcare costs each year.

A weekly delivery that makes a difference

Steve Honyotski receives 10 meals at his Boston home each week, cooked fresh and delivered cold or flash-frozen. They're ready to eat after just a couple of minutes in the microwave.

"The carrot ginger soup is my favorite," Honyotski said.

Honyotski, 71, lives with several chronic conditions, including diabetes, obesity, and high blood pressure. He said he's noticed improvements in his health since he started eating medically tailored meals. He needs less insulin to control his diabetes, and he's lost enough weight to delay a knee replacement surgery.

For now, those meals will keep coming. And Massachusetts' Medicaid director, Ryan Schwarz, said the state will seek federal approval to continue medically tailored meals in the coming years. "We feel very strongly committed to continuing these services," he said.

In North Carolina, researchers found that food and housing supports lowered Medicaid spending over time. Yet North Carolina state lawmakers suspended the services in 2025 over budget worries. After budget deliberations this summer, state legislators changed course and decided to partially fund the program.

Sponsor Message

"To me, that's a signal of what might occur in other states as these Medicaid cuts hit," said Hager, the UMass researcher. "Even though they have the authority to run these programs, it might be a lot harder for the states to actually implement them."

This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with WBUR and KFF Health News.

World.title: Canadian citizen detained at U.S. border crossing, questioned about voting for hours
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Paige Adamson was on her way home from a birthday dinner in Tsawwassen, B.C., on Sept. 15 when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing.

It was a regular stop that Adamson — a Canadian citizen who has lived in Point Roberts, Wash., as a U.S. permanent resident for 14 years — had grown used to.

But this time, they had a new question for her.

"The very first thing she asked was, 'Have you ever voted in a federal U.S. election?'" said Adamson.

Adamson, 61, said she told the border agent she had never voted in a federal election.

"They immediately said, 'Park over here and come into the office.'"

Paige Adamson says she has travelled across the border without issue for all of the 14 years she lived in the U.S. But recently, she faced hours of questioning after being accused of falsely claiming she was a U.S. citizen. (CBC News)

What happened next, Adamson said, was a nearly six-hour-long process — where she went through secondary inspection just after 9 p.m., was interrogated until after 2 a.m. and signed documents before being admitted into the U.S.

One of the documents CBC News reviewed said Adamson "must surrender for removal from the United States, if so ordered."

Lawyers who spoke with CBC News said U.S. voter registration systems can sometimes catch non-citizens up in errors, and one of them says he has seen an uptick in non-citizens being questioned in the last week.

Grounds for removal

According to documents provided by Adamson, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) alleges she falsely claimed she was a U.S. citizen "for the purposes of registering to vote in Whatcom County, Washington state."

The department also alleges Adamson voted in Washington state's 2018 general election.

DHS cites those allegations as grounds for removing Adamson from the U.S.

Adamson said she was questioned by U.S. border services agents for hours. (Tyson Koschik/CBC)

But Adamson maintained during questioning, a transcript reviewed by CBC News showed, that she has never voted in a federal election and doesn't remember ever voting in a state election — though she acknowledged receiving a ballot and may have been registered.

Adamson is now scheduled to appear for a hearing in Seattle, and is grappling with potentially being removed from the state she has lived in since 2012.

"My anxiety is over the top," she said.

A broader trend

In the past week and a half, immigration lawyer Len Saunders said he has received calls from three people — including Adamson — about being detained at the border and questioned about voting.

One, he said, was a Blaine, Wash., resident who crosses the border daily to work as a nurse in B.C.

Saunders said three near-identical situations like this in such a short period is unprecedented in his career that stretches back more than 25 years.

The Blaine-based lawyer told CBC News there could be hundreds of Canadians facing similar issues, and expects more cases as Canadians cross the border during the holidays.

"This is just the tip of the iceberg," he said.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders is seen in Blaine, Wash., on Jan. 9, 2026. He says that he's seen a recent uptick in U.S. permanent residents being questioned over voter registration. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)

B.C. immigration lawyer Chris Anders said border enforcement is "way, way stricter and tougher" than at any point in the last two decades.

He said the databases used by border officials are constantly expanding, meaning something that did not cause problems for someone previously could suddenly pop up during a new entry.

Voter registration issues

Washington state automatically registers some eligible voters when they get or renew a driver's licence or state ID, but the state says the system is tied to proof of U.S. citizenship.

But internal Washington Department of Licensing emails, obtained by the non-profit Federation for American Immigration Reform through a Freedom of Information request, show instances where non-citizens were registered to vote.

"A lot of Canadians say, 'Well, I thought I was entitled to [vote] because I went in, got my driver's licence and they registered me to vote,'" said Saunders.

Saunders said that in those situations, he has told clients to immediately deregister and submit a declaration saying they "unknowingly registered or unknowingly voted," and that used to be a consistent solution.

"Now, it seems to be a completely different scenario during this current administration."

The detainment

In an email to CBC News, a spokesperson for the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) said when a permanent resident arrives at a port of entry, officers screen their documentation against federal and state databases.

The CBP says if those records indicate "potential unlawful voter registration, illegal voting, or a previous false claim to U.S. citizenship," the individual is subject to "rigorous examination and detailed questioning."

Depending on the case, an individual may face "prolonged" immigration inspections, receive a notice to appear and formal removal proceedings, the spokesperson said.

WATCH | Questions about border questioning answered: Are U.S. border agents allowed to search my phone? Your border questions answered | Duration 8:40

Adamson said she wasn't offered water until around the five-hour mark of her detainment, and no one asked whether she needed to use the bathroom.

"I was basically treated like a criminal," she said.

She said the large Canadian population in Point Roberts — an exclave of the U.S. located just south of Delta, B.C. — has left her concerned that some of her neighbours could face similar problems.

"This beautiful little place, it's kind of being invaded," she said.

World.title: Why is it so difficult for Ukraine to take down Russia's jet-powered drones?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When a Russian drone slammed into a high-rise residential building in Kyiv around 8 a.m. Friday, killing a 14-year-old boy and injuring several others, the remnants of a jet engine were plainly visible among the broken glass and blackened debris on the pavement.

Russia's latest battlefield innovation — jet-powered drones — has been used to carry out strikes on the Ukrainian capital, including attacks targeting offices, data centres and warehouses.

The weapons, which have been pummelling Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine for weeks, have often been able to evade Ukrainian air defences because they fly at higher altitudes and at much higher speeds, reaching more than 600 km/h.

"It's not easy to intercept. You need to intercept [at] a similar speed or faster," said Volodymyr Khomenko, head of the Explosive Ordnance Disposal Department of the National Police of Ukraine.

"For faster drones, we need faster interceptors."

WATCH | Kyiv — a city under seige by Russian drones: 24 hours in Kyiv: Living through Russian drone strikes | Duration closed caption 9:33 Kyiv is a city under siege, the target of Russia’s new strategy, which uses the latest jet-powered drones to strike Ukraine’s capital city around the clock. Regular sirens send weary residents to the nearest shelter, underpass or metro station, but in a city where an air alert punctuates 11 hours of a 24-hour period, daily life carries on.

What are jet-powered drones?

According to Ukrainian officials, Russia began testing its jet-powered strike drones two years ago in the Chernihiv region, north of Kyiv and near the border with Belarus.

Unlike earlier models of Shahed drones, which were based on Iranian designs and included piston engines , the new versions are equipped with turbojet engines. Ukrainian military intelligence officials have said some of those engines are being sourced from China.

There are three models of Geran jet-powered drones, with the latest being the Geran-5. Its design differs significantly from earlier versions. Instead of a triangular shape, it looks more like a cruise missile, with aerodynamic fins.

The Geran-5 can cruise at about 600 km/h, roughly three times the speed of the earlier Shahed models that began attacking Ukrainian cities in 2022.

How often is Russia using them?

Khomenko told CBC News that he believes about half of the drones currently being launched at Ukraine are jet-powered, while the other half are older models. But he says the balance is shifting rapidly.

Ukraine's Air Force said Russia fired 2,800 jet-powered drones at Ukraine in August, almost twice as many as in July.

Firefighters clear debris from the site of a jet-powered drone strike in Kyiv on Friday. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

In recent weeks, Russia has been sending the drones in small waves, often resulting in multihour air-raid alerts in Kyiv. Air defences can be heard throughout the city alongside the sound of explosions.

Unlike older models, which emit a buzzing sound that's been compared to a motorcycle, the jet-powered drones are quieter. Instead, residents often report hearing a whooshing sound as they fly through the air.

When a drone crashed into the high-rise apartment building on Friday, Alice Boyko told CBC News she didn't think she heard the air-raid siren until after the explosion. She lives in the same building that was struck, but her apartment is on the opposite side.

"To be honest, I was more afraid of the missiles, but now I worry about drones, too.

"You never think that this is going to happen to you."

Alice Boyko, centre, shelters with her family members in a parkade during an air-raid alert in Kyiv Friday after a jet-powered drone slammed into her building. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

Why are they so hard for air defences to intercept?

Ukraine's Air Force has said that it's intercepting about 60 per cent of the jet-powered drones, compared with more than 90 per cent of earlier models.

During air-raid alerts in Kyiv, mobile units armed with heavy machine guns and shoulder-mounted surface-to-air missile systems track threats in the sky. Above them, fighter jets, including F-16s, try to shoot the drones down.

Ukraine has also developed a large fleet of interceptor drones during the war. But the models currently in the field are not fast enough to intercept the jet-powered drones.

Borys Dolyna, a commander of a Ukrainian interceptor-drone company, told CBC News that the jet-powered drones move so quickly that they can be difficult to see even on the video feeds from interceptor drones. In some cases, he says, they appear as little more than a small pixel on the screen.

He says he's seen jet-powered drones several times, but their speed was so great that his team had no chance of intercepting them.

What is Ukraine doing about it?

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said the country is trying to accelerate production of newly designed interceptors capable of bringing down the Russian drones.

While officials have reported a number of successful interceptions, the technology is still in the trial phase.

Cory Woods, a Canadian working as a drone-interceptor pilot in Ukraine who is normally deployed in the eastern part of the country closer to the front, says drone warfare is evolving so rapidly that it has become what he describes as a "cat-and-mouse game."

Cory Woods, a Canadian from Alberta fighting in Ukraine, says drone battles in the war are turning into 'dogfights' and that the newer Russian jet-powered drones are a 'very challenging' problem. (Angela Johnston/CBC)

"Every time the enemy makes an innovation and alters their technology or their tactics, we have to respond and change ours," he said in an interview with CBC News from Kyiv.

"Once they pick up on that, they change it again, and so it's constantly going back and forth."

However, Woods says that if Ukraine is to seriously blunt Russia's ability to use strike drones across the country, its military must have weapons capable of targeting the factories where the drones are made and the sites where they're launched.

"There's no point in hitting the arrow if you let the archer live," he said.

"Russia has massive manufacturing capabilities. They've been gearing up for this for years. They've stockpiled a lot."

World.title: In UN address, Anand takes jab at 'great powers' disrupting global order
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In an address to the United Nations General Assembly on Saturday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the world is facing profound challenges in the global order as great powers walk away from economic co-operation, while state sovereignty is too often treated 'with disdain.'

State sovereignty 'has been treated with disdain,' Anand says in UN address

Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand says Canada's foreign policy is guided by establishing autonomy in strategic fields to limit superpower coercion, along with aspirations to lead middle powers.

"Great powers are walking away from global economic co-operation, dismantling economic integration," Anand said Saturday in Canada's annual address to the United Nations General Assembly.

"In the face of this rupture, Canada's goal is to achieve greater strategic autonomy," she said at the green marble dais.

Anand's speech echoed Prime Minister Mark Carney's rhetoric over the past year about middle powers forging deeper ties and working with countries on shared goals, including states that aren't close partners.

She said that involves emerging technologies, critical minerals, defence production and energy — as well as the rule of law and respect for sovereignty.

WATCH | Canada needs to 'meet the moment,' Anand says of global lansdcape: Foreign affairs minister says government needs to ‘meet the moment’ as global landscape shifts | Duration closed caption 18:02 Chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton speaks with Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand about her trip with Prime Minister Mark Carney to diversify Canadian trade ahead of Davos and the international response to his speech to the World Economic Forum. Plus, retired Dutch admiral Rob Bauer, who chaired the NATO Military Committee, discusses U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to annex Greenland, what tension remains in the alliance and how far the deal with NATO will go to subdue Trump’s desire for the U.S. to own the Arctic island.

"We are facing serious challenges in the global order," Anand said.

"We will lead other middle powers to act collectively and decisively, because middle powers are playing a key role in building the framework for the new international order — which is being established as we speak."

Anand used an analogy that she said comes from her roots in rural Nova Scotia.

"The tide does not wait; you must move with it."

Anand addresses the UN General Assembly on Saturday. (Eduardo Munoz/Reuters)

Anand said state sovereignty "has been treated with disdain" but that Canada will defend that principle, and work toward stability and common rules.

She said that is why Canada is calling for a just peace in Ukraine, self-determination for Palestinians and Israelis, and an end to hate-based violence.

"We were tragically reminded of the scourge of antisemitism again when a gunman carried out an attack on a synagogue in Belleville, Ont.," she told the UN.

"Canada is an open, pluralistic society, with a public square full of robust and civil debate. Our success is underpinned by this civility, by our democratic institutions and by respect for our differences," she said.

For the second year in a row, Anand spoke instead of Carney, who was at the UN from Monday to Wednesday but whose officials said he could not deliver Canada's address due to scheduling issues.

The UN schedules foreign ministers later in the rotation during the annual high-level week, with weekday, daytime speeches reserved for heads of state and government. Anand spoke late Saturday afternoon.

WATCH | Trump UN speech filled with threats: Trump delivers boastful UN speech brimming with threats | Duration closed caption 2:40 U.S. President Donald Trump delivered a boastful, combative speech to the United Nations General Assembly in which he mused over 'annihilating' Iran and even hinted at U.S. regime change in Cuba, prompting the Cuban delegation to walk out.

Anand also voiced support for the NATO alliance, amid an increase in warnings from European leaders about Russian hybrid attacks. She cited a recent defence agreement between Denmark, its autonomous territory Greenland and U.S. President Donald Trump.

"This agreement is yet another reminder that North America and Europe are stronger together. And as a founding member of NATO, our commitment to the transatlantic alliance is ironclad," Anand said.

To that end, Anand reiterated work being done to better secure the Canadian Arctic, saying this is occurring in lockstep with Indigenous Peoples.

Anand said Canada supports the International Criminal Court amid Washington's quest to dismantle the institution. Her comments come as Canadian critics argue Ottawa is not calling out American coercion, including the sanctioning of a Canadian judge for her work at the ICC.

She reiterated Canada's bid for a seat on the UN Human Rights Council, through a vote expected in one year.

Anand said Ottawa is pursuing "values-based realism" while advocating for democracy in Iran, the return of Ukrainian children kidnapped by Russia and work to end Haiti's gruesome gang crisis.

WATCH | Ukraine president addresses UN assembly: Zelenskyy targets Russia’s finances in UN speech | Duration closed caption 6:51 After nearly five years of war, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy addressed the UN General Assembly in New York, laying out Kyiv’s strategies to drain Russian resources and end the conflict.

Her speech mentioned gender equality, LGBTQ+ rights, Sudan's civil war, Hamas attacks on Israel, Israeli settler violence against Palestinians and safe approaches to artificial intelligence.

Anand also said Canada is ready to work with whoever UN members elect as their next secretary general, referring in French to the role in the masculine and feminine titles.

That comment followed the Trudeau government calling for a woman to be the next secretary general, in September 2024. The Carney government has not repeated that call.

World.title: Helicopter crashes outside Montreal, killing all 4 occupants
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A helicopter crashed Saturday afternoon in Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville, roughly 55 kilometres southeast of Montreal, killing all four people on board, police said.

Police are investigating after a helicopter crashed in a field near the Rang des Écossais off Highway 10 in the municipality of Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville on Saturday afternoon.

Sûreté du Québec spokesperson Brigitte Dorsainville said it happened at around 2:30 p.m. ET and the helicopter was on fire when first responders arrived.

Dorsainville said all four occupants on board were declared dead at the scene.

Sainte-Brigide-d'Iberville is located roughly 55 kilometres southeast of Montreal.

Police said Saturday evening that the helicopter likely encountered difficulties shortly after takeoff and crashed not far from its departure point, according to early information.

The SQ did not specify where the helicopter took off from.

The identities of the victims have yet to be released. Police said they believe the helicopter was a "private aircraft."

The fire has since been brought under control and the SQ's major crimes unit has taken over the file.

Transport Canada to appoint minister's observer

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada confirmed it has deployed a team of investigators to the crash site in a statement to CBC News.

Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon took to social media to express his condolences.

"My thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragedy," he wrote, adding that safety of civil aviation operations is a top priority for Transport Canada.

MacKinnon said the federal government is monitoring the situation and will provide necessary support. He also announced that Transport Canada will appoint a "minister's observer."

The observer's role is to monitor the response alongside the TSB and provide the minister with updates on the investigation. The observer can also help identify regulatory issues or safety deficiencies.

World.title: 'It's totally worked': B.C. man uses motion-activated zombie to scare bears away from garbage
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Squamish, B.C., homeowner is using a motion-activated Halloween decoration to scare bears away from his garbage bins.

Stephen Fryer has been dealing with bears constantly in the Brackendale neighbourhood, about 50 kilometres north of Vancouver.

"They're around us every single day," Fryer said.

Officials say animals are looking for food at lower elevations, after drought and wildfires at higher elevations have reduced their food sources. Fryer is one homeowner who is trying a creative way to keep the bears out of his garbage.

He stores his bins outside, as he does not have a garage, and the bears often tip the bins to get inside.

"The garbage, the handles have been like chewed off — not ripped off, chewed off, because they're trying to get into it," Fryer said.

Using a hook, Fryer reinforced the bins with a strap to his house to prevent the bears from tipping his bins. He does not have a garage and said the bears have tried to tear off his organic garbage bin. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)



Fryer decided to reinforce the bins to the side of his house with a bolt and strap — but that didn't work either.

"One of them finally figured out how to rip it out of the wall and pulled the ... I-hook out of the wall and off the strap," Fryer said.

His wife had asked for the Halloween decorations to be set up in September, and that's when Fryer got an idea to put a motion-activated zombie on top of the garbage bins.

"It absolutely scared the bear to the point where it it peed itself," Fryer said.

WATCH | Squamish man uses Halloween decorations to keep bears out of garbage: Squamish man uses Halloween decorations to keep bears out of garbage | Duration closed caption 2:13 A Squamish homeowner is using a motion-activated Halloween decoration to give a good scare. Stephen Fryer is hoping it will be enough to keep hungry bears away from his garbage in the Sea-to-Sky community.

Surveillance video shows a burly black bear sniffing the bins. Moments later, the zombie lets out a scream and pops up.

"Another one came by, and it went off," Fryer said.

Since the zombie was installed, the bears have been deterred.

"As funny as that is, it's totally worked," Fryer said.

Fryer said he believes a fed bear is a dead bear, and wanted to prevent them from getting into his garbage bins. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)

More than 30 bears killed

In Squamish, 90 tickets have been issued in connection with the wildlife attractant bylaw, which includes leaving garbage out and not picking up fruit from fallen trees.

"The number of complaints we're getting is pretty high each day," said Sgt. Chris Doyle with the BCCOS's Sea-to-Sky zone.

A total of 33 black bears were killed by BCCOS in 2025. In the first seven months of 2026, 33 bears have been killed. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)

The BCCOS said more bears are being seen at lower elevations.

"There's a lot less berries at higher elevations than there should be for a normal year, and that's likely driving a lot of the conflict," Doyle said.

Between January and July this year, conservation officers have responded to 13,672 calls regarding black bears in B.C.

At least 33 black bears have been killed in the first seven months of the year. September is often the deadliest month, with nine being killed last year.

Bears killed after entering stores

A bear wandered into a Squamish grocery store on Sept. 17 around 3 p.m. PT through automatic sliding doors.

Video captured the bear walking near the produce section of the store, and shortly after, it left through the sliding doors.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) said the bear also entered another business in the downtown area.

When officers arrived, the bear was outside the store. Officers tranquillized the bear and killed it.

An adult male black bear entered Stong's Market in downtown Squamish on Sept. 17. The B.C. Conservation Officer Service said the bear has a conflict history in the downtown area and was 'dispatched' due to public safety concerns. (Submitted by Tim Langille)

In a statement, the service said the bear was killed "due to public safety concerns".

A similar incident occurred in Hope recently when a black bear and its cub entered a pharmacy on Sept. 20 through automatic sliding doors.

BCCOS confirmed the mother bear was killed and the cub was released into a wilderness area.

"Bears that pose a serious threat to public safety, such as those that display a minimal fear of people or are conditioned to non-natural food sources, are not candidates for relocation or rehabilitation, as the risk is simply far too great," said the service.

Calls for change

Advocates argue that more can be done to prevent bears from being killed.

Holly Reisner with North Shore Black Bear Society said there has been an increased level of bear activity in B.C.

"These automated doors are just allowing bears to enter," Reisner said. "The bears are very attracted by any type of odour."

A black bear in a residential area of Squamish on Aug. 14 2026. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)

She's encouraging businesses to consider replacing the doors so bears cannot enter.

Lesley Fox, executive director of The Fur-Bearers, said a bear walking through a doorway should not be a death sentence.

"The question should be what the bear actually did, whether they posed a genuine threat, and whether reasonable non-lethal options were available," Fox said.

She suggests better security features be installed.

"These are preventable problems," Fox said.

World.title: Powerful storm causes widespread flooding, outages in northeast U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A slow-moving, powerful storm crept along the coast of the northeast U.S. on Saturday, producing high winds that knocked out electricity to tens of thousands while whipping up big waves and heavy rains that created dangerous conditions in some places.

Tens of millions of people were in the path of the nor'easter, which was forecast to affect the mid-Atlantic area and New England throughout the weekend. Around 100,000 customers in the region were without electricity Saturday.

The forecast showed no immediate reprieve. There will be "a lot of high winds, a lot of high tides and heavy rain possibility over the next few days for the northeastern U.S.," said Bob Oravec, lead forecaster with the National Weather Service in College Park, Md.

In the coastal New Jersey borough of Surf City, water flooded the streets and inundated some homes.

Kenny Formica, owner of Surf City Marina on the Jersey Shore, was trying to keep busy Saturday as he sat at home watching water rise inside his marina through surveillance cameras.

Waves pound the coast in Scituate, Mass., on Saturday. (Joseph Prezioso/AFP/Getty Images)

Water getting inside the building is rare, Formica said. The last time he remembers it happening was during Hurricane Sandy, which he said caused more than $4 million in damage to his business.

Ahead of the storm, Formica said workers secured dock lines, moved loose items and equipment out of harm's way and parked the marina's trucks and forklifts at the highest point of the property. By Saturday morning, even those were nearly surrounded by water.

Formica said he woke Saturday to messages from customers reporting missing boats and Jet Skis. He said one customer sent him a video around 4 a.m. showing his 25-foot (7.6-metre) boat after it had blown off its lift.

"This is like an 8,000-pound [3.6-tonne] boat and, you know, a $150,000 boat — just gone," Formica said.

In Edgewater, N.J., along the Hudson River, water had spilled into a large parking lot packed with cars. Video posted to social media showed one car nearly submerged, with just its sunroof poking above the water, as people moved other vehicles farther from the rising tides.

Storm upends flights, events

The storm forced a change of plans for many people. Hundreds of flights were cancelled at Boston Logan International Airport, as were the vast majority of flights at the popular Massachusetts tourist destinations of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket.

The Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs — both gearing up for the playoffs during the final weekend of the regular Major League Baseball season — had to shuffle the schedule for their three-game series. They played a double-header Friday in Boston to try to avoid the storm. Then MLB rescheduled their finale on Sunday to occur in Florida, at the home of the Tampa Bay Rays.

Meanwhile, Ed Sheeran cancelled his high-profile concerts Friday and Saturday at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Mass.

A nearly empty terminal at Boston Logan International Airport on Saturday. (CJ Gunther/Reuters)

Farther south, a highway closure on North Carolina's Hatteras Island scrambled Jayden Sink and Kimberly Laprad's Saturday wedding plans.

The Virginia couple had made it onto the island before the storm, but most of their roughly 45 guests were stranded on the other side of the closure, the Island Free Press reported.

A local campground offered a new venue, cabins and an officiant, and a DJ volunteered to provide music. Organizers invited anyone on the island to come celebrate with the couple Saturday afternoon.

East Coast officials urge caution

Nor'easters are not unusual as New England moves into fall, but this one is coming early in the season.

State officials along the East Coast urged people to use caution. Delaware Gov. Matt Meyer took to social media Saturday to implore people to keep an eye on the forecast.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said coastal flooding is the biggest threat, but the storm will also bring heavy rains, powerful winds and waves as high as six metres.

"The rain is underway and while it's only half an inch or so thus far, mark my words: Much more is coming," the governor said early Saturday.

World.title: Jacob Tremblay can relate to the Unabomber. No, really
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

It's uncomfortable to make any comparison — especially to the actor's face — between Ted Kaczynski, the mass-murdering ecoterrorist widely known as the Unabomber, and Jacob Tremblay, the cherubic former child actor behind films with titles as fuzzy and feel-good as Good Boys and Wonder.

There is some additional context here: After all, we are talking about the 19-year-old Canadian's portrayal of Kaczynski in the Unabomber Netflix movie, which dropped Friday.

But it still feels genuinely offensive to imply that there's any weightier parallel between the two. Which is why it's so surprising when Tremblay himself offers something like it, all on his own.

"I really had a hard time relating to Ted for the most part. But once I was there on set — the script is written so beautifully, of course you can really feel empathetic towards this guy," he says during a video call promoting the film.

WATCH | Jacob Tremblay on the message of Unabomber: Canadian actor Jacob Tremblay embraces his dark side in new film | Duration closed caption 1:54 From Room to his turn as Ted Kaczynski in Unabomber, Jacob Tremblay discusses his evolution as an actor, the awkwardness of being the youngest in the room and why the film's message about the importance of loving and valuing children is so critical.

It is a somewhat striking idea. Even as he points to the terrible, inexcusable crimes Kaczynski committed later, Tremblay keeps returning to his inability to resist relating to him.

"What I found, and what I really held on to," he says, "was the idea of being the youngest person in the room."

He's referring to the stranger-than-fiction beginning to Kaczynski's story — the near-singular plot focus of the Janus Metz-directed film. A math prodigy, the Chicago native was propelled to academic heights at Harvard University at just 16.

Through that early enrolment, he eventually became, at the time, the youngest-ever assistant professor at University of California, Berkeley (at which he would twice plant bombs, some 20 years later).

"You know, in this industry, I'm also often the youngest person there," Tremblay says. "So I could kind of relate to that feeling of awkwardness and not really fitting in."

Bigger backstory

The subject matter, of course, runs deeper than that. At Harvard, Kaczynski was also wrapped up in one of the most bizarre historical confluences of the last century.

After he was selected as a vulnerable test subject for what many have theorized was part of the CIA's top-secret MK-Ultra mind-control experiment, psychologist Henry Murray encouraged the young math student's nascent theories and developed his delicately blooming self-confidence.

He then had him strapped to a chair, wired with electrodes, and saw those same ideas mocked with surgical precision. The subjects were given, in Murray's words, "vehement, sweeping, and personally abusive" critiques that systematically tore them down.

Russell Crowe, left, appears as Henry Murray alongside Jacob Tremblay as Ted Kaczynski in Unabomber. (Philippe Bosse/Netflix)

In the movie, the goal is to win the Cold War. If America can figure out how to break young men's minds, they can theoretically then break the minds of captured enemy combatants. And if the goal is to learn how to destroy a person's self-worth, who easier to start with than a precocious, self-unassured child?

The resultant screaming and scheming villainy we get onscreen is an against-type performance for Tremblay, in what he calls a fun change. His filmography, he says, is built around his desire to never play the same character twice, while flitting between as many genres as possible.

But it's this one that has that personal parallel to return to. Because if you're to believe some sources, that was Kaczynski's rosebud, though he had long denied those sessions affected him much at all. Going by the film, they were a gross betrayal of the societal duty to protect children — producing a man who would go on to mail deadly letter-bombs to authority figures for decades.

Given that this role comes so soon after Tremblay's performance as a boy manipulated into armed resistance against the federal government in Sovereign , the pattern is hard to ignore. The theme of "a young, impressionable mind, driven by trauma, really, to do violent things," as Tremblay characterizes it, that he also deems Unabomber's key message.

"How important it is to treat children with love … and teach them how much value they have," he says. "Because on the flip side of that, if a child isn't loved as much, it's harmful and it causes violence. It really does."

It also comes as the industry in which he came up goes through another period of reckoning. Following former child actor Hayden Panettiere's overdose death earlier this year, Canadian actor Alison Pill wrote a New York Times op-ed calling child acting "extractive, exploitative and nonconsensual" while proposing it should be banned entirely.

Nicky, Ricky, Dicky & Dawn's Casey Simpson, among others, pushed back against a ban — but said propelling a child to stardom basically guarantees they will later feel like a failure, regardless of what they achieve as an adult.

WATCH | Jacob Tremblay on his obsession with filmmaking: Canadian actor Jacob Tremblay discusses his passion for filmmaking | Duration closed caption 0:48 Beyond acting, Jacob Tremblay reveals his deep love for the collaborative nature of being on set and his commitment to shadowing the crew to learn the art of storytelling from behind the camera.

Tremblay does not make this comparison so directly. And from his earliest memories, his relationship with acting was obsessive fascination: After his first film role in Smurfs 2 at five years old, he says he remembers his mother asking him if this is what he would like to keep doing. Not only did he say yes — he said he couldn't picture ever doing anything else.

That has stayed. After Tremblay briefly flirted with the idea of going to film school, director Mike Flanagan advised him to simply spend as much time as possible on set to prepare for his growing yearning to write and direct.

Even still, as clear as the path to acting may have been, the question of whether he consciously chose it is tougher to answer.

"It's hard to say, 'OK, well, I really wanted to do this when I was five years old,'" he says. "Because I'm sure I couldn't fully understand what it meant to be an actor, or in film, at five years old."

That leads to the difficult comparison: Kaczynski, the young man raised to an incredibly high level while still too young to handle it, is destroyed. Is that in any way similar to Tremblay's experiences — breaking into fame with his role in the film Room at just eight years old — even if he didn't know what he was signing up for?

"You try and find those parallels, for sure. And I can imagine how different my life would be without this career. It's hard to even think about, right?

"It makes me really feel for someone who — like Ted, who has so much talent at a young age and had so much potential," he says.

"I just really hope that people watching this movie can think about this going forward — about talented people, people with skills. And how they want to elevate them and bring them up in life, rather than using them."
