Lesotho, a small African kingdom that emits almost nothing, told the UN it needs climate money. Its prime minister also put a number on Lesotho youth unemployment: 38 percent.

Lesotho is a landlocked mountain country of about 2.4 million people, entirely surrounded by South Africa. Prime Minister Sam Matekane addressed the 81st UN General Assembly in New York on Friday, 25 September 2026.

Climate change is no longer a future threat but a present reality, he said, according to the UN’s official summary. Climate justice, he added, demands adequate and accessible finance from developed countries.

A roundabout on a main road in Maseru, Lesotho’s capital. (Photo: Wikimedia Commons / Paramente Phamotse, CC BY-SA 3.0)

A small country most outsiders cannot place

Lesotho sits high in southern Africa’s mountains; even its lowest point is well above 1,000 metres. It is one of only three countries in the world entirely enclosed by another state.

Its economy is tiny: about US$2.6 billion in 2025, World Bank data show. That is less than a thousandth of Britain’s economy, spread across roughly 2.4 million people.

The country lives on a few pillars. Garment factories sell clothing to the United States, and highland dams sell water to South Africa’s industrial heartland.

Diamond mines add export income. Wages sent home by people working abroad, mostly in South Africa, equal about a fifth of national output.

What Matekane said in New York

The speech built a single argument, according to the UN summary. Small, poor and peaceful countries keep their side of the bargain, and the rich world should keep its side.

Matekane said Lesotho has restored peace and stability after periods of political and security unrest. Its experience, he argued, shows that preventive diplomacy remains the best way to avert conflict.

On climate, he pointed to severe floods, droughts, land degradation and damaged roads and bridges. Least developed countries emit little, he said, yet carry a disproportionate share of the damage.

He asked developed countries for adequate and accessible climate finance and technology. He also named his government’s own tool, a Just Energy Transition Fund.

The fund is meant to expand renewable energy, create jobs and reduce the country’s dependence on work abroad. He also backed permanent African seats on a reformed UN Security Council.

The 38 percent problem

The most concrete number in the speech concerned Lesotho youth unemployment. It remains at 38 percent, Matekane said, urging partners to keep their official development assistance, or aid, promises.

He also called for fairer international financial institutions, such as the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Poor countries often say these lenders charge them too much and listen too little.

The source and age range behind the 38 percent figure are not clear. The International Labour Organization (ILO) modelled estimate for ages 15 to 24 was about 25 percent in 2025.

Either way, joblessness is a national emergency. In July 2025 the government declared a state of disaster over unemployment, as US tariffs hit its garment exports.

Why migration is personal for Lesotho

For generations, people from Lesotho have crossed into South Africa to work in its mines, farms and homes. Migration, Matekane said, is not an abstract concept for his country but a daily lived reality.

He said migration benefits both the countries people leave and the countries they reach. Protecting migrants’ dignity, regardless of status, is a legal obligation and a moral imperative, he added.

The main audience for that passage sits in Pretoria as much as in New York. South Africa has seen repeated campaigns against foreign workers, and many people from Lesotho work there without papers.

The money matters too. Personal remittances equalled about 21 percent of Lesotho’s economy in 2025, according to World Bank data.

Why water and clothing matter more than speeches

Lesotho’s real leverage is water and textiles. The Lesotho Highlands Water Project already sends water to the Johannesburg region and generates hydropower at home.

Its second phase, built around the Polihali Dam, is under construction and will raise those flows. Royalties from South Africa for that water are among the government’s steadiest incomes.

The garment industry employs tens of thousands of people, mostly women. It depends on the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA), a US scheme giving duty-free access to American shoppers.

AGOA lapsed in 2025 and received only a short renewal in early 2026. In early September President Donald Trump signed a further two-year extension, running to 2028.

What this means for expats, travellers and investors

Lesotho hosts a small foreign community in Maseru, the capital, mostly aid workers, dam contractors and clothing buyers. Nothing in the speech changes visa or business rules.

The practical message is that the government is shopping for climate and energy finance. Investors in water, solar and wind will find a receptive government, and labour-heavy projects will get political priority.

For travellers, the loti is pegged one-to-one to the South African rand, and rand notes are accepted. On 26 September 2026 both traded at about 16.30 to the US dollar, according to open.er-api.com.

What is not known

The size, backers and first projects of the Just Energy Transition Fund have not been disclosed. It is also unclear whether Matekane secured any new commitments from donors in New York.

No fresh figure for overall unemployment, as opposed to Lesotho youth unemployment, was given. The survey behind the 38 percent figure has not been identified.

World.title: Mozambique Petrol Shortage Returns to Coal Hub Tete, One Pump Left
World.content:
Mozambique · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country Mozambique, on Africa’s south-east coast, has about 36 million people and no oil refinery. Its economy, about US$22 billion in 2025 (World Bank), is smaller than Vermont’s.

— Why it matters Tete, a city on the Zambezi river in the west, is the country’s coal-mining hub. Mines, lorries heading to Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe, and motorbike taxis all depend on trucked-in fuel.

— Why now Petrol ran short again in Tete from Thursday afternoon, 24 September, into Friday’s public holiday. It is at least the third such squeeze in the city since early 2025.

— What happened Broadcaster STV found only one station selling petrol on 25 September. Drivers and motorbike-taxi riders queued for hours; other stations had taped off their petrol pumps.

— The numbers Official petrol price since May: about US$1.47 a litre. Street sellers in Tete charged up to about US$2.51 a litre in early September, close to double.

— What it means for you Visitors and firms in Tete should keep tanks full and allow for queues. Officials warn that street fuel is stored and sold in unsafe conditions.

— Still open No official has explained this week’s shortage or said when supply will return to normal. A crackdown on illegal sellers announced on 7 September is also untested.

A Mozambique petrol shortage has returned to Tete, the country’s inland coal hub. One filling station was left to serve the whole city.

A square in Pemba, northern Mozambique. Petrol shortages have hit several Mozambican cities, Tete among them, since 2025

The latest Mozambique petrol shortage struck Tete city from Thursday afternoon, 24 September, and lasted into Friday morning. Mozambique is a country of about 36 million people on Africa’s south-east coast, and it imports all the petrol it uses.

Tete sits on the Zambezi river, far inland from the Indian Ocean ports. It is the centre of the country’s coal industry and a staging post for lorries bound for Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

One pump for a whole city

A tour of the city by STV, a private Mozambican television channel, found only one pump selling petrol. Long queues of drivers and motorbike-taxi riders formed, and many waited several hours to fill up.

At the other stations, tape around the pumps signalled that petrol had run out. Some stations were selling only diesel, the report in the daily O País said.

The timing hurt. Friday, 25 September, was Armed Forces Day, a public holiday, when motorbike-taxi riders had hoped to carry more passengers and earn more.

O País said neither the authorities nor station operators had explained the cause. Nor had anyone given a date for supplies to return to normal.

A shortage that keeps coming back

This is not the first Mozambique petrol shortage to hit Tete this year. On Wednesday, 8 April 2026, only two stations in the city had petrol. The business daily Diário Económico reported it, citing the newspaper Notícias.

Diesel stayed available then, as it did this week. The city also went through a similar squeeze in March and April 2025, when local papers reported just one working pump.

During that 2025 crisis, Deputy Energy Minister Inocêncio Impissa said there was fuel in the ports. The problem, he said, was getting it to towns such as Tete.

The state fuel company Petromoc warned that a US dollar shortage was delaying bank guarantees and payments to foreign suppliers. IMOPETRO, which then bought fuel abroad for all Mozambican distributors, said stocks covered at least 22 days.

Prices jumped in May

On Wednesday, 6 May 2026, the government raised fuel prices after trying to hold them for about two months. It blamed the war in the Middle East, which pushed up world oil prices.

Petrol rose 12.1 percent, from 83.57 meticais (about US$1.31) to 93.69 meticais (about US$1.47) a litre. Diesel rose 45.5 percent, from 79.88 meticais (about US$1.25) to 116.25 meticais (about US$1.82).

The figures were announced by Paulo da Graça, chairman of ARENE, the national Energy Regulatory Authority. The regulator sets prices by region, so the pump price in Tete can differ slightly.

At the new petrol price, a US gallon costs about US$5.56. Conversions here use 63.82 meticais to the US dollar, the open.er-api.com rate on 26 September 2026.

President Daniel Chapo, visiting Tete the next day, called the rise inevitable. He said the crisis was global and Mozambique’s prices remained among the region’s lowest, the Portuguese agency Lusa reported.

The street market fills the gap

When pumps run dry, roadside sellers step in. In early September, Tete street sellers charged 140 to 160 meticais (about US$2.19 to US$2.51) a litre for petrol and diesel.

That is close to double the official price, O País said. In districts such as Mateus Sansão Muthemba, where supply has been irregular, some residents still rely on the informal trade.

On Monday, 7 September, Otávio Semba, director of the provincial infrastructure service, announced a multi-agency team to step up inspections. He said action would follow against anyone selling fuel without a licence.

Mr Semba also said the shortage of recent months was easing, as stations were again receiving regular deliveries. Less than three weeks later, the queues were back.

Officials worry about more than prices. Fuel kept in homes and roadside containers carries a real fire risk, and it is sold outside any legal controls.

Why Tete is exposed

Every litre of petrol sold in Tete arrives by road or rail from a coastal port. Any delay in unloading, paying for or trucking fuel shows up first in inland cities.

A Mozambique petrol shortage also weighs on the mining economy around Tete. Heavy mine vehicles use diesel, but many staff and small suppliers drive petrol cars and motorbikes.

Motorbike-taxi riders told STV that the shortage cut into their earnings. Hours in a queue are hours without passengers.

The wider scramble for Africa’s minerals and infrastructure is covered in Africa: The New Scramble. Reliable fuel supply is a quiet but real part of that story.

What to watch next

The first test is how quickly petrol returns to Tete’s pumps after the holiday weekend. A longer gap would push more drivers back to the street sellers.

The second is whether the government or the fuel companies explain the cause. In 2025, the answers pointed to dollar shortages and road bottlenecks rather than a lack of fuel.

The third is price. Any new adjustment by ARENE would change the gap between the pump and the roadside, which reached almost double in September.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Tete short of petrol again? No official cause has been given for the shortage that began on 24 September 2026. In a similar crisis in 2025, officials blamed transport bottlenecks and a shortage of US dollars for fuel imports. How much does petrol cost in Mozambique? Since May 2026 the official petrol price has been 93.69 meticais (about US$1.47) a litre. Street sellers in Tete charged 140 to 160 meticais (about US$2.19 to US$2.51) in early September. Is it safe to buy fuel from street sellers in Tete? Provincial officials say the trade is illegal and risky, because fuel is stored and sold outside legal conditions. A multi-agency inspection team was announced on 7 September 2026. What should travellers to Tete do? Fill up whenever a station has petrol, allow extra time for queues and check local news before long drives. Diesel has generally stayed available during the petrol shortages.

World.title: South Africa Could Meet Its Climate Targets Without Trying, Analysts Warn
World.content:
South Africa · ENERGY

Key Facts — The country About 65 million people, Africa’s most industrialised economy. Output was about US$427 billion in 2025, a little smaller than Denmark’s. Coal still generates most of its electricity.

— Why it matters Under the 2015 Paris climate deal, each country sets its own emissions cap, called a Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). Weak caps from big coal users make the global warming limits harder to reach.

— Why now On Friday 25 September, news site GroundUp and data publisher The Outlier argued the country could meet its caps without extra effort.

— What happened A draft national inventory, gazetted on 29 May 2026, puts net 2024 emissions at about 444 million tonnes. That is already inside the 2025 target range.

— The numbers Caps of 350 to 420 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent for 2030. The 2035 range is 320 to 380 million tonnes.

— What it means for you Investors and exporters should watch the gap. Loose targets could cost South Africa climate finance and expose its goods to carbon border charges abroad.

— Still open Whether the government tightens its range, and whether delayed coal-plant closures push energy emissions back up before 2030.

South Africa’s emissions targets may be met with almost no extra effort, a new analysis argues. Critics say that makes them a formality rather than a real climate commitment.

Kusile, a coal-fired power station run by the state utility Eskom in Mpumalanga province, in 2019 (Photo: JMK, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

South Africa is the most industrialised economy in Africa and still relies on coal for most of its electricity. That makes its climate pledges a test case for coal-dependent emerging markets everywhere.

On Friday 25 September, Cape Town news site GroundUp and data publisher The Outlier examined whether the country is on track. Their answer was yes, but mostly because the bar is low.

What the targets say

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, every country sets its own emissions cap, called a Nationally Determined Contribution, or NDC. South Africa’s cap for 2030 is a range of 350 to 420 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent.

Carbon dioxide equivalent is a common unit that converts all greenhouse gases into the warming effect of carbon dioxide. The 2030 range dates from the country’s updated NDC of September 2021.

In October 2025 the government submitted a second NDC with a 2035 range of 320 to 380 million tonnes. It keeps net zero as the goal for 2050.

Both ranges include the carbon that forests, grasslands and other land absorb. That detail matters, because the land has recently done much of the work.

Why the targets look easy to hit

The draft tenth national greenhouse gas inventory was gazetted for public comment on 29 May 2026. It puts gross 2024 emissions at about 478 million tonnes.

After subtracting about 33 million tonnes absorbed by land, net emissions come to about 444 million tonnes. That figure already falls within the range the country set for 2025.

Emissions peaked around 2008 and 2009 and have drifted down unevenly since. GroundUp notes the Presidential Climate Commission, a state advisory body, ties that fall mostly to economic stagnation and power cuts, not policy.

GroundUp also reports on government-commissioned research from the University of Cape Town. It found that existing policies could bring 2035 emissions to between 289 and 359 million tonnes.

That would put the country at or below its 2035 range without new measures. “The targets are so unambitious that we could hit them by doing what industry and government have already promised to do, without lifting a finger further,” said Déna Jansen.

Jansen is an analyst at Just Share, a Cape Town shareholder-activism group. She told GroundUp that “a target that doesn’t ask anything of you isn’t anything more than a formality.”

What independent analysts say

Climate Action Tracker is an independent research project run by Climate Analytics and the NewClimate Institute. It rates South Africa’s overall climate effort as “insufficient”.

In its December 2025 review, the tracker said the 2035 target implies a cut of 16 to 29 percent from 2022 levels. A fair share of the effort to hold warming to 1.5°C would need a 40 percent cut.

The tracker also found the 2035 range less ambitious, relative to a 1.5°C path, than the 2030 range. If every country acted like this, it says, warming could reach about 3°C.

It praised some features, such as an economy-wide target set in absolute tonnes. It also urged the government to narrow the ranges, which leave wide room for interpretation.

The coal problem underneath

The easy headline hides a harder reality in the energy sector. That sector covers fuel burned for power, industry and transport.

It emitted about 375 million tonnes in 2024, according to the draft inventory. That alone exceeds the lower end of the 2030 target.

After rolling power cuts eased in 2024, the state utility Eskom burned more coal and energy emissions rose. Total emissions fell only because land was estimated to absorb more carbon, an estimate the inventory treats with caution.

To reach the top of the 2030 range, net emissions must fall by about another 24 million tonnes. Reaching the bottom would require a cut of about 94 million tonnes.

The national electricity plan retires about eight gigawatts of coal capacity by 2030. GroundUp notes this depends on six gigawatts of new gas power being ready, which is uncertain.

Eskom has already pushed the closure of five coal stations to 2030, citing delays in private power projects. Each delay keeps more coal burning for longer.

The law behind the pledges

President Cyril Ramaphosa signed South Africa’s first Climate Change Act in July 2024. The law lets the government set sectoral emission targets and carbon budgets for large companies.

Critics say whether South Africa’s emissions targets bite depends on how firmly those budgets are enforced. Several key clauses were deferred when the law took effect in 2025, which slowed that process.

What it means for investors and exporters

Jansen warned that a credibility gap could cost South Africa access to international climate finance. It could also expose exports to carbon charges in the countries that buy them.

The European Union’s carbon border levy is the clearest example. It prices the emissions embedded in imports such as steel and aluminium. Charges apply to goods imported since January 2026, and importers start buying the certificates to pay them in February 2027.

For companies operating in South Africa, the carbon intensity of coal-based electricity feeds into the cost of almost everything they produce. Cleaner power would lower that exposure over time.

What to watch next

The first test is whether the government uses the Climate Change Act to set binding carbon budgets that go beyond current plans. Analysts will also watch the final version of the 2024 inventory.

The deeper question is whether South Africa’s emissions targets act as a ceiling or a floor. For now, the evidence suggests they describe where the economy is heading anyway.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are South Africa’s climate targets for 2030 and 2035? The 2030 cap is 350 to 420 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent. The 2035 cap is 320 to 380 million tonnes, with net zero planned for 2050. Why do analysts say the targets are too easy? Net 2024 emissions of about 444 million tonnes already sit inside the 2025 range. Climate Action Tracker says the 2035 goal means a 16 to 29 percent cut from 2022, against a fair 40 percent. Is South Africa on track to meet them? Not guaranteed. Energy emissions rose after power cuts eased in 2024. Closures of five coal stations have slipped to 2030 because new capacity is delayed.

World.title: Three Fibre Cuts in One Day Knock Out Mobile Service in Northern Ghana
World.content:
Ghana · EXPAT

Key Facts — The country Ghana, in West Africa, has about 35 million people and an economy of roughly US$114 billion, slightly larger than Luxembourg's. Its poorer north relies heavily on mobile networks.

— Why it matters Buried fibre-optic cables carry the traffic behind calls, mobile data and mobile money. Road works and illegal gold mining keep cutting them, and repairs cost operators millions.

— Why now On Saturday, 26 September, the communications minister said three separate routes feeding the north and the eastern Oti Region had been cut on the same day.

— What happened Cuts on routes run by MTN, Telecel and the state IT agency left 1,215 mobile sites without service or badly degraded.

— The numbers 694 older 2G/3G sites and 521 faster 4G sites were hit. Ghana logged 8,578 fibre cuts by early September, costing operators over US$20 million.

— What it means for you In the north, expect patchy calls, data and mobile-money payments during outages. Carry some cash and offline maps; a second network's SIM may help.

— Still open The regulator said repairs were under way on Saturday afternoon, but full restoration had not been announced. The causes of the three cuts are still being investigated.

Three Ghana fibre cuts on one day have degraded or knocked out 1,215 mobile sites in the north and the Oti Region. Calls, mobile data and mobile money in those areas all depend on those sites.

A Telecel office in Tamale, the largest city in northern Ghana, where mobile networks carry calls and payments (Photo: Samaru Samaru, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Ghana, a West African country of about 35 million people, runs much of daily life over mobile networks. Its communications minister, Samuel Nartey George, disclosed the outage on Saturday, 26 September.

The damaged routes serve the five regions of Ghana's north and parts of Oti, a newer region on the Togo border. They belong to two private operators and a state agency.

What the three cuts knocked out

The first cut hit the Kintampo–Buipe route, on the section run by MTN Ghana, at 04:19 GMT. MTN, a South African group, is Ghana's largest mobile operator.

The second struck the Wakawaka–Bamboi route, on Telecel Ghana's section, at 11:36 GMT. Telecel Ghana is the former Vodafone Ghana.

The third hit the Hohoe–Jasikan route at 11:25 GMT. That section belongs to the National Information Technology Agency (NITA), the state body that runs government networks.

Ghana keeps Greenwich Mean Time all year, so these are also local times. The first break came before dawn and the other two late in the morning.

How many sites went down

The minister said 694 2G and 3G sites and 521 4G sites were suffering service denial or significant degradation. That is 1,215 sites in all.

2G and 3G are older network generations that handle voice calls and basic data. 4G is the faster standard most people use for mobile internet.

Mobile money, the phone-based payment system many Ghanaians use every day, depends on the same towers. A mast that loses its fibre link can stay switched on yet carry no traffic.

The minister made that point at a government briefing on 7 September. “It's not because there is no service, but because the fibre has been cut,” he said.

Who is fixing it, and how fast

Teams from MTN Ghana, Telecel Ghana and NITA were sent to find the causes and restore service. They work under the National Communications Authority (NCA), Ghana's telecoms regulator.

The minister said he was confident restoration would begin within a few hours. He apologised to customers and residents in the affected regions.

His statement named no cause for any of the three cuts. The NCA said later on Saturday that repair work was ongoing, with no restoration timeline.

A problem that keeps coming back

Saturday's Ghana fibre cuts add to a long run of damage. Ghana had recorded 8,578 fibre cuts in 2026 by early September, the minister told the 7 September briefing.

He said operators had spent more than US$20 million this year repairing them. “That's money that without the fibre cut we could have used to build new sites,” he said.

Road building under the Big Push, the government's flagship road programme, caused 49% of the cuts. Illegal gold mining, known locally as galamsey, caused about 25%.

Private developers and other activities accounted for the remaining 26%. The full picture is in our earlier report, Ghana Has Counted 8,578 Fibre Cuts This Year, and Paid US$20m to Mend Them.

The yearly totals swing widely. The minister cited about 3,900 cuts in 2021, more than 10,000 in 2022 and about 8,000 in 2025.

Why the north is exposed

Ghana's five northern regions are Northern, Savannah, North East, Upper East and Upper West. Tamale, the largest northern city, lies hundreds of kilometres from the capital, Accra.

The minister said all three damaged routes supply capacity to those five regions. Losing three on one day leaves few backup paths for the traffic.

Oti, created in 2019 from part of the Volta Region, borders Togo to the east. The Hohoe–Jasikan route runs from the Volta Region into Oti.

What it means for residents, visitors and business

For anyone travelling in northern Ghana, patchy calls and data are a real risk during outages like this one. Carrying some cash and offline maps is a sensible precaution.

A SIM card from a second operator can help, though this incident hit routes used by several networks. Shops and firms relying on card terminals or mobile money should plan for downtime.

For investors, the figures describe a real operating cost. Every dollar spent on repairs, the minister argues, is a dollar not spent on new coverage.

The pattern is familiar across Africa, where fibre expansion often outruns protection of the cables. For a broader view, see Africa: The New Scramble.

What to watch after the Ghana fibre cuts

The first test is how quickly the 1,215 sites come back online. The second is whether the operators name a cause for each cut.

Beyond this week, the question is whether road builders and miners can be kept away from buried cables. The minister has framed every repair bill as money lost to new coverage.

Frequently Asked Questions

World.title: Kenya Lecturers Set to Strike as Universities Report US$770 Million Hole
World.content:
Kenya · BUSINESS

Key Facts — The country Kenya, East Africa’s business hub, has about 57.5 million people. Its economy, about US$136 billion in 2025 (World Bank), is roughly a thirtieth the size of Britain’s.

— Why it matters Kenya runs more than 30 public universities, funded by the state and student fees. Lecturers are public employees, and their pay is set through national union deals.

— Why now The lecturers’ union has called a nationwide strike from Friday 2 October. The government has not promised in writing to pay for a new 2025–2029 pay deal.

— What happened On 23 September, vice-chancellors told the pay regulator the state owes universities over Sh100 billion (about US$770 million) and cannot fund the deal.

— The numbers Budget estimates for 2026/27 left student loans and scholarships about Sh72 billion (about US$556 million) short, according to Treasury figures reported in June.

— What it means for you Foreign students, visiting researchers and partner institutions should expect disrupted teaching from 2 October. Companies relying on campus contracts face payment delays.

— Still open Whether the Treasury commits in writing before the deadline, and whether the strike goes ahead or is suspended by talks or a court.

Kenya’s public university lecturers plan to strike from 2 October. Their bosses say the state already owes them more than US$770 million.

Nairobi’s skyline seen from Nairobi National Park. The capital hosts several of Kenya’s largest public universities (Photo: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

Kenyan public universities say they cannot pay for a new lecturers’ pay deal without fresh money from the national Treasury. They told the state pay regulator that the government owes them more than Sh100 billion (about US$770 million).

Kenya is East Africa’s largest economy and a regional centre for higher education. Its lecturers are public employees, and their pay is agreed nationally between unions, universities and the government.

The warning lands days before a planned nationwide strike. The lecturers’ union says its members will stop work at midnight on Friday 2 October.

All figures here are converted at KES 129.5 per US dollar (open.er-api.com, 26 September 2026).

What the universities told the regulator

The Salaries and Remuneration Commission (SRC) sets and advises on public-sector pay in Kenya. It asked vice-chancellors to confirm what money they had to fund the 2025–2029 collective bargaining agreement, or CBA.

A CBA is a pay and conditions deal negotiated between employers and a union. The SRC said it needed the figures to judge whether the deal was affordable.

In a letter dated 23 September, the Vice-Chancellors’ Committee of public universities answered bluntly. Its chair, Professor Daniel Mugendi, said the state had never fully paid what it owed under the current funding model.

“The outstanding amount presently standing at over Sh100 billion,” he wrote, according to the Daily Nation. That is about US$770 million in unpaid state funding.

The vice-chancellors asked that the extra cost of the new deal be “fully funded by the National Treasury”. They said absorbing it from existing allocations would further strain institutions already in serious financial difficulty.

What the Sh100 billion figure measures

The Sh100 billion (about US$770 million) is the universities’ own estimate of arrears. It covers money they say the government owes but has not sent since the funding model changed.

That model is the Student-Centred Funding Model, introduced in 2023. It ties state money to each student admitted and each course offered, mixing government scholarships, loans and household contributions.

The SRC has told universities that the new pay deal will be funded through this same model. In practice, each university would pay lecturers from the money it receives per student.

The universities reject that. They say the per-student money already falls short of their existing wage, teaching and running costs.

Why the lecturers plan to strike

The Universities Academic Staff Union (UASU) represents teaching staff at public universities. It issued a seven-day strike notice at a Nairobi press briefing on 24 September.

Its secretary-general, Dr Constantine Wasonga, said the government had failed to honour a return-to-work deal signed on 5 November 2025. That deal ended an earlier strike by lecturers.

The union says the SRC told university unions on Monday 21 September that no written funding promise existed. Neither the Ministry of Education nor the Treasury had committed to pay the deal from the national exchequer.

Without that promise, the SRC could not issue the formal advice needed for the government to make a pay offer. The union says talks have therefore been “an exercise in futility”.

UASU also objects to any plan to fund lecturers from student fees or commercial income. It argues that academic staff are public officers whose pay must come from public funds, as Kenya’s constitution requires.

“We cannot have CBAs funded from students,” Dr Wasonga told the Daily Nation. Other public education workers, he noted, concluded their own 2025–2029 deals last year.

A wider squeeze on higher education

The pay fight comes on top of a hole in student financing. Budget estimates for 2026/27, reported in June, showed a large gap at two state funders.

The Higher Education Loans Board (HELB), which lends to students, was allocated Sh56.3 billion (about US$435 million). It needed Sh112.1 billion (about US$866 million), leaving a gap of Sh55.8 billion (about US$431 million).

The Universities Fund, which pays scholarships, faced a further shortfall of Sh16.26 billion (about US$126 million). Together, the two gaps come to Sh72.06 billion (about US$556 million).

Reports at the time estimated that nearly 689,000 students might not receive full support. That student-funding gap is separate from the Sh100 billion (about US$770 million) the universities say they are owed.

Parliament is also considering the Tertiary Education Placement and Funding Bill, 2026. UASU wants it to guarantee that lecturers are paid from the exchequer.

What it means for foreigners

A strike would halt teaching at Kenyan public universities, which host exchange students and joint research projects. International students should check with their university about exams and term dates.

Foreign partners running research grants or campus contracts should plan for delays. Universities already say they cannot meet existing obligations.

For investors, the standoff is a test of how Kenya handles public wage demands on a tight budget. Lecturer strikes have been a recurring feature of Kenyan campus life.

What to watch next

The first test is whether the Treasury issues a written funding commitment before 2 October. That would let the SRC advise on a pay offer and could avert the strike.

If no commitment comes, the strike is set to begin at midnight on Friday. Talks, conciliation by the labour ministry or a court order could still delay it.

The deeper question is who pays for Kenyan public universities: the state, students or the institutions themselves. The answer will shape the sector well beyond this pay round.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why are Kenyan university lecturers threatening to strike? The lecturers’ union says the government has not honoured a November 2025 return-to-work deal. No written Treasury commitment exists to fund the 2025–2029 pay deal from public funds. When would the strike start? The union says lecturers will stop work at midnight on Friday 2 October 2026, unless the government acts first. How much do the universities say they are owed? Vice-chancellors say the state owes them more than Sh100 billion, about US$770 million, in unpaid funding since the current model began in 2023. What is the Salaries and Remuneration Commission? It is the Kenyan body that sets and advises on public-sector pay. It must judge whether the lecturers’ pay deal is affordable.

World.title: South African Party Declares War on Broken Municipalities Before Vote
World.content:
South Africa · POLITICS

Key Facts — The country South Africa (64.7 million people) is Africa’s most industrialised economy, with 2025 output of about US$427 billion (World Bank), close to Denmark’s. Its 257 municipalities run water, power and roads.

— Why it matters Town and city councils, not the national government, deliver most tap water, electricity and refuse collection. Many are close to insolvent, so homes and firms often pay for generators, boreholes and private security.

— Why now Every municipal council is elected on Every municipal council is elected on 4 November 2026 . Parties are launching manifestos, and ActionSA, founded in 2020 by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, unveiled its own.

— What happened On Saturday 26 September 2026, Mashaba launched a nine-point manifesto at Johannesburg City Hall. He was “declaring war on broken municipalities” and promised reliable basic services.

— The numbers Ratings Afrika, a credit analytics firm, puts the 2025 operating deficit of 128 municipalities at R39 billion (about US$2.4 billion). That is up from R35 billion (about US$2.1 billion).

— What it means for you Anyone living, investing or running a business in South Africa depends on the local council for power, water and permits. Check a town’s service record before committing money there.

— Still open Whether ActionSA wins enough seats to govern, and with whom. It rules out pre-election coalition deals and says any partnership must follow the results and a written programme.

A South African opposition party has promised to fix the failing town councils that leave millions without reliable water and power. The pledge comes five weeks before nationwide local elections.

Johannesburg at sunset, with Ponte Tower and the Hillbrow Tower. ActionSA launched its manifesto at the city’s City Hall. (Photo: Frankbel, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

ActionSA, a South African party founded by former Johannesburg mayor Herman Mashaba, has declared war on broken municipalities. It launched its local election manifesto at Johannesburg City Hall on Saturday 26 September 2026.

South Africa’s 257 municipalities supply most water, electricity, roads and refuse services. Many are deep in debt, and all their councils face voters on 4 November 2026.

Who is ActionSA and what did it launch?

Mashaba, a businessman, ran Johannesburg from 2016 to 2019 and founded ActionSA in 2020. He now leads the party as president and is its candidate for Johannesburg mayor.

The party is outside the national coalition government in Pretoria. At local level, however, it already holds the mayoralty of Tshwane, the metro that includes the capital.

“Across South Africa, residents are witnessing their municipalities collapse around them,” Mashaba said in his speech. He said voters were “gatvol”, a South African slang word for fed up.

Mayoral candidates from several cities presented parts of the plan before Mashaba closed the event. The party published the text of his speech the same day.

A nine-point plan for failing councils

The first pledge is basic services: clean tap water, steady electricity, maintained roads, working sewers and regular refuse collection. The second is financial discipline.

ActionSA promises fully funded budgets, less wasteful spending, fair tariffs and better metering and billing. It says residents should be charged accurately for what they actually receive.

Further points cover merit-based appointments, transparent tenders and protection for whistle-blowers. The party also promises more municipal law-enforcement officers and stronger municipal courts.

For business, it pledges less red tape and clear turnaround times for municipal approvals. It also promises to restore run-down city centres and tackle hijacked buildings.

The remaining points cover informal settlements, public transport, illegal dumping and disaster readiness. ActionSA also says its councillors will scrutinise spending, whether in government, coalition or opposition.

The money behind broken municipalities

Independent data support the party’s diagnosis. In July, Ratings Afrika, a credit analytics firm, put the 2025 operating deficit of 128 municipalities at R39 billion (about US$2.4 billion).

That was up from R35 billion (about US$2.1 billion) a year earlier. The cumulative effect is a liquidity shortfall of R128.7 billion (about US$7.9 billion), meaning bills far exceed available cash.

The firm’s average financial sustainability score fell to 27 out of 100, from 31 in 2021. Rand figures here are converted at 16.30 rand per US dollar (open.er-api.com, 26 September 2026).

The Auditor-General of South Africa, the state’s independent auditor, paints a similar picture. Its 2024-25 report on municipal audits covers four financial years from 2021-22.

Over that period, councils ran up R24.12 billion (about US$1.5 billion) in fruitless and wasteful expenditure. Irregular expenditure, meaning spending that broke procurement or other rules, reached R145.21 billion (about US$8.9 billion).

Of that irregular spending, R40.14 billion (about US$2.5 billion) came in 2024-25 alone. Unauthorised spending, beyond approved budgets, totalled R118.13 billion (about US$7.2 billion).

Treasury has already squeezed the worst offenders

In July, National Treasury, South Africa’s finance ministry, withheld the July 2026 equitable share from 69 municipalities. The equitable share is the main national grant that pays for basic services.

Treasury cited unfunded budgets, unchecked irregular spending and unpaid bills to Eskom, the state power utility, and to water boards. The affected councils included the metros of Johannesburg and Nelson Mandela Bay.

On 28 July, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana said the money would be released to protect services. He stressed that the release was conditional and that the councils had not yet fixed their failings.

By that date, 20 of the 69 had received their full allocation and 21 a partial one. The remaining 28 had received nothing.

Coalitions will decide who runs the cities

In several big metros no party has held a majority since 2016, so coalition deals decide who governs. ActionSA says it will not enter pre-election pacts.

Mashaba said voters decide first, the programme comes second and political positions come last. Any coalition, he added, must have a clear programme and clear accountability.

Past coalitions in Johannesburg and elsewhere have collapsed repeatedly, with mayors replaced mid-term. That instability has itself slowed repairs to water and power networks.

What broken municipalities mean for business

For foreign investors, companies and residents, the municipal crisis is a direct cost. Unreliable water and power push firms towards generators, solar systems and boreholes.

Slow approvals delay building and property projects. ActionSA’s promise of fixed turnaround times would help, but only where it wins power or a strong coalition role.

The broader contest for capital across the continent is covered in Africa: The New Scramble. Reliable cities remain one of South Africa’s main selling points.

What to watch before 4 November

Other parties are launching their own manifestos in the coming weeks. Voters will compare ActionSA’s record in Tshwane with its promises for Johannesburg and other cities.

Treasury’s follow-up on the 69 councils will also shape the debate. The result on 4 November will show whether anger over services reshapes local politics.

Frequently Asked Questions

World.title: Western Sahara: US Backs Morocco and Says the Status Quo Cannot Last
World.content:
WESTERN SAHARA · DIPLOMACY

Key Facts The country. A disputed desert territory on Africa’s Atlantic coast, about the size of Colorado, with roughly 600,000 people. Morocco, a country of about 37 million, controls most of it and calls it its southern provinces.

A disputed desert territory on Africa’s Atlantic coast, about the size of Colorado, with roughly 600,000 people. Morocco, a country of about 37 million, controls most of it and calls it its southern provinces. Why it matters. Spain left in 1975. The Polisario Front, an independence movement backed by neighbouring Algeria, still wants a referendum. It is Africa’s last big unresolved decolonisation dispute.

Spain left in 1975. The Polisario Front, an independence movement backed by neighbouring Algeria, still wants a referendum. It is Africa’s last big unresolved decolonisation dispute. Why now. The mandate of MINURSO, the UN mission watching the ceasefire since 1991, expires on 31 October. The UN Security Council must renew, reshape or end it.

The mandate of MINURSO, the UN mission watching the ceasefire since 1991, expires on 31 October. The UN Security Council must renew, reshape or end it. What happened. On Friday 25 September, US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau backed Moroccan sovereignty after meeting Morocco’s foreign minister. “This status quo cannot be maintained,” he said.

On Friday 25 September, US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau backed Moroccan sovereignty after meeting Morocco’s foreign minister. “This status quo cannot be maintained,” he said. Who is involved. Washington, Rabat, Algiers and the Polisario. Trump adviser Massad Boulos says US-brokered talks have held three rounds without agreement.

Washington, Rabat, Algiers and the Polisario. Trump adviser Massad Boulos says US-brokered talks have held three rounds without agreement. What it means for you. Firms eyeing the territory’s ports, fisheries or green hydrogen get stronger US cover. European courts still limit EU trade deals there, so legal risk remains.

Firms eyeing the territory’s ports, fisheries or green hydrogen get stronger US cover. European courts still limit EU trade deals there, so legal risk remains. Still open. Whether the Council keeps MINURSO, whether Algeria joins the vote, and whether the Polisario answers Morocco’s autonomy plan.

One-stop reference Company Intelligence Every listed company in Latin America — financials, ownership and structure for 1,450+ companies across 26 exchanges, in one place. Browse the directory →

Washington has told Morocco the five-decade stalemate must end, five weeks before the UN decides whether its peacekeeping mission in the territory survives.

The United States has again backed Morocco’s claim to Western Sahara, a disputed stretch of desert on Africa’s Atlantic coast. Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau, the number two at the US State Department, made the point in New York on Friday, 25 September 2026.

He spoke after meeting Nasser Bourita, Morocco’s foreign minister, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. The timing matters: the UN Security Council must decide the future of its mission in the territory by 31 October.

What the Americans actually said

Landau left little room for nuance. The two sides “reaffirmed the centuries-old friendship” between their countries, he told reporters, as well as a shared vision for developing the region under Moroccan sovereignty.

He said the United States wants to work with Morocco and the other parties to end the conflict for good. The dispute has dragged on for more than 50 years, he added, and “this status quo cannot be maintained.”

He also called relations between Washington and Rabat, the Moroccan capital, the best they have ever been. The words were reported by Morocco World News and the Moroccan news site Yabiladi.

The meeting capped a busy stretch. On 16 September the United States, Morocco and Israel issued a joint statement backing Moroccan sovereignty and Rabat’s 2007 autonomy plan.

A US envoy admits the talks have stalled

A second US voice added a sober note. Massad Boulos, President Donald Trump’s special adviser for Arab and African affairs, met Bourita in New York earlier in the week.

Boulos then told the French broadcaster France 24 that three rounds of talks had produced no agreement. The rounds brought together the foreign ministers of Morocco, Algeria and Mauritania, plus Polisario leaders.

“We are awaiting the Polisario Front’s responses to the Moroccan autonomy plan,” Boulos said. He conceded that “we don’t have an imminent solution within reach.”

He was notably softer on Algeria, Morocco’s rival and the Polisario’s main backer. Algeria is helping, he said, but “cannot impose a solution” on the movement.

Boulos has kept that channel open. He was received by Algeria’s President Abdelmadjid Tebboune in Algiers on 13 September and met Algerian Foreign Minister Ahmed Attaf in New York on 24 September.

The October deadline

The UN mission, known by its French initials MINURSO, was set up in 1991. Its job was to organise a vote on independence that has never taken place.

The current rules come from Security Council Resolution 2797, adopted on 31 October 2025 with a US draft. It made Morocco’s autonomy plan the basis for talks and called genuine autonomy the most feasible outcome.

That resolution passed 11 to none, with China, Russia and Pakistan abstaining and Algeria not taking part. It extended MINURSO for one year, to 31 October 2026.

The Council must now renew, reshape or retire the mission. Morocco presented six parameters for the negotiations at the UN this week, but their full text has not been published.

Rio Times set out the stakes of the vote in its earlier report, UN Must Decide the Future of Western Sahara Mission MINURSO by 31 October. At the time, Washington had not spelled out its position.

Money as an argument

Rabat pairs diplomacy with concrete. Its development plan for the southern provinces, launched in 2015, started with 77 billion dirhams (about US$8.0 billion).

Dirham figures here use 9.59 dirhams to the US dollar, the open.er-api.com rate on 26 September 2026. The plan has funded the Dakhla Atlantic Port, a 1,055-kilometre expressway from Tiznit to Dakhla, and desalination plants.

In 2025 Morocco picked investors for six green hydrogen projects in its southern regions, worth 319 billion dirhams (about US$33.3 billion). The message to Washington is that recognition comes with investable projects attached.

What it means for foreigners

For investors, the US line lowers political risk on the Moroccan side of the dispute. Yet the EU’s top court ruled in October 2024 that EU trade deals with Morocco cannot cover the territory without its people’s consent.

For travellers, Laayoune and Dakhla, the main towns, are reached through Moroccan airports. Western governments warn against going near the sand wall that separates Moroccan and Polisario-held areas.

The other side of the table

The pro-independence camp is weaker but not silent. Namibia told the General Assembly this week that the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination must be respected.

The Polisario Front still holds roughly a fifth of the territory, east of Morocco’s sand wall. Its self-declared Sahrawi republic remains a member of the African Union.

Several African and Arab states, however, have opened consulates in Laayoune and Dakhla. That is a quiet way of recognising Moroccan control.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the United States will table a new resolution, or whether Algeria will take part in the October vote. The Polisario had not publicly responded to Landau’s remarks by Saturday.

Nor is it clear what happens to the mission’s staff if the Council lets the mandate lapse. Morocco’s six negotiating parameters also remain unpublished in full.

World.title: South Africa Suspends Over 50,000 Social Grants as Treasury Tightens Sassa Checks
World.content:
South Africa · Social Policy

Key Facts —Suspensions. Sassa suspended more than 50,000 social grants in the first quarter of the 2026/27 financial year after reviewing about 100,000 recipients under tightened National Treasury conditions. —Reason. Most suspensions were for non-compliance with review requirements — beneficiaries who did not respond to notices, missed review appointments, or whose income or circumstances no longer met the criteria. —Scale. Nearly 45% of South Africans rely on a social grant; the social assistance budget stands at R260 billion (about US$16 billion) for 2026/27. —Savings. Cross-checks against bank, tax, student-aid, payroll and prison data are saving the state about R44 million (roughly US$2.7 million) a month, according to Sassa chief executive Themba Matlou. —Not final. A suspension is not a cancellation: beneficiaries who complete their review within the notice period can have their payments reinstated.

South Africa’s welfare agency has cut off more than 50,000 social grants in a single quarter as a Treasury-driven verification drive tightens eligibility checks on a system that supports nearly half the population.

Sassa offices and paypoints handle reviews for millions of grant recipients across South Africa.
