World.title: Burnham’s AI agenda is already in disarray thanks to Trump
World.content:
Within the space of a week, however, Trump trashed any hopes that America will participate in global agreements on AI and POLITICO revealed that AISI’s usually privileged access to new AI models is now being delayed by the White House – which told leading AI firms OpenAI and Anthropic not to share their models with the U.K. until U.S. testers have finished ascertaining that they don’t pose a threat to American systems.

So if Burnham wants to stick to his plan of making U.K. the center for brokering international AI harmony he has to figure out how to bring the U.S. onside, or else press on without the U.K.’s closest ally.

When approached by POLITICO, a U.K. government spokesperson said: “The U.K. is a world leader in AI security, and the AI Security Institute continues to work closely with the U.S. government, international partners and leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.”

Special relationship problems

The U.K. already has a track record for convening global meetings on AI safety, but it has also tended to stick by the U.S. when deciding whether to sit out specific international agreements.

In 2023 the U.K. hosted the Bletchley Park Summit on AI safety, which produced an agreement on the opportunities and risks of AI signed by 28 countries, crucially including the U.S. and China.

However, at the Paris iteration of the summit in 2025 the U.K. declined to sign a new declaration on the ethical development of AI alongside the U.S.

World.title: Pope Leo XIV draws 800,000 faithful to Paris before emotional Lourdes pilgrimage
World.content:
France welcomed Pope Leo XIV to Paris on Saturday, as hundreds of thousands of people gathered along the Champs-Élysées to see the pontiff travel by popemobile to an outdoor Mass.

 

Waving flags and cheering, the crowds lined a 2-kilometre route from near the Arc de Triomphe towards Place de la Concorde. The Vatican estimated that about 800,000 people attended the Mass, exceeding the 600,000 who had registered in advance. Leo stopped repeatedly to wave to the crowd and bless children and babies before reaching the ceremony.

After the Paris Mass, Leo travelled to Lourdes, where he began his pilgrimage on Saturday evening with a silent prayer at the Grotto of the Apparitions. The site is associated with the visions reported by Bernadette Soubirous, then aged 14, in 1858. On his first full day in Lourdes, the pope walked barefoot part of the way to the sanctuary, greeting pilgrims and pausing to speak with families who had travelled from across Europe. He spent several minutes in personal prayer inside the basilica before meeting privately with shrine rectors and chaplains.

On Sunday, Leo is due to meet French bishops and celebrate another outdoor Mass at the sanctuary. He is also scheduled to meet sick people and seven survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy and personnel, before concluding the visit with a Rosary and torchlight procession.

World.title: Pope Leo arrives in Lourdes for Second Leg of France visit after historic Paris crowds
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV arrived in Lourdes on Saturday evening, landing at Tarbes-Lourdes-Pyrénées International Airport to begin the next stage of his four-day France visit, hours after drawing hundreds of thousands of worshippers to an outdoor Mass at Paris' Place de la Concorde.

 

Leo opened his pilgrimage in Lourdes with a prayer at the Grotto of the Apparitions, the site where Catholics believe the Virgin Mary appeared to Bernadette Soubirous in 1858 and one of the faith's most-visited shrines.

On Sunday, the pope will meet with French bishops before celebrating an outdoor Mass in the sanctuary's Prairie, followed by the Angelus prayer. In the afternoon, he is due to meet staff and sick people at the Accueil Notre-Dame and hold a private meeting with contemplative religious sisters.

Pope Leo XIV prays at the Grotto of the Apparitions of Massabielle, in Lourdes, France, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. AP Photo

Leo will also meet privately with seven survivors of sexual abuse by priests and other Catholic personnel — a moment likely to be closely watched by critics who argue the church has not done enough to address the issue. Some survivors' groups have criticised the Vatican's choice to meet with individuals rather than representatives of established advocacy organisations. The visit to Lourdes will close Sunday evening with one of the sanctuary's signature rites, a Rosary recitation and torchlight procession.

A record-breaking mass in Paris

Leo's arrival in Lourdes capped a whirlwind of roughly 32 hours in the French capital, where he paraded through central Paris in his popemobile, addressed UNESCO's headquarters, and celebrated an open-air Mass that drew far more people than organisers had anticipated.

Around 600,000 people had registered in advance for Saturday's Mass at Place de la Concorde, but the Vatican estimated actual turnout at roughly 800,000 — about 200,000 more than expected. Some 2,400 priests and deacons and about 100 bishops took part in the service.

Faithful along on the Champs Elysees avenue follow a Mass celebrated by Pope Leo XIV at the Place de la Concorde in Paris, Saturday, Sept. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Thomas Padilla) AP Photo

As the pope travelled down the Champs-Élysées toward the Concorde, crowds lined a security perimeter stretching nearly two miles from the square past the Arc de Triomphe. Metro stations along the route were closed as part of the security operation, and chants of "Leo! Leo!" rang out as he passed. Parents lifted babies and young children toward the popemobile throughout the ride, and the pope reached out to touch dozens of them.

In his homily, Leo urged the faithful not to keep their beliefs private but to let their faith be visible enough to bring comfort to others.

French President Emmanuel Macron did not attend Saturday's Mass and is not expected to attend any of the pope's Masses during the visit. His wife, Brigitte Macron, was present, alongside Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.

A test of faith in a secularising country

The visit has doubled as a message to French Catholics to hold onto their faith even as church attendance declines nationally. Leo began the trip on Friday with a visit to the newly restored Notre-Dame Cathedral, the first papal visit there since the fire that devastated the building in 2019.

Speaking earlier Saturday at the Catholic Institute of Paris, the pope said he had been struck by the growing number of adults converting to Catholicism in France, describing it as a small but resilient flame worth protecting. Adult baptisms in the country have nearly tripled since 2016, reaching about 13,000 this year — though the increase, also seen recently in Spain, hasn't reversed the broader decline. France recorded 513,000 baptisms in 1980, compared with 186,000 in 2024.

Observers noted that Saturday's crowds and their enthusiasm echoed other moments of mass celebration on the Champs-Élysées in recent decades, including France's World Cup victories in 1998 and 2018.

Many of those who turned out, organisers said, were not just practising Catholics but those who came simply to witness the event.

World.title: Azerbaijan marks its Remembrance Day looking forward to a future of peace
World.content:
Azerbaijan marks the annual Remembrance Day with a nationwide tribute to the soldiers who lost their lives during the 44-day war in 2020, but also with a renewed hope brought by the historic peace between Azerbaijan and Armenia, after decades of bitter conflict.

 

The events of that autumn in 2020 changed the 30-year status quo generated by the dissolution of the Soviet Union which had brought decades of deep-rooted conflict and regional stagnation between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

The cessation of hostilities in November 2020 reshaped the strategic landscape of the region establishing a new political framework which culminated with the two former rivals reaching a peace agreement which includes borders delimitation, the start of a reconciliation process, but also kickstarting an economic expansion and launching new regional transport corridors for global opportunities.

Six years after the end of the war, this legacy has transitioned from post-war recovery into active regional integration and development. The true dividends of this hard-won peace are now materialising not just in diplomatic halls, but on the ground, fundamentally altering the economic landscape of the South Caucasus.

Armenia's Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, left, and President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, right, shake hands during a Board of Peace meeting in Washington, February 2026 Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Opening the railways

The most visible sign of this evolving relationship is the movement of rail freight, and following the lifting of transit restrictions by Azerbaijan in late 2025, a steady flow of cargo has travelled towards Armenia.

Routed primarily via Azerbaijan Railways from Bilajari station towards the Boyuk Kasik junction at the Georgian border, shipments move into Armenia.

This transport artery facilitates both direct bilateral sales and international transit and has established a new economic dynamic.

According to state customs data, direct exports from Azerbaijan to Armenia between January and August 2026 reached over $17 million (over €15 million). While this accounts for just 0.08% of Azerbaijan's total global exports, the physical volume is substantial.

Direct shipments have included approximately 17,000 tonnes of diesel fuel and roughly 5,000 tonnes of AI-92 and AI-95 petrol.

The trade even saw a brief reciprocal exchange, with Azerbaijan recording a symbolic $960 in imports from Armenia in March.

The route also serves as a vital corridor for third-country transit.

Recent freight shifted around Azerbaijani territory includes nearly 60,000 tonnes of agricultural products, such as wheat, barley, and buckwheat, alongside more than 9,000 tonnes of fertiliser and over 1,400 tonnes of propane gas.

Industrial materials are also moving steadily through the corridor, comprising 1,114 tonnes of coal, 608 tonnes of timber, and 133 tonnes of aluminium.

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, left, and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev attend Outreach/BRICS Plus format session at the BRICS Summit October, 2024

A new era of digital transit

Beyond physical rail freight, bilateral cooperation has achieved significant progress in the digital domain. The two countries have implemented a digital transit agreement between national operators AzerTelecom and Telecom Armenia.

Under this arrangement, a portion of Armenia’s international internet traffic is routed across Azerbaijan. Both companies noted that such agreements aim at "diversifying connection routes in the region" and "increasing the reliability of telecommunication networks".

This cooperation also aligns with broader regional infrastructure goals, including the Digital Silk Way project. In return, the arrangement allows Azerbaijan to transmit data traffic to its Nakhchivan exclave directly through the Armenian telecommunications network.

Restoring infrastructure

Both countries are laying the groundwork for expanding multi-directional transit. While physical exports from Armenia across Azerbaijani territory are not yet active, official frameworks anticipate future integration.

The Armenian government’s state programme for 2026 to 2031 outlines plans to build full-scale commercial ties with Azerbaijan and unblock regional transport links following a final peace treaty.

Meanwhile, regional transport infrastructure is being restored rapidly, including ongoing railway construction in the Ordubad direction.

Once a comprehensive peace agreement is finalised, the full opening of transport corridors is expected to enable Armenia to utilise Azerbaijan's transit network for broader international trade, establishing a fully interconnected economic corridor across the South Caucasus.

A historic summit in Washington

This deepening economic integration is underpinned by key high-level diplomatic milestones.

The strategic framework for the current bilateral political process was formalised on 8 August 2025 during a historic trilateral summit in Washington.

Hosted at the White House by US President Donald Trump, the meeting brought together Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev and Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan who signed the joint declaration for the comprehensive peace agreement.

President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev and PM of Armenia, Nikol Pashinyan shake hands as US President Donald Trump sits between them, 8 August 2025 Copyright 2025 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.

Building trust towards reconciliation

Meanwhile, the normalisation process is also extending beyond state-level diplomacy and taking root at the community and institutional levels.

Armenia supported Azerbaijan’s successful bid to host the UN Climate Change Conference (COP29) in Baku, while Azerbaijan supported Armenia’s candidacy for membership in the Eastern European Group COP Bureau.

In April 2026, the "Peace Bridge" format facilitated a fourth round of dialogue between Armenian and Azerbaijani civil society representatives in the town of Gabala.

Participants from both nations emphasised the importance of crossing borders and maintaining consistent dialogue to prepare their respective societies for the eventual outcomes of a final peace treaty.

Furthermore, civil engagement is progressing alongside the joint development of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit corridor through Armenia's Syunik region that connects Azerbaijan directly to its Nakhchivan exclave.

On 18 September 2026, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan was awarded the Hessian Peace Prize during a formal ceremony at the Hesse State Parliament in Wiesbaden, Germany.

The award recognises efforts to establish peace in the South Caucasus and has provided a platform for a notable diplomatic gesture.

During the ceremony, Pashinyan publicly expressed his gratitude for the peace process with Azerbaijan. Acknowledging the leaders' joint efforts, the Armenian prime minister stated that the Azerbaijani president was "equally deserving of this award" for his contribution to regional peace.

World.title: Oktoberfest halfway through: Is closure of the Wiesn back on the cards?
World.content:
The traditionally particularly busy "Italian weekend" is just around the corner and on 26 and 27 September will mark the halfway point of this year's Oktoberfest. After the extreme overcrowding last year, organisers are looking with particular attention at visitor flows in 2026.

 

On the middle Wiesn Saturday in 2025, the festival grounds reached their capacity limits, so that access to the Theresienwiese had to be temporarily closed due to overcrowding.

In parts of Wirtsbudenstraße there was such a crush at the time that nobody could move forwards or backwards – visitors spoke in videos of "nightmare" scenes on the verge of a mass panic.

The upcoming weekend is traditionally referred to as the "Italian weekend", as tens of thousands of guests from the neighbouring country flock to Munich at this time. According to the Oktoberfest press office, the term has developed historically over decades, without a specific historical trigger or an exact start year.

The mass influx is fuelled above all by the short journey from northern Italy over the Brenner Pass by car, coach or motorhome. Regional public holidays and long weekends in the Italian September calendar also offer the ideal opportunity for a short break. The Italian flair on the festival grounds is unmistakable: Munich daily newspapers often print their front pages in two languages on these days, and Italian Carabinieri as well as fire crews from Bolzano support Munich police directly on site with patrols and communication.

To prevent critical overcrowding like last year in good time, the city is increasingly relying on a network of surveillance cameras and AI-based crowd-tracking software.

Incidentally, those who made it to the Wiesn stayed longer. An analysis of mobile phone data showed that visitors remained on the festival grounds an average of 15 minutes longer than in 2025. The absolute peak period in the first week was between 17:00 and 18:00 each day.

World.title: "Respectable women in long skirts": Tajani under fire in memes and international media
World.content:
Despite having apologised and despite Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's attempts to put an end to the controversy that erupted during the week, Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani's comments about choosing a life partner on the basis of criteria such as the length of the skirt she should wear continue to spark negative reactions against the minister, crossing national borders and turning him into the subject of memes shared on social media.

 

During a speech at an event organised last week, Tajani said he would advise marrying serious women who wear "longer skirts". "Perhaps less eye-catching, but more reliable, more serious, someone who will be a good mother, who will remain faithful to the love she seals with marriage," the foreign minister went on, explaining that he would always choose "the pretty, serious, credible one, who keeps the family together, who is there, who you know will always have an answer and is there when you call."

After facing a torrent of criticism, Tajani apologised. "I am very sorry that some of my remarks, taken out of a much more wide-ranging speech, have been misunderstood. I apologise if some people felt offended by what I said, but I have never intended to offend women, I have never done so in my life, either in private life or in public," Tajani said on the sidelines of his visit to New York for the UN General Assembly. But it was not enough.

The criticism of Tajani

The minister's remarks have been roundly condemned by opposition parties, trade unions and the Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI). Female senators from the Democratic Party, Italia Viva, the Greens and Left Alliance, the Five Star Movement and the Autonomies group gathered at Palazzo Madama wearing skirts.

"This is an act of freedom to say that we are free to dress as we wish. We believe that women's freedom is measured by every act of freedom, including the length of a skirt or any other choice that women want to make without being judged by men," said Italia Viva group leader Raffaella Paita, who came up with the idea.

"His words are proof of the intrinsic and unconscious patriarchy, so much so that Minister Tajani then tried to justify himself and apologised, but his justification is even worse. They do not realise what they are saying because it is ingrained in them. Instead we need to show that those remarks are unacceptable," said Simona Malpezzi of the Democratic Party, who posted the group's photo.

The initiative also came in response to comments by the leader of Futuro Nazionale, Roberto Vannacci, who, weighing in on Tajani's words, said: "Between a woman in a long skirt and a woman in a short skirt, I always prefer a woman without a skirt," added the former general. "I do not care about silly criticism. I love women, a gift of the universe," Vannacci later wrote on social media, posting images of the statues of the Venus de Milo and the Venus of Candia, both half-naked.

Many other opposition MPs also posted pictures of themselves wearing skirts, as did some men, including Florence city councillor and Democratic Party member Andrea Ciulli, who shared a photo of himself created with artificial intelligence in which he is wearing a skirt, with the caption "The length of a skirt does not measure a woman's worth, her freedom does".

"Tajani is now a meme, he is no longer a minister," said former prime minister and Italia Viva leader Matteo Renzi, piling on the pressure. Memes depicting the minister in women's clothing have been circulating, and have also been picked up by international media including CNN and the BBC.

Unions and CEI against Tajani's comments

The CGIL union also issued a stinging response. "Pitting the 'flashy' woman against the 'serious', 'reliable' and 'good mother', even invoking the length of her skirt, revives an old model of society in which it is still men who decide how women have to be in order to be considered respectable," the union said, adding: "Institutions have a responsibility: to remove stereotypes and obstacles to the full participation of women, not to reproduce the former and weaken the safeguards against the latter. Starting with making the full right to work effective by overcoming existing pay and career disparities. The quality of democracy is also measured by the power that women can really exercise."

The CEI's secretary, Monsignor Giuseppe Batur, responding to a question about the remarks made by Tajani and Vannacci, said: "Every word, every way of looking at women must be filled with respect and admiration; for us Christians the first place where the Word became flesh is a woman's womb, and for those who have faith this forever shapes the way we look at women." "Through our gaze we enter into a relationship with others; towards men, women, children and older people we must show respect, and towards women that respect must be at its highest, given the extent to which they can be the object of superficial glances," Batur added.

Meloni and the majority defend Tajani

Democratic Party leader Elly Schlein in recent days called on Prime Minister Meloni to comment, but Meloni downplayed Tajani's words and urged people not to "blow them out of proportion", saying they were just an "awkward phrase". "I have already answered, I would not exaggerate and I do not think we should make it the main topic of Milan Fashion Week," Meloni said while attending an event during Fashion Week in Milan.

Tajani was later defended by other members of the government, including Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, who wrote on X: "Tajani did not tell women how they should dress, he explained, as a father, what kind of partner he would recommend to his son, on the basis of his own upbringing and values. Anyone who feels offended, in one case or the other, is naturally free to say so. But the fact that an opinion jars with someone does not necessarily mean that it limits their freedom. Deciding instead to silence someone else means failing to respect their freedom."

"You talk about women's freedom, but why not fight for those women who are prisoners of their husbands and cannot take part in the life of the country? For religious reasons you accept that there are slaves in Italy, including polygamy. Consistency would require you to join us in fighting against the burqa," said Stefania Pucciarelli of the League.

World.title: Fat Bear Week returns as Alaska's biggest bears compete for the crown
World.content:
Sixteen bears are competing in this year's tournament, with last year's winner, Chunk, officially known as Bear 32, hoping to defend his title. Chunk reportedly weighed 544 kilograms when he won last year's contest.

 

Now in its 12th year, Fat Bear Week invites people around the world to vote for the bear they believe has been most successful at gaining weight ahead of hibernation.

Speaking to the Associated Press, Mike Fitz, a resident naturalist at Explore.org, explained that the competition highlights how crucial weight gain is to the bears' survival. Because they do not eat during hibernation, they must consume enough food in roughly six months to sustain themselves for the entire year.

But choosing a winner is not simply a matter of identifying the heaviest bear.

"This year, I think it's pretty tough to predict. I mean, there's a few bears that are larger than others, but it's not necessarily about body mass alone. We want people to consider the bears' stories as well, because getting fat means different for a big adult male who's maybe trying to dominate access to the best fishing spots at Brooks Falls," he explains.

Why getting fat is essential for survival

Katmai National Park and Preserve is home to approximately 2,200 brown bears. The competition, which began in 2014, was designed to raise public awareness of the animals and their remarkable preparations for winter.

Adult male brown bears typically weigh between 270 and 410 kilograms, although particularly large males can exceed 450 kilograms after feeding extensively on salmon. Females are generally about one-third smaller.

During hibernation, the bears neither eat nor drink and can lose around a third of their body weight.

Fitz also highlighted the importance of healthy salmon populations to the bears' survival. He pointed to the abundant sockeye salmon runs in Alaska's Bristol Bay region as an example of what healthy river ecosystems can support.

According to Fitz, the region demonstrates why protecting and restoring salmon populations elsewhere in North America is so important, particularly in areas where salmon numbers are declining.

Beyond celebrating the bears' impressive size, the competition also offers an insight into their daily lives.

Fitz said viewers can observe everything from bears enjoying a successful fishing session and playing with one another to the difficulties faced by mothers trying to feed their cubs or coping with the loss of their young.

"We get to see their their joys when they have a belly full of fish, we get to see them having fun when they're playing with another bear in a friendly manner and we get the see the real hardships that they experience the mother struggling to feed their cubs, the mothers who maybe lose cubs for instance".

The competition's final round is scheduled for Tuesday, 29 September, when the public will decide which bear takes this year's title.

And for those who can't get enough of Fat Bear Week, Google has added an interactive surprise: Searching for "Fat Bear Week" brings up a small bear on the screen that users can feed salmon, helping it gain enough weight to survive winter hibernation.

World.title: Six dead after explosion causes building to collapse in central Athens
World.content:
Six people have been confirmed dead after a building where they were staying collapsed in Athens.

 

The building collapsed following an explosion on Friday morning in the Plaka district of the Greek capital.

Four US tourists had been staying on the first floor of the building while a couple - a 78-year-old British man and a 77-year-old Greek woman - lived on the second floor. The process of formally identifying the bodies is ongoing.

Fire crews are now winding down the operation after hours of searching through the rubble.

Around 30 firefighters, using six vehicles, took part in the search, with three specially trained dogs also deployed.

Rescue teams used geophones to try to detect possible sounds beneath the rubble, as well as specialist cameras to pinpoint locations where people might be trapped.

The explosion occurred shortly after 7:30 am on Friday and also caused damage to neighbouring properties and vehicles.

Two women were freed from a nearby building on Friday and transported to hospital. Another person suffered minor injuries from flying debris.

Authorities are meanwhile working to determine the cause of the blast.

The fire service, police, and medical crews remain at the scene, with a team from the Arson Crimes Division also investigating the incident.

World.title: Adieu, dear listeners!
World.content:
This week is the final Sound Kitchen program, and it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listeners Corner’s” with Paul Myers, plus a special musical choice from me to you. Just click the “Play” button above to join the feast!

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October, and today’s show is our last meal together. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 7 February: I asked you a question about the 68th annual Grammy Awards that took place on 1 February. You were to re-read our article “French DJ wins Grammy for Lady Gaga remix” and send in the answer to this question: Which six artists were given “Lifetime Achievement” awards?

The answer is, to quote our article: “On Saturday evening, Nigeria's Fela Kuti was posthumously awarded a lifetime achievement award, becoming the first African artist to receive the distinction.

The king of Afrobeat was one of several artists to receive the award, including Cher, Whitney Houston, Carlos Santana, Paul Simon and Chaka Khan.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question, suggested by RFI Listeners Club member Alan Holder from the English Isle of Wight. Alan’s question was: “What would be your ideal gift from your best friend or spouse? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Mohamed Elsayed Abd Elraheim from Elsharkya, Egypt. Mohamed Elsayed is also this week’s bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club members Hans Verner Lollike from Hedehusene, Denmark; Helmut Matt from Herbolzheim, Germany; Kashif Khalil from Faisalabad, Pakistan, and last but not least, gentle Debashis Gope from West Bengal, India.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 14 February: That week, I asked you a question about the Benin Bronzes, the trove of Nigerian sculptures and artifacts that were looted by colonial powers.

One of the most well-known organizations working for the return of these works is in Nigeria: it’s the National Commission for Museums and Monuments – the NCMM- which requested the return of bronzes from Britain that were looted from the Kingdom of Benin during the British Benin Expedition of 1897. Some of the sculptures date to the fourteenth century, but the bulk of the collection dates to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

And that week, the NCMM had a win, as my good colleague Melissa Chemam noted in her article: “Cambridge University museum set to return Benin bronzes to Nigeria”.

You were to re-read Melissa’s article and give the details of the artefacts to be returned. What did Melissa name in her article about the Benin Kingdom artworks that went home to Nigeria?

The answer is, to quote Melissa: “Among the returned bronzes that will travel in the coming months are wood and ivory sculptures, as well as commemorative heads of King Oba and Queen Mother Lyoba Idia.

The term ‘Benin bronzes’ refers to objects crafted from brass and ivory as well as bronze, which were seized during the colonial-era military expedition.”

The bonus question you answered that week was: “What do you know after all these years? What have you found are important life truths?

The winners are: Faithful RFI Listeners Club member Jayanta Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Jayanta is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners are RFI Listeners Club member Nasyr Muhammad from Katsina State in Nigeria, as well as RFI English listeners M. Ganesan from Goa, India, and three listeners from Bangladesh: Rafiq ul Islam from Naogaon, as well as Abdul Mannan and Mahfuza Akhter, both from Chapainawabganj.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Minor Swing” by Django Reinhardt and Stephane Grapelli, performed by the composers with Le Quintette Hot Club de France; "Water No Get Enemy" by Fela Kuti, performed by Fela Kuti and Africa ’70; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer; “L'hymne à l'amour” by Edith Piaf and Marguerite Monnot, sung by Edith Piaf, and “I Wish You Love” by Charles Trenet and Léo Chauliac, performed by Laufey with the Iceland Symphony Orchestra conducted by Hugh Brant.

World.title: Podcast: Pope in secular France, vultures and farmers, first divorce law
World.content:
With its strong commitment to secularism, France is not an obvious place for Pope Leo XIV to stage an appearance, but his visit is drawing interest from Catholics and non-Catholics alike. After nearly disappearing from France, vultures are making a comeback, but their return has created new tensions with farmers. And France's revolutionary first divorce law from 1792.

Advertising

Some 800,000 people have signed up to see Pope Leo XIV on his first official visit to France, a secular country where the Catholic faith no longer dominates. Francois Mabille, head of the Geopolitical Observatory of Religion at the French Institute for International and Strategic Affairs, looks at why France is of interest to the Vatican, and young people of different religions talk about what Pope Leo means to them. (Listen @0'00)

Vultures all but disappeared from France by the 1940s as people sought to eradicate the scavenger birds. A programme to reintroduce the four European vulture species to the Grands Causses plateaux in the southern Massif Central has been sucessful – so successful that some farmers say there are now too many. We visit a vulture feeding station to explore the close relationship between vultures and agriculture, and the tensions that arise with the return of wild species. (Listen @20'00)

In 1792, France introduced one of Europe’s first and most liberal divorce laws, as part of a broader revolutionary effort to enact liberté, egalité et fraternité in the family itself. (Listen @14'00)

Episode mixed by Cecile Pompeani.

Spotlight on France is a podcast from Radio France International. Find us on rfienglish.com, Apple podcasts, Spotify or your favourite podcast app.

World.title: Spain: Thousands protest in Madrid against housing crisis
World.content:
Tens of thousands rallied in the Spanish capital after an 87-year-old woman was dramatically evicted from her home this week. Protesters called for measures to curb rising costs and reduce evictions.

Tens of thousands of people protested in central Madrid on Saturday to denounce Spain's housing crisis.

The demonstrators called for better protection for tenants, anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.

The march through the center of the Spanish capital was called after an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, was evicted from her apartment where she had lived for seven decades.

Protesters carried signs reading 'we are all Maricarmen' Image: C. Carvajal/JNA/ZUMA/picture alliance

The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent ahead of a general election next year.

Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth has put pressure on the already limited housing supply in the cities. The Bank of Spain estimated a shortage of 550,000 homes across the country last year.

Toxic tourism — Mallorca's housing crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Protesters camp out in Puerta del Sol

Government authorities estimated that around 25,000 people had shown up to protest against Spain's growing housing crisis. The Madrid Tenants' Union, which organized the protest, said over 300,000 had taken part.

Once the rally wrapped up, some activists set up a protest camp in the city center's Puerta del Sol square with plans to stay put. Some even pitched up tents to stay the night, or until the police forcibly removed them.

Police officers looked on at about a dozen tents, surrounded by thousands of protesters, news agency AFP reported from the scene.

Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownership Image: Tomas Calle/JNA Press/Sipa USA/picture alliance

Rallying around Abascal

The protest was triggered by Maricarmen Abascal's dramatic eviction on Wednesday from the house she had lived in for decades.

Abascal was greeted by supporters as she was removed from her home on a stretcher and loaded onto an ambulance.

"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse. "And we can't keep maintaining this. Housing is a right, and we don't have it," she said.

According to Spanish media, Abascal's father first rented the home in the upscale Retiro neighborhood in 1956. After her parents died, she continued to live in the flat, which had a rent cap at the time.

Spain: Tourism boom worsens housing crisis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In 2018, the building changed ownership, and Urbagestion, an investment fund, bought the unit, raising the rent from €500 ($570) to €2,650 ($3,018).

Abascal had been offered an opportunity to buy the apartment before this but could not afford it.

The fund later lowered her rent to €1,650, but Abascal could not afford that either. Courts had blocked her eviction three times previously and extensive media coverage turned her into a symbol of the crisis.

"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.

"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted," she added.

World.title: Germany news: EU ministers meet for migration showdown
World.content:
09/26/2026 September 26, 2026 Mass protests against cuts to social services

Hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets of cities across Germany on Saturday to voice their opposition to planned government spending cuts and call for a stronger welfare state.

Trade unions said a total of 175,000 took part in the protests, including in Nuremberg (over 20,000), Stuttgart (16,000), Frankfurt (15,000), Hanover (13,000), Essen (12,000), Berlin (5,500) and elsewhere under the slogan: "Hard-earned! Your work. Your health. Your pension."

Speaking in the western city of Essen, German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) leader Yasmin Fahimi criticized plans by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's coalition government to reform working hours and pensions, and warned against cuts to social security benefits.

"We will not simply allow what we have built up over many years in terms of social standards to be taken away from us," she said.

'Participation, self-determination, pension system, health system' - the blocks holding up 'democracy,' said protesters in Frankfurt Image: Bernd Kammerer/Presse- und Wirtschaftsdienst/picture alliance

Pension reform has been the focus of attention for months in Germany, while automobile giant Volkswagen has also announced sweeping job cuts.

The issues played a central role in the recent state elections in Berlin and the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, which resulted in disastrous defeats for Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU).

Nevertheless, the chancellor insisted earlier this month: "The reforms must go ahead."

Christiane Benner, leader of the trade union IG Metall, warned in Nuremberg against scaling back social security in times of restructuring and job cuts, for example in the automotive sector.

German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) leader Yasmin Fahimi spoke to crowds in Essen Image: Friedrich Stark/epd

"Economic change can only succeed with confidence in the future and with solidarity," she said.

German employers, however, accused the trade unions of a "ritual refusal to reform."

Steffen Kampeter, chief executive of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), told the DPA news agency that "the trade unions say 'no' to almost every change" and accused them of "dreaming of the world of yesterday."

World.title: Backlash over data centers tests Europe's AI ambitions
World.content:
Massive data centers needed to run AI are triggering protests across Europe. Their operators counter that they boost digital sovereignty and energy independence.

Like coal-fired power plants and wind turbines, few people actually want a data center in their backyard. But they do want to use their services. As a global debate rages about the potential dangers of artificial intelligence, there are also many local discussions about where exactly the data centers needed to train and run AI should be built.

This is currently a major issue in Europe, where many governments and companies have decided that they would prefer to store data in Europe rather than in the United States, which is the global leader in computing. But more digital sovereignty in Europe will mean more consumption of the continent's resources.

According to the German Ministry for Economic Affairs, for every kilowatt-hour of electricity consumed, an average of between 0.4 and 4.4 liters (0.8 and 9.3 pints) of water is used to cool data centers, with the water either evaporating or being diverted back to tanks in a warmed state.

What happens when data centers lose power? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Massive water consumption

The summer that just ended was the hottest on record in Europe — in some areas, water use was restricted for residents, agriculture and even nuclear power plants. The summers are expected to get warmer, so many are wondering about the potential water consumption of data centers in the future.

They are also worried about the high electricity consumption of the centers. Fingrid, Finland's national grid operator, recently forecast that electricity consumption would rise by almost 40% if all projects with signed connection agreements were implemented in full.

This week, the European Commission announced a new scheme for data centers to increase transparency on their energy and water use. Those with a capacity of more than 500 kW will receive an efficiency grade that will also take into account their contribution to the grid, such as the reuse of waste heat. "Tripling our data center capacity cannot mean tripling the pressure on our grids, our water and our energy bills," said Teresa Ribera, the Executive Vice-President of the European Commission for a Clean, Just and Competitive Transition.

Several data centers are currently under construction in Europe Image: Maksim Zabarovskii/imageBROKER/picture alliance

Data centers in urban hubs and rural areas

Europe's most powerful data centers have primarily been built near the major cities of Frankfurt, London, Amsterdam, Paris and Dublin (FLAP-D) because of high connectivity, proximity to users and businesses, and well-established ecosystems with specialized engineers and secure supply chains.

However, according to a report by the investment group CBRE, the situation is changing as these markets face power and grid infrastructure constraints. New data centers are being built in the Dutch city of Groningen, Barcelona in Spain or the Belgian capital Brussels, as well as in more rural areas.

And as this happens, there are more and more protests taking place, both on and offline. Earlier this month, hundreds turned up for a protest in front of tech giant Google's offices in the Austrian city of Linz, demonstrating against its already advanced plans to build a data center in the small town of Kronstorf.

Hundreds protested against a Google data center saying that AI needed democracy Image: APA-Images/picture alliance

Earlier this month, bestselling Irish author Sally Rooney successfully led a campaign to overturn planning permission for a proposed data center in the village of Killala, arguing that it would breach national climate policy.

In central France, meanwhile, several elected officials in the village of Etrechet have resigned over Google's plans to build a massive data center, which, at full capacity, would require between 880 megawatts and 1.1 gigawatts of electricity or the equivalent of the total output of a nuclear power plant. Etrechet mayor Florence Laurent told the French daily Le Monde that she was resigning out of a "sense of powerlessness, since the village has no decision-making power" regarding the project.

Some operators of data centers argue that the facilities can be built in such a way that they save energy. A large data center currently being built in Marseille will reportedly use a cooling system that requires 30% less power and consumes no water.

Other data centers, in Scandinavia, for example, use waste heat from the servers and route it into district heating networks via heat exchangers and pumps.

This spring, the German energy company E.ON published the results of a survey that found nearly three-quarters of people would be more likely to welcome data centers near residential areas if they fed their waste heat into the heating network.

Data centers face backlash from US communities To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Data center operators also argue that the facilities can serve the public by connecting the batteries that usually provide backup power to local grids so that there is uninterrupted service in the event of power outages or at times of peak demand.

For proponents of building more data centers in Europe, the facilities not only contribute to the continent's digital sovereignty but also help to strengthen energy independence.

Monir Ghaedi contributed to this article, which was translated from German.

World.title: China, US agree to set up channel for AI safety incidents
World.content:
Following the summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, the two superpowers pledged to set up a "communication channel" for AI incidents and boost coordination on military matters.

Beijing and Washington promised to expand dialogue on AI safety and between the countries' militaries while also cutting tariffs on about $30 billion (€26.3 billion) of "non-sensitive goods."

The pledges follow the three-day summit between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in the US.

US President Trump described the summit in an online post as "one of Friendship, Strength, and Success" for both nations.

Trump-Xi summit: Results or just symbolism? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China's President Xi was more constrained, saying the two sides agree on "strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity."

Beijing and Washington to improve military communication

On Saturday, with Xi back in Beijing, China said the two sides agreed to a mutual tariff reduction on roughly $30 billion of "non-essential" goods. This applies to exports such as agricultural products or holiday decorations.

The Chinese statement also confirmed that the two side will be setting up a "communication channel" for AI incidents.

"Artificial intelligence technologies are continuously developing, all parties can strengthen exchanges, discuss in-depth and seek consensus in light of the latest situation," the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.

A new round of AI-focused dialogue is due to be held in November.

The two nations will also accelerate their work on military crisis communications, Beijing said, without providing details.

Xi to travel to the US again in December

The US had previously announced that Beijing and Washington agreed to extend their "trade truce" agreed by Trump and Xi in Busan last October. The agreement, which saw China suspending its controls on rare earths and the US cutting back on some of its tariffs, was due to expire on November 10. According to US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, the deal will remain in effect until January.

Trump hosts China's Xi for state visit To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The White House also said the two sides addressed American concerns about rare earths supply "with the goal of ensuring shipment levels return to appropriate levels." China also agreed to import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the US in 2027 and 2028, according to the Trump administration.

While Donald Trump confirmed the Iran war was also on the agenda during the US talks, no major breakthroughs were reported on the issue. However, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said both sides agreed that Iran should not have nuclear weapons, and no country should impose transit tolls on international waterways, in reference to the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump and Xi are due to meet twice more by the end of the year, with Trump expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation ​summit in China in November and Xi expected back in the US for a G20 summit in December, which is due to be hosted in Trump's National Doral Miami golf club.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Trump rejects Iran proposal to reopen Strait of Hormuz
World.content:
US President Donald Trump says he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and put an end to hostilities. "I'd like to make a deal, too," he said. "But that deal would not be acceptable."

US President Donald Trump said on Saturday he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and bring about an end to hostilities.

"I reject their proposal ... I rejected their deal," Trump told reporters at the White House in Washington, DC.

Iran had proposed an initiative aimed at reopening the strategic waterway at the UN General Assembly in New York, which it said could put an end to fighting within seven days.

Tehran said the proposal had been transmitted to Washington via Qatari mediators.

What did Trump say?

"They want to make a deal to open the Hormuz Strait immediately because they're losing so badly," said Trump, claiming: "We're winning tremendously."

Earlier, a US official had told Reuters that discussions with Iran, conducted through mediators, were "positive and constructive."

But the Wall Street Journal reported that Trump was skeptical that Tehran would meet his demands. He reportedly told staff that a renewed bombing ‌campaign ​is likely following the November US midterm elections.

"They want to make a deal and I think that's fine," said Trump. "What they want to do is ​immediately open the Hormuz Strait ... because they have no money coming in, because they get their money from the Hormuz Strait."

Iranian ports are currently under a US blockade as Washington attempts to pressure Tehran into lifting its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz. The key waterway remains largely closed to international shipping despite claims by Trump that the US is control of it.

"I'd like to make a deal, too," said Trump. "But that deal would not be acceptable."

Hours earlier, the US President had posted an image on social media calling the Strait of Hormuz the "Trump Strait."

Iran offers plan to reopen Strait of Hormuz within 7 days To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Strait of Hormuz: What was the Iranian proposal?

Meanwhile, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, who was on his way back to Tehran after attending the UN General Assembly in New York, told CBS News the proposal had been developed "in coordination" with Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei.

He said the process would have begun "from the very day they accept it."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, who met with Trump's envoy Steve Witkoff earlier in the week, said the plan had foreseen a cessation of all hostilities across the Middle East, including in Lebanon, with the Strait of Hormuz to be reopened on the seventh day of the truce.

He said the conditions were the same as those laid out in a memorandum of understanding signed with the US earlier this year, which called for the release of frozen Iranian assets, the lifting of sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: Paris: Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass before huge crowd
World.content:
The pope addressed around 700,000 people during a Mass at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees. Leo XIV is on a four-day visit to France.

Pope Leo XIV on Saturday celebrated Mass for hundreds of thousands of worshippers in central Paris.

The Vatican said some 700,000 people were in attendance for the open-air service at the Place de la Concorde, near the Champs-Elysees.

What do we know about the Mass?

The Mass began mid-afternoon after the pontiff traveled down the French capital's iconic avenue in his popemobile, cheered by the faithful lining the route.

News agencies described how the crowd stretched ‌2.2 kilometers (1.4 miles) across ⁠central ⁠Paris, with many waving white and yellow flags and pressing against security barriers for a glimpse of the pontiff.

Some 700,000 people were said to have attended the mass Image: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP

At the Mass site, a huge white canopy was erected to serve as a makeshift altar for Leo to deliver his service, which lasted an hour and half.

Dozens of screens were installed to allow worshippers to follow the proceedings.

In his homily, Leo asked worshippers not to keep their faith to themselves. He urged Catholics to find happiness in faith, not material things.

"Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied," he said. "From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France."

"Only God can fill the emptiness within us," said the pope.

Pope Leo urged Catholics to find happiness in faith, not material things Image: Franck Derouda/SIPA/picture alliance

Crowds began queuing hours before the service began, with many parents and children among those hoping to catch a glimpse of the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics.

"It's a big event; we've come to share the Christian fervour," teacher Sylvie Leclerc told the AFP news agency.

"You don't hear much from us Catholics, but now we're going to make some noise! But to proclaim love, peace, joy," she added.

Earlier on Saturday, the pope visited a social center and later met with adults who had recently been baptized.

It is Pope Leo's first visit to France Image: Alberto Pizzoli/AFP

Leo's first trip to France as pope

Pope Leo is on a four-day visit to France that will see him travel to Lourdes and Metz, as well as Paris. It's his first visit to France since becoming pope last year.

On Friday, around 300,000 people gathered to see the pontiff as he waved from his popemobile on the way to the restored Notre Dame Cathedral, which had to be restored after a devastating fire in 2019.

French President Emmanuel Macron did not appear at the Mass. However, far-right leader Marine Le Pen and centrist Edouard Philippe have confirmed their attendance.

Leo makes first official papal visit to France in 18 years To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Russia expected to intensify hybrid war on Europe
World.content:
Drone explosions, airspace violations, arson attacks: Poland, Romania, and Moldova are now regularly targeted in Russian attacks against Ukraine. More governments are calling these attacks deliberate acts of aggression.

Just a few months ago, Russia's war was an distant reality for many people in Europe outside of Ukraine. If Russian drones occasionally entered the airspace of countries like Poland or Romania, even official statements seemed strangely dismissive and abstract. Even after a Russian drone struck a high-rise apartment building in the eastern Romanian city of Galati in late May this year, many EU and NATO representatives hesitated to accuse Russia of intentional action. At most, there was discussion of hybrid warfare.

The situation has changed radically since the summer. Drone overflights have become almost daily in certain parts of central and southeastern Europe, and there have even been crashes and explosions, particularly in countries bordering Ukraine. Alerts are becoming more frequent, with authorities increasingly having to close airspace or suspend operations at airports, as unauthorized flights are detected. Russia has been bombing border crossings, infrastructure and trains in Ukraine, but very close to other borders. Acts of sabotage are also increasingly common.

For the Baltic states, Poland, Moldova and Romania in particular, the war has long ceased to be "hybrid." More and more, politicians in these countries are saying that Russia is acting deliberately.

Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Drones violate Moldovan and Romanian airspace

This became evident this week in an unprecedented manner. Moldova recorded four drones entering Moldovan airspace, two of which exploded in Moldovan territory. Wreckage of another was also found. The country's northern airspace was closed temporarily.

Two drones also violated Romanian airspace; with one crashing near the northern town of Solca. A nearby border crossing with Ukraine a few dozen kilometers away was closed as a result. NATO aircraft were scrambled near the Danube Delta.

The wreckage of a drone found in Moldova Image: Polizei der Republik Moldau

The scrambling of NATO aircraft has become more common in response to Russian air attacks in Ukraine.

In Poland, NATO fighter jets were scrambled twice in response to Russian attacks near the border with Ukraine. Two Polish border crossings were evacuated after a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station near the village of Wola Krobowska, 40 kilomters (ca. 25 miles) south of the Polish capital Warsaw, on Wednesday night. The station is used to route internet traffic through Poland to Ukraine.

On the same day, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter violated Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds according to the Polish military.

Polish Prime Minister Tusk says Europe needs to prepare

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke very bluntly in Krakow on Thursday and said that Russia was refining its "disgusting forms of pressure" and Poland must be prepared for them.

Russian President Vladimir Putin "wants to exhaust Ukraine by destroying its industrial and energy infrastructure, but he also wants to exhaust Europe," Tusk said. He added that there was a suspicion that the fire at the Starlink ground station had been deliberate.

Earlier this month, Tusk had already warned the Polish parliament that there might be Russian drone and even missile attacks against those who supported Ukraine.

Donald Tusk has warned that Poland has to prepare for possible drone attacks Image: Lukasz Glowala/REUTERS

Moldovan President Maia Sandu also reacted very strongly on Thursday, saying that Russia's war was a danger to all of Europe and reasserting Moldova's support for Ukraine.

In Romania, reactions were less clear. Defense Minister Radu Miruta said that not more than a "diplomatic protest" was needed, though he acknowledged that the drone that had crashed in Solca had new technical features, which suggested it could be a newer type of Russian jet-powered drone.



In New York on Wednesday, in his address to the United Nations General Assembly, Romanian President Nicusor Dan had said: "We are in the fifth year of the illegal, unprovoked and unjustified war of aggression waged on a large scale against Ukraine by a permanent member of the Security Council." He had added that as the "EU member state with the longest border with Ukraine, Romania has directly felt the effects of this war through repeated violations of our airspace."

And he too reasserted support for Ukraine: "We have said it before, and we say it again: Romania will stand with Ukraine and its people, who are acting in legitimate self-defense, for as long as it takes."

Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Romania would stand by Ukraine Image: Heather Khalifa/AP Photo/picture alliance

Attacks on western Europe from the Mediterranean?

Meanwhile, there is growing speculation that Russia could expand its war to Western Europe. On Thursday, the Spanish newspaper El Mundo published information about a CIA report warning that Russia could be preparing drone attacks on Italy, France and Spain. The attacks could be launched from international waters in the Mediterranean and from vessels that were part of Russia's shadow fleet.

There has been no official confirmation so far. French President Emmanuel Macron said that that the CIA had not informed France of this information, but he did say that the possibility Russia could launch an attack against Europe was "plausible."

French President Emmanuel Macron said the CIA had not warned France of possible drone attacks from international waters Image: Ludovic Marin/AFP



At a press conference in Denmark on Thursday, politicians and military officials warned that Russia was expected to intensify its hybrid war against the West and NATO in the coming months. The situation is currently the most serious since the end of the Cold War," said Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus.

This article was originally published in German.

World.title: Germany's FM Wadephul meets Lavrov on UNGA sidelines
World.content:
Skip next section We are pausing our coverage

09/27/2026 September 27, 2026 We are pausing our coverage

The debate has closed for the day and will resume again for its final session on Monday.

Here's a recap of the main developments on Saturday:

Johann Wadephul used his speech to the General Assembly to warn of the threat of AI, highlight the need for urgent UN reforms, and slam Russia for its war of aggression in Ukraine.

His Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov, for his part, accused Germany and other European countries of "doing everything" to thwart talks to help end the conflict between Russia and Ukraine.

But the biggest headlines today came from the foreign ministers' rare meeting away from the general debate.

Wadephul described the meeting, their first since Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, as an "intense conversation" that again highlighted the deep divisions between them.

Lavrov said the meeting was unnecessary and that no progress had been made.

Away from the war in Ukraine, the foreign ministers from India and Saudi Arabia called for de-escalation in the conflict in the Middle East and for maritime navigation to be fully restored and protected.

The conflict is sure to feature heavily in the United Arab Emirates' appearance on Monday during the final session of the debate, while another speech worth watching could be that of Kim Son Gyong, North Korea's representative.

World.title: La estafa del falso empleado de banca
World.content:
Recibir un SMS que alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en nuestra cuenta bancaria puede evitar que seamos víctima de un robo, excepto si no ha sido el banco quien realmente lo ha emitido

En la estafa del falso empleado de banca el delincuente primero envía un mensaje con una alerta sobre un movimiento sospechoso en la cuenta y facilita un enlace o un número de teléfono al que llamar. Ya en la conversación, intenta convencer a la víctima de que su dinero está en peligro para que autorice operaciones que resultarán fraudulentas

En 2025, Instituto Nacional de Ciberseguridad (INCIBE) registró 25.133 casos de phishing. Durante los dos últimos años, tanto la Policía Nacional como la Guardia Civil y el Banco de España han emitido alertas sobre el aumento de las llamadas de falsos empleados bancarios.

TÉCNICAS DE MANIPULACIÓN

Autoridad Suplantan a profesionales pertenecientes a bancos a los que la víctima concede poder y confianza Urgencia Crean la sensación de que hay poco tiempo para actuar, lo que evita que la víctima reflexione o consulte con alguien Sobrecarga de información técnica Emplean jerga bancaria para intimidar y hacer creer que dominan una situación compleja Aumento gradual de las peticiones Incluye a la víctima en grupos de aplicaciones de mensajería para hacerle creer que mucha gente ya está ganando dinero

CIBEREXPERTO NOMBRE Jordi Sánchez CARGO Experto en fraude de CaixaBank “Durante la llamada, el estafador te hace creer que te está guiando para solucionar tu problema, pero en realidad, está intentando que tu hagas exactamente lo que necesita, emitir operaciones bancarias, descargar aplicaciones o facilitar información, como códigos o datos de tarjetas” Play / Pause CÓMO EVITAR LA ESTAFA DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA 1 Sospechar de mensajes inesperados. No clicar en ningún enlace que aparezca en el mensaje ni llamar al número que ofrecen. Ante la duda, siempre se debe llamar a los números oficiales del banco 2 Desconfiar de la urgencia y de las amenazas.Mensajes como “Su cuenta será bloqueada” buscan que se actúe sin pensar 3 No compartir claves ni códigos de verificación. El banco nunca solicitará contraseñas u otros códigos de seguridad 4 No descargar archivos ni instalar aplicaciones. Los estafadores pueden pedir que se descarguen programas que en realidad les están dando acceso al teléfono de la víctima

Una estafa que ha evolucionado. Este fraude comenzó como un SMS y una llamada, pero hoy se dan variantes como la que busca robar información de las tarjetas bancarias mediante el uso de la tecnología NFC del teléfono móvil. Este sistema de comunicación inalámbrica permite compartir información entre otros, tarjetas y móviles, y realizar pagos sin contacto. Los estafadores solicitan a la víctima que se descargue una aplicación maliciosa y que acerque la tarjeta al smartphone. Así, sus datos son enviados a otro teléfono de los atacantes, donde crearán una tarjeta de forma virtual con la que intentar sacar dinero o comprar en comercios.

El teléfono puede parecer auténtico. Los estafadores pueden hacer que en la pantalla del móvil de la víctima figure el mismo número que utiliza el banco para atender a sus clientes o que el SMS aparezca en el mismo hilo que las comunicaciones legítimas mediante una técnica que se conoce como spoofing (que significa suplantación).

Conocen datos personales de su víctima. En muchos casos, disponen de información de su objetivo, como el banco del que es cliente, parte del DNI o la dirección de correo electrónico.

Si ya se ha caído en la estafa. Se debe poner en conocimiento del banco de inmediato para que se puedan adoptar las medidas operativas oportunas. También es muy importante guardar las evidencias, como capturas de pantalla, SMS, correos y registro de llamadas. Presentar una denuncia ante la Policía Nacional o la Guardia Civil.

OTROS CASOS DEL FALSO EMPLEADO DE BANCA

World.title: El curioso caso de los barrios con nombres inventados por las inmobiliarias en México
World.content:
Mientras las torres de lujo avanzan sobre zonas tradicionales y las familias enfrentan una presión creciente para vender sus casas y marcharse, las inmobiliarias rebautizan las colonias populares

Una imponente escultura metálica circular recibe a los visitantes del Cuadrante Polanco, un conjunto residencial de imponentes torres de departamentos en una zona de rápida transformación de Ciudad de México. En la acera de enfrente se construyen dos edificios más. Las torres del otro costado también aparecieron en los últimos cinco años. La grama (césped) está bien cuidada, los locales comerciales son prístinos y los guaruras (personal de seguridad privada) hacen sus rondas. Lo único que parece fuera de lugar es que, en realidad, no estamos en Polanco: las inmobiliarias que han levantado este nuevo barrio ostentoso han tomado prestado el nombre de la colonia de lujo por excelencia de la ciudad, con la que colindan.

La megalópolis de Ciudad de México, dividida en sus variopintas colonias —o urbanizaciones—, atraviesa una transformación acelerada y nada discreta. New Polanco, como se le dice con sorna, se asienta sobre manzanas que hasta hace pocas décadas constituían un parque industrial. En las inmediaciones conviven sedes de multinacionales, museos y concesionarios de Ferrari con fábricas de harina, estaciones eléctricas y hasta una planta cervecera que llena el aire con olor a cebada. El barrio, como otros similares en la ciudad, también es una expresión de los factores que están cambiando la cara a las zonas tradicionales y desplazando a las comunidades en las principales ciudades del país.

Un hombre camina en la cerrada Andrómaco, en Ciudad de México. Rodrigo Oropeza

Los expertos lo han definido como una doble crisis en el mercado: de oferta y de asequibilidad, traducida en el alza sostenida de los precios de compra y renta y en la inclinación del portafolio hacia unidades de mayor valor. La gentrificación se come los barrios populares y obliga a los habitantes que han convivido durante generaciones a buscar nuevos rumbos, muchas veces en las periferias. También produce barrios que no existen en los mapas o demarcaciones oficiales: “Condesa Sur”, “Roma Oriente” y “Reforma Norte” se apropian de los nombres de las urbanizaciones de mayor plusvalía con las que limitan, en un intento por justificar los altos precios.

“Pero esto no es Polanco. Lo quieren hacer para atraer más gente para vender sus departamentos”, corrige Alfredo Sánchez, funcionario público retirado que ha vivido toda su vida, 68 años, en la “Cerrada de Andrómaco”, un pasillo angosto que recorre la distancia de una cuadra y alberga coloridas casas de dos o tres pisos a ambos lados. El contraste es tangible. El vecindario popular, un vestigio de lo que fue la zona, se ha quedado atrapado entre un centro comercial y un parque infantil que, detrás de altas murallas, forma parte de las áreas comunes de un conjunto de torres residenciales.

Algunos habitantes de las casi 60 familias que viven ahí dicen que sienten la presión de las inmobiliarias para vender sus casas y ceder el espacio a nuevos complejos. Y aunque pueda parecer una oferta tentadora, aceptarla no les permitiría seguir viviendo en su zona: las propuestas rondan los 2 millones de pesos (unos 115.000 dólares), mientras que un departamento en el área cuesta más del doble, cerca de 350.000 dólares.

Vista aérea de la cerrada Andrómaco, en Ciudad de México. Emiliano Molina

En las principales ciudades —Ciudad de México, Guadalajara y Monterrey—, cerca del 78% del inventario digital de vivienda corresponde a propiedades de alto valor, según una radiografía del sector elaborada por Propiedades.com, un sitio web inmobiliario. “Esta configuración refleja una brecha importante entre la oferta digitalizada y las necesidades de vivienda asequible para una gran parte de la población”, agrega el estudio del segundo semestre del 2025.

La empresa, que rastrea aumentos de hasta 180% en las rentas en zonas de la capital, detalla que el encarecimiento ha desplazado a residentes hacia áreas aledañas con precios más accesibles, aunque estas “zonas de contención” comienzan a registrar un aumento en la demanda e indicios de revalorización. La Condesa y la Roma, donde palpita el corazón de la gentrificación de la capital, han empezado a desbordarse hacia otras comunidades, donde las fachadas art déco, que florecieron desde 1925, dan paso a edificios con gimnasio, terrazas y áreas infantiles.

En agosto de 2026, el precio promedio por metro cuadrado de vivienda en Ciudad de México se elevó un 4,4% y alcanzó cerca de 3.500 dólares, consolidándola como el precio más alto del país, de acuerdo con el seguimiento del banco Banorte. Según estudios académicos, es también la segunda ciudad más costosa de Latinoamérica, solo por detrás de Montevideo, en Uruguay, según el Relevamiento Inmobiliario de América Latina (RIAL) de la Universidad Torcuato Di Tella, en Argentina.

Fachada de la cerrada Andrómaco, en Polanco, el 10 de septiembre. Rodrigo Oropeza

La Administración de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum ha reconocido el problema estructural, que también golpea el desempeño de la economía, y anunció el año pasado la meta de edificar y financiar 1,8 millones de viviendas populares, para beneficio de 12 millones de familias. En paralelo, el partido gobernante Morena promueve iniciativas legislativas en Ciudad de México para evitar que las desarrolladoras se asimilen a colonias de mayor plusvalía, en un intento que han denominado de publicidad engañosa y voracidad inmobiliaria. “Cuando cambia el nombre de un barrio, cambia quién puede vivir en ese barrio”, ha dicho la diputada local de Morena Cecilia Vadillo, quien promueve la propuesta.

Sin embargo, en la Cerrada de Andrómaco, que se ha hecho viral en redes sociales como reflejo de la disparidad, se quejan del abandono mientras temen por lo que pasará en los próximos años, mientras los servicios de electricidad y agua se han encarecido y han empezado a presentar fallas, dicen, ante el alto consumo de los vecinos. “Los políticos vienen, toman nota y se van. Nos preocupa que llegue un presidente al que se le bote la canica y nos diga que nos vamos porque nos vamos, con una indemnización que no nos alcance para vivir en la ciudad”, se queja José Mendoza, de 63 años. Su familia ha vivido en este pequeño vecindario durante tres generaciones. “Los de allá”, dice señalando los edificios en la otra acera, “quisieran que desapareciéramos”.
