World.title: Starlink ground station in Poland hit by fire in suspected arson attack
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A fire last night at a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was caused deliberately, says digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski. The facility is used to provide internet services across the region, including in Ukraine, which relies heavily on Starlink connections. Although the fire is still being investigated, “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian”, says Gawkowski. 🔴 Gawkowski o pożarze stacji Starlink. "Element wojny hybrydowej" Wicepremier Krzysztof Gawkowski ocenił pożar stacji Starlink na Mazowszu jako celową próbę zakłócenia łączności. – Wiele wskazuje na to, że pożar stacji Starlinków na Mazowszu to kolejny element wojny hybrydowej… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) September 24, 2026 Firefighters were called out at around 9 p.m. on Wednesday to the facility, which is located in the village of Wola Krobowska, just south of the capital Warsaw. Due to suspicions that the fire had been caused deliberately, police and officers from the Internal Security Agency (ABW) were also later dispatched to the scene. “We’re dealing with an arson attack that was intended to impact critical telecommunications infrastructure that influences internet operation,” Gawkowski, who also serves as deputy prime minister, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday morning. In a separate interview with TVP, the minister said that the facility is owned by Polish state telecommunications operator Exatel and “provides internet transmission through Poland, and also to Ukraine”. He noted that other internet providers use Exatel’s facility, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which is the owner of Starlink. Starlink terminals have been vital in Ukraine during Russia’s war against the country. Gawkowski told TVN that “the modus operandi in this case is clearly Russian” and “is another element of the hybrid warfare we are facing”. Poland has been one of the primary targets for Russian sabotage operations in Europe, including a series of arson attacks. “The Russians want to paralyse critical infrastructure, cut off water, gas and electricity, paralyse the internet,” said the minister. “All these processes have one goal: to incite panic and stir up emotions.” However, in his remarks to TVP, Gawkowski acknowledged that, for now, “it is impossible to say” for sure whether Russia was behind the attack. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 The spokesman for Poland’s security services, Jacek Dobrzyński, likewise told TVN that “at this stage it is still too early to talk about the causes or motives of this fire”. However, he confirmed that “everything points to arson”. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also told broadcaster RMF that “this could be an act of sabotage, and we are taking that into account, so nothing can be ruled out here, especially since these are sensitive elements that ensure satellite communications”. Polish news service Defence24 notes that ground stations are used by Starlink to connect its satellite constellation with terrestrial communications infrastructure. The facility in Poland, alongside one in Lithuania, serves the entire Central and Eastern Europe region, including Ukraine. Tu nieco więcej o roli stacji naziemnych w systemie Starlink. https://t.co/EYys481dSi — Mariusz Marszałkowski (@MJMarszalkowski) September 24, 2026 Earlier this month, a fire broke out at a drone plant in Poland belonging to WB Electronics, which supplies the armed forces of Ukraine and Poland, among others. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that there was “no doubt” the fire was caused deliberately, and that Russia was likely behind it. The Polish government has in recent months warned that Russia is planning to escalate its hybrid actions against Poland and other countries in the region, including through acts of sabotage, disinformation, and potential airspace and border violations. In July, a Russian missile entered Polish airspace before landing in a field in eastern Poland. On Wednesday this week, the same day as the fire in Wola Krobowska broke out, a Russian helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace. World.title: Bolt and Lucid Plan 25,000 Autonomous Vehicles Across Europe
World.content:
Bolt and U.S. electric vehicle maker Lucid Group have announced a partnership to develop autonomous mobility services in Europe, with plans to deploy more than 25,000 fully autonomous vehicles across European cities over the coming years.

The vehicles will be based on Lucid’s upcoming Midsize platform and use NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference architecture and development platform for autonomous vehicles.



The companies plan to develop the vehicles for SAE Level 4 autonomous driving, which allows vehicles to operate without human control within defined conditions.

Bolt says the project is part of its wider ambition to have 100,000 autonomous vehicles operating on its platform by 2035.

The companies will work together from the early stages of vehicle development. Bolt will contribute traffic and mobility data, operational experience and knowledge of European markets, while Lucid will provide its software-defined vehicle platform and automotive technology.

Bolt will also define requirements covering the vehicle, software, safety and passenger experience. Its autonomous driving division will oversee the partnership and develop the infrastructure needed to operate the fleet.

This will include vehicle dispatch, charging, maintenance, remote assistance and customer support. Bolt also plans to own and operate the autonomous vehicles itself.

Rollout will depend on local regulations

The companies have not yet announced which European cities will receive the service first.

Bolt and Lucid said launches will take place city by city and depend on local regulations, official approvals and operational readiness. The companies also plan to work with autonomous driving technology providers, European regulators and policymakers before introducing the service.

For the foreseeable future, autonomous vehicles on the Bolt platform will operate alongside vehicles driven by human drivers.

Lucid’s side of the project will be led by Lucid Technologies, a newly established division bringing together artificial intelligence, advanced driver-assistance systems, autonomous driving and other digital technologies.

Bolt currently operates in more than 850 cities across 50 countries and says its platform serves more than 200 million customers. Its services include ride-hailing, car-sharing, electric scooters and food and grocery delivery.

Lucid Group, listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker LCID, develops electric vehicles and related technologies. The company operates manufacturing facilities in Arizona and Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Prague Airport Works to Speed Up Border Checks for Non-EU Travellers
World.content:
Prague Airport and the Czech Ministry of the Interior are preparing additional measures to reduce waiting times for passengers arriving from non-Schengen countries following the introduction of the EU Entry/Exit System (EES).

The new system has made border checks more complex, particularly for travellers from outside the EU. Prague Airport says it has already introduced several measures aimed at keeping passenger flows moving during busy periods.



Airport staff, known as the Red Team, are assisting passengers in the terminal, directing them through the new procedures and providing information where needed. The airport has also adjusted passenger flow corridors based on data collected since the system was introduced.

One of the main issues identified so far is the self-service registration process. According to the airport, a significant number of passengers do not complete their registration at the kiosks, which can lead to additional delays at passport control.

Prague Airport is therefore examining the entire journey from the registration kiosks to passport control and looking at ways to make the process easier, particularly for families and older passengers.

“Data has shown us that the most common delays occur when people interrupt the registration process at the terminals,” said Radomír Lašák, Chairman of the Board of Prague Airport. “Together with the Police of the Czech Republic, we are not merely putting together temporary stopgaps but are redesigning the entire process so that it remains resilient even during peak periods.”

Further measures are also being prepared at the European level, including the possibility of allowing passengers to complete parts of the EES registration before departure. Airlines could also provide passengers with information about the process during flights.

The Czech Ministry of the Interior and the Immigration Police are working with Prague Airport on the next steps and have committed additional resources to help manage the new system.

Interior Minister Lubomír Metnar said the authorities’ priority was to maintain security standards while limiting the impact of the new procedures on passengers.

The airport said it will continue monitoring passenger flows and adjusting its procedures based on actual operations, particularly during peak travel periods.

World.title: Czech Statehood Day 2026: What Is Open and What to Do in Prague
World.content:
September 28 is a public holiday in the Czech Republic, marking Czech Statehood Day and the feast of St. Wenceslas. This year, the holiday falls on a Monday, giving many people a three-day weekend.

For anyone planning to spend the day in Prague, however, there are two practical questions: which shops will be open, and what can you do around the city?



Where you can shop on September 28

Under Czech legislation regulating retail opening hours, shops with a sales area of more than 200 square meters must close on September 28.

The restriction applies throughout the day and covers large supermarkets, hypermarkets and home improvement stores.

Smaller shops with sales areas of up to 200 square meters are exempt and can open at their owners’ discretion. Petrol stations and pharmacies can also operate.

Other exceptions include shops located at airports, railway stations and bus terminals, as well as retail outlets inside healthcare facilities.

Why September 28 is Czech Statehood Day

The holiday commemorates Prince Wenceslas, a member of the Přemyslid dynasty who became one of the central figures in Czech history.

Wenceslas was killed by his brother Boleslav I on September 28, 935, in Stará Boleslav. His death later became the foundation of a cult that developed around him from the late 10th century onward.

His remains were transferred to Prague in 938 on Boleslav’s orders and buried in the Rotunda of St. Vitus. The reasons behind the transfer are not known with certainty, but the move helped strengthen Wenceslas’s status as a religious figure while also reinforcing Prague’s position as the center of the emerging Czech state.

Over the following centuries, Wenceslas became the patron saint of the Czech lands and an important symbol of Czech statehood.

The connection between Wenceslas and Czech political tradition was further strengthened under Charles IV, who commissioned the Crown of Saint Wenceslas. The crown became one of the principal symbols of the Czech monarchy and remains part of the Czech Crown Jewels.

See the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle

September 28 is also the final day of this year’s exhibition of the Czech Crown Jewels at Prague Castle.

The jewels are being displayed in Vladislav Hall as part of the exhibition Habsburgs 500. Admission is free, and the display also includes a coronation robe dating from 1653 and other historical objects.

The exhibition closes at the end of the day on September 28.

Government buildings open to visitors

Several normally restricted buildings will also be accessible to the public.

Straka Academy, the official seat of the Czech government, will open its doors on September 28. Visitors can see the government meeting room, ceremonial areas and the building’s garden.

The program also includes an interactive exhibition called Journey of the Republic. Tours are free and begin at 10 a.m., with the final group scheduled to leave at 5 p.m.

The Ministry of Finance on Letenská Street will also welcome visitors. Tours start at 9:30 a.m. and include the ministry’s historic premises and the former monastery.

Museums and other attractions

The National Technical Museum in Letná will remain open on September 28, giving visitors access to its permanent exhibitions.

The Postal Museum will also be open.

For those looking for a more traditional Prague attraction, September 28 will be the final chance this year to ride the historic Letná Carousel.

Another option is the National Museum, where the Přemyslids exhibition examines the history of the dynasty that ruled the Czech lands during the country’s early medieval period.

The exhibition runs until October 15, 2026, making the public holiday particularly relevant for visitors interested in the history behind Czech Statehood Day.

World.title: Bangkok Gears Up for the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings
World.content:
All eyes are on Thailand as the country prepares to host the 2026 International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank Group (WBG) Annual Meetings, also known as the 2026 Annual Meetings or AM2026 Thailand.

Running from 12-18 October 2026, at the Queen Sirikit National Convention Center (QSNCC) in Bangkok, the event will mark Thailand’s second time hosting the meetings, following its first in 1991. This will make Thailand one of only three nations to have hosted the IMF–WBG Annual Meetings twice.



The IMF–WBG Annual Meetings, held for two consecutive years in Washington D.C. and every third year in one of the 191 member countries, serve as a gathering of top economic figures from around the world. By covering a broad range of issues, the meetings aim to strengthen global financial stability, combat poverty, and ensure inclusive economic growth and job creation.

Thailand’s selection to host again in 2026 highlights how the country has advanced over the past three decades in terms of its institutional progress, economic resilience, and sustained engagement with international partners. As host, Thailand brings decades’ worth of experience in economic transformation and regional leadership to the table.

The “Olympics of Finance”

Often dubbed the “Olympics of Finance,” the meetings are set to attract more than 15,000 participants, including finance ministers, central bankers, economists, business leaders, civil society representatives, and journalists from the IMF and World Bank’s 191 member countries, including the Czech Republic.

The Annual Meetings will be held under the theme of “Thailand’s New Horizons: Empowering People, Building Resilience”. Therefore, the meetings will focus on enhancing people’s potential and creating opportunities, with the goal of fostering a financial and economic system that is safe, sustainable, and inclusive.

Under the theme, the government plans to showcase four policy priorities it believes are increasingly relevant in an era marked by geopolitical fragmentation, economic volatility, and demographic change. These are indeed the issues that warrant serious conversation and sincere collaboration among the global community and all stakeholders to address them in the most efficient way:

Digital Transformation: The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems.

The first centers on digital transformation and artificial intelligence, using the examples from Thailand’s Digital Public Infrastructure, including PromptPay and cross-border QR payment systems. Connected Economy: A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored.

A second pillar focuses on what is called “Building Resilience in a Fragmented World”. In order to achieve this, the concept of a “Connected Economy” capable of bridging divides between competing blocs while strengthening supply chains and investment links will be explored. Climate Finance: The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change.

The third pillar addresses climate finance, with emphasis on reforms to help countries adapt to climate change. Longevity Economy: The final priority seeks to turn the challenges of ageing populations into new sources of economic growth.

Alongside these focus areas, the Bank of Thailand plans to unveil the “Bangkok Blueprint,” an international framework developed jointly with the IMF and the World Bank aimed at combating digital financial fraud and strengthening trust in the digital economy.

Readiness in All Aspects

According to the Fiscal Policy Office, Thailand’s overall readiness has been assessed at “Grade A” following months of coordination between the Ministry of Finance, the Bank of Thailand, and the IMF–World Bank Annual Meetings Secretariat.

Preparations extend beyond the conference venue. Authorities have developed contingency plans for traffic management, emergency responses, and arrangements for high-level foreign officials. A working group has also been established to address cybersecurity matters.

Beyond Tourism: A Regional Economic Capital

Beyond its long-established reputation as a world-renowned tourist destination, the 2026 Annual Meetings offer Thailand an excellent opportunity to present another dimension of the Kingdom to the international community.

AM2026 reinforces Thailand’s standing as a trusted international partner while highlighting its growing role as a regional economic capital and a hub for finance, investment, policy innovation, and multilateral dialogue in Southeast Asia. Having said that, countries and companies vying for economic and business opportunities cannot overlook Thailand and its potential to become an important impetus for their long-term prosperity and growth.

World.title: Hotline for Foreigners in Czechia: Tips to Save Time and Frustration
World.content:
Reaching the Client Centre for residence-related questions in Czechia requires patience.

More than 2,000 calls are received every day, so some waiting time is unavoidable.

However, you can significantly reduce your waiting time by calling during less busy hours, which are published through the authority’s official channels.



It is also worth having your identification document number ready before calling. This can speed up the process, particularly if you are calling to book an appointment.

Those who do not want to wait on the phone can use other ways to get in touch. Answers to many common questions are available in the Frequently Asked Questions section of the Information Portal for Foreigners (ipc.gov.cz).

If your matter is not urgent or your question is more complicated, you can also contact the centre by email at [email protected].

The current status of your application can be checked online using the dedicated service on the same portal.

When it comes to appointments, most bookings can be made through your personal account on the Information Portal for Foreigners.

You only need to book by phone in three cases: to provide biometric data, to inspect your case file, or to collect a residence card as an EU citizen.

World.title: Czech President Warns NATO Allies May Need to Shoot Down Russian Aircraft
World.content:
Czech President Petr Pavel has warned that NATO may eventually need to shoot down Russian aircraft or drones that deliberately violate the alliance’s airspace.

Speaking to Fox News Digital in New York during the U.N. General Assembly, Pavel said Russia was testing NATO’s readiness and could interpret continued restraint as a sign of weakness.

“There might be the time when we will have to shoot down some of these planes or unmanned vehicles that are testing our readiness,” Pavel said.



Pavel said the alliance needs to distinguish between accidental airspace violations and deliberate incursions in which an aircraft ignores warnings to leave.

“If it is deliberate and the violator doesn’t respond to our measures, then we will have to act, because otherwise Russia simply would push further on,” he said.

His comments came after a series of incidents involving Russian aircraft and drones near NATO territory.

On Wednesday, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace after crossing from the Kaliningrad region. According to Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command, the helicopter travelled around 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds.

On Thursday, Romania also scrambled two F-16 fighter jets after an unidentified aerial target entered its airspace from the direction of Ukraine. The object later crashed near the country’s border with Ukraine, with no casualties reported.

Pavel said Russia’s actions reminded him of incidents during his time at NATO, when Russian aircraft repeatedly tested the responses of allied forces.

“They are, on one hand, provoking. On the other, testing what will our reaction be,” he said.

In a speech to the U.N. General Assembly on Wednesday, Pavel said Russia’s “aggressive posture poses a direct threat to European security” and warned that the risks were increasing.

The Czech president also questioned whether Russia was genuinely prepared to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine. He said Moscow would need to agree to a ceasefire before entering meaningful negotiations without conditions.

World.title: New Sports Complex Opens in Prague’s Riegrovy Sady
World.content:
A new sports complex has opened in Riegrovy Sady, giving residents of Prague 2 access to a refurbished court, parkour equipment, a climbing wall and an outdoor fitness area.

The facility, next to the TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady building, was officially opened Tuesday afternoon. The renovation and installation of new equipment cost CZK 8.7 million, excluding VAT.



The site is intended for people of different ages and can be used for several sports. The refurbished court is suitable for football and basketball, while the new equipment includes a parkour area, climbing wall and a small fitness zone.

The project forms part of the district’s longer-term plans for Riegrovy Sady. Officials said the upper section of the park has lacked sufficient space for outdoor sports and exercise.

The sports area occupies land that until last year was used by two unauthorized structures, the Ice Magic ice sculpture exhibition and the Containall sports and cultural center.

The district is also considering a much larger project for the site. A multifunctional hall for sports and cultural events could eventually replace the current outdoor facility.

Petr Janů, deputy chairman of TJ Sokol Královské Vinohrady, previously said the goal was to create a building designed to remain in place for decades or longer.

The project is still at an early stage. Prague 2 plans to discuss the design with local residents, heritage authorities and Prague’s Institute of Planning and Development. An architectural competition is also expected to be held.

World.title: Prague Taxi Drivers Could Be Tested on Czech and Local Geography
World.content:
Prague taxi drivers could soon be required to demonstrate their knowledge of Czech and the city’s geography.

The Chamber of Deputies approved the change on Wednesday as part of an amendment to the Road Traffic Act. The legislation does not automatically introduce testing in Prague or other Czech cities. Instead, it would give municipalities the authority to impose such requirements.



Under the amendment, municipalities could test taxi drivers on their legal rights and obligations, their Czech language skills to the extent necessary for the job, and their knowledge of locations within the municipality that are relevant to taxi services.

The bill now goes to the Senate.

What the new rules could mean for taxi drivers

The issue has been debated in Prague for some time, particularly as the taxi industry has changed with the rapid growth of app-based services.

Pirate Party leader Zdeněk Hřib introduced a more detailed proposal in May. That version included specific provisions defining what drivers could be required to know and what would fall outside the scope of the tests.

For example, the proposal said drivers should not be expected to demonstrate encyclopedic knowledge of Prague’s landmarks. Transport Minister Ivan Bednárik of the SPD, however, argued that the Pirate Party’s proposal had legal shortcomings.

A shorter amendment submitted by ANO MP Patrik Nacher ultimately became the version approved by the Chamber of Deputies.

Supporters of the change say taxi driving has increasingly become a profession with few formal qualification requirements beyond holding a driving licence.

The explanatory report accompanying the legislation argues that the sector has attracted foreign workers who may have limited knowledge of Czech, local traffic rules and the city in which they operate.

Critics, meanwhile, have raised concerns about the potential impact on fares. They argue that additional requirements could increase the cost of entering the profession and eventually lead to higher prices for passengers.

No English requirement in the legislation

The approved amendment refers specifically to knowledge of the Czech language. It does not introduce an English-language requirement, even though some taxi drivers in Prague also have limited English skills.

The legislation would apply to taxi drivers regardless of whether they operate independently or through digital platforms such as Uber and Bolt.

Foreign nationals make up roughly half of Prague’s registered taxi drivers, reflecting the sector’s long-standing reliance on foreign workers and recently arrived migrants.

World.title: French man caught in Hungary jailed for 26 years over murder of Argentine rugby star
World.content:
A French former soldier arrested in Hungary while fleeing towards the Ukrainian border has been sentenced to 26 years in prison for killing former Argentina rugby international Federico Martín Aramburu in Paris.

A Paris court found Loïk Le Priol, 32, guilty of murder on Friday, bringing to an end a trial that began on 7 September. The court did not find that the killing had been premeditated. His associate Romain Bouvier, 35, was convicted of attempted murder and sentenced to 19 years in prison, Reuters reported.

“The narcissistic, intrusive and uncontrollable rage of Loïk Le Priol ultimately led to the gratuitous killing of Mr Aramburu,” the presiding judge said.

Both men were former members of Groupe Union Défense (GUD), a violent far-right organisation that has since been dissolved and banned in France.

His escape ended at the Hungarian-Ukrainian border

Le Priol’s connection to Hungary dates back to the days immediately after Aramburu’s killing.

On the evening of 22 March 2022, a then 27-year-old French national arrived at the Záhony road border crossing and attempted to leave Hungary for Ukraine. Hungarian police checking his documents discovered that French authorities had issued a European arrest warrant for murder. Police detained him on the spot.

Le Priol told officers that he had a military background and intended to travel to Ukraine to fight following Russia’s invasion. Hungarian police also found three knives in his vehicle, leading to separate proceedings over the possession of particularly dangerous objects.

A Budapest court subsequently approved his transfer to France, and Le Priol agreed to the simplified extradition procedure. He was handed over to French authorities later that month.

If you missed it: Tiger last year, marmoset this time: Hungarian man caught with yet another exotic animal

Fatal confrontation in central Paris

Aramburu, 42, was killed in Paris in the early hours of 19 March 2022 following an altercation near Boulevard Saint-Germain. The confrontation began after the two groups argued at a café and continued outside after security staff removed those involved from the venue.

Bouvier fired first and wounded Aramburu. Le Priol then fired the shots that proved fatal, according to the findings presented at trial. Aramburu died at the scene.

Prosecutors had sought 27 years in prison for Le Priol and 20 years for Bouvier. The jury ultimately imposed sentences one year shorter in each case.

The presiding judge said Le Priol had been driven by a desire to kill and described the two men as sharing a fascination with weapons and violence. Le Priol, who had admitted firing the fatal shots during the trial, asked Aramburu’s family for forgiveness in his final statement to the court.

Who was Federico Aramburu?

Federico Martín Aramburu was a former Argentine international who won 22 caps for his country and spent much of his club career in France, including spells with Biarritz and Perpignan.

He was also part of Argentina’s squad at the 2007 Rugby World Cup, where the team finished third.

More than four years after the shooting, Friday’s verdict concludes the main criminal trial in a case whose manhunt unexpectedly stretched from central Paris all the way to Hungary’s eastern border.

World.title: Hungary Weekly Briefing: Immunity battle, intelligence shake-up and a weaker forint
World.content:
Parliamentary immunity is back at the centre of Hungarian politics, while intelligence reforms, public-money investigations and a weaker forint add to a busy week.

This week’s Hungary Weekly Briefing looks at the latest institutional battles, as prosecutors seek to lift the immunity of Prime Minister Péter Magyar and two former ministers in separate cases.

We also examine the continued overhaul of Hungary’s intelligence services, fresh investigations into the use of public money, and the economic uncertainty created by a weaker forint for businesses and homebuyers.

Beyond politics and the economy, the briefing covers a violent Budapest assault involving a British tourist, upcoming changes to the capital’s public transport and a first look at Hungary’s 2027 calendar, including six guaranteed long weekends.

World.title: PM Magyar confirms wealth tax from January as egg-throwing disrupts Szolnok rally
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar used the latest stop of his nationwide tour to restate several major government plans, including a new wealth tax, asset recovery and constitutional reform. His appearance in Szolnok was also briefly disrupted when an egg was thrown towards the stage.

Magyar addressed supporters in Szolnok’s Kossuth Square on Saturday, the third stop of his new nationwide tour following events in Veszprém and Pécs. The tour is expected to visit 15 provincial cities before concluding in Budapest.

One of his clearest pledges concerned the planned wealth tax, which would target individuals with assets exceeding HUF 1 billion. The prime minister said the measure would take effect from 1 January, calling it one of Tisza’s most important and most widely supported campaign promises.

He accused pro-Fidesz media of launching a new campaign against the tax and argued that the criticism was driven by those with the largest fortunes. Magyar also made a sarcastic reference to billionaire businessman Lőrinc Mészáros and his wife, Andrea Várkonyi, while insisting that the government intended to introduce the measure as promised.

Asset recovery and constitutional reform

Another major part of the two hour-speech focused on recovering public assets allegedly lost under previous governments.

Magyar told those who might eventually be held responsible for financial damage to the state that repayment could count as a mitigating circumstance under criminal law.

“They know the Hungarian State Treasury’s bank account number, and we are waiting for the transfer.”

He also renewed his criticism of Hungary’s prosecution service, accusing prosecutors of having watched while the country was, in his words, “looted like during the Mongol invasion”.

Magyar also repeated that a broader constitutional process would begin and criticised the county-level administrative system inherited from the Orbán governments. He argued that county assemblies had too often functioned as political patronage hubs, rewarding loyalists rather than relying on qualified professionals, and claimed that the system had also been used to keep mayors under political pressure.

He said his government wanted to replace what he described as a “feudal” structure with a more professional administration.

If you missed it: Germany and Hungary revive defence ties – Leopard tanks, joint exercises and Ukraine on agenda

Szolnok electrolyte plant ruled out

Turning to a local issue, Magyar said no electrolyte plant would be built in Szolnok while the Tisza government remains in office.

Supporters gather at Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s rally in Szolnok on 26 September 2026. Photo: Screenshot / Facebook – Péter Magyar

The planned KunlunChem factory has faced strong local opposition and had already run into several obstacles before Saturday’s statement.

Egg thrown towards Magyar during Szolnok speech

The event was also disrupted shortly after Magyar began speaking. According to Index, the prime minister was talking about his recent private audience with Pope Leo XIV when his bodyguards suddenly appeared behind him after something was thrown towards the stage. The livestream did not initially make clear what the object was, and Magyar first appeared to believe that a drink had been thrown.

Magyar interrupted his speech and addressed those responsible:

“I would like to ask the Fidesz trolls not to throw drinks, because there are many civilians here, and I do not think any of our elderly compatriots or children deserve to have water or beer poured over them. If you want to pour it over me, come up here, no problem.”

He then attempted to continue his speech, although several further shouts from the crowd repeatedly interrupted him. It later emerged that an egg had been thrown towards the prime minister.

After Tisza MP Andrea Rost addressed the audience, Magyar returned to the stage and spoke at greater length about the incident. He said Tisza supporters had not gone to rival political events during the election campaign to whistle at speakers or throw eggs, and argued that those disrupting his event were acting out of political frustration.

Magyar asked his supporters not to be angry with them, claiming that some former Fidesz voters were struggling with the loss of a political community and leaders they had previously trusted.

Footage recorded by Kontroll at the scene showed plain-clothes police officers detaining the man suspected of trying to hit Magyar with an egg. The man reportedly told reporters that he regretted missing the prime minister’s head. He resisted the officers as they moved to detain him and was eventually taken to the ground.

World.title: Tiger last year, marmoset this time: Hungarian man caught with yet another exotic animal
World.content:
A Hungarian man already under investigation over a tiger cub has run into trouble again after police found a common marmoset in his car.

The National Bureau of Investigation (NNI) is once again investigating the case of a man from Tiszafüred who was found with a tiger cub last year. This time, officers discovered a common marmoset in his car, police.hu reported.

The NNI’s Environmental Crime Unit has been investigating the man on suspicion of damaging nature since November 2025, when a tiger cub believed to have been smuggled into Hungary was found during a search of his home.

The young tiger was initially taken to the Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden, where it was given the name Pablo. It was later transferred to the Veresegyháza Bear Sanctuary, where it currently lives.

Police find another exotic animal in his car

On 24 September, officers stopped the man during a routin roadside check in Pomáz, a town north of Budapest.

Inside his vehicle, they found another exotic animal: a common marmoset, a small primate native to South America.

According to police, the origin of the animal could not be established because it had no documents proving where it came from and no individual identification marking. Hungarian authorities also said that private individuals are not permitted to keep the animal in Hungary.

“The small monkey, found in a cat carrier in the suspect’s boot during the police operation, appears to be a healthy male based on the initial examination. Following the check-up, Director General and Chief Veterinarian Dr Endre Sós took a faecal sample, after which our colleagues transferred the newcomer to the zoo’s quarantine facility, where he is currently being kept under observation.” – The Budapest Zoo and Botanical Garden wrote.

Man placed in pre-trial detention

Investigators questioned the man again as a suspect over the unauthorised keeping of the animal. This time, however, the authorities took further action.

Given that the man was already under investigation over the earlier tiger case, police treated the new discovery as a repeat offence. He was taken into custody, and a court later ordered his pre-trial detention.

The investigation is now examining both exotic-animal cases, including the circumstances in which the marmoset came into his possession.

If you missed it: Adorable tiger cub discovered during drug raid in Hungarian town – videos

Budapest Zoo warns against keeping wild animals as pets

Keeping large predators and other protected or specially regulated exotic animals is subject to strict rules in Hungary, and authorities launched a criminal investigation into the circumstances surrounding the animal’s arrival in the country.

The Budapest Zoo used the case to underline why wild animals should not be kept as pets. It stressed that proper food and veterinary care are only part of animal welfare: social species also need contact with their own kind and living conditions that reflect their natural behaviour.

A marmoset may appear comfortable around people, the zoo noted, but that does not mean its needs are actually being met.

World.title: Travel alert: Multiple crashes hit Hungary’s M1, M7 and M0 motorways as weekend traffic builds
World.content:
Drivers in Hungary faced a difficult Saturday as a series of crashes disrupted traffic on major motorways and roads across the country. The latest collision occurred on the M1 near Tatabánya, one of the main routes between Budapest and the Austrian and Slovak borders, while other accidents affected the M0 ring road, the M7 motorway and roads in Budapest and several regional cities.

As Blikk reported, emergency services were called to six traffic accidents across Hungary in less than an hour on Saturday morning, between 11:01 and 11:59. In several locations, roads or ramps had to be closed, while a rescue helicopter was dispatched to one of the scenes.

New crash on the M1 near Tatabánya

Two vans and a passenger car collided at kilometre 56 of the M1 motorway near Tatabánya, on the side heading towards Budapest.

According to Hungary’s disaster management authority, material from the crash was spilt onto the carriageway, and firefighters were working to clear the road. Traffic disruption was reported in the area.

The latest collision came shortly after another serious disruption on the same motorway.

Earlier on Saturday, five vehicles collided near Szárliget and Óbarok. Útinform reported an eight-kilometre queue towards Budapest and around three kilometres of congestion in the direction of Hegyeshalom following that crash.

Drivers travelling between Budapest and western Hungary or Austria should therefore expect longer journey times on the M1.

Rescue helicopter called to crash near the M0

Another accident occurred at Gyál, just outside Budapest, where a passenger car and a motorcycle collided on Kőrösi Road near an access ramp to the M0 motorway. A rescue helicopter was sent to the scene and the affected ramp was closed while emergency services worked there.

The M0 forms the main ring road around Budapest and is widely used by international traffic avoiding the city centre, particularly drivers travelling between the M1, M5 and other motorways.

Accident on the M7 near Lake Balaton

An accident also disrupted travel on the M7 motorway, one of Hungary’s busiest tourist routes. Near Balatonvilágos, at kilometre 92, a car travelling towards Budapest left the motorway and ended up among bushes beside the road.

Both people inside the vehicle were able to get out without assistance. Firefighters had to use chainsaws to clear branches and vegetation around the car before they could secure the vehicle. Ambulance crews were also called to the scene.

The M7 connects Budapest with Lake Balaton and, further south-west, routes towards Croatia and Slovenia, making disruptions particularly relevant to tourists and international drivers.

By early Saturday afternoon, another accident was also causing congestion on the M7 near Pákozd. Two cars collided at kilometre 54 on the side heading towards Letenye, leaving only one lane open and creating a queue of almost four kilometres, according to traffic information cited by local media.

Crash also causes disruption in Budapest

Budapest itself was not spared from Saturday’s series of accidents. Shortly before noon, a car crashed into a tree at the intersection of Gergely Street and Alkér Street in Kőbánya, Budapest’s 10th district.

Two people were inside the vehicle. Emergency services worked at the scene under a full road closure, which also affected public transport in the area.

Another collision occurred in Ónod in north-eastern Hungary, where two cars carrying a total of four people crashed near the junction of Nyéki, Rákóczi and Szent István streets.

Drivers advised to check conditions before travelling

Traffic conditions may change quickly as damaged vehicles are removed and roads reopen.

Travellers heading towards Austria or Slovakia via the M1, Lake Balaton or Croatia via the M7, or around Budapest on the M0 should check live traffic information before setting off and allow additional travel time.

The M1 is particularly affected, with multiple crashes occurring on the motorway within a relatively short period on Saturday.

World.title: Scholars, not suspects: Stipendium Hungaricum student responds to controversial ‘migrant bus’ post
World.content:
A controversial photo of a bus near Hungary’s Austrian border sparked speculation about illegal migration – but the passengers were actually Stipendium Hungaricum students. One of them now explains what happened and why the incident matters.

The author, Hassan Farooq, is a final-year International Relations student at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), studying in Hungary under the Stipendium Hungaricum programme. The views expressed in this article are his own.

Around mid-August, a bus stopped at a rest area near Fertőendréd, close to Hungary’s border with Austria. Women wearing headscarves and dark-skinned men stepped off during the break.

A photograph of the passengers soon appeared online, accompanied by questions and speculation about who they were and why they were there. The answer was considerably less mysterious.

They were Stipendium Hungaricum scholarship students returning from a visit to Sopron, where they had spent the day learning about the city’s Roman heritage, the 1921 referendum and the founding of the Hungarian state.

Hungary’s National Union of Students (HÖOK) quickly responded, saying that the people photographed were scholarship students rather than illegal migrants. Political influencer Virág Gulyás, who shared the image, stood by her decision to raise questions about the bus and later challenged HÖOK’s response.

As one of the thousands of Stipendium Hungaricum students currently studying in Hungary, I believe the episode deserves a closer look.

Hungary has every right to debate migration, border protection and who is allowed to enter the country. But international students who came here through a Hungarian government scholarship programme should not become collateral damage in that debate.

Who was actually on the bus?

There is nothing controversial about a country enforcing its immigration laws or protecting its borders. Those are legitimate responsibilities of any state. But that was simply not what this particular bus was about.

Stipendium Hungaricum is a Hungarian government scholarship programme launched in 2013. It operates through bilateral agreements between Hungary and partner countries and is managed by the Tempus Public Foundation under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade. Students do not simply arrive in Hungary without a formal process.

Applicants submit their documents through the scholarship system and, depending on their country, through the relevant sending partner. They then go through nomination, university admission and selection procedures before receiving a scholarship.

The competition is considerable: For the 2026/27 academic year, the programme received more than 113,000 applications from around the world.

Hungarian universities participating in the programme offer hundreds of courses taught in English and other foreign languages, attracting students from Africa, Asia, the Middle East, Europe and beyond.

This is not an informal route into Hungary. It is an international higher-education programme created, funded and promoted by the Hungarian state.

More than 100,000 applications

Stipendium Hungaricum has become one of the most visible elements of Hungary’s international higher-education strategy. Demand has continued to increase.

The University of Debrecen alone received almost 44,000 Stipendium Hungaricum applications for the 2026/27 academic year, according to university figures. International students are now a familiar part of university life in Budapest, Debrecen, Szeged, Pécs and other Hungarian cities.

They study medicine, engineering, economics, international relations and dozens of other subjects. Many of us came to Hungary precisely because the Hungarian government actively encouraged us to do so.That is what makes the Fertőendréd incident particularly striking.

The students photographed at the rest stop had been invited to Hungary through a government-backed scholarship programme and admitted to Hungarian universities. They were returning from a programme designed to teach them more about Hungary when their presence suddenly became a source of suspicion online.

The issue is not whether journalists or members of the public are allowed to ask questions.Of course they are. But journalism should also involve checking easily verifiable facts before an insinuation is allowed to take on a life of its own.

What does Hungary get in return?

Stipendium Hungaricum is not simply financial support given to foreign students. One of its wider goals is to build long-term academic, professional and personal relationships between Hungary and scholarship holders’ home countries.

Thousands of students leave Hungarian universities every year as doctors, engineers, researchers, economists and other professionals. Some return home. Others continue their studies or careers elsewhere. Many remain connected to Hungary through universities, professional networks and alumni communities.

For Hungarian universities, international students can also contribute to research partnerships, international rankings and a more diverse academic environment. University towns benefit as well.

International students rent apartments, shop locally, use services and take part in campus and city life.

And Hungary gains something less easily measured: thousands of people who return home with first-hand experience of the country and who may continue talking about Hungary for decades. That kind of connection is difficult to achieve through traditional diplomacy alone.

Scholars, not suspects

Hungary deserves a serious discussion about immigration policy. It deserves a serious discussion about border protection too. But those discussions should distinguish between illegal migration and foreign students who entered Hungary legally through a programme established by the Hungarian government itself.

The people photographed near Fertőendréd had gone through formal application procedures, had been admitted to Hungarian universities and were taking part in an educational programme.

They were not an unexplained threat.

They were students.

And before a photograph becomes evidence of something more alarming, that is the sort of basic fact worth establishing first.

World.title: While flying, Hungarian minister opens up about father lost in national airline tragedy
World.content:
For Hungary’s economy and energy minister, flying carries an unusually personal meaning. Asked about aviation while travelling on board a plane, István Kapitány recalled his father, a Malév chief pilot who died in a crash near Paris when the future minister was not yet one year old. Decades later, aviation would unexpectedly become a constant part of Kapitány’s own life as well.

“The first thing that usually comes to mind is my father, who was a chief pilot at Malév and flew a great deal,” Kapitány said.

His father was a professional pilot for Malév, Hungary’s former national airline. Kapitány said that despite choosing an entirely different profession himself, flying ultimately became a major part of his own life as well.

Working for a large international company meant travelling constantly. According to the minister, he visited 85 countries by air over the course of his career.

“I chose a job in which I ended up flying more in my life than my father did,” he said.

His father, also named István Kapitány, was the captain of Malév Flight 355, one of the most serious accidents in the history of Hungary’s former national airline.

From turboprops to giant Airbuses

Kapitány described an unusually wide range of flying experiences accumulated over several decades. He recalled travelling on everything from small turboprop aircraft to large Airbus and Boeing jets.

Yet despite spending so much time in airports and aircraft cabins, he said flying never became something he simply endured as part of the job. He continues to enjoy not only aircraft themselves, but also the social side of travelling: meeting new people, discovering different cultures and striking up conversations during flights.

“I love the whole atmosphere,” he said.

He summed up his enthusiasm with a characteristically Hungarian comparison, saying he likes aircraft at least as much as Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy likes trains and buses.

If you missed it: Hungary’s energy minister shares when the country could leave Russian gas

A plain tragedy near Paris

Behind Kapitány’s enthusiasm for flying lies a deeply personal family history. His father, István Kapitány Sr, was a Malév chief pilot who died in an air crash when Kapitány was less than a year old.

On 23 November 1962, Malév Flight 355 was travelling from Budapest to Paris, with a stop in Frankfurt. The aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-18V registered as HA-MOD, crashed while approaching Paris-Le Bourget Airport near Roissy-en-France.

A Malév Ilyushin Il-18 photographed in April 1972. Photo: Lars Söderström / Wikimedia Commons

All 21 people on board – 13 passengers and eight crew members – were deceased. István Kapitány Sr was the aircraft’s captain. Aviation accident records show that he had accumulated more than 10,000 flying hours by the time of the crash.

Kapitány was born in December 1961, meaning he was not yet one year old when his father died. French, Hungarian and Soviet experts tried to determine the exact cause of the crash, but were unable to reach a definitive conclusion.

Despite losing his father in an aviation disaster, Kapitány himself became fascinated with flying. He has previously recalled that he wanted to follow in his father’s footsteps and become a pilot. Ultimately, however, he chose a different career, partly at the request of his family.

World.title: Births fall sharply in Hungary – could the population really drop to 5 million by 2100?
World.content:
Hungary has recorded another sharp fall in the number of births, while deaths slightly increased in August compared with a year earlier. The latest figures add to a long-running demographic trend that has seen the country’s population decline for decades, even as fewer deaths have somewhat moderated the natural population loss so far this year.

According to preliminary data released by the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH) and reported by MTI on Friday, 5,922 children were born in Hungary in August 2026, while 9,452 people died.

The number of births was 7.4% lower than in August 2025, representing 475 fewer newborns. Meanwhile, deaths increased by 0.9%, or 87 people, year on year. As a result, Hungary recorded a natural population decrease of 3,530 people in August, compared with 2,968 in the same month last year.

The August decline is part of a much longer demographic trend: Hungary’s population has been shrinking for decades, while the number of births has continued to fall in recent years.

Fewer children born in Hungary

Between January and August, 46,497 children were born, 3.5% or 1,663 fewer than during the same period in 2025.

Births fell by 3.4% between January and March and by 4.7% between May and August compared with the corresponding periods of last year. April was the only exception, when the number of births rose by 1.8% year on year.

Hungary’s estimated total fertility rate also declined, from 1.31 to 1.29 children per woman. The indicator estimates how many children a woman would have over her lifetime if the fertility patterns observed during the period remained unchanged.

The difference between births and deaths produced a natural decrease of 34,900 people between January and August. That was slightly smaller than the 35,374 recorded a year earlier, primarily because fewer people died. Birth numbers, however, continued to decline.

More than 51,000 more deaths than births in 12 months

Between September 2025 and August 2026, 70,354 children were born in Hungary, 5.1% fewer than during the preceding 12 months. Over the same period, 122,056 people died, which means the number of deaths exceeded the number of births by 51,702.

Natural population decrease should not be confused with the total change in Hungary’s population, as immigration and emigration also affect the number of people living in the country. The latest figures nevertheless fit into a demographic decline that has been underway for decades.

What about the warning that Hungary could have only 5.2 million people by 2100?

The latest KSH data come only weeks after a separate long-term demographic forecast attracted considerable attention in Hungary.

As we previously reported, demographer Pál Péter Tóth warned at the 64th Annual Meeting of the Hungarian Economic Association that, if current demographic trends continue, Hungary’s population could fall to around 5.2 million by 2100.

The KSH’s own forecasts are also scenarios rather than predictions of an inevitable future. Under its medium scenario, Hungary’s population could also fall significantly, to around 6.8 million by 2076.

What the latest data do show is that the immediate trend has not reversed: fewer children are being born, and Hungary continues to record substantially more deaths than births.

If you missed it: Shocking warning by demographer: Hungary could have just 5 million people by 2100

Marriages also fell sharply in August

The KSH figures also showed a significant decline in marriages during the month. A total of 5,633 couples married in August, 12% or 739 fewer than in August 2025.

Across the first eight months of the year, however, the picture was slightly different. A total of 31,287 couples married between January and August, 1% more than during the same period last year. The KSH also stressed that the latest 2026 vital statistics are preliminary.

World.title: Bosnia Court Blocks Republika Srpska From Funding Secessionist Lobbying
World.content:
Bosnian lawmaker Denis Zvizdic, who initiated teh legal challenge. Photo: EPA/FELIPE TRUEBA.

Bosnia’s Constitutional Court on Friday declared that budgetary funds used by Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity to pay foreign consulting firms to lobby for independence violate the state’s constitutional architecture.

The ruling targets a consulting agreement signed between the Republika Srpska Representative Office in Vienna and a Montreal-based firm, Dickens & Madson Canada Inc., which listed “the independence of Republika Srpska” as a core political objective.

The legal challenge was initiated in April by a state-level lawmaker, Denis Zvizdic, who argued that using taxpayers’ funds to lobby against Bosnia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity was unconstitutional.

A 2008 ruling allowed the entity to engage foreign firms for general economic promotion. However, the court has now established that funding campaigns explicitly promoting secession represents an assault on the constitutional order.

“The Constitutional Court hereby prohibits all payments from the budget of Republika Srpska regarding the consulting services contract concluded with Dickens & Madson Canada Inc.,” the court said. “Financing lobbying services for goals that run counter to the Constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina is strictly incompatible with the constitutional order.”

The applicant, Zvizdic, welcomed the announcement, saying the entity had weaponised massive public funds for anti-state campaigns.

“Public money cannot be used to finance lobbying aimed against the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, its territorial integrity, sovereignty and its institutions,” Zvizdic stated.

“This binding decision establishes a clear legal standard: citizens’ money must serve development and investment, not the undermining of the state,” he added.

Under Bosnia’s state-level laws, entities possess no constitutional right to unilateral secession. Furthermore, ignoring or violating a binding order of the Constitutional Court carries severe penalties.

The court said the full text of the judicial decision will be delivered to all parties and published on its official website within the month.

World.title: Serbia Sees First TV Debate Between Ruling Party and Student List
World.content:
Serbia’s first election debate ahead of October 25 polls aired on TV on Thursday night, pitting former prime minister and current speaker Ana Brnabic – third on the government’s “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia” list – against Mirjana Nikolic, Rector of the University of Arts in Belgrade and a candidate on the rival “Student List – Students Win”.

The debate on the N1 TV channel was supposed to focus on education but quickly expanded into a wider confrontation over the anti-government student movement, the media, universities and the overall political situation.

Nikolic said she was initially apprehensive about debating a senior ruling-party official but welcomed the chance to present the Student List’s programme.

She said her previous meetings with Brnabic at parliament’s Education Committee had been marked by confrontation, adding that the televised debate offered a chance for both sides to present their programmes.

The appearance was notable because ruling SNS officials have largely avoided N1 during previous election campaigns and Brnabic last appeared in 2017.

“To be honest, I was not particularly happy to come to N1 this time either, given the way your television station has, over the past ten years, engaged in what I see as the dehumanisation of my President and my friend,” Brnabic said.

She accused N1 of having spread false information but said she had agreed to appear after Vucic encouraged her to give the television station “a chance”, following its change of management.

The debate quickly became heated, including an exchange over Nikolic’s alleged refusal to shake Brnabic’s hand.

The candidates also clashed over the student-led university blockades. Brnabic said students had been discriminated against “thanks to the Student List and the blockades”, while Nikolic accused her of promoting a misleading narrative about the protests and about how universities functioned.

On education, Brnabic defended the SNS record in government, pointing to higher teachers’ salaries, increased education spending and investment in science and technology infrastructure.

Nikolic challenged the figures, arguing that nominal salary increases did not necessarily mean education workers were better off, and questioned delays to university infrastructure projects.

She also criticised Brnabic’s understanding of Serbia’s education system, telling her: “As a professor, I have to tell you – Ana, you failed, you failed the exam.”

Nikolic said the Student List advocated free education, equal opportunities for students and teachers and the modernisation of the education system.

The debate was the first in a series of thematic election debates announced by N1 ahead of the October 25 parliamentary election.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Czechia Restricts Rules for Russian Diplomats Travelling
World.content:
Sikorski confronts Lavrov as tensions rise; Russian helicopter enters Polish airspace

Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski used a UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to deliver a direct message to his Russian counterpart, Sergey Lavrov: that after more than four years of full-scale war, Russia had failed to achieve its central objectives in Ukraine, and lacked the economic weight to outlast the countries supporting Kyiv. “You have been trying to conquer Donbas for over 12 years and Kyiv for over four,” Sikorski said. Ukraine, he noted, has only one-tenth of Russia’s GDP. But Poland alone has almost half Russia’s GDP, while Europe has roughly 10 times as much and NATO 25 times as much. “You can still kill a lot of people, but you cannot win,” Sikorski said. “You can stop this imperial war of choice at any time.” He ended by addressing Lavrov personally: “Sergey, I know you’re listening. Tell your boss: enough is enough.”

Hours before Sikorski spoke in New York, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter flying from the Kaliningrad region crossed into Polish airspace north of Braniewo at 11:08 on Wednesday. According to Poland’s Operational Command, it penetrated about 300 metres into Polish territory and remained there for 42 seconds. Warsaw scrambled fighter jets and raised the readiness of its ground-based defences. The Operational Command said the flight pattern suggested Moscow was again probing Poland’s ability to respond. The pressure continued on Thursday morning, this time from attacks inside Ukraine. PM Donald Tusk said Russian strikes close to the Polish border forced authorities to evacuate the border crossings at Hrubieszow and Dorohusk. “Just as we were talking, Ukraine was attacked again near the Polish border,” Tusk said during a meeting with Bulgarian PM Rumen Radev. He warned that “autumn and winter may be critical”.

The incidents come as Warsaw is seeking stronger security guarantees from Washington and dealing with an unexpected hitch in talks over a permanent US military presence. Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz had been due to meet his US counterpart Pete Hegseth at the Pentagon on Wednesday, with a permanent US Army base in Poland among the expected topics. The visit was cancelled at Washington’s urgent request, officially because of a scheduling conflict connected with Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US. No replacement date has been announced. The timing caused unease in Warsaw. Onet reported, citing unnamed government sources, that some Polish officials suspect Hegseth may be seeking to slow discussions on the permanent base. Subsequent reporting, however, indicated that the Pentagon initially tried merely to change the meeting’s time before cancelling it, suggesting the explanation may be less straightforward. The uncertainty comes days after Donald Trump said “significant progress” had been made towards establishing a US Army base in Poland and suggested its location could soon be announced.

World.title: Fading Away: Sicily’s Ancient Albanian Community Fears its Identity Risks Erasure
World.content:
Piana degli Albanesi sits among the fertile mountains of western Sicily, overlooking farmland and a lake whose waters have receded dramatically.

Its Arbereshe name is “Hora e Arbereshevet”, or, “Town of the Arbereshe”, the only one among the several other Italian towns to maintain a distinct name connected to the ethnic group that inhabits it.

The word “Hora”, explains Mayor Rosario Petta, as he walks through the town’s cobbled streets, is an old Albanian word for a town or homeland that is no longer commonly used in modern Albanian.

In Piana, however, the name is everywhere. It appears on street signs, public buildings and local businesses, a reminder that this is not simply a Sicilian town with an unusual history. It is the centre of one of Italy’s most important ethnolinguistic communities.

Petta says that in Albania, the Arbereshe are almost mythical figures –reminders of a version of Albania that disappeared centuries ago but still exists in these communities.

There is a strange historical relationship between the two sides.

The people of Piana look towards Albania as the ancestral land from which their communities emerged. Meanwhile, in Albania, the Arbereshe represent a living connection to an older version of Albanian language and culture that they can no longer experience in their homeland.

But the community in Piana is shrinking.

Over the past five years, according to Petta, the town has lost more than 20 per cent of its population. Its official population is now below 6,000, although the actual number of people living there is believed to be lower.

“The more people we lose, the more our ancient heritage is threatened,” Petta said.

The reasons are familiar across rural southern Italy: limited employment, young people leaving for larger cities or abroad, and the decline of traditional agriculture.

In Piana, climate change is adding another layer to the crisis.

The olive groves around Piana are increasingly exposed to drought, extreme temperatures and wildfires.

In 2023, wildfires destroyed several hectares of land around the town. The water crisis is also affecting farmers directly.

“We have felt the water crisis a lot and it is reflected in the quantity, quality and timing of our produce,” Claudio said.

Harvests have been brought forward as summers become longer and hotter. Trees are showing signs of stress that were previously unusual.

“The summer season is longer,” he added. “This year the grape harvesting season came earlier because of weather changes.”

The climate crisis, therefore, threatens more than individual farms. Agriculture has historically been one of the ways Arbereshe communities have remained rooted in their villages and integrated within Italian and Sicilian society. If farming becomes economically unsustainable, one of the remaining reasons for younger people to stay also disappears.

The Scalia siblings are trying to make agriculture part of the solution.

Their company was established in 2022, building on an olive grove planted in 1998. Their aim is to combine modern agricultural practices with the cultural heritage of Piana.

Their products are organic, with the longer-term ambition of securing territorial recognition such as the IGP designation. Alongside olive oil, they produce honey and other agricultural products, including plums.

The names of their products pay homage to their Arbereshe heritage. One of them, “Filari”, refers to the rows of olive trees while evoking “fili d’oro”, the golden threads used in traditional Arbereshe clothing.

The point is to make the connection between agriculture and culture more visible.

“Few people invest in agriculture and innovation in these historical times,” Claudio Scalia said. “Those who do struggle to live exclusively from it these days. To keep our farming culture alive, we are also taking on other jobs to financially sustain ourselves in a more stable way.”

Children no longer speak the language

World.title: Bringing the Balkans into Schengen: a Win-Win Scenario for Europe
World.content:
How would all this work? The member states would ask the Commission to prepare a roadmap of criteria: the Schengen acquis.

That means external border control, visa policy, the Schengen Information System, police cooperation and data protection – reinforced by rule-of-law conditions.

The Commission would report on progress every six months, and once a country met all the criteria, the member states would have to give their consent in the Council.

Reforms and the closer cooperation they bring can strengthen security rather than weaken it. When the Schengen area grew from 15 to 24 members in 2007, Germany’s then Interior Minister, Wolfgang Schauble, said: “We will have a gain in security, not a loss.”

The main argument against admitting Western Balkan countries has recently evaporated. For over a decade, several EU interior ministers saw the Western Balkan borders as a brake on irregular migrants and asylum seekers heading from Turkey and Greece into central Europe.

The admission of Bulgaria and Romania to the Schengen area in 2025 overturned that. Why would anyone on that route cross several tightly controlled borders when they could travel from Greece through Bulgaria and Romania to Hungary and Austria without ever leaving the Schengen area?

Reforms and eventual membership would meanwhile help to stabilise the region’s most fragile states – Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Kosovo, where Bosniaks, Serbs and Albanians live on both sides of the borders. As EU membership has receded into the distant future, the dangerous narratives of the late 1980s, that led to the wars of the 1990s, are returning, and with them ideas of redrawing borders along ethnic lines (floated by the presidents of Serbia and Kosovo in 2018).

The recent state funeral in Belgrade for Bosnian Serb wartime military commander Ratko Mladic, convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, is only the latest reminder of that.

It is precisely because these forces are gaining ground that the EU needs a stronger counter-offer. Schengen could be one. It does not move borders but makes them invisible, as they are between France and Germany, or Lithuania and Poland.

But you cannot make a border invisible before its status is settled, and the line between Serbia and Kosovo is the very thing being fought over. Settling it would become the price of a prize that’s within reach. It is a far stronger incentive than EU membership, which is at least a decade away.

Several countries already belong to Schengen but not the EU: Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. Unlike with earlier Schengen enlargements, this time no new external borders would be required. Surrounded by Schengen members, the borders of the Western Balkan countries could simply be collapsed inwards.

Offering such a roadmap would cost the EU little, and only serious reformers would ever join. Yet the process alone would hand the EU influence and win back some of its lost credibility. More importantly still, it would offer the Balkans something better than more quarrels over where lines should run. Borders would no longer matter.

Kristof Bender is Deputy Chairman of the European Stability Initiative (ESI).

A German version of this article first appeared in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung (NZZ).

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Mr Who? Professor in Race Against Time to Convince Serbia’s Undecided Voters
World.content:
On one hand, Ilija Srdanovic’s greatest asset might be his lack of political baggage. On the other, his obscurity may prove a hindrance.

With the 56-year-old medical professor from Novi Sad, northern Serbia, now the figurehead of a grassroots movement to unseat Serbia’s ruling party and president, voters will give their verdict on October 25.

Largely unknown to the wider Serbian public until this month, Srdanovic has been thrust into the spotlight, his every move and utterance picked over by tabloids and pro-government broadcasters.

Srdanovic hails from the city where 16 people were crushed to death in November 2024 when a concrete canopy at a newly renovated railway station collapsed, triggering an outpouring of anger and frustration at what many Serbs say is the mismanagement, corner-cutting and corruption that has flourished during 14 years of rule by the Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, and President Aleksandar Vucic.

Chosen by the students who took up the call for change, Srdanovic finds himself effectively going head-to-head with Vucic, a seasoned politician and, his critics say, an autocrat in the mould of Viktor Orban.

World.title: Millions Still Being Spent on Tito’s Dilapidated Galeb Ship
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – Millions are still being spent on Tito’s dilapidated Galeb ship, with deadlines broken and no museum in sight.

The (in)famous, rusty old vessel Galeb has a history stretching from its construction back in the 1930s, through sinking during WWII to the status of Tito’s ship and a symbol of the Non-Aligned Movement. It is still waiting for its final conversion into a museum. Index reports that in more recent years, its story has been reduced to moves between different shipyards, successive deadline overruns and constantly rising costs. Around €22 million has so far been invested in the renovation and conversion, partly from EU funds.

more repairs, more deadlines

Galeb is now going to the Viktor Lenac Shipyard for the repair of damage caused in February, when a Turkish cargo ship hit it. The cost of the repair will be covered by the insurance of the Turkish ship, and at the same time the regular annual overhaul will also be carried out. President of the Management Board of the Viktor Lenac Shipyard, Luka Hrboka, confirmed the price of the works. “The amount is €860 thousand including VAT. The whole ship was built in the riveted system and that could be a bit more demanding than on some standard ship,” Hrboka stated for RTL. The ship should return to the Rijeka Port in about one month.

Project burdened by postponements

The museum on Galeb was supposed to open its doors back in 2021. The last announced deadline was February of this year. Now the opening has been postponed to the end of the year. Rijeka Mayor Iva Rinčić believes that the project was problematic from the start.

“I think there was a series of, I will dare to say, wrong decisions, from the purchase itself to, of course, the costs that exceeded the deadlines and so on. Now we are in a situation that in talks and negotiations with the Central Agency for Financing and Contracting of EU Programmes and Projects we are trying to open the ship and bring the project to an end so that we avoid as many penalties as possible,” Rinčić said.

the museum display is ready

From the Museum of the City of Rijeka they say that around 90 percent of the permanent display is ready. The exhibition will, through original objects, cover the entire history of Galeb, and not only the period related to Josip Broz Tito.

“Tito recognised it as an interesting vessel. He observed a military exercise of the Yugoslav Navy and, when he saw that the ship was very interesting, it simultaneously became both a school ship and his residential yacht for travels around the world. Of course we document all those attractive moments on the ship,” explained the spokesperson of the Museum of the City of Rijeka, Velid Đekić. That Galeb as a museum will certainly attract visitors is also believed by Rijeka resident Slavko Vanino. “Enemies will also come and will spit on it there,” he joked and added that the ship will certainly attract attention. After a series of unforeseen problems and broken deadlines, hope remains that Galeb will finally be opened to the public by the end of the year.

World.title: Patients of One Croatian Hospital Will Need to Pay While Waiting for an Examination!
World.content:
September the 27th, 2026 – Patients of one Croatian hospital will have to pay while waiting for an examination. It’s safe to say the users of Pula Hospital are far from impressed with these latest rules.

The body that came up with these new rules would do well to remember that people generally do not come to hospital because they want to, but because they have to. As of the 1st of October, parking charges will begin in the grounds of Pula Hospital: the first hour is free, and every subsequent started hour costs two euros. Poslovni reports that that sounds simple until you sit in the waiting room and realise that you don’t actually know whether you will be called in ten minutes or in two hours.

People generally aren’t rocking up at a hospital because they fancy a break. They come sick, injured, worried, devastated, waiting for test results, sitting down anxiously awaiting examinations, or as concerned companions to someone who cannot manage alone. It isn’t a walk in the park, nor is it predictable. Then, in addition to worrying about their health or the health of their loved ones, they now also apparently need to make sure they find mental room think about the clock that is ticking outside in the car park. After three hours of stay, the bill will amount to four euros, regardless of whether you spent the time at an examination or waiting for an examination.

The hospital says that by charging it wants to free up spaces for patients and that is a goal that makes sense. However, in typical Croatian style, this idea lacks logic and hasn’t been properly thought through whatsoever. It is hard to ignore that the bill will also be paid by those who are there precisely as patients with more than enough going on. Free parking is, however, provided for people on dialysis during the procedure and for oncology patients for the duration of any active therapy. While that is of course a good thing, it leaves even more room for confusion.
