World.title: How the Lions claimed their moments to overcome a dominant Freo
World.content:
The footy season is a marathon, not a sprint.

Each game goes for about three hours, a long amount of time in our increasingly attention starved society. Multiply that by the 218 games over several months and the time starts to add up.

Especially if you are in one of the highest profile jobs in footy.

"The level of intensity that's required to be a senior coach, because it is a lifestyle, it never leaves you alone," premiership winning coach Chris Fagan said after the grand final.

In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

"It's 365 days a year, seven days a week. It's just always in your head. You're always thinking about the club and what's next."

In the era of short form video and instant takes, being involved in football nearly forces you to do the opposite.

You don't scroll through football games, you absorb them.

But football games, especially important ones, aren't one continuous event. They are made up of a series of moments and contests that separate the winner from the loser.

The bigger the stakes, the more important those discrete moments are. It's also something that newly minted three-time premiership coach Fagan has previously attested to.

"Finals come down to moments," Fagan told afl.com.au in 2020.

It was a theme he has repeatedly come back to, year after year. Win enough of those moments at the right time and you might just win the premiership. It's a formula that the Lions have ridden to their spot as maybe the most successful side of the modern era.

The importance of moments is something that wasn't lost on his opposite number coming into the finals.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained earlier in September.

Those moments also turned the 2026 grand final into one of the greatest in recent history. It was in those moments that the two-time champion Lions became three-time champions.

By winning enough moments at the right time Brisbane was able to overcome the biggest lead in time-on in a final since at least 2001.

Much of the 2026 grand final played out the way that the 2026 season had progressed, with Fremantle in control. On paper, Fremantle not just dominated proceedings but played in a way that took away Brisbane's strengths.

"Fremantle deserved to win that game today. They were better," Fagan said.

"They were better than us for longer periods. They were killing us at clearance and contested possession, particularly in that third quarter and we couldn't get any territory. They had a lot of inside 50s. They had more shots."

On paper, Fremantle should have won the game and done so comfortably.

But Brisbane won the moments that mattered.

"It's a little bit like this group has become this team that seems to need to get themselves into a dire situation before they can actually produce their best," Fagan said.

This is how Brisbane won the 2026 grand final.

A tight first half

It wasn't just a late swing that made the game a classic. This year's grand final had twists and turns almost from the first bounce. The first half saw nine lead changes through the first two stanzas, with the two sides often trading goals.

Despite this, more things were breaking Fremantle's way than Brisbane's early.

In the first half Fremantle was able to control the game in ways that Brisbane usually thrive. The Dockers were able to effectively neutralise the Lions' usually strong clearance game through the first half, both gaining position and hitting the scoreboard.

While the Lions broke even at around the ground stoppages, the Dockers were able to dominate centre clearances and piled on three goals from the middle.

The Dockers were also able to effectively outmanoeuvre the Lions in the air. The Lions have traditionally had the best mark differential of any team, with Fremantle one of the few to seriously challenge them.

However Fremantle dominated the marking battle, with their tall timber taking the upper hand. Fremantle also seemed to find a way to isolate Brisbane's shaky defence, with Patrick Voss seemingly finding a weak spot in their defensive set up.

Even when the Lions were able to dominate field position — such as the ten minute or so burst in the middle of the second quarter — they were unable to pile on the points.

The only thing keeping the Lions in the game was their maniacal forward half pressure. The Lions managed nine first half tackles inside their own 50 to just two from the Dockers. Brisbane was also able to translate this into a four goal edge in front half intercept scoring in the half.

At the end of the first half, the margin was the same before a ball was kicked in anger. Instead of four quarters to decide the premier, there would be just two.

The back end

For much of the third quarter it looked like the control Fremantle were able to exert on the game was starting to pay off on the scoreboard. While the game still stayed within a couple of goals, Brisbane didn't look out of it.

That was until Fremantle piled on 14 points in around five minutes, seemingly creating enough of a barrier to preserve the Flagmantle dream.

Some things slowly started to turn Brisbane's way despite the Dockers looking like they were gaining an unassailable lead. The Lions were slowly able to gain ascendancy in the air, managing 15 marks on the lead in the second half to nil.

They were also slowly able to quell Caleb Serong's gigantic influence on the game, particularly at stoppage. After collecting 12 clearances in the first three quarters Serong managed just one in the final period.

Most importantly the Lions started to work out how to pierce the league's best defence absent its most important piece — captain Alex Pearce.

"We had to play a bit smaller and we missed his leadership across the back end of the game and clearly missed his leadership late. He gives us so much in that aspect of the game," Longmuir said after the game about Pearce's game-ending Achilles injury.

Before the injury Brisbane managed just one goal from set shots, with three coming after the injury. The Lions struggled to move the ball effectively up ground before his injury, but found the paths to goal over time. It's also easy to imagine how Pearce would have settled the ship once it started going down fast in the end.

Of course, those last four minutes are the things dreams — and nightmares — are made of. Will Ashcroft winning three straight centre clearances from the same spot, with every Lion rising around the young star.

The moments and the missed missed opportunities

In the end it's the moments that will resonate the longest after this magical grand final. We will remember how Ashcroft won the ball in the middle late, and how LOgan Morris kicked straight. We will remember Josh Dunkley's defensive prowess and Ryan Lester's last ditch effort to save a goal.

Brisbane didn't have any passengers, nor did Fremantle. That's what made the Norm Smith Medal so hard to choose this year, and so controversial.

Unfortunately the memories for Fremantle will be more bitter than sweet. If they had to map out what the perfect game would look like for them — scoring aside — it would have looked something like what played out in the end.

"Obviously for you know four quarters we played "Fremantle football" and it's the last two minutes we didn't take our moments," Norm Smith medallist Shai Bolton said after the game.

For now, it's Brisbane's day to celebrate yet again. Especially those four minutes and 18 seconds in the last quarter where Brisbane overcame Fremantle, a seventeen point deficit and, yes, Wharfie Time to cement their place as one of the greatest teams in football history.

World.title: Brisbane Festival 2026: Our favourite shows
World.content:
Brisbane Festival has wrapped up for another year, with the month of September bringing an incredible range of events to the river city.

There's been something for everybody, from world-slaying nostalgia acts to out-of-the-box theatrical creations, and everything in between.

All part of Brisbane's ambitious push to become a true world city ahead of the 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games, the festival has centred the creative verve of Queensland and beyond on the shores of the Brisbane River.

More than 1.7 million people attended ticketed and free events produced by almost 2,000 artists over the course of the festival, including 535,000 people who visited the festival village at South Bank.

Artistic director Ebony Bott said her first year at the helm had seen the festival's box office haul jump 46 per cent from 2025.

"There has been a generosity and an openness in the way Brisbane has responded that has been incredibly moving to witness," Ms Bott said.

"I'm immensely proud of what we've made, but more than anything, I'm leaving these weeks with an even greater sense of what is possible here."

Here are seven shows we caught at Brisbane Festival in 2026.

World.title: Thousands rally against Spain's housing crisis after 87yo's eviction
World.content:
Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets in Madrid to protest against Spain's housing crisis and ask for protective measures for tenants, anti-fraud rules and a ban on evictions without alternative housing.

The protest on Saturday came in reaction to the dramatic eviction on Wednesday of an 87-year-old woman from the Madrid apartment she had lived in for decades.

"We're here because housing is a problem that already affects all of society, all ages and classes," said protester Dora Garcia, a 55-year-old nurse.

"And we can't keep maintaining this.

" Housing is a right and we don't have it. "

Taken out of her home on a stretcher in the upscale Retiro neighborhood, María del Carmen Abascal was greeted by protesters and supporters as she was loaded into an ambulance.

Some demonstrators held up their house keys as they protested for more housing rights. (Reuters: Alejandro Martinez Velez)

Spanish media reported that Ms Abascal's father first rented the property in 1956 and she continued as the tenant after her parents died, during which time there was a rent cap.

The building changed ownership in 2018, and Ms Abascal was offered the opportunity to buy the apartment but could not afford it, according to the Madrid Tenants' Union, which organised Saturday's protest.

Incomes have not kept pace with rising costs in Spain, leaving many out of the housing market. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Urbagestión, an investment fund that later bought the unit, raised her monthly rent from 500 euros ($810) to 2,650 euros ($4290).

It subsequently lowered the rent to 1,650 euros ($2670), which Abascal still could not afford on her pension, the union said.

Courts blocked three previous attempts to evict her.

Extensive media coverage turned Ms Abascal into a symbol of Spain's housing crisis.

Demonstrators hold a banner reading "Not one Maricarmen more" in support of the evicted pensioner. (Reuters: Alejandro Martinez Velez)

"This whole housing situation is heartbreaking. Maricarmen has been, in a way, the last straw that sparked this social unrest, but we've been dealing with this whole issue for a long time now," said protester Simón de la Riva, 43, a teacher.

"It's unacceptable that vulture funds are buying up homes, that people can't afford to live, that entire families are being evicted, and that an elderly woman has been evicted."

At the end of the march, protesters sat down in the Puerta del Sol plaza with apparent plans to stay put.

Some even pitched tents to stay at least the night or until police forcibly removed them.

At the end of the march, some demonstrators set up a camp at the Puerta del Sol square. (Reuters: Susana Vera)

Rising costs and a housing shortage are pricing many Spaniards out of the market, despite strong economic growth in Europe's fourth-largest economy.

Incomes have not kept pace. Analysts say tourism and immigration-driven population growth in cities have placed further pressure on the limited housing supply.

The Bank of Spain estimated that the country had a shortage of about 550,000 homes last year, with Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia accounting for a substantial share.

Spain ranks near the bottom of countries in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development for public rental housing, which represents less than 2 per cent of its available supply.

The European Union average is 8 per cent.

Spain previously built homes with public funds that were later sold into private ownership, removing them from the public housing stock.

"I haven't managed to defend my home, but I have fought so that others can learn to fight for what's theirs," Ms Abascal said on Friday.

She spoke from her hospital bed after the eviction in a video shared by the tenants' union.

AP

World.title: Cyclist 'died eight times' before getting a new heart
World.content:
Wollongong cyclist Cameron Butcher likes to say he has nine lives.

After he had a pacemaker installed in his early 20s, he recorded the eight times it saved his life.

The first came at just age 22 when the device shocked his heart back into rhythm as he lay unconscious on the grass after picking up a frisbee.

Things became even more serious when he experienced four shocks in the space of 10 minutes.

Cameron in hospital after receiving his new heart. (Supplied)

"The heart kind of just gave out and I was put on the transplant list," Mr Butcher said.

" A week later I got the call to go in and get a new heart. "

Nearly two years on from his heart transplant, the 26-year-old elite cyclist is the fittest he's ever been and is competing in the Australian Transplant Games which kicked off in Launceston on Saturday.

The long road to a diagnosis

As a 20-year-old, Mr Butcher was mountain biking and road racing around Australia until he was struck down by severe fatigue.

He was initially misdiagnosed with poor liver function, but over time his symptoms continued to worsen.

"They found I was having three seconds between heartbeats and my left ventricle, which is the one that sends blood out to the rest of the body, had become really inflamed and enlarged and wasn't doing its job," he said.

Cameron Butcher got back on the bike just five weeks after his heart transplant. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

Tests revealed Mr Butcher's heart was working at about a third of normal capacity.

A pacemaker was implanted but his heart began to fail.

Confronting his mortality at 24 was something he never expected.

"Getting that diagnosis of heart failure was probably the best thing that happened to me because for two and a half years I was trying to work out what was wrong," Mr Butcher said.

"I died eight times, so I always tell people I have nine lives."

Remarkable recovery

Less than five weeks after his transplant, Mr Butcher was back on the bike.

Cameron trains on Mount Keira in the Illawarra. (ABC News: Brooke Chandler)

"The first week [after the transplant] wasn't too pleasant," he said.

"But by the second week I was up [walking] and about doing 15 laps of the ward per day.

" I'm now the fittest I've ever been. "

Within six months, he won the mixed relay section of the 2025 Peoplecare Triathlon in Wollongong.

He also placed second at the 2025 Road Nationals in the transplant category, and won his age group in the 60-kilometre Willo Mountain Bike Race in March.

Celebration of life

The biennial transplant games is an Olympic-style sporting event for those who have undergone a transplant.

They were first organised by British transplant surgeon Dr Maurice Slapak in 1978 after he became inspired by a kidney recipient he ran with.

Chris Thomas, the CEO of Transplant Australia. (ABC Sport: Chris Taylor)

Chief executive of Transplant Australia Chris Thomas described the event as a celebration of life.

"Every participant owes their life to someone else," he said.

"They're people who were really once at death's door contemplating their future and then miraculously, someone has given them an organ to enable them to live.

"It's a really good opportunity to bring our community together to learn from one another."

Cameron Butcher with his mum post-heart transplant. (Supplied)

Mr Butcher will be competing in cycling, tennis, swimming and six-a-side soccer.

"I'm really competitive about the cycling stuff, but the other stuff's just a bit of fun and never been to Tassie before," he said.

The games will run until October 3.

World.title: OpenAI breach proves need for more data centres, major parties say
World.content:
Labor and Coalition MPs have maintained that Australia must open its doors to AI investment in the wake of OpenAI's data breach, in order to ensure the country has a seat at the table to shape the technology's development.

OpenAI disclosed this month that one of its autonomous agents gained unauthorised access to Medicare health statistics held by Services Australia in June by finding a security workaround.

AI leaders, including OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, have been warning that AI is advancing too quickly and its development should be slowed to give society a chance to catch up.

Open AI has paused training of its latest models following reports of the rogue agents breaching multiple government systems, according to Associated Press.

The government has recommitted to introducing "safeguards" against AI in the wake of the Services Australia breach, though those safeguards have not been detailed.

Yesterday, Environment Minister Murray Watt suggested a government taskforce would consider whether Australian law currently allowed for prosecution if a rogue AI agent inappropriately accessed information, "and if it doesn't, that's obviously something we will take into account in developing our new AI standards".

But neither the government nor the Opposition believe it would justify a withdrawal from the AI race, and the data centre rush that would secure access to AI compute and avoid total foreign dependence for the technology.

OpenAI's confession to its 'credit', says Coalition

Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume told ABC's Insiders program that the government should not try to chase down OpenAI over its voluntary disclosure.

"AI is inevitably going to be part of Australia's future, we want to make sure we are part of the conversation, but certainly the way to go about that is not to threaten criminal action against US counterparts and those trusted partners that we are relying on," Senator Hume said.

"This time, we could only have found out about it because OpenAI fessed up and said that something went wrong."

Jane Hume says the government should not finger wag at OpenAI, which made a voluntary disclosure of its breach. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

The government said while little actual damage was done by OpenAI's breach it was a "serious" and unprecedented incident, with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also directly raising in his meeting with Sam Altman why it had taken the company months to notify Services Australia.

At the United Nations General Assembly, Mr Albanese urged other middle powers to band together to influence the development of artificial intelligence, which is largely being led by AI rivals China and the United States.

US President Donald Trump rejected calls to regulate AI development, saying the US could not lose its lead to China, saying "whoever wins AI wins".

Shadow Defence Minister James Paterson told News24 that he doubted OpenAI's breach was the first — just the first to be disclosed.

"I think it is to OpenAI's credit that they told us," Senator Paterson said.

"This is the first time an Australian government has ever been notified that there has been a breach of this kind from an AI agent. I doubt, personally, this actually is the first time.

"It would not shock me at all if there had been other breaches in the past by AI agents … I guarantee you that if this was an AI company based in the People's Republic of China, and it engaged in a breach of Australian government networks, they will not be sending an email to any inbox to let us know."

Australia can't afford to write off AI Australia may want AI to live up to its promise, but has just experienced how easily things can go wrong. The challenge now is figuring out how to harness one without getting blindsided by the other.

Senator Paterson said Australia had a rare opportunity to gain a seat at the table of global AI regulation by establishing data centres in Australia for AI training.

"The truth is right now we are an irrelevant jurisdiction for AI regulation — we are a man shouting at the clouds — but if we get the investment here then we will have a say," Senator Paterson said.

Defence Minister Richard Marles told News24 there was "no hiding" from AI.

"We need to be engaging here. I mean, this technology is coming. There is no putting your head in the sand. And the more we engage with it, the more we have agency," Mr Marles said.

"We are seeking to engage with these companies, engaging in investment in Australia is an important economic opportunity. It is critically important for our national security.

"But, fundamentally, if there is a lesson to be drawn from this last week, what it also will give us is much more agency in terms of shaping the way this technology is developed and making sure that it's developed in a way that is safe for humans."

Richard Marles says the breach proves the need for Australia to play a role in shaping AI. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Senator Paterson said he supported a number of reforms to strengthen AI safety, including mandatory notifications of breaches, independent evaluators and assessors of models, and a complaints pathway for people to report issues with AI.

But the Coalition has also questioned whether the government had done enough to shield Australia's systems from AI, and has criticised Services Australia's four-day delay in raising the breach with the Australian Signals Directorate.

The agency had established a dedicated inbox for breach notifications, but Senator Paterson said it was "extraordinary" that the inbox wasn't being constantly monitored and reported.

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young has demanded that OpenAI chief Sam Altman appear at a parliamentary inquiry into AI.

"These big AI companies want to set up shop very quickly, before there is a real understanding of the threats of this technology," Senator Hanson-Young said.

"While we see the big AI companies themselves warning of how powerful their technology could be, they are still really pressuring government to get out of the way while they roll out the infrastructure. That's all a bit rich, frankly."

Mr Altman cannot be compelled to appear before the inquiry because he is overseas.

Senator Paterson said OpenAI should provide relevant senior officials to engage with that inquiry.

World.title: Purple pubs because heartbreak hotels for Freo's hometown faithful
World.content:
Fremantle fans have been left heartbroken following a shock seven-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday's grand final.

Despite the Dockers leading for most of the game, the Lions were able to claw back a 17-point deficit with just four minutes left in the final term.

In Fremantle, more than 40,000 people took over the Cappuccino Strip and sold out venues across the Port city.

The atmosphere in Fremantle was electric for the first three quarters — at one venue, fans were screaming and jumping on tables.

However, there was a noticeable shift in the atmosphere as the minutes ticked away late in the game, with many fans visibly distressed as the Lions piled on late goals.

Fremantle fans knew their long wait would continue as Logan Morris sealed the game for the Lions. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

At the siren, collective moans of disappointment echoed throughout Fremantle's venues.

At one point, tension led to a physical altercation in the crowd with multiple police and security trying to break up the fight.

One man was escorted away by police, with an ambulance called to attend to a woman seen on the ground.

Devastated fans

Fans were seen holding each other and crying.

It wasn't a happy end to the carnival atmosphere that saw huge crowds spill onto the streets of Fremantle to cheer their beloved Dockers on. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

One fan, Layla, said she felt sad but hopeful because of the fight the Dockers put up.

"I genuinely thought we had it," she said.

"And then in the last minute, my heart just broke."

Harry Thorn (right) says he's disappointed but stays faithful. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

Harry Thorn was also in Fremantle to watch the game. He said it ran in his family to support the Dockers.

"I'm a little bit disappointed that we've never won a [grand] final, but we're gonna get there one year," he said.

" And then we'll get our own three-peat. "

Tayla Bowden was brought to tears when the final siren rang and said she was left devastated and shocked.

Tayla Bowden (left) says she was left shocked and Chelsea Bowden (right). (ABC News: Pip Waller)

She said being a Fremantle supporter was about a balance of hope and despair at the same time.

"We have stuck with them for 32 years and we love them, no matter what. We haven't got a premiership yet, it's hard," she said.

"They're hard to love and you can't help but love them at the same time. The culture is the biggest thing.

" What is not to love about them? "

Fremantle's Cappuccino Strip cleared quickly after the loss, with some devoted fans remaining in the city venues.

Fremantle Dockers's signs had been taken down. (ABC News: Pip Waller)

Some of the Fremantle dockers signs had been taken down with rubbish on the streets.

Fremantle's players and travelling party were due to return to Western Australia today.

World.title: Surfing town marks 30 years since fatal Gracetown cliff collapse
World.content:
For Stephen Duggan, September 27, 1996 started out like any other Friday but when the news of a coastal cliff collapse reached his family farm, he did not hesitate to act.

Driving down to his local beach, racing across the sand, Mr Duggan and his friend John dug for hours with their bare hands, searching for survivors.

"We were just working so frantically, we were just pulling dirt out," he said.

Wreaths placed at the memorial in Gracetown, marking 30 years since the tragedy. (Supplied)

Thirty years ago, students, teachers and parents flocked to Huzza's Beach for an inter-school surfing competition in Gracetown, 271 kilometres south of Perth.

Inclement weather saw people take shelter under the cliffs, which suddenly gave way, killing five adults and four children.

Extraordinary rescue efforts

The sole survivor of the incident was 11-year-old Sara Otto.

Mr Duggan was one of the people who discovered her under the rubble and saved her life.

"We came across a girl who had possibly been saved by a rock falling down and hitting her on the head, which had then kept a lot of sand off her face," he said.

Surfers in the water at one of Gracetown's famous surf breaks. (ABC South West: Bridget McArthur)

Mr Duggan recalls the mammoth risks taken on by community members who raced to help in the search.

"[One man] drove his backhoe through the water, through metres of salt water, over rocks and over parts of the reef to get his machine to the area," he said.

"[Another man] drove his excavator over the edge with an extended boom, down a pretty steep embankment to get it to the bottom.

"The actions of those two guys were pretty encouraging, pretty strong and, under today's circumstances, pretty dangerous."

Holding memories close

Skye Thompson's father, Lindsay, was among those who died.

Skye Thompson at a beach in Gracetown. (ABC South West: Anthony Pancia)

She said that while her childhood memories of her father were fading, she holds close what she does remember.

"He gave me the feeling that I was loved," Ms Thompson said.

"After 30 years, there are only a few memories that really stick.

"For a girl, just to be loved by your father is something really special — I always carry that memory."

Ms Thompson was just 12 and competing at the surfing competition in Gracetown, on Western Australia's south-western coast, when her world changed forever.

Lindsay Thompson died in the Gracetown cliff collapse in 1996. (ABC News)

"A lot of us kids were witnesses to the cliff collapse," she said.

"But we're also witness to the community coming together and how fast people came to volunteer, from really young people to older people as well."

Ms Thompson said she always sought out a body of water on the tragedy's anniversary.

"We try and get in a swim and get out in the ocean or maybe have a surf and remember our friends and family."

Surfing legacy lives on

Gracetown Grommets surfing competition was created in honour of those who died.

This year it celebrated its 30th competition.

Cowaramup Bay Boardriders Association president Ian Andreson said the incident sent shock waves through the surfing community.

Hundreds of surfers paddled out to pay homage to those who lost their lives in the tragedy. (ABC News)

"For decades we have sheltered under those cliffs, away from the sun or the wind or the rain," he said.

"To have that happen with the locals was just an absolute tragedy."

Mr Anderson said he had seen grandchildren of those who died in the collapse compete in the event.

"That continues as a family legacy, the commitment of the families and to surfing — that's phenomenal," he said.

A monument placed in honour of the nine people who lost their lives in the tragedy. (Supplied)

Ms Thompson said seeing young surfers in the water at Gracetown would make her father happy.

"He'd be absolutely stoked to see all these young people and the amount of girls in the water," she said.

World.title: Six bodies recovered from rubble of Athens building after explosion
World.content:
The bodies of six people have been recovered from the rubble of a two-story house after a suspected gas explosion in an historic part of the Greek capital, Athens, according to local authorities.

Documents and belongings found with four of the victims, two men and two women, indicated they were citizens of the United States, according to Greek state broadcaster ERT and other local reports.

The tourists, two American couples, had been renting an apartment on the first story of the building and were expected to check in to catch a flight from Athens airport but did not show up, a police source told Reuters.

Dozens of firefighters using cameras, sensors and rescue dogs were called to the scene to search for victims. (AP: Yorgos Karahalis)

The other two people killed were an elderly British man and his Greek wife, who lived on the second story of a three-story building, ERT reported.

The blast occurred in the Plaka district on Friday, local time, and was believed to have been caused by a major gas leak, Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said.

Mr Doukas also said that neighbouring buildings were damaged and evacuated after the explosion.

"We are talking about an incredible disaster," he said.

The building where the explosion occurred appeared to have been completely destroyed. (AP: Yorgos Karahalis)

Plaka lies at the foot of the Acropolis, Greece’s most visited ancient monument.

Two women were injured in an adjacent building on Lysikratous Street, the fire department said.

The owner of the ground-floor apartment, Mathaios Artavanis, told the Kathimerini Daily he was absent at the time of the blast.

The search-and-rescue operation involved 30 firefighters and three dogs.

Rubble from the debris was blasted across the street from the home and damaged nearby buildings. (AP: Yorgos Karahalis)

They were initially looking for an elderly couple who lived in one apartment and four tourists who were staying in another as they removed debris from the building.

Cameras and sensors were used by the rescuers to locate the bodies of the six victims, fire brigade spokesman Vassilis Vathrakogiannis said in a televised briefing.

An investigation into the explosion has since been launched, after reports were made of a gas smell.

A year ago, locals in Plaka warned the city and utility companies about the risk of gas leaks or short circuits, according to a letter by the residents' association published by Kathimerini.

The residents had urged a fire drill to identify possible weaknesses in the emergency response plans for the district.

Video from the scene showed rubble strewn across the street and parked cars crushed by falling debris.

Resident Andreas Martzaklis said all those rescued from the adjacent building were tourists.

The pastor of a nearby church said a service on Sunday would be held outdoors because the building had been damaged.

World.title: Forty years ago, this Brisbane band was the next big thing. What went wrong?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Forty years ago, this Brisbane band was the next big thing. What went wrong? Nick Dent September 27, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If anyone in Brisbane ever could be, the Atkinson boys, Darren and Greg, seemed destined to be rock stars. They grew up in Oxley, streets away from both Ed Kuepper (the Saints) and Robert Vickers (the Go-Betweens), both of whom they knew from delivering them fruit for their parents’ greengrocery business. Brisbane band Ups and Downs in the 1980s: Peter Shaw, John Flade and Greg Atkinson, with Darren Atkinson in front. Facebook Better still, their dad, Geoff Atkinson, was a popular DJ on 4BC and 4BK during the 1950s and ’60s, had a music TV show on QTQ9, Teen Beat, had interviewed the Beatles, and nurtured the boys’ love of music by bringing the latest records home from work. At the end of the 1970s, with Darren on drums and Greg on bass and lead vocals, they put together a band called 42nd Street, moved to Sydney, and promptly and acrimoniously broke up.



But everything would change when they returned to Brisbane and (in 1983) formed the legendary guitar-pop band Ups and Downs with guitarists John Flade and Peter Shaw. Two singles they released in Brisbane, Living Inside My Head and Perfect Crime, started a buzz down south, including a positive review in The Sydney Morning Herald, so they headed back to Sydney and were signed by Polygram sub-label True Tone Records. “It was a great time for guitar bands,” Darren recalls. “The time was right for a group like us, so we had a lot of early success.” Ups and Downs around the time of Sleepless. “Back then, there were so many venues throughout Sydney suburbs, you could play at least three or four nights a week.



“The time was right for a group like us, so we had a lot of early success.” Ups and Downs were part of the Paisley Underground – an indie rock movement inspired by 1960s psychedelia, but with a darker edge. “We didn’t want to just be labelled as a ’60s copyist band,” Darren says, admitting, “we created part of that ourselves by wearing paisley shirts on stage”. Their efforts culminated in their best-known single, The Living Kind: a jangle-pop ode to longing that skirted the lower reaches of the singles chart and got them an ARIA nomination for Best New Talent (Crowded House won that year). So why did it all go wrong? Why aren’t Ups and Downs talked about in the same breath as another Brisbane guitar band of the era, the Go-Betweens?



First there was the handling of the band’s 1986 release Sleepless, the 40th anniversary of which they are celebrating with a national tour. “We didn’t do a whole album,” says Darren. “It’s actually a mini-album which is, to this day, a bad marketing idea.” With just seven tracks, Sleepless was all killer, no filler, and the band were told people would love it. “But it actually went against us, because we couldn’t get into the mainstream album charts. We sold lots on the independent front, but the sales weren’t recognised.” With their management, they took the view True Tone were not supporting their commercial potential.



“We tried to extract ourselves from that [contract], and that meant we pretty much couldn’t record and didn’t play much,” Darren says. Adding keyboard player Trevor O’Neill, Ups and Downs were able to sign to Mushroom Records two years later and finally release a full album, Underneath the Watchful Eye. But when the A&R rep who signed them was sacked, they found themselves the label’s unloved child. Worse still, by the time they re-emerged, a new generation of guitar bands had stolen their thunder. “I think the defining moment was a gig at Selena’s at the Coogee Bay Hotel. It had Ratcat, the Hummingbirds, Falling Joys and Caligula, all new bands, and we were down towards the bottom of the bill,” Darren says. “We decided, well, things don’t last forever,” Greg says.



The brothers started a new band, Big Heavy Stuff, with a grungier sound, which found airplay on Triple J and supported Radiohead on their OK Computer Australian tour. After three deals with three different labels, they fizzled out in the new millennium. Kristin Black, who DJs the weekly 4ZZZ show Heyday, says Ups and Downs were Brisbane’s answer to the Church. The Paisley Above Ground: Ups and Downs now. “Sleepless, or Flawless as I have called it, is a brilliant mini album,” she says. “Combining a moody instrumental opener, with chiming guitar tracks, an unlikely but brilliant Neil Diamond cover [Solitary Man] – it just works.



“There’s something about siblings singing in harmony, they do it best.” Related Article Radio ‘Where’s our transmitter?’ How the Whitlam dismissal nearly silenced radio 4ZZZ To mark 40 years of Sleepless, Ups and Downs are reuniting to tour it. They also have a new EP, Radio Is Dead, a fresh and evocative release showcasing the band’s ethereal guitar textures and otherworldly vocal harmonies. With cover art depicting the Atkinsons’ dad in his radio prime, it’s their first new release since 2017 comeback album The Sky’s In Love With You.



“Greg’s voice doesn’t seem to have aged a day in 40 years,” Black says. “I’m thrilled there’s new Ups and Downs music in the world.” Ups and Downs still boast their original line-up, with the addition of extra bassist Alex Ronayne. “I don’t think we had any intention of ever getting back together,” Darren says. “But about 10 years later, someone wanted to put our song on a compilation album, and suddenly it’s ‘do you wanna do a show?’ and next thing we’re ‘maybe we could get back together’. “It’s not just a nostalgia thing, you know,” Greg says. “For us, it’s reigniting that creative intensity that we had back then.” “Unfortunately, being hungry for success – it comes with a really dark, competition side,” Darren says. “What’s beautiful about doing it now is there’s none of that, honestly.



“We felt lucky to still be able to do this and still enjoy it.” Ups and Downs play the Crowbar Brisbane, Friday, October 2; Wallaby Hotel, Mudgeeraba, Saturday, October 3; Crowbar Sydney, Friday, October 9; and Hamilton Station Hotel, Newcastle, Saturday, October 10. World.title: ‘My preference is to stay’: What is Sam Walker worth should he star in a Roosters premiership?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘My preference is to stay’: What is Sam Walker worth should he star in a Roosters premiership? Christian Nicolussi September 27, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sam Walker is 80 minutes away from winning a premiership with the Sydney Roosters – and justifying the climbing price tag that was floated during preliminary contract negotiations with the Bondi club. Walker overcame a serious ankle injury to play an instrumental role in the Roosters’ 36-20 win over the Dolphins in their preliminary final triumph on Friday night. Roosters halfback Sam Walker. Getty Images The team was in such control in the latter stages of the match that Roosters coach Trent Robinson had the luxury of giving his star playmaker an early mark with an eye on Sunday’s decider. Walker hit pause on contract talks with the Roosters last month. The difference between what his management was chasing and what the Roosters were prepared to pay was around $1 million over four years.



The Queenslander’s camp, as reported by this masthead, was holding out hope for close to $1.7m a season from 2028. If the 24-year-old inspires the first Roosters title since 2019, and then plays a key role for Australia at the World Cup – especially as there are concerns over Nathan Cleary’s foot – Walker will be in hot demand after November 1, should he become a free agent. Loading Walker said after Friday’s win, his immediate focus had been on his recovery, including the use of a hyperbaric chamber, but he was keen to remain in the red, white and blue. “For sure, like I said, my preference is obviously to stay at the Roosters,” Walker said.



“But for now, I’m not thinking anything about that. “My job is to go out there and perform, play football, and the rest will take care of itself. Sam Walker gets a cuddle from Billy Smith during his excellent comeback game from injury. Getty Images “There’s not a glimmer of thought about that [contract situation] at the moment. It’s about winning next Sunday.” The Roosters head into the grand final knowing it will be the last appearance for Daly Cherry-Evans (Hull FC), as well as rugby-bound teammates Mark Nawaqanitawase and Angus Crichton.



With skipper James Tedesco off contract at the end of next year, and now a year-to-year proposition, and uncertainty about Spencer Leniu’s future at Bondi next year, the Roosters will have space in the cap to accommodate Walker. Cherry-Evans was mindful not to get caught up in Walker’s contract talks, and said: “I love this club, which is crazy to say after 12 months, but the people have been nothing but amazing towards me and my family. Loading “And if Sammy feels the same thing, then he’ll say. “When the time’s right, he will sort that out. But my opinion on it will [mean] very little, which is how it should be.”



Walker suffered a syndesmosis injury against the Dolphins in round 26, about a fortnight after he parked contract negotiations, and there were initial fears he wouldn’t play again this season. “But once I had the surgery, I was pretty clear and pretty focused on getting back for this game,” Walker said. Related Article NRL 2026 The moment DCE knew he could win a premiership with the Roosters “I’m really grateful for the staff and the medical team at the Roosters – they’ve done an amazing job helping me out, and also the club to believe in me to let me play. It was obviously a massive risk for them as well. “I can’t wait [for Sunday]. It’s going to be an exciting week, but none of that matters unless we go out there and perform for 80 minutes. That’ll be our goal, and that’s all we’re focusing on.”



Walker grew up a Roosters fan, despite constant attempts to convert him into being a South Sydney supporter while his father and uncle, Ben and Chris, were playing at the Bunnies. The Roosters’ only injury concern heading into grand final week is Connor Watson. He suffered a concussion against the Dolphins and will have to obtain clearance from an independent doctor to play before he exits for St George Illawarra in 2027 en route to the PNG Chiefs in 2028. World.title: ‘Loitering in the shallows’: Winter shark surveillance led to hundreds of beach evacuations
World.content:
PoliticsNSWSharks ‘Loitering in the shallows’: Winter shark surveillance led to hundreds of beach evacuations Michael McGowan September 27, 2026 — 11:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Shark surveillance drones patrolling NSW waters over winter for the first time led to hundreds of beach evacuations, including one for a two-metre great white swimming “in the shallows” on Sydney’s northern beaches. In total, data released by the NSW government on Sunday showed there were more than 1200 shark detections by drone operators in July and August, leading to 360 interventions including alarms, jet ski deployments and beach evacuations. Shark surveillance drones patrolling NSW waters. NSW Government The incidents reports, compiled by the Department of Primary Industries, make for chilling reading; they include a massive four-metre bull shark spotted 50 metres offshore at Urunga on the Mid North Coast, and a pack of seven “chasing a whale” at Lennox Head. The two-metre great white was spotted “loitering” about 150 metres offshore at South Narrabeen at about midday in early July, before two more were seen about 10 minutes later. After multiple sharks were sighted, at about 1pm a two-metre great white seen “tracking north” was “in the shallows” about “30 metres from shore”.



The drone surveillance logs include others spotted by drones close to swimmers at Warriewood on the northern beaches and Woolgoolga, near Coffs Harbour. The winter drone program was announced after a spate of fatal shark attacks, including the death of surfer Mercury Psillakis, 57, at Dee Why last September and 12-year-old Nico Antic in Vaucluse. Premier Chris Minns last week met Psillakis’ twin brother Mike and widow Maria, as well as Coogee shark attack survivor Leah Stewart. Those attacks led the government to announce it would roll out year-long drone surveillance, as well as a trial of artificial intelligence to identify sharks. Work is under way to procure and build a trial AI system to assist drone pilots with shark detection and species identification. Maria Psillakis, Mike Psillakis, Premier Chris Minns and shark attack survivor Leah Stewart. Instagram Minns warned at the time that increased surveillance was likely to lead to more sharks being spotted – but this was not necessarily evidence of an increase in population. The winter drone surveillance resulted in hundreds of beach evacuations, including multiple closures at popular Sydney swimming spots such as Bondi, where a two-metre shark spotted 100 metres offshore in July was one of multiple shark sightings.



Other popular beaches such as Manly, Dee Why and Cronulla were all evacuated multiple times. Related Article Sharks ‘I did think she was going to die’: How strangers saved shark attack victim Leah Stewart The shark data was released as the government announced expanded drone surveillance covering 97 beaches across the state from the beginning of the spring and summer school holidays. A total of 73 drones will patrol beaches from 6.15am to 6.30pm in October and from 6am to 7.30pm in December. It will also roll out seven remotely operated drones at beaches including Crowdy Head, Avalon and Mona Vale. Primary Industries Minister Tara Moriarty said the $120 million drone program was one of the most comprehensive in the world.



“A foundational platform in our new program is drone technology, that is delivering eyes in the sky across our state’s popular beaches, looking out for the target sharks – white, bull and tiger – and then enabling countermeasures,” she said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Nothing is quite what it seems in this comedy of menace
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Harold Pinter’s The Homecoming is performed at the Athenaeum

MUSICAL THEATRE: Spamalot returns to Melbourne

MUSIC: Metal band Health finishes their show with an invite to Cherry Bar

THEATRE: Luke makes its world premiere at Red Stitch

MUSIC: Kristian Bezuidenhout performs Handel and Bach with the MSO

THEATRE

The Homecoming ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 3 The lights come up to reveal two characters in a living room and it doesn’t take long for the sense that something is off-kilter to take hold. A pugnacious aged patriarch and ex-butcher named Max (Richard Piper) blathers on in an unpunctuated stream of consciousness to the uninterested Lenny (Ben Geurens) – we don’t find out the two are family until Max admonishes the louche Lenny for speaking such to his “lousy filthy father”. Richard Piper as Max in The Homecoming. Ben Fon The barely concealed hostilities are extended to the diametrically gentle Sam (David Field), Max’s chauffeur brother and the hulking wannabe boxer Joey (Eddie Orton), Lenny’s younger brother. No one and nothing are quite as they seem in Harold Pinter’s 1965 comedy of menace The Homecoming, even once you account for the virulent sexism, barely concealed hatred, and dearth of familial love between these characters.



The intrigue deepens when all four of them retire to bed and the taciturn Teddy (Peter Houghton) enters the house, accompanied by his enigmatic wife Ruth (Kate Kendall). Teddy has effectively been estranged from his family for six years and now resides in America, with neither his wife nor family acquainted with each other. A series of decidedly strange interactions between all the characters leave audiences none the wiser as to what is about to unfold in this claustrophobic domestic setting. Under the direction of Greg Carroll, a slowly creeping sense of foreboding and listlessness overtakes the play, only strengthening its grip on the audience as it unfolds. The world Pinter has ensconced these characters in exists in and of itself, ungoverned by the moral sensibilities and social mores of the now, let alone that of the 1960s when this play first premiered in London. Peter Houghton as Teddy and Kate Kendall as Ruth. Ben Fon Absurdist and fantastical despite its realist underpinnings, The Homecoming lulls its audience into an illusion of normalcy. When social contracts are broken with seemingly no repercussions, the play’s (and our) grasp on reality loosens – shining an uncomfortable spotlight on the confronting misogyny on display, calling into rebuke the meaning of the familial ties traditionally held so dear, and questioning the unspoken rules that allow society to function as it does. The famed Pinter Pause allows the requisite space for these consternations to fester. A muscular black room is the fitting backdrop for the exertion of these men’s fragile, toxic masculinities, while Amelia Carroll and Margaret Goy’s costume design is a stunning cloak of civility that masks the innermost depravations of these characters. Clad in a babydoll dress throughout, Ruth is read as childlike and guileless – a misnomer that allows her to exert the full force of her feminine wiliness.



The strength of a production like The Homecoming lives and dies by its ensemble cast, and this one is uniformly excellent. Kendall is a particular highlight as the otherworldly, cosmically unflappable Ruth, simultaneously an antidote against the testosterone-soaked aggression of the men around her and the sun around which their neediness, desperation and contemptibility orbit.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair MUSICAL THEATRE

Spamalot ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 4 You’d think that after 51 years a joke might stop being as funny as it once was. And yet, sitting in the dark watching two men debate how one swallow – or perhaps two, if they were holding some sort of string – might transport a coconut across countries, I found myself laughing as though it were the first time I’d heard this conversation. From left: Jesse Vasiliadis, Gareth Isaac, Stephen Curry, Ethan Jones and Noah Skape. Ben Fon Monty Python and the Holy Grail first hit cinemas in 1975, and Spamalot, “a new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture” takes the key plot and a handful of songs from the film, adds a whole lot more, and twists the story off into new directions as needed. The musical, itself now 20 years on from when it took Broadway by storm and took out the Tony Award for best musical, still feels vibrant and fun and silly.



A spoof of the Arthurian legend, the story sees King Arthur (Stephen Curry) seeking knights to join his round table before being tasked by God (a video recording of Eric Idle) to find the Holy Grail. While many jokes and scenes are lifted directly from the original film and other Python works, Spamalot, with book and lyrics by Idle, and music co-written by John Du Prez, is its own thing. Jaz Flowers and Ethan Jones as the Lady of the Lake and Sir Galahad. Ben Fon The songs written specifically for Spamalot hold their own against the older, more established tunes. Idle takes great delight in breaking the fourth wall in creative ways, and musical theatre itself is a key pillar of the story, with nods to everything and everyone from West Side Story to Liza Minnelli. Jaz Flowers as the Lady of the Lake steals almost every scene she’s in – her powerful command of every note makes light work of the parade of vocal challenges thrown her way. Her skill as a singer is matched only by her comedic timing. Her meta duet with Ethan Jones as Sir Galahad in The Song That Goes Like This is a particular highlight.



Python humour remains evergreen because it is untethered from time. When it isn’t purely revelling in the absurd, it is taking aim at themes that sadly never grow old (inequality, bigotry, cowardice), joyfully ratcheting up the classics (fart jokes), and being gleefully persnickety when it comes to wordplay. With a talented cast who all appear to be enjoying every minute on stage, Spamalot is just the right amount of silly.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux MUSIC

Health ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, September 20 Metal always straddles the serious and the absurd. Tonight Los Angeles industrial metal band Health enters the stage to the theme song from Neon Genesis Evangelion. Health in 2026 is all machine beats and processed guitar riffs, with wan, emotive vocals. Richard Clifford Internet wags call Health’s brand of industrial metal “cum metal”. The band sells t-shirts that say “Sad Music For Horny People”. Tonight’s show is an industrial crush of guitar, drums, big feelings, and dudes swishing their long, lustrous hair, faces melted in metallic bliss. That’s the audience, by the way – I can’t really see the band, they’re swaddled in smoke and light, as it should be.



At the start of their career, Health put out two acclaimed albums of dancey noise rock, heavy, colourful and dynamic. Since then they’ve distilled their sound into something more structured: the glam of industrial metal, with hints of shoegaze and gothic rock. Have they polished the metal a bit too thin over the years? Health in 2026 is all machine beats and processed guitar riffs, with singer Jake Duzsik’s wan, emotive vocals. John Famiglietti opens the show with a pitch-perfect Aussie accent Richard Clifford But they push forward, and their fans come with them. Almost everything in tonight’s set is from their last two albums, Rat Wars and Conflict DLC, and just a few earlier tracks, notably Major Crimes and Tears (written for video games Cyberpunk 2077 and Max Payne 3), and We Are Water, from their 2009 second album Get Color. They’re at their peak when it all builds to something manic, like in Future of Hell and Shred Envy. A template emerges, in which something jagged and hard rears its head briefly, before they cut the decibels for Duzsik’s verses, which all merge into one overwrought cloud.



Like all metal shows, there’s an air of generosity and camaraderie between the crowd and the band. Bassist/producer John Famiglietti opens the show with a pitch-perfect Aussie accent (“You sick c---ts, we’re gonna rip your f--kin’ dicks off!“) and ends it by inviting everyone to Cherry Bar for the afterparty, before crowdsurfing to the sound booth. His people love him.

Reviewed by Will Cox THEATRE

Luke ★★★★

Red Stitch, until October 11 Local playwright Angus Cameron has teamed up with Red Stitch for the world premiere of Luke – a disturbing, emotionally complex three-hander that weaves a provocative play of ideas into a psychological mystery of troubling currency. Will Lonsdale, Olga Makeeva and Dion Mills in Luke Parenthesy I was bewildered by the opening sequence. Two adults race across a living room playing dress-ups. They’re engaged in some kind of private game, based on the Bolshevik assassination of the Romanovs during the Russian Revolution, but something about the scene feels off, inauthentic somehow.



A clever reason for this will remain an enigma until well after we discover that the pair are high school teachers in country Victoria. It’s 2007, and Damon (Dion Mills) and Olena (Olga Makeeva) are unwinding at term’s end after a gruelling night of parent-teacher interviews. When Chris (Will Lonsdale) – the school’s 19-year-old rowing coach and a former student of Damon’s – joins them, the games continue. Some of the playfulness is literary or historical – a relic of the ludic flamboyance essential to Damon’s pedagogic style. He’s an inspiring educator, discreetly gay, and his mentor-like relationship with Chris, who came out to Damon as a student, is tinged by affection and by a body of queer knowledge excluded by the official (read heteronormative) education system. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Parenthesy When conversation turns to a never-seen character, Luke – a year 11 student leaving the school after inappropriate attention from a member of staff – the game mutates through a series of twists, with a possible child sex abuse scenario, and its consequences, playing out over decades. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Mills’ suspect teacher has the charisma, passion, idealism, and sheer eccentricity of a gifted educator. There’s no question he leaves a mark on his students: his scenes with Lonsdale’s Chris are tender and haunted – enlivened by the irrepressible joy they both take in the learning game, as well as the shadow of barely repressed desire.



Olena is the fulcrum of the play, and Makeeva is riveting as, through veiled parable and a clipped and embittered realism, the character weighs the truth of a situation in which the righteousness of her own acts is called into question. She is a staunch counter to Chris – a young man heavily invested in his own righteousness, and solipsistic in the performance of it. Editor's pick Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said Luke tackles such uncomfortable subjects as the erotics of education and the ethics of making art from life. It has stern things to say about the cultural amnesia afflicting Australian literature and drama, and it brings child protection concerns into contact with the reality of homophobia, knowing the ancient slur – the one that equates homosexuality with paedophilia – has never quite ceased to echo. Yet this haunting play celebrates, too, the solidarity and strangeness of found family, the clandestine solidarity and the mentorship relations that can exist between queer men finding their tribe.



In this, it has an artistic genealogy that can be traced back to some of the most fearless and unsettling voices in queer Australian literature – the implied pederasty in David Malouf’s short story Under Southern Skies, say, or Frank Moorhouse’s The Everlasting Secret Family – updating the issues to a world of changing mores in which progressive rhetoric can disguise more difficult and painful human truths.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead MUSIC

Handel and Bach ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, September 19 Many Melbourne concertgoers will remember the stylish flair with which Australian fortepianist Kristian Bezuidenhout performed the complete Beethoven piano concertos with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra on the cusp of COVID. Kristian Bezuidenhout at an earlier concert. Marco Borggreve Returning with some of that flair, Bezuidenhout directed the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra from the harpsichord in this program of works by Bach and Handel.



Focusing particularly on rhythm and dynamics, Bezuidenhout brought crisp grandiloquence to the many French-style introductions on the program, whether to Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 1 in C major or the Overture to Handel’s Admeto. There was also a general rhythmic buoyancy which lent itself well both to the dance-infused Bach Suite and Suites Nos. 1 and 2 from Handel’s familiar Water Music. Carefully shaped dynamics applied to the whole orchestra made sense of the rise and fall of phrases and provided some well-judged dramatic contrasts. Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews These are unapologetically political songs, and this artist is unapologetically herself Despite overall clarity, it was in Bezuidenhout’s arrangement of Bach’s incomplete Contrapunctus XIV from The Art of Fugue that the listener might have longed for some more granular detail in terms of articulation and pliability of tone in individual lines. Such qualities were more apparent in Handel’s Concerto grosso in D minor, Op. 3, no. 5 which followed. Fine wind and brass playing hallmarked the second half. Beginning with the Sinfonia from Bach’s Cantata No. 52 (otherwise recognisable as the opening of Brandenburg Concerto No. 4) followed by the Water Music, the horns and oboes took up Bezuidenhout’s brisk tempos with alacrity.



Oboists Johannes Grosso and Ann Blackburn together with horn players Lucie Krysatis and Abbey Edlin crowned the festive mood of the Handel; their timbre setting up piquant contrasts with the strings, trumpets providing an additional regal air in the second suite. Thanks to Bezuidenhout, the MSO proved it can bring some idiomatic lightness to the glories of the baroque.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: Forty years ago, this Brisbane band was the next big thing. What went wrong?
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCity life Forty years ago, this Brisbane band was the next big thing. What went wrong? Nick Dent September 27, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If anyone in Brisbane ever could be, the Atkinson boys, Darren and Greg, seemed destined to be rock stars. They grew up in Oxley, streets away from both Ed Kuepper (the Saints) and Robert Vickers (the Go-Betweens), both of whom they knew from delivering them fruit for their parents’ greengrocery business. Brisbane band Ups and Downs in the 1980s: Peter Shaw, John Flade and Greg Atkinson, with Darren Atkinson in front. Facebook Better still, their dad, Geoff Atkinson, was a popular DJ on 4BC and 4BK during the 1950s and ’60s, had a music TV show on QTQ9, Teen Beat, had interviewed the Beatles, and nurtured the boys’ love of music by bringing the latest records home from work. At the end of the 1970s, with Darren on drums and Greg on bass and lead vocals, they put together a band called 42nd Street, moved to Sydney, and promptly and acrimoniously broke up.



But everything would change when they returned to Brisbane and (in 1983) formed the legendary guitar-pop band Ups and Downs with guitarists John Flade and Peter Shaw. Two singles they released in Brisbane, Living Inside My Head and Perfect Crime, started a buzz down south, including a positive review in The Sydney Morning Herald, so they headed back to Sydney and were signed by Polygram sub-label True Tone Records. “It was a great time for guitar bands,” Darren recalls. “The time was right for a group like us, so we had a lot of early success.” Ups and Downs around the time of Sleepless. “Back then, there were so many venues throughout Sydney suburbs, you could play at least three or four nights a week.



“The time was right for a group like us, so we had a lot of early success.” Ups and Downs were part of the Paisley Underground – an indie rock movement inspired by 1960s psychedelia, but with a darker edge. “We didn’t want to just be labelled as a ’60s copyist band,” Darren says, admitting, “we created part of that ourselves by wearing paisley shirts on stage”. Their efforts culminated in their best-known single, The Living Kind: a jangle-pop ode to longing that skirted the lower reaches of the singles chart and got them an ARIA nomination for Best New Talent (Crowded House won that year). So why did it all go wrong? Why aren’t Ups and Downs talked about in the same breath as another Brisbane guitar band of the era, the Go-Betweens?



First there was the handling of the band’s 1986 release Sleepless, the 40th anniversary of which they are celebrating with a national tour. “We didn’t do a whole album,” says Darren. “It’s actually a mini-album which is, to this day, a bad marketing idea.” With just seven tracks, Sleepless was all killer, no filler, and the band were told people would love it. “But it actually went against us, because we couldn’t get into the mainstream album charts. We sold lots on the independent front, but the sales weren’t recognised.” With their management, they took the view True Tone were not supporting their commercial potential.



“We tried to extract ourselves from that [contract], and that meant we pretty much couldn’t record and didn’t play much,” Darren says. Adding keyboard player Trevor O’Neill, Ups and Downs were able to sign to Mushroom Records two years later and finally release a full album, Underneath the Watchful Eye. But when the A&R rep who signed them was sacked, they found themselves the label’s unloved child. Worse still, by the time they re-emerged, a new generation of guitar bands had stolen their thunder. “I think the defining moment was a gig at Selena’s at the Coogee Bay Hotel. It had Ratcat, the Hummingbirds, Falling Joys and Caligula, all new bands, and we were down towards the bottom of the bill,” Darren says. “We decided, well, things don’t last forever,” Greg says.



The brothers started a new band, Big Heavy Stuff, with a grungier sound, which found airplay on Triple J and supported Radiohead on their OK Computer Australian tour. After three deals with three different labels, they fizzled out in the new millennium. Kristin Black, who DJs the weekly 4ZZZ show Heyday, says Ups and Downs were Brisbane’s answer to the Church. The Paisley Above Ground: Ups and Downs now. “Sleepless, or Flawless as I have called it, is a brilliant mini album,” she says. “Combining a moody instrumental opener, with chiming guitar tracks, an unlikely but brilliant Neil Diamond cover [Solitary Man] – it just works.



“There’s something about siblings singing in harmony, they do it best.” Related Article Radio ‘Where’s our transmitter?’ How the Whitlam dismissal nearly silenced radio 4ZZZ To mark 40 years of Sleepless, Ups and Downs are reuniting to tour it. They also have a new EP, Radio Is Dead, a fresh and evocative release showcasing the band’s ethereal guitar textures and otherworldly vocal harmonies. With cover art depicting the Atkinsons’ dad in his radio prime, it’s their first new release since 2017 comeback album The Sky’s In Love With You.



“Greg’s voice doesn’t seem to have aged a day in 40 years,” Black says. “I’m thrilled there’s new Ups and Downs music in the world.” Ups and Downs still boast their original line-up, with the addition of extra bassist Alex Ronayne. “I don’t think we had any intention of ever getting back together,” Darren says. “But about 10 years later, someone wanted to put our song on a compilation album, and suddenly it’s ‘do you wanna do a show?’ and next thing we’re ‘maybe we could get back together’. “It’s not just a nostalgia thing, you know,” Greg says. “For us, it’s reigniting that creative intensity that we had back then.” “Unfortunately, being hungry for success – it comes with a really dark, competition side,” Darren says. “What’s beautiful about doing it now is there’s none of that, honestly.



“We felt lucky to still be able to do this and still enjoy it.” Ups and Downs play the Crowbar Brisbane, Friday, October 2; Wallaby Hotel, Mudgeeraba, Saturday, October 3; Crowbar Sydney, Friday, October 9; and Hamilton Station Hotel, Newcastle, Saturday, October 10. World.title: ‘My preference is to stay’: What is Sam Walker worth should he star in a Roosters premiership?
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘My preference is to stay’: What is Sam Walker worth should he star in a Roosters premiership? Christian Nicolussi September 27, 2026 — 12:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sam Walker is 80 minutes away from winning a premiership with the Sydney Roosters – and justifying the climbing price tag that was floated during preliminary contract negotiations with the Bondi club. Walker overcame a serious ankle injury to play an instrumental role in the Roosters’ 36-20 win over the Dolphins in their preliminary final triumph on Friday night. Roosters halfback Sam Walker. Getty Images The team was in such control in the latter stages of the match that Roosters coach Trent Robinson had the luxury of giving his star playmaker an early mark with an eye on Sunday’s decider. Walker hit pause on contract talks with the Roosters last month. The difference between what his management was chasing and what the Roosters were prepared to pay was around $1 million over four years.



The Queenslander’s camp, as reported by this masthead, was holding out hope for close to $1.7m a season from 2028. If the 24-year-old inspires the first Roosters title since 2019, and then plays a key role for Australia at the World Cup – especially as there are concerns over Nathan Cleary’s foot – Walker will be in hot demand after November 1, should he become a free agent. Loading Walker said after Friday’s win, his immediate focus had been on his recovery, including the use of a hyperbaric chamber, but he was keen to remain in the red, white and blue. “For sure, like I said, my preference is obviously to stay at the Roosters,” Walker said.



“But for now, I’m not thinking anything about that. “My job is to go out there and perform, play football, and the rest will take care of itself. Sam Walker gets a cuddle from Billy Smith during his excellent comeback game from injury. Getty Images “There’s not a glimmer of thought about that [contract situation] at the moment. It’s about winning next Sunday.” The Roosters head into the grand final knowing it will be the last appearance for Daly Cherry-Evans (Hull FC), as well as rugby-bound teammates Mark Nawaqanitawase and Angus Crichton.



With skipper James Tedesco off contract at the end of next year, and now a year-to-year proposition, and uncertainty about Spencer Leniu’s future at Bondi next year, the Roosters will have space in the cap to accommodate Walker. Cherry-Evans was mindful not to get caught up in Walker’s contract talks, and said: “I love this club, which is crazy to say after 12 months, but the people have been nothing but amazing towards me and my family. Loading “And if Sammy feels the same thing, then he’ll say. “When the time’s right, he will sort that out. But my opinion on it will [mean] very little, which is how it should be.”



Walker suffered a syndesmosis injury against the Dolphins in round 26, about a fortnight after he parked contract negotiations, and there were initial fears he wouldn’t play again this season. “But once I had the surgery, I was pretty clear and pretty focused on getting back for this game,” Walker said. Related Article NRL 2026 The moment DCE knew he could win a premiership with the Roosters “I’m really grateful for the staff and the medical team at the Roosters – they’ve done an amazing job helping me out, and also the club to believe in me to let me play. It was obviously a massive risk for them as well. “I can’t wait [for Sunday]. It’s going to be an exciting week, but none of that matters unless we go out there and perform for 80 minutes. That’ll be our goal, and that’s all we’re focusing on.”



Walker grew up a Roosters fan, despite constant attempts to convert him into being a South Sydney supporter while his father and uncle, Ben and Chris, were playing at the Bunnies. The Roosters’ only injury concern heading into grand final week is Connor Watson. He suffered a concussion against the Dolphins and will have to obtain clearance from an independent doctor to play before he exits for St George Illawarra in 2027 en route to the PNG Chiefs in 2028.
