World.title: ‘Loitering in the shallows’: Winter shark surveillance led to hundreds of beach evacuations
World.content:
PoliticsNSWSharks ‘Loitering in the shallows’: Winter shark surveillance led to hundreds of beach evacuations Michael McGowan September 27, 2026 — 11:52am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Shark surveillance drones patrolling NSW waters over winter for the first time led to hundreds of beach evacuations, including one for a two-metre great white swimming “in the shallows” on Sydney’s northern beaches. In total, data released by the NSW government on Sunday showed there were more than 1200 shark detections by drone operators in July and August, leading to 360 interventions including alarms, jet ski deployments and beach evacuations. Shark surveillance drones patrolling NSW waters. NSW Government The incidents reports, compiled by the Department of Primary Industries, make for chilling reading; they include a massive four-metre bull shark spotted 50 metres offshore at Urunga on the Mid North Coast, and a pack of seven “chasing a whale” at Lennox Head. The two-metre great white was spotted “loitering” about 150 metres offshore at South Narrabeen at about midday in early July, before two more were seen about 10 minutes later. After multiple sharks were sighted, at about 1pm a two-metre great white seen “tracking north” was “in the shallows” about “30 metres from shore”.



The drone surveillance logs include others spotted by drones close to swimmers at Warriewood on the northern beaches and Woolgoolga, near Coffs Harbour. The winter drone program was announced after a spate of fatal shark attacks, including the death of surfer Mercury Psillakis, 57, at Dee Why last September and 12-year-old Nico Antic in Vaucluse. Premier Chris Minns last week met Psillakis’ twin brother Mike and widow Maria, as well as Coogee shark attack survivor Leah Stewart. Those attacks led the government to announce it would roll out year-long drone surveillance, as well as a trial of artificial intelligence to identify sharks. Work is under way to procure and build a trial AI system to assist drone pilots with shark detection and species identification. Maria Psillakis, Mike Psillakis, Premier Chris Minns and shark attack survivor Leah Stewart. Instagram Minns warned at the time that increased surveillance was likely to lead to more sharks being spotted – but this was not necessarily evidence of an increase in population. The winter drone surveillance resulted in hundreds of beach evacuations, including multiple closures at popular Sydney swimming spots such as Bondi, where a two-metre shark spotted 100 metres offshore in July was one of multiple shark sightings.



Other popular beaches such as Manly, Dee Why and Cronulla were all evacuated multiple times. Related Article Sharks ‘I did think she was going to die’: How strangers saved shark attack victim Leah Stewart The shark data was released as the government announced expanded drone surveillance covering 97 beaches across the state from the beginning of the spring and summer school holidays. A total of 73 drones will patrol beaches from 6.15am to 6.30pm in October and from 6am to 7.30pm in December. It will also roll out seven remotely operated drones at beaches including Crowdy Head, Avalon and Mona Vale. Primary Industries Minister Tara Moriarty said the $120 million drone program was one of the most comprehensive in the world.



“A foundational platform in our new program is drone technology, that is delivering eyes in the sky across our state’s popular beaches, looking out for the target sharks – white, bull and tiger – and then enabling countermeasures,” she said. Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Nothing is quite what it seems in this comedy of menace
World.content:
Key points THEATRE: Harold Pinter’s The Homecoming is performed at the Athenaeum

MUSICAL THEATRE: Spamalot returns to Melbourne

MUSIC: Metal band Health finishes their show with an invite to Cherry Bar

THEATRE: Luke makes its world premiere at Red Stitch

MUSIC: Kristian Bezuidenhout performs Handel and Bach with the MSO

THEATRE

The Homecoming ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 3 The lights come up to reveal two characters in a living room and it doesn’t take long for the sense that something is off-kilter to take hold. A pugnacious aged patriarch and ex-butcher named Max (Richard Piper) blathers on in an unpunctuated stream of consciousness to the uninterested Lenny (Ben Geurens) – we don’t find out the two are family until Max admonishes the louche Lenny for speaking such to his “lousy filthy father”. Richard Piper as Max in The Homecoming. Ben Fon The barely concealed hostilities are extended to the diametrically gentle Sam (David Field), Max’s chauffeur brother and the hulking wannabe boxer Joey (Eddie Orton), Lenny’s younger brother. No one and nothing are quite as they seem in Harold Pinter’s 1965 comedy of menace The Homecoming, even once you account for the virulent sexism, barely concealed hatred, and dearth of familial love between these characters.



The intrigue deepens when all four of them retire to bed and the taciturn Teddy (Peter Houghton) enters the house, accompanied by his enigmatic wife Ruth (Kate Kendall). Teddy has effectively been estranged from his family for six years and now resides in America, with neither his wife nor family acquainted with each other. A series of decidedly strange interactions between all the characters leave audiences none the wiser as to what is about to unfold in this claustrophobic domestic setting. Under the direction of Greg Carroll, a slowly creeping sense of foreboding and listlessness overtakes the play, only strengthening its grip on the audience as it unfolds. The world Pinter has ensconced these characters in exists in and of itself, ungoverned by the moral sensibilities and social mores of the now, let alone that of the 1960s when this play first premiered in London. Peter Houghton as Teddy and Kate Kendall as Ruth. Ben Fon Absurdist and fantastical despite its realist underpinnings, The Homecoming lulls its audience into an illusion of normalcy. When social contracts are broken with seemingly no repercussions, the play’s (and our) grasp on reality loosens – shining an uncomfortable spotlight on the confronting misogyny on display, calling into rebuke the meaning of the familial ties traditionally held so dear, and questioning the unspoken rules that allow society to function as it does. The famed Pinter Pause allows the requisite space for these consternations to fester. A muscular black room is the fitting backdrop for the exertion of these men’s fragile, toxic masculinities, while Amelia Carroll and Margaret Goy’s costume design is a stunning cloak of civility that masks the innermost depravations of these characters. Clad in a babydoll dress throughout, Ruth is read as childlike and guileless – a misnomer that allows her to exert the full force of her feminine wiliness.



The strength of a production like The Homecoming lives and dies by its ensemble cast, and this one is uniformly excellent. Kendall is a particular highlight as the otherworldly, cosmically unflappable Ruth, simultaneously an antidote against the testosterone-soaked aggression of the men around her and the sun around which their neediness, desperation and contemptibility orbit.

Reviewed by Sonia Nair MUSICAL THEATRE

Spamalot ★★★★

Athenaeum Theatre, until October 4 You’d think that after 51 years a joke might stop being as funny as it once was. And yet, sitting in the dark watching two men debate how one swallow – or perhaps two, if they were holding some sort of string – might transport a coconut across countries, I found myself laughing as though it were the first time I’d heard this conversation. From left: Jesse Vasiliadis, Gareth Isaac, Stephen Curry, Ethan Jones and Noah Skape. Ben Fon Monty Python and the Holy Grail first hit cinemas in 1975, and Spamalot, “a new musical lovingly ripped off from the motion picture” takes the key plot and a handful of songs from the film, adds a whole lot more, and twists the story off into new directions as needed. The musical, itself now 20 years on from when it took Broadway by storm and took out the Tony Award for best musical, still feels vibrant and fun and silly.



A spoof of the Arthurian legend, the story sees King Arthur (Stephen Curry) seeking knights to join his round table before being tasked by God (a video recording of Eric Idle) to find the Holy Grail. While many jokes and scenes are lifted directly from the original film and other Python works, Spamalot, with book and lyrics by Idle, and music co-written by John Du Prez, is its own thing. Jaz Flowers and Ethan Jones as the Lady of the Lake and Sir Galahad. Ben Fon The songs written specifically for Spamalot hold their own against the older, more established tunes. Idle takes great delight in breaking the fourth wall in creative ways, and musical theatre itself is a key pillar of the story, with nods to everything and everyone from West Side Story to Liza Minnelli. Jaz Flowers as the Lady of the Lake steals almost every scene she’s in – her powerful command of every note makes light work of the parade of vocal challenges thrown her way. Her skill as a singer is matched only by her comedic timing. Her meta duet with Ethan Jones as Sir Galahad in The Song That Goes Like This is a particular highlight.



Python humour remains evergreen because it is untethered from time. When it isn’t purely revelling in the absurd, it is taking aim at themes that sadly never grow old (inequality, bigotry, cowardice), joyfully ratcheting up the classics (fart jokes), and being gleefully persnickety when it comes to wordplay. With a talented cast who all appear to be enjoying every minute on stage, Spamalot is just the right amount of silly.

Reviewed by Elizabeth Flux MUSIC

Health ★★★★

Forum Melbourne, September 20 Metal always straddles the serious and the absurd. Tonight Los Angeles industrial metal band Health enters the stage to the theme song from Neon Genesis Evangelion. Health in 2026 is all machine beats and processed guitar riffs, with wan, emotive vocals. Richard Clifford Internet wags call Health’s brand of industrial metal “cum metal”. The band sells t-shirts that say “Sad Music For Horny People”. Tonight’s show is an industrial crush of guitar, drums, big feelings, and dudes swishing their long, lustrous hair, faces melted in metallic bliss. That’s the audience, by the way – I can’t really see the band, they’re swaddled in smoke and light, as it should be.



At the start of their career, Health put out two acclaimed albums of dancey noise rock, heavy, colourful and dynamic. Since then they’ve distilled their sound into something more structured: the glam of industrial metal, with hints of shoegaze and gothic rock. Have they polished the metal a bit too thin over the years? Health in 2026 is all machine beats and processed guitar riffs, with singer Jake Duzsik’s wan, emotive vocals. John Famiglietti opens the show with a pitch-perfect Aussie accent Richard Clifford But they push forward, and their fans come with them. Almost everything in tonight’s set is from their last two albums, Rat Wars and Conflict DLC, and just a few earlier tracks, notably Major Crimes and Tears (written for video games Cyberpunk 2077 and Max Payne 3), and We Are Water, from their 2009 second album Get Color. They’re at their peak when it all builds to something manic, like in Future of Hell and Shred Envy. A template emerges, in which something jagged and hard rears its head briefly, before they cut the decibels for Duzsik’s verses, which all merge into one overwrought cloud.



Like all metal shows, there’s an air of generosity and camaraderie between the crowd and the band. Bassist/producer John Famiglietti opens the show with a pitch-perfect Aussie accent (“You sick c---ts, we’re gonna rip your f--kin’ dicks off!“) and ends it by inviting everyone to Cherry Bar for the afterparty, before crowdsurfing to the sound booth. His people love him.

Reviewed by Will Cox THEATRE

Luke ★★★★

Red Stitch, until October 11 Local playwright Angus Cameron has teamed up with Red Stitch for the world premiere of Luke – a disturbing, emotionally complex three-hander that weaves a provocative play of ideas into a psychological mystery of troubling currency. Will Lonsdale, Olga Makeeva and Dion Mills in Luke Parenthesy I was bewildered by the opening sequence. Two adults race across a living room playing dress-ups. They’re engaged in some kind of private game, based on the Bolshevik assassination of the Romanovs during the Russian Revolution, but something about the scene feels off, inauthentic somehow.



A clever reason for this will remain an enigma until well after we discover that the pair are high school teachers in country Victoria. It’s 2007, and Damon (Dion Mills) and Olena (Olga Makeeva) are unwinding at term’s end after a gruelling night of parent-teacher interviews. When Chris (Will Lonsdale) – the school’s 19-year-old rowing coach and a former student of Damon’s – joins them, the games continue. Some of the playfulness is literary or historical – a relic of the ludic flamboyance essential to Damon’s pedagogic style. He’s an inspiring educator, discreetly gay, and his mentor-like relationship with Chris, who came out to Damon as a student, is tinged by affection and by a body of queer knowledge excluded by the official (read heteronormative) education system. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Parenthesy When conversation turns to a never-seen character, Luke – a year 11 student leaving the school after inappropriate attention from a member of staff – the game mutates through a series of twists, with a possible child sex abuse scenario, and its consequences, playing out over decades. Iain Sinclair’s direction guides three excellent performances. Mills’ suspect teacher has the charisma, passion, idealism, and sheer eccentricity of a gifted educator. There’s no question he leaves a mark on his students: his scenes with Lonsdale’s Chris are tender and haunted – enlivened by the irrepressible joy they both take in the learning game, as well as the shadow of barely repressed desire.



Olena is the fulcrum of the play, and Makeeva is riveting as, through veiled parable and a clipped and embittered realism, the character weighs the truth of a situation in which the righteousness of her own acts is called into question. She is a staunch counter to Chris – a young man heavily invested in his own righteousness, and solipsistic in the performance of it. Editor's pick Arts Three titans of politics, sport and media had a meeting in the 1980s. A new play imagines what was said Luke tackles such uncomfortable subjects as the erotics of education and the ethics of making art from life. It has stern things to say about the cultural amnesia afflicting Australian literature and drama, and it brings child protection concerns into contact with the reality of homophobia, knowing the ancient slur – the one that equates homosexuality with paedophilia – has never quite ceased to echo. Yet this haunting play celebrates, too, the solidarity and strangeness of found family, the clandestine solidarity and the mentorship relations that can exist between queer men finding their tribe.



In this, it has an artistic genealogy that can be traced back to some of the most fearless and unsettling voices in queer Australian literature – the implied pederasty in David Malouf’s short story Under Southern Skies, say, or Frank Moorhouse’s The Everlasting Secret Family – updating the issues to a world of changing mores in which progressive rhetoric can disguise more difficult and painful human truths.

Reviewed by Cameron Woodhead MUSIC

Handel and Bach ★★★★

Melbourne Symphony Orchestra, Melbourne Recital Centre, September 19 Many Melbourne concertgoers will remember the stylish flair with which Australian fortepianist Kristian Bezuidenhout performed the complete Beethoven piano concertos with the Freiburg Baroque Orchestra on the cusp of COVID. Kristian Bezuidenhout at an earlier concert. Marco Borggreve Returning with some of that flair, Bezuidenhout directed the Melbourne Symphony Orchestra from the harpsichord in this program of works by Bach and Handel.



Focusing particularly on rhythm and dynamics, Bezuidenhout brought crisp grandiloquence to the many French-style introductions on the program, whether to Bach’s Orchestral Suite No. 1 in C major or the Overture to Handel’s Admeto. There was also a general rhythmic buoyancy which lent itself well both to the dance-infused Bach Suite and Suites Nos. 1 and 2 from Handel’s familiar Water Music. Carefully shaped dynamics applied to the whole orchestra made sense of the rise and fall of phrases and provided some well-judged dramatic contrasts. Related Article ★★★★★

Melbourne live reviews These are unapologetically political songs, and this artist is unapologetically herself Despite overall clarity, it was in Bezuidenhout’s arrangement of Bach’s incomplete Contrapunctus XIV from The Art of Fugue that the listener might have longed for some more granular detail in terms of articulation and pliability of tone in individual lines. Such qualities were more apparent in Handel’s Concerto grosso in D minor, Op. 3, no. 5 which followed. Fine wind and brass playing hallmarked the second half. Beginning with the Sinfonia from Bach’s Cantata No. 52 (otherwise recognisable as the opening of Brandenburg Concerto No. 4) followed by the Water Music, the horns and oboes took up Bezuidenhout’s brisk tempos with alacrity.



Oboists Johannes Grosso and Ann Blackburn together with horn players Lucie Krysatis and Abbey Edlin crowned the festive mood of the Handel; their timbre setting up piquant contrasts with the strings, trumpets providing an additional regal air in the second suite. Thanks to Bezuidenhout, the MSO proved it can bring some idiomatic lightness to the glories of the baroque.

Reviewed by Tony Way The Booklist is a weekly newsletter for book lovers from Jason Steger. Get it delivered every Friday.

World.title: More rain, snow forecast as severe weather system moves north
World.content:
Heavy snow is trapping cars and trucks in the South Island, with several major roads closed or restricted as strong winds and rain move over the country.

SH7 between the turnoff to Hanmer Springs and Springs Junction, including Lewis Pass, is now closed because of heavy snow.

NZTA said there is no detour and people should avoid the area or delay their journeys if possible.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6405684778112

On SH73, the sections between Otira and Arthur's Pass, and Springfield and Castle Hill, are closed to towing vehicles, with snow chains required.

MetService warns the Tararua Range could receive another 40 to 60mm of rain on top of what has already fallen, while another 5 to 10cm of snow is forecast for parts of Canterbury.

Orange warnings remain in place for heavy rain in the Tararua Range, heavy snow in Canterbury and severe winds across parts of the lower North Island.

The Tararua Range is expected to receive peak rainfall rates of 15 to 20mm an hour from late this morning.

MetService said streams and rivers could rise rapidly, with surface flooding, slips and difficult driving conditions possible.

In the Canterbury High Country and plains near the foothills south of Arthur's Pass, another 5 to 10cm of snow is expected to settle above 400 metres, with lesser amounts down to about 200 metres.

A severe weather system moving north over the country is bringing further heavy rain, snow and severe gales across central New Zealand on 27 September 2026. Screenshot / MetService

The snow is expected to ease from the south in the afternoon.

Severe west to northwest winds gusting up to 120km/h are forecast in exposed parts of Wairarapa, the Tararua District and Hawke's Bay south of Hastings.

A warning for Wellington is in place until noon, with northwest winds gusting up to 120km/h in exposed places before switching to strong or gale southerlies around midday.

The change could briefly bring southerly gusts of up to 90km/h.

NZ Transport Agency said roading crews were helping vehicles stuck on SH8 near Lake Pūkaki because of heavy snow.

Motorist Kyle Dinz said he was stuck near Lake Pukaki due to heavy snowfall while travelling on SH8 on Sunday 27 September 2026. Supplied / Kyle Dinz

Kyle Dinz said he was caught in standstill traffic near Lake Pūkaki, behind several heavy trucks stuck on the road.

He eventually made it to Lake Tekapo, where he said the snow was even heavier.

Heavy snow blankets vehicles near Lake Tekapo on 27 September 2026. Supplied / Kyle Dinz

NZTA also closed a section of road between Springfield and Castle Hill, including Porters Pass, to towing vehicles and advised drivers to use snow chains.

A driver told RNZ their car slid while crossing Porters Pass at about 9.30am because of the snow, forcing them to turn back.

Snow falls on Porters Pass on Sunday morning, 27 September 2026. Supplied / Tracey Hunter

NZTA has issued snowfall warnings for SH8 between Omarama and Tarras, including Lindis Pass, SH85 between Omakau and Kyeburn, and the Crown Range Road.

MetService has also issued warnings for Porters Pass, which is expected to receive 10 to 15cm of snow above 600m between 10am and 4pm.

Arthur's Pass could get 2 to 4cm above 700m between 11am and 4pm.

A snowfall warning has also been issued for the Crown Range Road, where snow showers could affect the road around midday.

The Desert Road (SH1) is also under a snowfall warning from 7pm Sunday until 1am on Monday.

Several watches are in place across the country.

A Heavy Snow Watch remains in place for the Canterbury High Country and plains near the foothills about and north of Arthur's Pass, with rain expected to turn to snow above 200m and heavy snowfall possible above 400m.

Strong Wind Watches are in place for parts of Hawke's Bay, Horowhenua, the Kāpiti Coast, the Marlborough Sounds and the Chatham Islands.

The Heavy Snow Watch for Central Otago, the Queenstown Lakes District, inland Clutha and Southland north of Lumsden has been lifted after the threat of warning-level snowfall passed.

World.title: Parliament's triennial warrant of fitness
World.content:
Spring at Parliament, where the oak trees feel a fresh flush of growth © VNP / Phil Smith

Spring is a time for reflection and renewal, and as the 54th Parliament came to a close this week, MPs agreed to an updated set of rules governing how Parliament operates: the 2026 Review of Standing Orders.

Audio player for " Parliament's triennial warrant of fitness " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/politics/1606510%2Fparliament-s-triennial-warrant-of-fitness

Parliament's triennial warrant of fitness The House Download MP3 12m

During question time, when something contentious happens, you might see MPs in the chamber promptly reach for their copy of the Standing Orders and thumb through the pages for the relevant rule, like a Scrabble player furiously flicking through the dictionary to see whether their word counts.

Every three years, MPs get the chance to review and change those rules. There are more than 400 of them, covering not just the legislative functions of Parliament, but also what MPs can and can't say in the House, how select committees operate, how members conduct themselves, and even what MPs are allowed to wear.

Of course, rules need to evolve to stay relevant. The triennial review is carried out by the cross-party Standing Orders Committee, which spends months considering how Parliament operates. Given that MPs aren't always the best judges of their own performance, the committee also spends time hearing from the public, experts, its own secretariat, academics, and other parliamentary tragics who take a keen interest in the finer details of how the place works.

The proposed changes are then debated and agreed to by the House on the final day before Parliament adjourns for the election campaign.

So, what's actually changed? Among the most notable recommendations included in the 2026 Review of Standing Orders were:

Urgency explanations: In cases of urgency where the government intends to move a bill straight from its first reading into the second reading (thereby skipping the select committee process) the member in charge must explain the specific reason for the omission.

Truncated select committee timelines: When referring a bill to a select committee for a timeframe shorter than the standard six months, the government must similarly explain "with some particularity" the reason for the shortened timeframe.

Select committee guidance: The inclusion of a purpose statement to steer select committee consideration, including what the committee should endeavour to learn from the public during the submission process.

Framework for the punishment of contempt: Plans for a scale of appropriate penalties for members who have been found guilty of contempt.

A new Legislative Scrutiny Committee: The establishment of a Legislative Scrutiny Committee that will consider some less controversial bills instead of them going through the Committee of the whole House stage.

Much clearer rules on which financial interests MPs have to make public.

Those changes and many more were agreed to unanimously on Wednesday afternoon during a debate that included each party with the exception of Te Pāti Māori.

Bizarrely, despite chairing the committee, Speaker Gerry Brownlee doesn't get the chance to speak in the House about the review he had spent the last 18 months overseeing. So, to hear it straight from the man himself, The House sat down with him to chat through what he described as "the most comprehensive review of Standing Orders since the start of the MMP electoral system." It is certainly one of the bigger ones.

Urgency

The use of urgency has increased over recent Parliaments, with the 54th passing more legislation under urgency than any recent Parliament. Parliamentary commentators, including the likes of Sir Geoffrey Palmer, have increasingly raised concerns over its usage, arguing that urgency should be used far more sparingly. Nevertheless, governments of all political stripes make use of it.

"Well, I think the whole committee recognised that urgency is something that you do have to have," Brownlee said. "[our] Parliament doesn't sit for a long period of time. We sit for …28 weeks [a year] now with another two weeks of scrutiny for the Estimates and then the [Annual Reviews]. So there's always pressure on time. The House sits for, I think it's about 13 hours [of debating] time each week. …So the real answer to having less urgency is to have more normal time. The willingness across the Parliament to change the sitting hours of the Parliament is not that great. So there'll always be urgency."

Parliament's Speaker, Gerry Brownlee laughs in response to a speech. VNP / Phil Smith

Urgency is especially contentious when it is used to skip the select committee stage, effectively locking the public out of this accessible forum for having a say on legislation. A rule change will require the Minister in charge of a bill to give "some kind of particularity about why the minister is progressing in that particular fashion," Brownlee says.

The justification threshold will ultimately still rest with Ministers, so they could still argue (as they have this term), that urgency is justified because a law change was in their coalition agreement. The House would then decide whether that constitutes a valid justification and vote on the urgency motion, though as the government always has a majority, it would almost certainly pass.

Submissions

While urgency has been a major talking point this term, so too has the massive increase in the volume of submissions made to select committees.

As of September 11, the 54th Parliament had received 697,330 written submissions, a vast jump compared to the previous term of Parliament, which itself saw a huge increase on that preceding it.

While greater public engagement in the Parliament is healthy for democracy, that surge has placed a real strain on Ministries and the Office of the Clerk (Parliament's secretariat).

Brownlee suspects the sheer scale of submissions has likely been propelled by the assistance of AI. Other commentators have put forward various explanations for the spike in engagement, but there is broad agreement that the trend shows no sign of slowing down.

Recognising this, the Standing Orders Committee explored options to accommodate the increase without curbing participation.

"You can't stop people making submissions. That would be inappropriate." Brownlee says.

He says that a new rule whereby consideration by select committee has specified goals "should allow select committees to really focus on… what they need to be doing. That will give guidance to the clerks who advise the committee on which submissions they might want to hear from or to respond to."

Plugging the gaps

A benefit of holding the Standing Orders Review toward the end of a parliamentary term is the opportunity to reactively address procedural issues and ambiguities that arose along the way, effectively trying to patch up those gaps in the system.

"Anything that comes up that is a little different is always tabulated, it's put there for the Standing Orders Committee toward the end of each Parliament to have a look at. This time we started around 18 months [ago]. This has been a longer process because [after] 30 years of MMP, [we said] let's have a look at some of the more substantial stuff."

You can listen to the chat with Gerry Brownlee, along with audio from the Standing Orders debate by clicking the link near the top of the page.

You can read the full 2026 Report of the Standing Orders Committee here.

World.title: Commerce Commission cracks down on cartels in public procurement
World.content:
The Commerce Commission says illegal bid-rigging in public procurement is costing New Zealand taxpayers around $360 million a year.

Chair Dr John Small said investigations were currently ongoing and public procurement was being targeted.

"I have a message for those involved in this illegal activity - we're coming for you.

"We take an extremely dim view of any illegal activity that rips off taxpayers."

Small said the commission was making cartels in public procurement a "specific enforcement priority",

"Both our Anonymous Reporting Tool and leniency programme continue to generate very strong leads."

But procurement was not the only sector being targeted.

"In addition, we are tackling all forms of cartel conduct. We have ongoing actions in the real estate and grocery sectors, while last year we saw the conclusion of cases involving customer allocation and price fixing in the courier sector and the bid-rigging of public roading contracts."

Government agencies spend about $51.5 billion a year on the procurement of goods and services.

The Commerce Commission defined bid-rigging as "an agreement among some or all the bidders about who should win a bid".

It said this led to procurers being unlikely to get the best value for money for their business, customers or taxpayers.

The commission said it also had an educational outreach programme to better inform different sectors and businesses, including those in procurement.

It urged anyone who becomes aware of cartels to report it to the Commission through the anonymous reporting tool.

For those involved in a cartel, it said they can apply for leniency.

World.title: National and Labour launch election 2026 campaigns
World.content:
Launches today in Auckland for National and Labour's campaigns set the scene for the next six weeks in what looks to be a knife-edge election.

Campaign launches are typically rah-rah affairs designed to rally party faithful, with both parties set to unveil new policies.

National's launch in central Auckland may indicate whether leader Christopher Luxon intends to focus on attacking Labour or bigging up National's record this term and promises to "build the future".

Labour's event in South Auckland will be a chance for leader Chris Hipkins to shift up a gear, having held his first public meeting of the campaign just two weeks ago when he told the crowd he was "just getting warmed up".

In 2023 Hipkins kicked off the campaign promising free dental care for everyone under 30.

His speech back then was interrupted by hecklers from Brian Tamaki's Freedoms Party at least four times, but they were drowned out by the crowd who Hipkins thanked for having his back.

National's 2023 launch came with no policy announcement, instead a "pledge card" listed eight of its priority promises - from lowering inflation and growing the economy to restoring law and order, and lifting school achievement.

During this campaign, parties will have to prove their ability to tackle New Zealanders' top five concerns: the cost of living, healthcare, the economy, unemployment, and housing, according to the latest Ipsos Issues Monitor.

The survey released this week showed Labour was still considered most capable of managing all of those, but it took a tumble on every measure, narrowing the gap with National on all but the cost of living.

National's ability to tackle the cost of living and the economy also tumbled, though the party made modest gains on healthcare and housing, and stayed the same on unemployment.

World.title: Hoarder's house catches fire in Blenheim
World.content:
Firefighters remain at the scene of a house fire north of Blenheim.

Fire and Emergency dispatched nine brigades to Spring Creek around midnight.

The house belonged to a hoarder, which a spokesperson told RNZ had "made the incident a lot more complicated".

"It took us a long time to extinguish as the fire had spread to a couple of trees, and car parts, and the like, that were in the yard.

"It went to, what we call, a fourth-alarm fire.

"We had about seven or eight pumps there at the height of the incident, plus several more water tankers."

A digger was still on site to pull apart debris, while firefighters dampened down the remaining hotspots.

World.title: What is Wharfie Time and how did it backfire for heartbroken Dockers?
World.content:
As the bells tolled around the MCG on Saturday, Fremantle fans screamed in exhilaration.

This was finally their moment in the premiership sun after 31 long years of waiting.

Wharfie Time had arrived, and with four minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, there was surely no way that the Dockers could bottle this one — particularly with their viral celebration in full swing.

And then it all fell apart.

What is Wharfie Time?

You will no doubt have heard about it by now.

Before this year the phrase "Wharfie Time" would likely never have passed your ears, and now it's all the AFL world can talk about.

Wharfie Time is a viral celebration the Dockers have been using sparingly in close games at Perth Stadium during the 2026 season.

It's only ever used after a Fremantle goal, it's only ever used once in a game, and it's designed to get the crowd up and about to inspire the Fremantle players to see the game out as strongly as possible.

The lights in the stadium dim, leaving only an eerie glow of purple, as the bells from ACDC's song Hells Bells toll through the stadium and the words "Wharfie Time" appear on the big screen.

The Dockers have recently gone all-in on embracing ACDC, with former lead singer Bon Scott buried in the area due to his family emigrating there when he was young.

A guitarist at the top of the stadium starts every game playing Hells Bells, with the whole show being Fremantle's answer to the after goal songs that the Brisbane Lions do, or Port Adelaide fans singing INXS's Never Tear Us Apart before a game.

But what does the phrase 'Wharfie Time' even mean?

Great question.

It all goes back to former Dockers skipper and now Sydney Swans boss Matthew Pavlich using the phrase in a pre-match rev up in 2009.

Pavlich was mic'd up before the match and was caught telling his teammates "put on your Superman capes boys, it's Wharfie Time", as can be seen at the 39 second mark of the video below.

When it happened nobody really knew what the hell he was talking about. The "Wharfie" part was in reference to the dock workers and the club's mascot being the Dockers, but mixing it with Superman capes reference was a little … odd.

It went down in viral footy moments folklore, on par with Brett Kirk's infamous "Thanks Basil" speech.

The Dockers went on to embrace the quirkiness of it all and started the Wharfie Time celebration this year.

How did it backfire in the grand final?

In the lead-up to the match there had been a heap of talk around whether the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time at the MCG.

The Lions and the Cats had been allowed to use their goal celebrations in the 2025 grand final, with Charlie Cameron's Take Me Home, Country Roads celebration a particular fan favourite, often appearing to lift the Lions when they needed it most.

On the morning of the grand final, it was finally properly confirmed — the Dockers would be allowed to use Wharfie Time in the 2026 decider.

Just after confirmation, Brisbane football manager Danny Daly confirmed to ABC Sport's Corbin Middlemas and Ben Cameron that coach Chris Fagan had played the tolling bells to his Lions players in their Friday afternoon meeting. He didn't elaborate further.

We then witnessed one of the great grand finals in the history of the game.

After an incredible to-and-fro throughout, with 4 minutes and 18 seconds left on the clock, Fremantle's Patrick Voss kicked a goal to put the Dockers up by 17 points.

The bells started to toll. Dockers fans went wild. It felt as if the end was nigh.

And the Lions came back from the dead.

Legendary Lions coach Leigh Matthews has always said that he thinks the absolute limit of how many goals a team can kick in a particular amount of time is one goal per minute left.

Four minutes left. Four goals for the Lions. Heartbreak for the Dockers.

Several Lions players would go on to elaborate on Daly's earlier reveal to ABC Sport, saying Fagan had told them to use Wharfie Time against the Dockers, energising their own game instead.

"We talked about Wharfie Time and making that our energy [before the game]," Lions midfielder Josh Dunkley said.

"When I looked around at centre bounce and Wharfie Time came on, we all looked at each other, and connected, grew a leg and got it done.

"It's unbelievable."

Other players would say they felt the Dockers thought they had it won, and that you could feel the energy immediately rise in the Brisbane camp.

It was an inspired bit of coaching.

Will the Dockers use Wharfie Time again?

As ABC Sport writer Dean Bilton wrote in his analysis of the game, "it's cursed forever now, those bells now more likely to trigger an untimely bout of PTSD than to inspire the Freo faithful".

The Dockers have not confirmed or denied, and we may have to wait until the first close clash at Perth Stadium next year to know if Wharfie Time has been finally laid to rest.

World.title: Darwin teen 'in shock' after being selected to play in FIFA under-15 World Cup
World.content:
Long before Mark O'Connor ever thought about donning the green-and-gold jersey, there was football in the streets of Darwin.

Back then, the now 15-year-old was just like any other kid playing kickabouts with his mates when his father signed him up to a local club.

He could not have imagined it would be the first step towards representing his country.

Mark has since played for local clubs Greater Palmerston United (GPU), Mindil Aces and Darwin Olympic and now is preparing to join Australia's U-15 FIFA World Cup squad in Baku, Azerbaijan next month.

Mark O'Connor says he never imagined he would be selected to represent Australia in soccer. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I'd say [I was] almost in shock, in disbelief, because I didn't expect any of this to happen," he says.

" And then I felt super excited, but also kind of in disbelief. "

For a Northern Territory teenager who never thought standing on the world stage was something that happened to kids from the Top End, the moment means everything.

"Ever since I was playing from a young age, this is the type of thing that I'd want to be selected for," he says.

Mark O'Connor has played for three local soccer clubs in Darwin including Darwin Olympic. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Raw Territory talent

Mark's success was built through Darwin's footballing community, with different clubs playing a crucial role in his development.

Darwin Olympic president Yianni Prouzos says Mark's selection is also recognition of the region's talent.

"Mark started off as a GPU player, then he had a few years at Mindil Aces, and he spent a fair bit of time at Darwin Olympic," he says.

"For the size of the population, I believe there is a lot of raw talent in the Northern Territory."

Yianni Prouzos says there is a lot of young talent in Darwin's local soccer scene. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

Even so, Mr Prouzos says Mark stood out, and he still remembers the first time he saw the marauding midfielder whose inspiration is Premier League giant, Liverpool's Steven Gerrard, play the game.

"The first time he took the pitch, the way he moved with the ball, change of direction of the body, amazing scanning," he says.

"Very small body, a lot of people target him, [but] he gets up.

"His determination, he keeps on coming back and back."

Mark O'Connor has been praised for his skill and determination. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

The underdog

Mark says playing football in the tropics, where travelling down south for tournaments often means arriving as the underdog, prepared him for the challenge ahead of facing some of the best young footballers in the world.

"The NT would never really, I'd say, do very well down south, so being the underdog a lot was quite challenging," he said.

"To play against some of the best junior players in the world, it's really special to me.

Mark O'Connor says his previous experience competing interstate has helped prepare him for the international games. (ABC News: Michael Franchi)

"I can see the levels that they're at and see how I compare to them as well."

Darwin Olympic teammate Anthony Reichstein says Mark's selection gives other Territory players something to aspire to.

"I think it gives a lot of the boys and girls up here a chance to make it now because they're clearly looking at Darwin now and it gives everyone a lot of hope," he says.

Beyond Darwin

Football Australia selected players from all nine of its member federations, with young footballers from metropolitan and regional areas earning a place in the national squad.

Talent identification lead Michael Cooper says that representation is particularly important for regional players.

"When you're in these regional areas, you do need that role model," he said.

"You do need to know that pathway is alive for you."

Michael Cooper says the opportunity to play for Australia is particularly important for regional players and their families. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

For Mark, the message is one he knows from experience.

"I started out at the same level as everyone else, playing for the same clubs in the NT," he said.

"And you can really make it to any level you want through enough hard work and dedication."

World.title: 'Hope your tummy OK': Neale responds to Ginnivan's Instagram post
World.content:
Brisbane Lions star Lachie Neale has sent a tongue-in-cheek message to Hawks gun Jack Ginnivan on social media, after Neale was controversially allowed to play in the grand final despite hitting Ginnivan off the ball in the preliminary final.

Neale was initially handed a one-game suspension for the gut punch on Ginnivan, in line with nine other players who were cited for similar incidents throughout the year.

But during an appeals hearing on Thursday evening, it was decided Neale could play in the grand final under "compelling and exceptional circumstances", in that the Lions star had a clean suspension record from his 321 games.

Neale went on to play an important role in Brisbane's stunning come-from-behind victory over Fremantle in the grand final.

Lachie Neale responds to a comment from Jack Ginnivan on his Instagram. (Instagram: @lachieneale)

The dual Brownlow Medallist posted a photo of himself with Brisbane's three premiership cups on Instagram after the match, which Ginnivan replied to with a cherry emoji, signalling the cherry on top of a brilliant career at the Lions.

Neale then replied, "Hope your tummy OK my guy," to Ginnivan in reference to the gut punch.

Ginnivan was uninjured in the incident, however the AFL had been cracking down on strikes to the body off the ball throughout the 2026 season.

The grand final, widely considered one of the most entertaining in history, is likely to be Neale's final game with the Lions.

Having started his career at the Dockers, Neale has spent eight seasons in Brisbane, but looks likely to move to Collingwood next season as a free agent.

"It doesn't feel real at the moment, but I'm sure it will sink in. I've absolutely loved my time at this footy club, they're an exceptional organisation from top to bottom and I can't thank them enough," Neale said after the game.

"It's been an incredible ride and the best eight years of my life.

"I'm going to miss them very much."

World.title: Bloodied de Minaur scores stirring Laver Cup win over in-form Zverev
World.content:
Alex de Minaur may have ended up with a bloodied knee from a typically fearless diving volley but he was happy to draw blood for Team World by saving a match point en route to downing Alexander Zverev at the Laver Cup.

Helping drag Andre Agassi's side back into the three-day event at London's O2 Arena, the Australian, who simply thrives in team competition, maintained his 100 per cent singles win record against Europe in Laver Cup duels, fighting back to defeat double grand slam champ Zverev 2-6, 7-6 (7-5), 11-9.

"If you can notice, my blood is red as well," De Minaur said, smiling at how Team World's scarlet shirts had seemed to reflect his bloodied right leg, which he had hurt when making the spectacular tumbling Boris Becker-like volley on his way to winning a point in the match tie-breaker.

"It was a very tough match. A tough battle. I left it all out there and got fortunate in the end to get the job done and I'm happy to give some points for Team World."

It was de Minaur's fourth singles win in three editions of the Cup in which he's yet to be defeated in singles combat, and his second-straight victory over Zverev after defeating the German in San Francisco last year as Team World won the title.

"We were in the same position last year and it worked out pretty well for us. We know we can do some damage. We know we're the underdogs, but we also know that we can step out on this court and light it up," de Minaur said.

His victory on Sunday morning AEST put Team World into the lead after Europe's 3-1 overnight lead had evaporated when American Learner Tien outlasted Italy's Flavio Cobolli in a baseline slugfest to secure a 6-3, 2-6, 10-7 victory in the opener to the second day.

But de Minaur's victory was rather more unexpected, especially with Zverev being on a rare roll, unbeaten in nine matches and fresh from both his US Open triumph and two Davis Cup wins.

But de Minaur had looked in good shape on Davis Cup duty in Queensland too and he never gave up the ghost, even when Zverev was serving for the match.

"Check his oil," Agassi had told de Minaur, trying to get him to force Zverev into a wearying war of attrition.

Even then, Zverev missed his big chance, serving for the match and a straight-sets win at 5-4 in the second stanza only to cough up two double faults that allowed de Minaur to break and level the match on a tiebreak.

The next crisis point for de Minaur was when Zverev gained match point in the first-to-10-point match tiebreak, only to play a conservative point.

De Minaur then earned a match point of his own and capitalised on the world number two coming up with a weak smash, which he returned with an irretrievable sharp down-the-line backhand to seal his two-hour win.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Emotions flowed as Lions went from a ‘very unlikely’ win to a threepeat
World.content:
There were moments last year when Sam Draper wondered if he would ever play again. It made the premiership medal around his neck feel almost surreal.

"I can't believe it. I got overawed with emotion at the end there. The tears started flowing. A lot of work's gone in to get to this point, so mate, I'm just so happy," Draper said in the rooms post-win.

Sam Draper left the Bombers after rupturing his Achillies tendon and moved to the Lions via free agency. (Getty: Darrian Traynor/AFL Photos)

The lively ruck suffered a season-ending Achillies tendon rupture while playing for Essendon in round six last year, before moving to Brisbane via free agency in the trade period.

He joined former West Coast captain Oscar Allen, who moved to the Lions ahead of their three-peat campaign this season.

"It doesn't feel real. I got really emotional at the end when I saw the high-performance team and just thanked them and the list manager Dom Ambrogio and Danny Daly [Lions football manager] just for believing in me and believing that I'll be back to my best," Draper said.

"I had the darkest moments of my life last year, and then to come out of that, and here I am today [winning a premiership]. It's just mental.

"I got so emotional when the siren went … I suppose, like, everything happens for a reason."

Sam Draper said he was overwrought with emotions after the premiership win. (Getty: Cameron Spencer/AFL Photos)

Draper was in career-best form when he went down with the injury and worried that if he did come back and play, he wouldn't be the same player.

"Will I have the same explosiveness, and things like that. A lot of work goes into Achilles rehab. It's very boring. So many calf raises, but I built my body back up [and] improved as a player, I reckon."

The improvement came while being surrounded by star players in a very successful side.

Draper left a struggling club in the Bombers, who finished 18th this year, to walk into a program with two back-to-back premierships under its belt.

Brisbane's belief sparks cruellest Fremantle collapse The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

When asked what made Brisbane so special, showman Kai Lohmann said it came down to connection.

"We're all really close friends and brothers, and even the staff as well. We have such a great connection, and yeah, it means a lot," Lohmann said.

" [It's] the brotherhood, how we are all one, and we just want to play for each other and we want to play for Fages [head coach Chris Fagan]. It's special. "

He added that having one premiership was special, but "three's just unbelievable".

Kai Lohmann says the Lions' "brotherhood" helped drive them to victory. (Getty: Quinn Rooney)

Lohmann was on the bench for the final four minutes, in which Brisbane came back from 17 points down to win the game. The Lions kicked the last four goals of the game; the last two off the boot of Logan Morris, who gave the Lions back the lead for the final siren.

"I was nervous as but it was a pretty cool [final] minute," he said, echoing his coach's thoughts in the post-match presser that the team was prepared for "Wharfie Time", which played with four minutes left on the clock.

" I think we tried to reverse card it and make it our own thing … So, Wharfie Time didn't really work. "

His teammate, Ryan Lester, said he thought the Lions' victory "looked very unlikely" when Docker Patrick Voss kicked a goal just before the four-minute mark to put them up by three majors.

He had just had an important tackle on Josh Treacy in the goal square, which made an almost-certain Dockers goal into a behind. But the Lions were still trailing by a significant margin with limited time left.

Lester had played in the previous three grand finals; defeating Geelong by 47 points in 2025, Sydney by 60 points in 2024 and falling short to Collingwood by four points in 2023.

So he knew what it was like to win by big margins, and go down by short ones.

Ryan Lester says it was party time after Logan Morris's goal. (Getty: Cameron Spencer/AFL Photos)

"But then Logan kicked that goal to put us seven points up and someone said there was only 10 seconds to go, and it was a bit of party time there," he said.

"It's just unbelievable to think that we're a three-time premiership team. You know, growing up, I looked at the Brisbane Lions and Hawthorn and those teams as just like immortal. It's unbelievable, and for us to join them is pretty cool.

"Particularly for me, like in 2022, I only played three games in the senior team and managed to break in in 2023, and ever since then, obviously we played in grand finals, so I feel very, very lucky the way my career has panned out and to be a part of this special team."

He admitted this year required "a bit of luck" for the team.

"I mean, when you look at the Hawthorn game and the Freo game, they could have gone either way really. And both [went] in our way. So, amazing."

World.title: Fremantle's recovery from inexplicable collapse begins by sitting in grief
World.content:
Fremantle's devastated players had not even left the field of play at the Melbourne Cricket Ground and the recovery from what is one of the most heartbreaking grand final losses ever had already begun.

The bowels of the MCG acted as a safety bunker for Freo's players, a sanctuary away from prying eyes in the aftermath of a crushing loss.

Fremantle's team bus was parked and ready to depart as family members, club employees and reporters filed in and out of the rooms.

In the greatest and cruellest of grand finals, only the Lions believed The AFL grand final has never felt so raw as in the five ballistic minutes that elevated the Brisbane Lions to legends and delivered Fremantle the most crushing defeat imaginable.

Amid the cloud of devastation, the rays of hope already began to shine through.

Before the players retreated to the rooms, their crestfallen loved ones looked to console them, even though it seemed an impossible task, before trying to impart whatever positive vibes they'd managed to summon.

Eventually the players started filtering through. Some in tears, some clutching their jerseys in disbelief, others simply looking into any space possible that meant they could avoid eye contact.

One middle-aged man, presumably a father of one of the players, embraced each of them, telling them to keep their heads up.

It is this positivity that will help Fremantle get back up off the canvas after an unspeakably traumatic defeat.

The loved ones of Fremantle's shattered players did their very best to summon positive energy in the changerooms in the immediate aftermath of the grand final. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir, a man who has overseen this team's rise to be a bona fide contender over the past seven seasons, admitted there was no way to soften the blow for his "devastated" charges.

Brisbane's incredible heist left Longmuir in tears before the final siren, and when he gathered his players on the ground in the immediate aftermath, the message was clear: "Have each other's back."

"We play an imperfect game that is full of mistakes, and every game that they have played across their journey they would have made mistakes, it just feels a bit bigger right now," he said.

" If we had've won, we would've won together. We lost, we lose together, so have each other's back. "

Brisbane's three-peat may have made winning premierships look easy, but it is anything but.

It is easy to forget that before their crowning moments of the last three years, the Lions too experienced significant heartbreak.

For some reason in sport, you often need to experience ultimate grief before you get the opportunity to experience ultimate joy.

The sporting Gods are cruel like that.

As difficult and gut-wrenching as it may be right now, Longmuir wants his players to sit in the grief.

Justin Longmuir got Fremantle's shattered players into a huddle on the field immediately after the final siren. (Getty Images: Daniel Carson)

"We're devastated, but we need to make sure that we've got each other's back and support each other and make sure we're not too hard on ourselves through this moment," he said.

"The time to move on is not now, and we've got to sit in this and help each other through it and then the time to move on and worrying about next year is down the track."

And what is to come of the now-infamous and probably haunted Wharfie Time? Do we ever see it again?

Longmuir continued the theme of positivity by saying he would like to see Wharfie Time return, downplaying the impact it had on Fremantle's collapse, but when your opponent openly speaks about using it as motivation, it is time to bury the gimmick.

Fremantle players admitted after the match that they thought they were home when the Wharfie Time bells tolled in the final quarter. (Getty Images: Michael Willson)

The bells tolling after Patrick Voss's goal with just over four minutes left certainly allowed Fremantle's fans to dare to dream, and in the aftermath, the players revealed they did as well.

Norm Smith Medal winner Shai Bolton and teammate Judd McVee both admitted they thought they were home, before the Lions avalanche, which the Norm Smith Medal winner described as a "blur".

"Finals football is all about moments and in the last four minutes we didn't take our moments and Brisbane probably did," Bolton said.

"They've got the experience and in the last four minutes they played their way and came home with the chocolates."

Fremantle players were left devastated after the final siren as they watched Brisbane receive the premiership cup. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Fremantle is a family club and will need to summon all that positivity to get over this.

"We'll stick together after this, we're like brothers," McVee told ABC Sport.

"Everyone plays a part in it. It is a very tight group here, and we just love each other."

Fremantle, like Brisbane three years ago, will be back. They are too young and too talented not to.

The Dockers ranked 13th in the league in experience in terms of games played and have the 11th-youngest list in the AFL.

Leigh Matthews's famous minutes and goals equation came up trumps for Brisbane in its time of need. (Getty Images: Morgan Hancock)

Like Brisbane under Chris Fagan, the Dockers also have the power of continuity behind them, something many of their rivals are chasing in a league that is increasingly obsessed with instant results over the ups and downs of a long journey.

One of the best-known adages in the AFL world is legendary former Brisbane coach Leigh Matthews's minutes and goals equation. Watch any close game and you are likely to hear commentators refer to it.

During his time as a coach, Matthews had always believed that you could still win a game if you had more minutes left than goals behind.

Brisbane needed three goals with four minutes remaining and wound up kicking four. Their legendary coach's equation came through again.

Never again will Fremantle's supporters or its players feel like a victory is truly in the bag.

Not when Matthews's equation is on their side, not when they get on a run midway through the third quarter, and certainly not when the Wharfie Time bell tolls, if it ever tolls again.

World.title: Roosters earn shot at perfect NRLW season with win over Canberra
World.content:
The Sydney Roosters are into their third consecutive NRLW grand final after halfback Tarryn Aiken's late try helped subdue the Raiders 20-10 at Sydney Football Stadium.

The final eight minutes of Saturday night's game were fairly frantic, with only a converted try between the sides after a four-pointer by Canberra's England international Hollie-Mae Dodd.

But Aiken might have wanted to ensure her team got to the decider after she missed out last year with an ACL tear.

The Roosters, who led 10-4 at half-time, have made it a celebratory weekend for the Tricolours after the NRL side's preliminary final win over the Dolphins in Brisbane on Friday night.

The Roosters' NRLW team are still nursing the hurt from losing the 2025 decider to the Broncos and would dearly love to add to their 2021 and 2024 premierships in the October 4 grand final.

It only took two minutes for the Roosters to start asserting their dominance.

Winger Jayme Fressard, after missing three matches with a hand injury, accepted a pass from her skipper Isabelle Kelly to score in the left corner.

The Roosters' second came off the back of a penalty against Raiders fullback Sheridan Gallagher for pulling Kelly's hair in stopping her 50-metre line break.

The ensuing set allowed prop Rima Butler through the front door.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

After a Jocelyn Kelleher conversion, the Roosters had sprung to a 10-0 lead.

The Raiders' first points came in the shadow of half-time from a battered and bruised Krystal Blackwell, who had been off the field for a minute to treat a bloody nose and grab a clean jersey.

The five-eighth returned in jersey No.25 and accelerated through a gap set up by her halves partner Zahara Temara to score in the 32nd minute.

In the second half, Blackwell needed the trainer to bring a towel to stem the blood flow.

The Roosters kept the pressure on, with Brydie Parker's boot denying Lili Boyle a try, before a swirling kick by Kelleher was allowed to bounce by Raiders winger Isabella Waterman.

Centre Jessica Sergis swooped to score her 17th try of the season and put the Roosters up 16-4.

Sergis then had a one-on-one steal on Blackwell with the Raiders on the attack as the Green Machine desperately tried to narrow the gap.

They did it with a Chante Temara short pass close to the line for Dodd to bust through to make it 16-10.

But Aiken made sure the Roosters were heading back to the premiership decider with an angled run to the line.

AAP

World.title: Russell wins Azerbaijan GP after Piastri disaster in Baku
World.content:
George Russell has claimed a nail-biting victory in Baku, holding off Max Verstappen by just 0.196 seconds to secure his third victory of the season.

Russell, who had never led a race from start to finish before in his career, narrowed the gap to his teammate Kimi Antonelli, who recovered from a 16th place start to finish fifth.

The Englishman was successfully holding Verstappen at arms length right up until the final moments of the last lap, when waved yellow flags for a Valtteri Bottas crash through the old town section of the track saw Russell lose power.

That allowed Verstappen to rapidly close the gap, but the Dutch four-times world champion ran out of time and had to settle for second.

George Russell led from start to finish for the first time in F1. (Getty Images: LAT Image/Alastair Staley)

"The first half of the race felt pretty plain sailing," Russell said.

"After the safety car I saw Max behind me, I knew he wasn't going to make it easy.

"He drove incredibly at the end of the race.

"When the yellow flag came out, I lifted off the power and, when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power.

"Max nearly got me on the line, which would have been a real shame.

"It is amazing to be back on the top step of the podium."

Earlier, Oscar Piastri let a promising position slip, locking up and spinning onto the run off area during his 40th lap to drop from third to 15th.

BAKU, AZERBAIJAN - SEPTEMBER 26: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes locks up heavily under braking during the F1 Grand Prix of Azerbaijan at Baku City Circuit on September 26, 2026 in Baku, Azerbaijan. (Photo by Alex Pantling/LAT Images) (Getty Images: Alex Pantling/LAT Images)

The Australian eventually finished in 14th and cut a dejected figure on what was a disappointing day for McLaren.

"I need to go and look because it certainly took me by surprise," Piastri said of his lock up.

"I didn't think I braked super late or super hard, just instantly locked both fronts.

"Just a disappointing end to the day, the first half of the race was very strong, so a shame to not have anything to show from it."

Piastri's teammate Lando Norris crashed out of the race on lap 36 when he was knocked out by the pair of Alpine cars, who collided at Turn One on a restart following a second safety car period of the race.

A turgid opening half of the race gave little indication of the drama to come in the second half.

Piastri, starting third, darted up the inside of Charles Leclerc on the opening corner and then led a procession of the two Red Bulls as Russell disappeared into the distance.

Verstappen appeared to be struggling with his medium tyres but did not allow his teammate Isack Hadjar to overtake, despite plenty of discussion taking place via the pit wall.

The action seemed set to continue in a static holding pattern until Alex Albon sent his car into the wall, precipitating the first safety car.

The restart caused chaos, Franco Colapinto locking up as he darted up the inside of Turn One, collecting teammate Pierre Gasly, who in turn knocked Norris out of the race.

Verstappen, who started eighth on the grid, had already overtaken Piastri at that point to move into second, but it was at the second restart that disaster befell the Australian, Piastri locking up his wheels while defending Hadjar and spinning into the run off area.

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

Tech.title: Apple hit with $5.7 billion in damages over haptic patents
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Haptics tech company Taction sued Apple in 2021, alleging it infringed two of its patents. Now a federal jury in San Diego has awarded Taction over $5.7 billion in damages. According to CNBC, “The lawsuit centered around U.S. Patent Nos. 10,659,885 and 10,820,117, which both involve vibration-based, tactile transducer technology that helps users feel a device responding to their input.”

Taction argued that Apple’s Taptic Engine in its Apple Watches and iPhones used technology that it had developed without a proper license, and the jury agreed. It found that Apple had infringed on two claims in one patent and one in the other. However, the jury did not find that Apple willfully infringed. Taction had accused Apple of reverse-engineering the tech from two Kannon gaming headsets.

Apple has said that it intends to appeal the decision. We’ve reached out for additional comment and will update the story if and when we hear back.

Tech.title: Decap is the man behind the drums behind your favorite song
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

I don’t think I’m going to hurt anyone’s feelings by pointing out that Decap doesn’t have the name recognition of Kendrick Lamar, Olivia Rodrigo, or Charli XCX. But his fingerprints are all over tracks from them, as well as many other artists, including Freddie Gibbs, Bad Bunny, Mac Miller, BTS, and even Ludwig Göransson’s score for Oppenheimer.

Nicholas Piantedosi, better known as Decap, is a record producer, but perhaps more importantly, he’s the man behind Drums That Knock, a series of sample packs that have found their way onto countless records across genres. The line is so successful that, after debuting in 2016, it’s now on its 11th installment. Kenneth Blume, formerly known as Kenny Beats, the producer behind hits from Denzel Curry, Vince Staples, Rico Nasty, Idles, and FKA Twigs, said that Decap “changed a million lives with a single snare.”

Unsurprisingly for a man so obsessed with low-end, he’s got a real beef to pick with phone speakers. And even with all the modern tools at his disposal in his digital audio workstation of choice, Ableton Live, he still can’t give up his trusty Boss SP-202 Dr. Sample from 1998.

What is your most indispensable tool?

Ableton Live. It’s how I get my ideas out.

Which is the most underappreciated?

The clipper. A soft clipper can give your drums that warm analog sound, or it can make them hit super hard. It’s the tool that changed my music.

What is one thing you wish you could change about your phone?

The speaker. I wish I could hear a fat 808 on my phone. A raw 808 with no processing is basically inaudible on a phone speaker. So many people listen to music all day on their phone without ever truly feeling the low end. If I can make my drums knock on a phone anyway, I’m doing something right.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

My Boss SP-202 sampler. It’s the first sampler I ever had, back in junior high when I first started making beats. I chopped my first samples on it, and it was the start of everything I’m doing now.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

Gatekeeping over gear. This idea that you’re not a real producer unless you use hardware, or unless you use this DAW or that one. It’s not true. If you’ve got a computer, you already have everything you need. The dopest producer might be a kid in North Africa with Skullcandy headphones. The only thing I care about is if you’re dope or not.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

My honest answer is nothing. I’m happy making the music I make, because it’s meaningful to me and it’s my expression. I don’t need to make anyone else’s.

What creation are you most proud of?

Creating a hard-hitting sound that I love and watching it make its way across genres.

What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?

From my dad. No matter what, make a decision and put a stake in the ground. But remember what a stake is. You can always pull it up and move it.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I meditate. It aligns my mind and my body, and when those two are lined up I can focus way more clearly. If the mind isn’t right, everything will always be a little off.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

The 3M technique: make it, mix it down, move on. It doesn’t have to be perfect. It’s about staying in the action of creation, because that’s where the magic happens.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Really good food. Living in Los Angeles, there’s no shortage of incredible restaurants, and I love going out for a nice dinner.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

“This all started with not wanting a real job”

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

Tech.title: Kids turned the comment section of an NPR podcast into a group chat
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Middle schoolers, likely blocked from other apps and social networks, apparently turned the Spotify comment section under an episode of NPR’s Wild Card into an impromptu group chat. In a new episode of This American Life, host Ira Glass digs into how the kids landed there and why. But it mostly boils down to kids getting creative to work around the restrictions placed on them.

When Glass asked one of the kids why they picked this particular podcast, they said, “We just, like, looked for podcasts that didn’t have many comments.” Which, obviously, hurt Glass’s feelings a bit.

Initially, showrunner Dave Blanchard thought the comments were a particularly odd strain of bot. “It was just like gibberish,” he tells Glass in the episode. The posts were “clipped, weird, incoherent,” he said, and loaded with emoji and shorthand. So he deleted them. Then one of the accounts posted, “so it deleted my com.” So Blanchard shared screenshots of the comments in NPR’s Slack.

Producer Hannah Chin almost immediately recognized the behavior not as bots, but as kids. “I was a kid who used weird parts of the internet not as they were originally designed to talk to my friends,” they said. “I talked back and forth with my friends on Google Docs,” demonstrating just how resourceful kids can be when cut off from traditional social media.

A similar thing happened last year with Ted Radio Hour.

Tech.title: OpenAI pauses training of its ‘most capable models’
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

As reports of OpenAI’s models breaking containment, hacking sites, and generally getting out of control pile up, the company has made the decision to pause training of its most powerful models. The decision was made after a model being tested within a sandbox exploited a loophole to gain internet access. The incident happened on September 20th, and “All training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use” remains paused as of Saturday evening, September 25th.

In addition, OpenAI revealed on Friday that its agents had inappropriately uploaded 53nimages from ChatGPT users to image-hosting sites. The company has not stated if the images were AI-generated, photos, or contained identifiable people. The company also revealed Friday that its models had attempted to hack the Department of Education’s website, and pulled data from the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The revelations are part of an ongoing review by OpenAI into the behavior of its models. As it dug into its records, following the Hugging Face hack, it’s uncovered more and more instances of “unexpected or concerning behavior.” It’s evidence not just of how difficult AI agents are becoming to control as they grow more advanced, but also of the challenge of tracking their actions. Their behavior can be unpredictable, and they’re smart enough to try and cover their tracks. This has led to growing calls from researchers, those within the industry, and even some CEOs to call for slowing the pace of AI advancement.

Tech.title: Can Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince save the web from AI?
Tech.content:
Today, I’m talking with Matthew Prince, who is CEO of Cloudflare. This episode is part of a two-part series on the future of business.

Matthew last joined us on the show about two and a half years ago, at what we thought then was a wild pivot point for the internet — and now it turns out things are even wilder because of AI, and Matthew and Cloudflare are right at the center of it.

Cloudflare found in June that bots made up more than half of internet traffic. That number just keeps going up as more and more AI companies scrape more and more of the web, and now as more and more AI agents try and do things for people on the web. Cloudflare sits between websites and all those agents, and allows website owners some level of control: Owners can block all those AI tools, allow them, or, as you’ll hear, only allow those that might pay money for access.

Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

So Matthew and I talked about how to control all these bots, what kind of mess they’re making of the web, and what kinds of information might be valuable in the future as some of the payment schemes come into focus. You’ll hear me ask pretty directly if some of the outcomes he’s describing are actually good — Matthew is a thoughtful guy, and his answer is something I’m still thinking about well after we had this conversation.

AI is also upending everything inside of Cloudflare. Earlier this year, the company laid off more than a thousand people — 20 percent of the company — and then Matthew wrote an op-ed about that decision that ran in the Wall Street Journal under the headline, “How I choose which Cloudflare employees to replace with AI.” That’s pure Decoder bait in every single dimension: AI, big controversial decisions, and org charts, all in one.

And one last thing, before we get going: You can subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Matthew Prince, CEO of Cloudflare. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Matthew Prince, you’re the cofounder and CEO of Cloudflare. Welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks for having me.

I’m really excited to talk to you again. It’s been about two years since you were on the show. I was just looking back over that episode and I said something to you like, “it’s a momentous time for the internet.” And I was not even close. It’s now an even more momentous time for the internet.

You are at the forefront of rebooting how companies work with AI. That is the most Decoder bait of all time. I want to talk about bots and the internet and publishers and Google and all the things that you are in the middle of. But let’s start at the very beginning.

Cloudflare is a complicated, important company. The last time you were on the show, you said, “Cloudflare is a service that makes the internet faster and protects it from bad guys.” Is that still how you would describe what Cloudflare does?

That’s usually what I say when I’m trying to answer a question at a cocktail party and I don’t want to talk to the person any more. What I say if I’m interested in talking to the person more is that Cloudflare is trying to rebuild the internet the way it should have been built from the beginning if we knew how important it was going to be.

We run a giant network. We’re in over 350 cities worldwide, literally thousands of data centers. We have equipment running in all those places, and then we do a handful of things. If you’re trying to put an application or content online, we make sure that it’s safe. If you’re a person or an employee online, we make sure that wherever you go online is safe. We help give people the ability to write applications that can scale to an entire internet audience and run on the infrastructure that we have. That’s the fastest-growing part of our business.

We’ve recently started to think about how the business model of the internet is changing dramatically and we’re trying to help shape what that future business model of the internet looks like and make it as healthy as possible.

Can I connect the dots between the business model of the internet, how the internet should have worked, and Cloudflare trying to build the internet as it should have been?

That is different than, “Cloudflare protects from bad guys.” I will note that’s what you said to me last time, which now makes me feel like you don’t want to talk to me at the cocktail party, but that’s fine. That’s a shift. It’s just a notable shift.
